title: Enhancing Law-Enforcement Audio Transcription: A LoRA-Based Adaptation of Whisper for BWC Footage
summary: Modern policing faces a "visibility paradox" where law enforcement agencies possess petabytes of Body-Worn Camera (BWC) footage that remains largely unutilized for accountability or systemic review due to the prohibitive labor costs of manual transcription. This research presents a framework for adapting the OpenAI Whisper architecture to the unique acoustic and linguistic challenges of the policing environment. By employing Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) through Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), we address the significant performance degradation observed in zero-shot models when confronted with high-stress scenarios, sirens, and radio interference. Crucially, we demonstrate that this adaptation is feasible on consumer-grade hardware (Acer Nitro local machine with NVIDIA 4GB GTX GPU) using 8-bit quantization and gradient checkpointing. We further integrate these transcriptions into a symbolic reasoning pipeline using a domain-specific ontology to transform raw audio into evidence-linked incident graphs, achieving a 93.7% lexicon mapping rate for the advancement of procedural justice and transparency.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a framework for fine-tuning OpenAI's Whisper speech recognition model for police Body-Worn Camera footage using LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning, making it feasible on consumer-grade hardware, and integrating transcriptions into a symbolic reasoning pipeline with a domain ontology to produce evidence-linked incident graphs for accountability and procedural justice.
AI.motivation: Law enforcement agencies have massive amounts of Body-Worn Camera footage that remains unutilized because manual transcription is prohibitively expensive. Zero-shot speech recognition models perform poorly in policing environments due to high-stress scenarios, sirens, and radio interference, creating a need for domain-adapted transcription that is also computationally accessible.
AI.method: The framework adapts OpenAI Whisper via Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), combined with 8-bit quantization and gradient checkpointing to enable training on consumer-grade hardware (Acer Nitro with NVIDIA 4GB GTX GPU). Transcriptions are then processed through a symbolic reasoning pipeline using a domain-specific ontology to map lexicon and construct evidence-linked incident graphs.
AI.result: The adapted model achieves a 93.7% lexicon mapping rate when integrated into the ontology-based symbolic reasoning pipeline, with successful fine-tuning demonstrated on consumer-grade hardware.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that domain-adaptive fine-tuning of speech recognition models for policing contexts is feasible on accessible hardware, and pairing it with symbolic reasoning enables automated transformation of raw BWC audio into structured, evidence-linked incident graphs—advancing procedural justice and transparency in law enforcement.

title: SKY-Piano: A Multimodal Piano Performance Dataset
comment: Accepted to the 27th International Society for Music Information Retrieval Conference (ISMIR 2026), Abu Dhabi, UAE. Project page: https://joonhyungbae.github.io/skypiano/
summary: Music information retrieval research on piano performance increasingly involves diverse modalities of data and annotations beyond audio and MIDI. We present SKY-Piano, a multimodal piano performance dataset that includes 11 hours of performance recordings of motion, multi-view video, audio, MIDI from 7 professional and 12 amateur pianists along with MusicXML scores. The performance pieces were selected considering playing technique, difficulty, and performer expertise on a shared core repertoire. The motion data include both hand and body motion, released in both flagged form, where samples lost to marker occlusion are marked as unreliable, and imputed form, where those gaps are reconstructed, together with Visual3D body-segment kinematics and other time-synchronized modalities. To easily browse different modalities of data at a glance, we provide an interactive web browser. In addition, we developed a fingering annotation model and tool for deriving pseudo fingering annotations from the MIDI and motion data. Lastly, we present MIDI-to-motion generation through a fine-tuning experiment as a use case of the dataset.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SKY-Piano, a multimodal piano performance dataset comprising 11 hours of synchronized recordings (motion, multi-view video, audio, MIDI, and MusicXML scores) from 19 pianists, along with tools for fingering annotation and an interactive browsing interface.
AI.motivation: Piano performance research increasingly needs diverse multimodal data beyond audio and MIDI to support tasks such as motion analysis, performance understanding, and generation. Existing datasets lack comprehensive, synchronized multimodal recordings spanning both amateur and professional performers with reliable motion capture and annotations.
AI.method: The dataset was constructed by recording 7 professional and 12 amateur pianists performing a shared core repertoire selected for playing technique, difficulty, and performer expertise. Motion data (hand and body) is released in both flagged form (marker-occlusion lost samples marked unreliable) and imputed form (gaps reconstructed), accompanied by Visual3D body-segment kinematics. A fingering annotation model/tool derives pseudo-fingering from MIDI and motion data, and an interactive web browser facilitates multimodal data exploration. A MIDI-to-motion generation fine-tuning experiment demonstrates the dataset's utility.
AI.result: The result is SKY-Piano, a dataset with 11 hours of time-synchronized multimodal piano performance data, including motion (flagged and imputed), multi-view video, audio, MIDI, and MusicXML scores, plus an interactive browser, a fingering annotation tool, and a MIDI-to-motion generation use case.
AI.conclusion: SKY-Piano provides a rich, accessible multimodal resource for piano performance research, enabling tasks such as fingering estimation and motion generation, with data reliability ensured through flagged and imputed motion streams.

title: Does EEG Foundation Models Transfer to Speech? A Benchmark on Overt and Imagined Speech Decoding
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables, submitted to IberSPEECH 2026
summary: EEG foundation models pretrained on thousands of hours have shown large gains over task-specific networks for motor imagery, seizure detection, sleep staging, and emotion recognition, but their transfer to speech decoding-arguably the most demanding non-invasive BCI application-remains untested. We present the first systematic benchmark of EEG foundation models against strong convolutional baselines for speech decoding, using two corpora: UGR-MINDVOICE (overt and covert Iberian Spanish) and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3 (imagined speech). We compare two foundation models (LaBraM, EEGMamba) against three established baselines (EEGNet, ShallowFBCSPNet, EEGConformer) under a unified preprocessing and fine-tuning protocol. Large-scale EEG pretraining yields no consistent advantage over a 16K-parameter CNN on speech tasks, indicating that current general-purpose EEG pretraining does not yet transfer to speech production and motivating speech-specific foundation models.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic benchmark of EEG foundation models (LaBraM, EEGMamba) against strong convolutional baselines (EEGNet, ShallowFBCSPNet, EEGConformer) for speech decoding, using two corpora (UGR-MINDVOICE and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3). Results show that large-scale EEG pretraining provides no consistent advantage over a 16K-parameter CNN for speech tasks, suggesting current general-purpose EEG pretraining does not transfer to speech decoding.
AI.motivation: EEG foundation models have shown gains in motor imagery, seizure detection, sleep staging, and emotion recognition, but their transferability to speech decoding—arguably the most demanding non-invasive BCI application—remains untested. This gap motivates a systematic evaluation.
AI.method: Two EEG foundation models (LaBraM, EEGMamba) are compared against three established convolutional baselines (EEGNet, ShallowFBCSPNet, EEGConformer) for speech decoding under a unified preprocessing and fine-tuning protocol, using two corpora: UGR-MINDVOICE (overt and covert Iberian Spanish) and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3 (imagined speech).
AI.result: Large-scale EEG pretraining yields no consistent advantage over a 16K-parameter CNN on speech decoding tasks, indicating that current general-purpose EEG foundation models do not yet transfer effectively to speech production tasks.
AI.conclusion: Current general-purpose EEG pretraining does not transfer to speech decoding, motivating the development of speech-specific EEG foundation models.

title: PanDent: Toward Comprehensive Tooth-Level Structure-Language Consistency in Dental Radiology
summary: Accurate evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in dental panoramic radiography (orthopantomogram, OPG) is limited by the lack of fine-grained, clinically reliable benchmarks that reflect expert interpretation. This work introduces PanDent, a large-scale, clinically grounded OPG benchmark built upon fine-grained, expert-validated tooth-level annotations. The dataset comprises 9,524 high-quality OPGs, each associated with comprehensive structured annotations produced by experienced dentists and further validated by an oral and maxillofacial radiologist, providing clinically reliable supervision for tooth-level diagnosis and reasoning. Clinically consistent radiology reports are constructed from expert-validated findings using clinician-defined reporting logic, establishing explicit correspondence between structured clinical evidence and free-text descriptions. This design enables evaluation of whether MLLMs generate reports that are not only linguistically coherent but also clinically consistent with expert-validated tooth-level findings. Experiments are conducted on diverse MLLMs, including state-of-the-art (SOTA) proprietary models, general-domain open-source models, and medical-specific models. Results show that current MLLMs can generate fluent reports, yet fail to produce clinically consistent descriptions, exhibiting substantial errors in fine-grained localization and tooth-level diagnosis. Fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves structure-language consistency, substantially enhancing visual localization accuracy and diagnostic correctness, and bringing model outputs closer to expert dental interpretation. These results establish PanDent as a rigorous benchmark for evaluating tooth-level clinical reasoning in MLLMs and a valuable resource for clinically grounded dental AI.

AI.tldr: PanDent is a large-scale, clinically grounded benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on dental panoramic radiography (OPG), comprising 9,524 expert-validated, tooth-level annotated images with structured clinical reports. Experiments show that current MLLMs produce fluent but clinically inconsistent reports, and fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves clinical consistency, localization accuracy, and diagnostic correctness.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation of MLLMs in dental panoramic radiography is limited by the lack of fine-grained, clinically reliable benchmarks that reflect expert interpretation, necessitating a benchmark with tooth-level annotations and clinically consistent reporting standards.
AI.method: The authors construct PanDent, a benchmark of 9,524 OPGs with expert-validated tooth-level annotations created by experienced dentists and verified by an oral and maxillofacial radiologist. Radiology reports are generated from these structured findings using clinician-defined reporting logic to establish explicit correspondence between structured clinical evidence and free-text descriptions. Diverse MLLMs (proprietary, open-source general-domain, and medical-specific) are evaluated on these tasks.
AI.result: Current MLLMs generate fluent reports but fail to produce clinically consistent descriptions, showing substantial errors in fine-grained localization and tooth-level diagnosis. Fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves structure-language consistency, visual localization accuracy, and diagnostic correctness, bringing outputs closer to expert dental interpretation.
AI.conclusion: PanDent serves as a rigorous benchmark for evaluating tooth-level clinical reasoning in MLLMs and provides a valuable resource for clinically grounded dental AI advancement.

title: Cocktail-Talker: Multi-Speaker Dialog Modeling in Noisy Social Environments with Turn Action GRPO
summary: Spoken dialog systems are typically designed for clean, dyadic interactions in which a single user and an assistant take turns speaking. Real-world social conversations, however, are often more ambiguous: multiple speakers may participate in the same conversation amid irrelevant speech and background noise. Each utterance may be directed to the assistant, addressed to another speaker, or completely irrelevant. In such settings, the assistant must decide not only what to say, but also whether to speak at all. In this paper, we introduce Cocktail-Talker, a speech LLM framework for multi-speaker spoken dialog modeling in noisy social environments. We model the assistant's behavior with three action tokens: <|respond|>, <|listen|>, and <|ignore|>, placed before a response or silence. Cocktail-Talker is trained via supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning to generate the appropriate action token and, only in <|respond|> mode, a speech response. To prepare the training data, we develop Cocktail-DialogGen, an LLM-based data pipeline that simulates realistic multi-speaker dialogs with speaker roles across diverse social settings. Together, these components take a step toward spoken dialog systems that interact more naturally and selectively in complex social environments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Cocktail-Talker, a speech LLM framework for multi-speaker spoken dialog modeling in noisy social environments, which uses three action tokens (<|respond|>, <|listen|>, <|ignore|>) to decide whether and how to respond, trained via supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning, with a companion LLM-based data pipeline called Cocktail-DialogGen for generating realistic training data.
AI.motivation: Traditional spoken dialog systems assume clean, dyadic, turn-taking interactions between a single user and an assistant. Real-world conversations are far more complex: multiple speakers may participate simultaneously, utterances may be directed to others or be irrelevant, and background noise is common. The assistant must decide not just what to say but whether to speak at all, a capability current systems lack.
AI.method: Cocktail-Talker introduces three action tokens—<|respond|>, <|listen|>, and <|ignore|>—placed before a response or silence to model the assistant's behavior. The model is trained via supervised finetuning followed by reinforcement learning to generate the appropriate action token and, only in <|respond|> mode, a speech response. Training data is produced by Cocktail-DialogGen, an LLM-based data pipeline that simulates realistic multi-speaker dialogs with speaker roles across diverse social settings.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates a step toward spoken dialog systems that can interact more naturally and selectively in complex social environments, effectively handling multi-speaker scenarios with irrelevant speech and background noise.
AI.conclusion: Cocktail-Talker and its companion data pipeline Cocktail-DialogGen enable spoken dialog systems to make selective participation decisions in noisy, multi-speaker social environments, moving beyond the restrictive clean dyadic interaction paradigm.

title: Improved Robustness in AI-Generated Music Detection
comment: Proceedings of the 27th ISMIR Conference, Abu Dhabi, UAE, November 08-12, 2026
summary: AI music generators leave predictable spectral artifacts determined by their architecture. Existing detectors exploit these artifacts with near-perfect accuracy on raw generated tracks, but their performance collapses under simple audio manipulations, such as speed modification or pitch shifting. We address this open robustness problem by introducing a frequency-scaling-invariant detection pipeline that aims to prevent this kind of attack by design. Our method maps audio onto a log-frequency axis via a log-STFT remapping. A single learned cross-correlation filter, combined with max-pooling, provides shift invariance at inference time. Training uses a hybrid loss that jointly supervises binary detection and artifact-peak localization, regularizing boundary weights. Because robustness to speed change is built in by design, the detector is also interpretable: it outputs both a binary decision and an estimate of the applied speed-change factor.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a frequency-scaling-invariant AI music detector that uses log-STFT remapping, a learned cross-correlation filter with max-pooling for shift invariance, and a hybrid loss supervising both binary detection and artifact-peak localization, making it robust to speed/pitch modifications by design while remaining interpretable.
AI.motivation: Existing AI music detectors achieve near-perfect accuracy on raw generated tracks by exploiting spectral artifacts, but their performance collapses under simple audio manipulations like speed modification or pitch shifting. This robustness gap under adversarial audio transformations motivates the need for a detector that is invariant to such attacks by design.
AI.method: The method maps audio onto a log-frequency axis via log-STFT remapping, uses a single learned cross-correlation filter combined with max-pooling to provide shift invariance at inference time, and trains with a hybrid loss that jointly supervises binary detection and artifact-peak localization while regularizing boundary weights.
AI.result: The detector achieves robustness to speed change built in by design, and additionally provides interpretability by outputting both a binary detection decision and an estimate of the applied speed-change factor.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-scaling-invariant detection can be achieved architecturally rather than through data augmentation or post-hoc defenses, yielding robust and interpretable AI music detection against speed/pitch manipulation attacks.

title: Theia: Large-Scale Multimodal Captioning and Automated Validation of the Incidents1M Dataset for Data-Free Distillation
summary: The deployment of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in critical domains like disaster management requires high-quality multimodal datasets, especially for transferring knowledge via Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (DFKD). However, existing datasets in this domain either entirely lack descriptive text, such as Incidents1M, or suffer from severe text-image semantic misalignment, such as CrisisMMD. In this work, we present a novel methodology to construct and automatically validate a large-scale multimodal dataset for disaster response. Starting from the vision-only Incidents1M, we successfully recovered 100,000 images and generated high-fidelity textual descriptions using two distinct Qwen3.5 architectures: a 4B dense model and a 35B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model. To ensure the generated captions provide reliable semantic anchoring for DFKD, we introduce an image-blind LLM-as-a-Judge validation pipeline leveraging Qwen3.5-9B. By intentionally obscuring the original image from the judge, this evaluator accurately simulates the modality gap of the student model during data-free distillation. Our evaluation across 173,179 label pairs demonstrates a high semantic agreement (78.65/100) between the two architectures. Furthermore, the automated evaluation reveals a conservative captioning behaviour, characterized by a high Precision (77.6%) and low Recall (46.0%). This minimizes the false positive noise, while simultaneously exposing underlying human annotation inconsistencies in the original ground truth. This work provides a scalable, LLM-validated multimodal dataset and a reproducible framework to advance cross-modal knowledge distillation.

AI.tldr: The authors construct and automatically validate a large-scale multimodal dataset for disaster response by recovering 100,000 images from vision-only Incidents1M and generating captions with two Qwen3.5 architectures (4B dense and 35B MoE). They introduce an image-blind LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline using Qwen3.5-9B that simulates the student model's modality gap in DFKD, achieving high semantic agreement (78.65/100) across 173,179 label pairs and revealing conservative captioning with high Precision (77.6%) and low Recall (46.0%), exposing inconsistencies in human-annotated ground truth.
AI.motivation: Critical domains like disaster management require high-quality multimodal datasets for DFKD, but existing datasets either lack descriptive text (Incidents1M) or have severe text-image semantic misalignment (CrisisMMD).
AI.method: The methodology involves (1) recovering 100,000 images from vision-only Incidents1M, (2) generating captions with two Qwen3.5 architectures (4B dense and 35B MoE) for cross-architecture consistency, and (3) validating captions via an image-blind LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline using Qwen3.5-9B that intentionally obscures images to simulate the modality gap of the student model during data-free distillation.
AI.result: Evaluation across 173,179 label pairs shows high semantic agreement (78.65/100) between the two caption generation architectures. Automated evaluation reveals conservative captioning with high Precision (77.6%) and low Recall (46.0%), minimizing false positive noise while exposing human annotation inconsistencies in the original ground truth.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a scalable, LLM-validated multimodal dataset and a reproducible framework to advance cross-modal knowledge distillation in disaster response applications.

title: Compact Representation of Mipmapped SVBRDFs via Shared Gaussians
summary: Spatially-varying BRDFs (SVBRDFs) are central to material representation in computer graphics, but their high-resolution, multi-channel, mipmapped textures impose a substantial storage burden. Existing compression methods face a fundamental trade-off: block-based compression provides random access and hardware-friendly decoding but exploits redundancy only within local blocks; image codecs offer strong rate-distortion performance but are not designed for direct real-time texture access; and neural texture compression achieves high compression ratios but requires neural inference during decoding, which introduces additional runtime overhead, especially on mobile platforms. We present Gaussian Texture Compression (GTC), a compact 2D Gaussian-based representation for mipmapped SVBRDF texture stacks that delivers high-quality compression with flexible rate-distortion trade-offs. Our method is based on a key observation that there are two dominant sources of redundancy in such data: across mip levels and across material maps. Both share a common underlying structure: the same spatial support is reused, with only level- or map-specific information attached. This property naturally suits 2D Gaussians, since each Gaussian explicitly separates its spatial footprint from the values it carries, allowing the footprint to be shared while the values vary per level and per map. Building on this property, GTC shares Gaussians along both redundancy dimensions and is trained via a progressive optimization pipeline. Experiments show that GTC achieves higher reconstruction quality and lower memory usage than ASTC, the industry-standard GPU texture compression format, while supporting random-access, non-neural decoding suitable for real-time rendering.

AI.tldr: GTC presents a compact 2D Gaussian-based representation for mipmapped SVBRDF textures that exploits redundancy across mip levels and material maps by sharing spatial footprints, achieving higher quality and lower memory than ASTC with non-neural, random-access decoding.
AI.motivation: High-resolution, multi-channel, mipmapped SVBRDF textures impose a substantial storage burden. Existing methods face trade-offs: block-based compression exploits only local redundancy, image codecs lack real-time texture access, and neural compression adds runtime inference overhead, especially on mobile platforms.
AI.method: GTC models SVBRDF texture stacks using 2D Gaussians that explicitly separate spatial footprints from carried values. Since redundancy exists across mip levels and material maps, Gaussians share spatial footprints along both dimensions while values vary per level and per map. The representation is trained via a progressive optimization pipeline.
AI.result: GTC achieves higher reconstruction quality and lower memory usage than ASTC, the industry-standard GPU texture compression format, while supporting random-access, non-neural decoding suitable for real-time rendering.
AI.conclusion: GTC demonstrates that a 2D Gaussian-based representation can effectively compress SVBRDF textures by exploiting cross-level and cross-map redundancy, providing a practical alternative to existing compression approaches with strong rate-distortion performance and real-time decoding efficiency.

title: OwlPath: Lossless Knowledge Compression for LLM Bug Repair
summary:
LLM-based software engineering agents are constrained by limited context windows: roughly 100K tokens must store structurally relevant code  subsets to resolve bugs. Standard retrieval models treat code as plain text, forcing agents to resolve multi-hop dependencies including subclass  chains, transitive callers and interface implementations through slow trial and error. We tackle this limitation with lossless knowledge  compression, encoding source code into an OWL2 ontology to answer structural queries using minimal relevant code fragments.
  We present OwlPath, an OWL2 reasoning layer atop CodeGraph, a widely used code intelligence platform with 500K+ GitHub stars, offering a unified  CLI for structural code retrieval. Powered by tree-sitter parsing, OwlPath supports multi-language repositories (Python, JavaScript,  TypeScript, Go, etc.) and encodes language-specific semantics into a unified OWL2 ontology. It adopts two complementary modules. First, a  transitive-closure engine fetches all structurally linked symbols via single SPARQL property-path queries, capturing multi-hop relations missed  by string matching. Second, the OWL Software Knowledge Map (OWL-SKM) precomputes a compact 3KB summary with module trees, core APIs and  issue-related symbols, directing agents to target modules in the first query.
  Evaluated on 18 SWE-bench Pro instances, OwlPath obtains a 68.4% strict-apply rate versus 66.7% for the CodeGraph baseline, cutting token usage  by 28.8% and runtime by 39.5%. In offline retrieval tests over 67 instances, OwlPath improves recall 2.06 times (0.464 vs 0.226) and reaches  88.1% hit rate compared to CodeGraph's 59.7%. On a 37-question structural retrieval benchmark, recall rises from 4.4% to 28.8%, with 69-80%  accuracy on transitive caller and interface tasks.

AI.tldr: OwlPath is an OWL2 reasoning layer atop CodeGraph that encodes source code into a unified ontology for lossless structural knowledge compression, enabling LLM-based software engineering agents to answer multi-hop structural queries with minimal context. It uses a transitive-closure engine for SPARQL property-path queries and a precomputed OWL-SKM summary, achieving 68.4% strict-apply rate on SWE-bench Pro, 2.06x recall improvement over plain-text retrieval, and significant token/runtime reductions.
AI.motivation: LLM-based software engineering agents are constrained by ~100K token context windows and must fit structurally relevant code subsets. Standard retrieval treats code as plain text, forcing agents to resolve multi-hop dependencies (subclass chains, transitive callers, interface implementations) through slow trial and error. The paper addresses this by proposing lossless knowledge compression via OWL2 ontologies to answer structural queries with minimal code fragments.
AI.method: OwlPath is built as an OWL2 reasoning layer on top of CodeGraph (500K+ GitHub stars), offering a unified CLI. It uses tree-sitter parsing to support multi-language repos (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, etc.) and encodes language-specific semantics into a unified OWL2 ontology. It has two complementary modules: (1) a transitive-closure engine that fetches all structurally linked symbols via single SPARQL property-path queries to capture multi-hop relations, and (2) OWL-SKM, which precomputes a compact 3KB summary containing module trees, core APIs, and issue-related symbols to direct agents to target modules on the first query.
AI.result: On 18 SWE-bench Pro instances, OwlPath achieves 68.4% strict-apply rate vs 66.7% for CodeGraph baseline, cutting token usage by 28.8% and runtime by 39.5%. In offline retrieval tests over 67 instances, OwlPath improves recall 2.06x (0.464 vs 0.226) and reaches 88.1% hit rate vs CodeGraph's 59.7%. On a 37-question structural retrieval benchmark, recall rises from 4.4% to 28.8%, with 69-80% accuracy on transitive caller and interface tasks.
AI.conclusion: OwlPath demonstrates that encoding source code into an OWL2 ontology provides a lossless, structurally-aware retrieval mechanism that significantly outperforms plain-text code retrieval for LLM agents. It improves retrieval recall, hit rate, and accuracy on multi-hop structural queries while reducing token consumption and runtime, making it a practical solution for context-limited LLM software engineering agents.

title: Recursive transformers for semiconductor thermo-mechanical reliability
summary: Transformer-based surrogate models are increasingly used to replace expensive first-principles simulation in engineering design. But conventional transformer architectures are often over parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets typical of engineering design spaces, where large simulation data is expensive to generate. Under these conditions, excess parameter capacity leads to overfitting rather than improved accuracy, while also incurring unnecessary memory and compute overhead. This motivates a shift towards architectures that focus on additional compute rather than additional learnable parameters. This paper presents a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms for surrogate thermo-mechanical analysis of advanced packages: a)Tiny Recursive Model, b) our proposed Depth Recursive transformer, c) and a simple recursive transformer. We systematically compare their predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, computational complexity (FLOPs), providing practical design guidelines for selecting recursive transformer architectures under resource-constrained scenarios. We validate this principle on two low-dimensional engineering prediction tasks: 1) thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages, where stress and warpage from thermal cycling must be evaluated repeatedly across a design-of-experiments sweep under costly finite element analysis (FEA). 2) Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver for capacitance field. Overall, recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small data engineering surrogate modeling.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates three recursive transformer paradigms—Tiny Recursive Model, a proposed Depth Recursive transformer, and a simple recursive transformer—as hardware-aware surrogates for engineering design. It shows that recursive weight-sharing transformers, which trade learnable parameters for additional compute, offer an effective balance between accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for low-dimensional, small-data engineering problems. Validation is performed on thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of semiconductor packages and a Laplace PDE solver for capacitance fields.
AI.motivation: Conventional transformer architectures are over-parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets typical of engineering design spaces, where expensive simulation limits data availability. Excess parameter capacity causes overfitting and unnecessary memory/compute overhead, motivating architectures that favor additional compute over additional learnable parameters.
AI.method: The authors propose a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer variants: a Tiny Recursive Model, a proposed Depth Recursive transformer, and a simple recursive transformer. They systematically compare predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, and FLOPs on two low-dimensional engineering tasks: thermo-mechanical stress/warpage prediction for semiconductor packages under thermal cycling (with FEA ground truth) and an iterative Laplace PDE solver for capacitance fields.
AI.result: Recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small-data engineering surrogate modeling, outperforming conventional transformer designs in resource-constrained settings.
AI.conclusion: For small, low-dimensional engineering datasets, recursive weight-sharing transformer architectures—particularly the proposed Depth Recursive transformer—are preferable to conventional transformers due to their superior parameter efficiency and competitive predictive performance, making them well-suited for resource-constrained engineering surrogate modeling.

title: Theatre Chapbooks At Scale: A Statistical Comparative Analysis of Typography
summary: We propose a statistical methodology that quantifies the similarity of typefaces between printed historical books. This provides a tool that accelerates philological analysis. Using character prototypes derived from clustering and aligning automatically extracted character images, the method defines a typeface distance between any two books. To produce actionable outputs, we develop an a contrario statistical framework to interpret the significance of the computed typeface distances. We apply the method to the philological study of 17 th -century Spanish printed theatre chapbooks in a quantity that exceeds the capabilities of systematic visual inspection by human experts. Our method enables the automatic comparison of Roman and Italic types extracted from different books. After validation by human experts, our method has led to new printer attributions being discovered, and former printer attributions being revised. This success strongly suggests that our method has the potential to enable digital bibliography on a larger scale than was previously possible.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a statistical framework for quantifying typeface similarity between printed historical books, enabling large-scale digital philological analysis. Using clustering and alignment of character images to derive character prototypes, the method computes typeface distances between books with an a contrario statistical framework for significance testing. Applied to 17th-century Spanish theatre chapbooks, the method enabled automatic comparison of Roman and Italic types, leading to new printer attributions and revisions of former ones after expert validation.
AI.motivation: The goal is to accelerate philological analysis by providing a quantitative tool for comparing typefaces across historical printed books, which currently requires systematic visual inspection by human experts that is infeasible at scale.
AI.method: Character images are automatically extracted from books, then clustered and aligned to form character prototypes. A typeface distance is defined between any pair of books based on these prototypes. An a contrario statistical framework is developed to determine the significance of the computed typeface distances.
AI.result: Applied to 17th-century Spanish printed theatre chapbooks beyond the scale of human visual inspection. The method automatically compares Roman and Italic types across books. After human expert validation, it produced new printer attributions and revised former ones.
AI.conclusion: The success of the method suggests it can enable digital bibliography on a larger scale than previously possible, providing a scalable tool for historical book analysis and printer attribution.

title: Multi-Head Attention Residuals
summary: Transformers propagate information across depth through a single additive residual stream: every sublayer reads only the most recent state. Attention residuals relax this by letting each sublayer attend, through a learned softmax. However, that read uses a single query shared across the entire width, so every feature subspace must read the depth history through one distribution. The cost of this forced compromise grows with how much the subspaces disagree about which layers to read, and disagreement grows with model width. We introduce Multi-Head Attention Residuals (MHAR): the routing query is reshaped into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history. The read becomes block-diagonal, the reshape adds zero parameters and negligible compute, and H = 1 recovers attention residuals exactly. Trained from scratch on a deduplicated Nemotron-based anneal corpus that is quality-filtered and STEM- and code-heavy, MHAR improves validation loss over a standard Transformer at 100M, 350M, and 1B (-0.061, -0.149, and -0.140). It achieves the best result among four methods in every setting, with the gain increasing from 100M to the larger scales. The head count is a real design axis rather than a free knob: validation loss is U-shaped with respect to H, with a flat optimum at H = 4 or H = 8 across scales. We adopt H = 8 for large-scale models; over-splitting beyond this point (H = 16) consistently gives back part of the gain. A direct probe of the trained queries confirms that learned subspace disagreement is the underlying driver. Fused Triton routing kernels increase attention-residual training throughput from 0.2-0.5x to 0.55-0.88x of the baseline while maintaining near-baseline peak memory. An identity-preserving conversion using delta attention residuals supports 8B mid-training, yielding improvements of +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Multi-Head Attention Residuals (MHAR), which reshapes the routing query in attention residuals into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history, making the read block-diagonal. This adds zero parameters and negligible compute. MHAR improves validation loss over standard Transformers at 100M, 350M, and 1B scales, outperforms four competing methods, is U-shaped in head count with optimum at H=4 or H=8, and supports 8B mid-training via delta attention residuals with gains on GSM8K and GPQA.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformers propagate information through a single additive residual stream where attention residuals use a single shared query across the entire width, forcing all feature subspaces to read the depth history through one distribution. This compromise becomes increasingly costly as model width grows because different subspaces disagree more about which layers to read.
AI.method: MHAR reshapes the routing query into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history. This makes the read block-diagonal, adds zero parameters and negligible compute, and reduces to attention residuals exactly when H=1. The implementation uses fused Triton routing kernels. An identity-preserving conversion using delta attention residuals enables 8B mid-training.
AI.result: MHAR improves validation loss over a standard Transformer at 100M, 350M, and 1B scales (-0.061, -0.149, -0.140), achieving the best result among four methods in every setting. Head count is U-shaped with flat optimum at H=4 or H=8, and H=16 over-splits. Triton kernels increase throughput from 0.2-0.5x to 0.55-0.88x of baseline. 8B mid-training yields +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.
AI.conclusion: Learned subspace disagreement is the underlying driver of the improvement, confirmed by directly probing the trained queries. MHAR head count is a real design axis rather than a free knob, with H=8 adopted for large-scale models. The method provides meaningful gains across scales and tasks while maintaining near-baseline peak memory.

title: HyperClaim: Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Hypergraph Reasoning for Video Misinformation Detection
summary: Video misinformation detection is often approached through global multimodal fusion or free-form multimodal reasoning. Both paradigms can under-represent localized authenticity cues that arise from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. Because such interactions are inherently higher-order, pairwise graph formulations are insufficient to capture multi-way cross-modal dependencies, whereas hypergraphs offer a suitable representation for these relations. We propose HyperClaim, a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for sample-level authenticity classification. Using the title or benchmark-provided paired text as a claim-like query, HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout. Without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, HyperClaim preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion tends to flatten. Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, it achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV, respectively, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights further reveal token- and frame-level structure.

AI.tldr: HyperClaim is a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for video misinformation detection that captures higher-order cross-modal interactions among query phrases, evidence text, and short frame spans, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on three benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Global multimodal fusion and free-form reasoning under-represent localized authenticity cues arising from higher-order coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal frame spans. Pairwise graph formulations are insufficient for these multi-way cross-modal dependencies.
AI.method: HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting for compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout.
AI.result: Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, HyperClaim achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV respectively, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights reveal token- and frame-level structure.
AI.conclusion: Hypergraphs effectively capture localized higher-order cross-modal and temporal authenticity cues for video misinformation detection without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, while preserving fine-grained structure that global fusion flattens.

title: A Query-Efficient Stochastic Volume Rendering Framework for Time-Varying Implicit Neural Volumes
summary: Time-varying implicit neural representations (INRs) provide a compact representation of scientific volumes and, for modalities such as dynamic X-ray computed tomography (CT), are often the only practical way to represent the data. However, interactive volume rendering of INRs is challenging, as cheap memory lookups are replaced by expensive neural inferences, hindering the performance. Therefore, conventional volume rendering methods such as ray marching with dense sampling are often impractical. While resampling, caching, and retraining can mitigate this cost, they compromise convenience and accuracy and become impractical for time-varying data. We tackle these challenges using a query-efficient stochastic volume rendering framework based on delta tracking. Our system employs a four-stage pipeline that exploits heterogeneous parallelism, using ray tracing cores for traversal and tensor cores for batched neural evaluation. Furthermore, we present strategies to reduce INR queries via ray budgeting and query pruning, thereby increasing per-frame performance. Using our renderer, many time-varying INRs can be rendered directly from their original representation. The system achieves ~30-40 FPS at 1024x1024 resolution on an RTX 4090 GPU and converges to high-fidelity images. Moreover, the system enables interactive temporal exploration of the continuous domain, with timestep updates taking approximately 1-2 ms.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a query-efficient stochastic volume rendering framework for time-varying implicit neural representations (INRs) using delta tracking, achieving interactive framerates (~30-40 FPS at 1024x1024 on RTX 4090) by leveraging heterogeneous parallelism across ray tracing and tensor cores, along with ray budgeting and query pruning strategies.
AI.motivation: Interactive volume rendering of INRs is challenging because traditional dense-sampling ray marching becomes impractical when neural network inferences replace cheap memory lookups. Existing mitigation strategies like resampling, caching, and retraining compromise convenience and accuracy, and become especially impractical for time-varying data.
AI.method: The system uses a delta-tracking-based stochastic volume rendering framework with a four-stage pipeline exploiting heterogeneous parallelism—ray tracing cores for traversal and tensor cores for batched neural evaluation. Ray budgeting and query pruning strategies are introduced to reduce INR queries and improve per-frame performance.
AI.result: The renderer achieves ~30-40 FPS at 1024x1024 resolution on an RTX 4090 GPU, converges to high-fidelity images, and enables interactive temporal exploration with timestep updates taking approximately 1-2 ms.
AI.conclusion: Many time-varying INRs can be rendered directly from their original representation, providing a practical and accurate solution for interactive visualization of dynamic scientific volumes without requiring resampling, caching, or retraining.

title: Do Context Files Help Coding Agents? A Two-Agent Ablation Study on Real Repositories
summary: Persistent context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) are standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, yet evidence for their effectiveness is contradictory. We present a controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), 17 real tasks from 3 repositories (15 shared + 2 Codex-only), and 288 evaluated runs with gold-test evaluation. Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent (bounded to <=10-15pp via equivalence testing). A failure-mode triage reveals why: agents fail on implementation skill---feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring---not missing repository knowledge that a context file could supply; a manipulation probe confirms the real AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass on either agent. We further show that borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman rho=0.75), offering a candidate explanation for prior contradictions: single-agent studies draw tasks from different agents' informative bands. We release all code, data, and analysis.

AI.tldr: A controlled ablation study across two frontier coding agents (Claude Code and Codex) and 288 evaluated runs shows that persistent context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) do not measurably improve task correctness (bounded to <=10-15pp via equivalence testing). Failure-mode triage reveals agents fail due to implementation skill (feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring) rather than missing repository knowledge, and a manipulation probe confirms context files never convert a near-miss to a pass. The study also finds task difficulty rankings are agent-specific (Spearman rho=0.75), explaining contradictions in prior single-agent studies.
AI.motivation: Persistent context files are standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, yet there is contradictory evidence about their effectiveness. The authors aim to provide rigorous, controlled evidence on whether context-injection strategy actually improves agent correctness.
AI.method: The study performs a controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), using 17 real tasks from 3 repositories (15 shared + 2 Codex-only), totaling 288 evaluated runs with gold-test evaluation. It includes failure-mode triage and a manipulation probe to test whether real AGENTS.md files convert near-misses to passes. Equivalence testing bounds the effect size, and Spearman correlation assesses cross-agent task difficulty alignment.
AI.result: Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent (effect bounded to <=10-15pp via equivalence testing). Failure-mode analysis shows agents fail on implementation skill—feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring—not missing repository knowledge. The manipulation probe confirms AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass on either agent. Task difficulty is agent-specific with Spearman rho=0.75.
AI.conclusion: The evidence suggests persistent context files do not materially improve coding agent correctness, and prior contradictory results in single-agent studies likely stem from tasks being drawn from different agents' informative difficulty bands. All code, data, and analysis are released for reproducibility.

title: Regularizing modality contribution drift in multimodal continual learning
summary: Multimodal continual learning (MMCL) aims to learn emerging knowledge from multimodal data while preserving knowledge. To mitigate forgetting, current MMCL methods usually focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity, but they overlook whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. We term this decision-level shift Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) and quantify it with the MCD score, which combines contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. Theoretical and empirical analyses further explain why current MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate this drift. To this end, we propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), which preserves the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks. Since MMCL settings differ in whether old exemplars are available, CMCDR includes both replay-based and replay-free versions. The replay-based version uses modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes on stored old samples, compares their contribution profiles between the current model and a frozen previous model, and constrains changes in old-sample modality-specific and interaction contributions. The replay-free version uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses, thereby regularizing the observed contribution profile without exemplars. Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering validate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Modality Contribution Drift (MCD), a previously overlooked phenomenon in multimodal continual learning where the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions shift across incremental tasks. The authors propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), which constrains changes in modality contribution structures, with both replay-based and replay-free versions to handle different MMCL settings.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal continual learning methods focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity but overlook whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. This decision-level shift, termed Modality Contribution Drift (MCD), is not reliably addressed by existing methods, motivating the need for a new regularization approach.
AI.method: CMCDR preserves the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks. It quantifies MCD using an MCD score combining contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. The replay-based version uses modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes on stored old samples, comparing contribution profiles between current and frozen previous models. The replay-free version uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses without exemplars.
AI.result: Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering validate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR. Theoretical and empirical analyses explain why current MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate MCD.
AI.conclusion: CMCDR effectively mitigates modality contribution drift in multimodal continual learning, addressing a gap overlooked by prior methods, with validated performance across multiple MMCL benchmarks and settings.

title: OVEarth-Bench: Evaluating Category Breadth and Query Diversity for Open-Vocabulary Earth Observation
summary: Open-vocabulary Earth observation (EO) aims to localize geospatial concepts specified in natural language rather than a fixed label set. Existing benchmarks, however, usually cover narrow category vocabularies or limited query forms. To fill this gap, we introduce OVEarth-Bench, which extends existing evaluation in two directions: category breadth, through broad hierarchical category coverage with positive and negative expressions, and query diversity, through vocabulary, referring, and reasoning queries. The benchmark supports mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol. We evaluate a broad set of general and EO-specific methods. The evaluation reveals that: (1) the performance of current methods remains limited, while broader category coverage yields more stable model rankings; (2) MLLM-based methods achieve the strongest overall performance; and (3) EO-specific methods generally underperform general models and rarely match the strongest methods. These findings provide guidance for future open-vocabulary EO method design and highlight the importance of developing more realistic, diverse, high-quality, and large-scale benchmarks for reliable evaluation. Our data and evaluation package are released at https://earth-insights.github.io/OVEarth-bench.

AI.tldr: OVEarth-Bench is a new open-vocabulary Earth observation benchmark that extends existing evaluation in two dimensions: category breadth (broad hierarchical categories with positive/negative expressions) and query diversity (vocabulary, referring, and reasoning queries), supporting mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol. Evaluations show current methods remain limited, MLLM-based methods perform best overall, and EO-specific methods generally underperform general models.
AI.motivation: Existing open-vocabulary EO benchmarks typically cover narrow category vocabularies or limited query forms, making them insufficient for reliable evaluation of methods that need to localize geospatial concepts specified in natural language.
AI.method: The benchmark extends evaluation along two dimensions: category breadth through broad hierarchical category coverage with positive and negative expressions, and query diversity through vocabulary, referring, and reasoning queries. It supports both mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol.
AI.result: Evaluation reveals: (1) current methods perform limitedly overall, though broader category coverage yields more stable model rankings; (2) MLLM-based methods achieve the strongest overall performance; (3) EO-specific methods generally underperform general models and rarely match the strongest methods.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide guidance for future open-vocabulary EO method design and highlight the importance of developing more realistic, diverse, high-quality, and large-scale benchmarks for reliable evaluation.

title: KernelGenBench: A Multi-Source and Multi-Chip Benchmark for LLM-based Kernel Generation
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/flagos-ai/KernelGenBench
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly increased the demand for efficient accelerator kernels, but kernel development remains a highly specialized and labor-intensive task. The recent rise of LLMs and agentic frameworks offers a promising pathway toward automatic kernel generation. However, despite rapid progress, there is still no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms. We present KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. It comprises two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source), evaluating 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip), measuring performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. Our large-scale evaluation, consuming over 15 billion tokens, shows: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling methods, while cuBLAS operators are the most challenging across all methods; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with even recent kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation remains highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaches 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling approaches.

AI.tldr: KernelGenBench is a unified benchmark for evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. It includes two sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS covering 210 operators from three sources, and KernelGenBench-MC measuring portability across six hardware platforms with 110 operators. Evaluation across 15+ billion tokens reveals that agent-based methods outperform pure LLM sampling, cross-platform performance degrades severely (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E), and autonomous kernel generation is highly cost-intensive with specialized agents consuming up to 5.19 million tokens per successful operator.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid progress in LLM- and agent-driven automatic kernel generation, there is no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms, making systematic assessment and fair comparison impossible.
AI.method: The paper introduces KernelGenBench with two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source) evaluates 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch-centric tasks, while KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip) measures performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. A large-scale evaluation consuming over 15 billion tokens was conducted comparing agent-based and pure LLM sampling methods.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling, with cuBLAS operators being the most challenging; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms with severe cross-platform degradation (AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation is highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaching 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling.
AI.conclusion: KernelGenBench establishes a unified evaluation framework for LLM/agent-generated kernels, highlighting that while agent-based approaches show promise, significant challenges remain in cross-platform portability, handling cuBLAS operators, and reducing the extreme computational cost of autonomous kernel generation.

title: VocalRender: Score-Native Singing Voice Synthesis for Real-World Composition
summary: Existing singing voice synthesis systems often require predefined durations, explicit duration prediction, or time-aligned acoustic guidance, which limits their compatibility with practical composition workflows. We propose VocalRender, a score-native system that directly synthesizes singing from lyrics, pitches, symbolic note values, and tempo. It uses an interleaved lyric--note representation and an autoregressive diffusion model to generate continuous acoustic latents while predicting the output length, eliminating the need for explicit duration prediction. Trained on a 2,300-hour singing dataset, VocalRender achieves strong intelligibility, strong melody control, and high speaker similarity across both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. Notably, it outperforms the strongest baseline by $0.42$ points in naturalness CMOS, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed score-native architecture.

AI.tldr: VocalRender is a score-native singing voice synthesis system that directly generates singing from lyrics, pitches, note values, and tempo without requiring predefined durations or explicit duration prediction, using an interleaved lyric-note representation with an autoregressive diffusion model trained on 2,300 hours of data.
AI.motivation: Existing singing voice synthesis systems require predefined durations, explicit duration prediction, or time-aligned acoustic guidance, which limits compatibility with practical composition workflows.
AI.method: VocalRender uses an interleaved lyric-note representation and an autoregressive diffusion model to generate continuous acoustic latents while predicting the output length, eliminating the need for explicit duration prediction. It is trained on a 2,300-hour singing dataset.
AI.result: VocalRender achieves strong intelligibility, strong melody control, and high speaker similarity across both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by 0.42 points in naturalness CMOS.
AI.conclusion: The score-native architecture is effective, demonstrating that direct synthesis from score-level inputs without explicit duration modeling can achieve state-of-the-art singing voice synthesis performance.

title: QQWorld: Quantile-Quantile Matching for World Model Regularization
summary: Latent world models enable efficient planning by predicting future states in a compact representation space, but their performance depends critically on the quality of the learned latent distribution. LeWorldModel (LeWM) regularizes its latents toward an isotropic Gaussian using the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective. We show that the corrective gradients of EP rapidly vanish for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled. To address this limitation, we propose QQWorld, which replaces EP with a quantile-quantile matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, thereby maintaining effective corrective gradients in the tails. We further develop cross-batch QQ, which enlarges the effective ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, and characterize its bias-variance trade-off. Across four control environments, QQWorld effectively improves the average planning success rate of LeWM, while consistently yielding better Gaussian alignment and thinner latent tails.

AI.tldr: QQWorld replaces the Epps-Pulley objective in latent world models with a quantile-quantile matching objective that preserves corrective gradients in the tails, improving Gaussian alignment and planning success across four control environments.
AI.motivation: Latent world models depend critically on the quality of the learned latent distribution. LeWorldModel (LeWM) regularizes latents toward an isotropic Gaussian using the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective, but the corrective gradients of EP vanish rapidly for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled and degrading planning performance.
AI.method: QQWorld proposes a quantile-quantile (QQ) matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, maintaining effective corrective gradients in the tails. It further introduces cross-batch QQ, which enlarges the effective ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, and characterizes its bias-variance trade-off.
AI.result: Across four control environments, QQWorld effectively improves the average planning success rate of LeWM, while consistently yielding better Gaussian alignment and thinner latent tails.
AI.conclusion: QQWorld addresses the tail-gradient vanishing problem of EP-based latent regularization via rank-matched QQ matching, leading to better-calibrated latent distributions and improved downstream planning performance.

title: MeshFM: 2D Features Are All You Need for 3D Shape Understanding
summary: We present MeshFM, an efficient feedforward framework for extracting rich features from 3D inputs. Our method distills 2D features from visual foundation models into 3D. We train a feedforward network to directly predict 3D features without requiring optimization during inference. The approach utilizes a two-stage training strategy. First, we optimize a feature field in 3D using only 2D feature supervision. Second, we train a network to regress this feature field. The entire procedure requires no 3D annotation, instead relying on the powerful information in 2D foundation models. We demonstrate that our learned features can be immediately applied to downstream tasks, including part segmentation, dense correspondence, and mesh deformation. Extensive experiments show that MeshFM, trained solely with 2D supervision, performs on par with methods trained explicitly with 3D supervision, even without task-specific fine-tuning. Moreover, our model is trained to be robust to extreme rotations of the input objects. Project page: https://threedle.github.io/MeshFM/

AI.tldr: MeshFM is an efficient feedforward framework that distills 2D features from visual foundation models into 3D features for meshes. It uses a two-stage training strategy—first optimizing a 3D feature field via 2D feature supervision, then regressing this field with a feedforward network—requiring no 3D annotations. The learned features generalize to part segmentation, dense correspondence, and mesh deformation, performing on par with 3D-supervised methods without task-specific fine-tuning and robust to extreme input rotations.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for extracting rich 3D features either require heavy optimization at inference time or rely on 3D annotations, which are expensive and scarce. The authors aim to build an efficient feedforward framework that leverages the powerful semantic and geometric information already captured by 2D visual foundation models, eliminating the need for both per-instance optimization and 3D labels.
AI.method: MeshFM employs a two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, a 3D feature field is optimized using only 2D feature supervision from visual foundation models, with no 3D annotation. In the second stage, a feedforward network is trained to directly regress this learned feature field. The network is trained to be robust to extreme rotations of input objects, enabling fast feedforward feature prediction at inference time.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that MeshFM, trained solely with 2D supervision, achieves performance on par with methods explicitly trained with 3D supervision across downstream tasks including part segmentation, dense correspondence, and mesh deformation—even without task-specific fine-tuning. It also exhibits robustness to extreme input rotations.
AI.conclusion: MeshFM demonstrates that powerful 2D foundation model features can be effectively distilled into a feedforward 3D feature extractor, achieving competitive performance against 3D-supervised approaches while being faster at inference and requiring no 3D annotations or task-specific tuning.

title: AgentS4D: Benchmarking Runtime Risks across the Execution Lifecycle of LLM-Based Workspace Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based workspace agents execute stateful, multi-step workflows across heterogeneous resources, external tools, and persistent state. Their safety must therefore be assessed from actions, side effects, and state changes throughout execution. Although recent benchmarks have advanced executable safety testing and trajectory-aware verification, they rarely provide a unified account of where risks enter, how they elicit unsafe behavior, which harms they target, and where supporting evidence appears during execution. We introduce AgentS4D, a sandboxed benchmark for lifecycle-wide runtime safety evaluation. Its four-dimensional runtime-safety framework uses six risk-entry sources, six induction strategies, and nine target harms to guide case construction, while seven lifecycle checkpoints organize post-run evidence. AgentS4D contains 328 risk-injected cases. We evaluate all 20 combinations of four harnesses (Hermes, OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex) and five LLM backends (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3, and Qwen3.7-Plus) on these cases, yielding 6,560 runs. Overall, 4,461 runs (68.0%) trigger prespecified unsafe signals. Across the 20 configurations, the observed safety of an agent system varies with both its harness-LLM pairing and how risk is introduced. Agent systems exhibit markedly different safety behavior when the same induction strategy reaches them through different risk carriers. They also respond differently to the same target harm when it is realized through different carriers and strategies. Moreover, 4,344 runs (66.22% overall) are unsafe yet complete. Thus, task completion cannot establish runtime safety, and testing only one form of a risk can conceal important weaknesses. Evaluations should examine complete agent configurations across diverse risk conditions and retain evidence throughout execution.

AI.tldr: AgentS4D is a sandboxed benchmark for lifecycle-wide runtime safety evaluation of LLM-based workspace agents, containing 328 risk-injected cases evaluated across 20 harness-LLM configurations (6,560 runs). Results show 68% trigger unsafe signals, 66.22% of runs are unsafe yet complete, and safety behavior varies with both the harness-LLM pairing and how risks are introduced, demonstrating that task completion cannot establish runtime safety.
AI.motivation: LLM-based workspace agents execute stateful, multi-step workflows across heterogeneous resources and persistent state, but existing safety benchmarks rarely provide a unified account of where risks enter, how they elicit unsafe behavior, which harms they target, and where supporting evidence appears during execution. A comprehensive runtime-safety evaluation framework is needed.
AI.method: AgentS4D introduces a four-dimensional runtime-safety framework using six risk-entry sources, six induction strategies, and nine target harms to guide case construction, with seven lifecycle checkpoints organizing post-run evidence. The benchmark contains 328 risk-injected cases evaluated across all 20 combinations of four harnesses (Hermes, OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and five LLM backends (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3, Qwen3.7-Plus).
AI.result: Across 6,560 runs, 4,461 runs (68.0%) trigger prespecified unsafe signals. Agent safety varies with harness-LLM pairing and risk introduction method. Agents behave differently when the same induction strategy reaches them through different risk carriers, and respond differently to the same target harm through different carriers and strategies. Notably, 4,344 runs (66.22%) are unsafe yet complete.
AI.conclusion: Task completion cannot establish runtime safety, and testing only one form of a risk can conceal important weaknesses. Evaluations should examine complete agent configurations across diverse risk conditions and retain evidence throughout execution.

title: DoTime: A Synthetic Benchmark Generator for Interventional and Counterfactual Time Series
summary: Most benchmarks for causal inference over time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation under-served exactly where it matters most, such as in healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science. We introduce \textbf{DoTime}, an open, scalable, and theoretically grounded generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, released as the \code{dotime} PyPI package together with four frozen evaluation suites. Beyond existing work, it adds capabilities absent from prior generators: continuous-time intervention \emph{windows}, counterfactual sampling modes with a positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs as a strict generalization of interrupted time series, non-stationary dynamics by construction with switching SCM parameters, and deterministic ramp and sinusoidal intervention profiles that place trends and structural breaks \emph{inside} the evaluation window. Moreover, it demonstrates the suitability of the generator as a prior for a causal foundation model reference implementation. The released suites span a training-scale snapshot of $100{,}000$ trajectories and eight named identification structures, each with exact ground truth: paired interventional trajectories from the same SCM throughout, and shared-noise counterfactuals in the continuous-time suite. We ship reference baseline implementations with an evaluation harness, and pose a falsifiable claim: interventional training buys a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over an observational model of identical capacity. It is tested across three training seeds per arm. Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional prior-fitted network's (PFN) gap is positive in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested.

AI.tldr: DoTime is an open, scalable generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, released as the dotime PyPI package with four frozen evaluation suites. It enables continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling with positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs, non-stationary dynamics, and deterministic intervention profiles. The authors show it works as a prior for a causal foundation model, demonstrating that interventional training yields a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over observational models of identical capacity.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for causal inference over time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation under-served in critical areas like healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science.
AI.method: DoTime generates multivariate temporal structural causal models with interventions, adding capabilities absent from prior generators: continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling with a positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs generalizing interrupted time series, non-stationary dynamics via switching SCM parameters, and deterministic ramp/sinusoidal intervention profiles. It ships four frozen evaluation suites with 100,000 training trajectories across eight named identification structures with exact ground truth, plus reference baselines and an evaluation harness.
AI.result: Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional prior-fitted network (PFN) shows a positive direction-accuracy gap over an observational model of identical capacity in every structure, trajectory length, and training seed tested (three seeds per arm).
AI.conclusion: Interventional training provides a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over purely observational models, and DoTime serves as a suitable and scalable data generator and prior source for causal foundation model development.

title: VETO: Towards Protecting Images From Frontier AI Editing
summary: The rise of powerful, accessible image-editing models such as FLUX.2 has brought high-fidelity editing within broad reach. Their capabilities now extend beyond localized modifications to extracting and recontextualizing objects and identities in entirely new scenes. By allowing prompt and generation tokens to attend directly to reference-image tokens, modern models blur the boundary between conventional editing and text-to-image synthesis. This expanded generative freedom also broadens the space of potential misuse, as harmful transformations are no longer confined to a predictable set of localized edits. Existing anti-edit defenses are designed to disrupt the semantic bottleneck of the reference-image encoding in legacy diffusion pipelines. However, newer editors distill reference information through joint-attention blocks, thereby often circumventing these protections. We therefore introduce VETO, a subtle anti-edit cloak that disrupts this inner mechanism through which modern models read the source image. Additionally, as existing editing benchmarks leave comprehensive recontextualizations largely untested, we introduce VetoBench, which evaluates defenses not only on conventional localized edits but also on broader contextual shifts. Across two contemporary editing models and three benchmarks, VETO consistently outperforms existing defenses while providing a stronger protection-fidelity trade-off.

AI.tldr: VETO is a subtle anti-edit cloak that disrupts the joint-attention mechanism modern image-editing models use to read reference images, introducing VetoBench to evaluate defenses against both localized edits and broader recontextualizations.
AI.motivation: Modern image-editing models like FLUX.2 now support recontextualizing objects into entirely new scenes via joint-attention blocks, which expand the space of potential misuse. Existing anti-edit defenses target the semantic bottleneck of legacy diffusion pipelines and are circumvented by newer editors that distill reference information through joint-attention, leaving a critical protection gap.
AI.method: VETO introduces a subtle anti-edit cloak designed to disrupt the inner joint-attention mechanism through which modern editing models read the source image.
