The paper also introduces VetoBench, a benchmark evaluating defenses not only on conventional localized edits but also on broader contextual shifts/recontextualizations.
AI.result: Across two contemporary editing models and three benchmarks, VETO consistently outperforms existing defenses while providing a stronger protection-fidelity trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Disrupting the joint-attention mechanism is an effective and more robust approach to anti-edit defense compared to legacy bottleneck-based methods, and evaluation must extend beyond localized edits to include recontextualization scenarios to properly assess defense efficacy.

title: RadHarmony: Radiological Data Handling in the Era of Agentic AI
summary: Training deep learning models on radiological images requires integrating heterogeneous datasets across different sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types. We present RadHarmony, an open-source Python library that provides a unified API for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting radiological datasets, with a primary focus on chest radiographs and early support for computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). RadHarmony standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, wraps MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching, and supports classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and radiology report text through a single interface, with an interactive visualization tool for dataset exploration and verification. To lower the barrier for integrating new datasets, RadHarmony introduces an AI-agent skill that guides the full integration workflow from raw data inspection through code generation and testing. We demonstrate the library's utility by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a reference vision transformer baseline that combines three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code. The code and pretrained model weights are available at https://github.com/f10409/RadHarmony.

AI.tldr: RadHarmony is an open-source Python library that provides a unified API for harmonizing and augmenting radiological datasets across 24 public datasets, supporting chest radiographs, CT, and MRI. It standardizes metadata, wraps MONAI datasets, handles multiple annotation types, includes an AI-agent skill for dataset integration, and demonstrates utility via a pretrained vision transformer baseline.
AI.motivation: Training deep learning models on radiological images is challenging due to heterogeneity across data sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types, creating a need for a unified tool to harmonize these datasets.
AI.method: RadHarmony provides a unified API for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting radiological datasets. It standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, wraps MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching, supports classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and radiology report text through a single interface, and includes an interactive visualization tool and an AI-agent skill for dataset integration workflow.
AI.result: The library successfully harmonizes three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code, demonstrated through pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a reference vision transformer baseline. Code and pretrained model weights are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: RadHarmony lowers the barrier for radiological dataset integration and harmonization, enabling unified training across heterogeneous medical imaging sources while providing extensible tooling for future dataset additions.

title: CrowdioSet and PaRIRset: Two Datasets Towards Live Music Source Separation
summary: Most Music Source Separation (MSS) models do not generalize well to live music recordings because they are trained on studio recordings alone, disregarding the venue acoustics, the speaker system's response and audience noise. We propose to bridge this gap by providing and training a model on two novel datasets. First, we present CrowdioSet: a noise dataset comprising 4800 real ambience tracks from Freesound and synthetic sing-alongs for the vocals in MUSDB18 and MOISESDB datasets, generated from zero-shot singing voice conversions. CrowdioSet enables effective audio denoising for live recordings, resulting in superior separation both in objective and subjective evaluations. Second, we introduce PaRIRset, a stereo impulse response dataset captured across 40 professional concert venues using a microphone array. Our results show that adding PaRIRset RIRs increases the performance of a MSS model compared to using real RIRs from Speech Enhancement tasks alone. We make the examples, code, model weights, PaRIRset, and CrowdioSet freely available to the public.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the poor generalization of Music Source Separation (MSS) models to live recordings by introducing two novel datasets: CrowdioSet (4800 real ambience tracks with synthetic sing-alongs for denoising) and PaRIRset (stereo impulse responses from 40 concert venues). Training on these datasets improves MSS performance on live music, outperforming models trained on studio recordings alone or with real RIRs from speech enhancement tasks.
AI.motivation: MSS models trained solely on studio recordings fail to generalize to live music due to unaccounted-for venue acoustics, speaker system responses, and audience noise. This domain gap significantly degrades separation quality in real-world live performance scenarios.
AI.method: The authors construct CrowdioSet, comprising 4800 real ambience tracks from Freesound and synthetic sing-alongs generated via zero-shot singing voice conversion for vocals in MUSDB18 and MOISESDB. They also introduce PaRIRset, a stereo impulse response dataset captured across 40 professional concert venues using a microphone array. MSS models are trained on combinations of these datasets to bridge the studio-to-live domain gap.
AI.result: CrowdioSet enables effective audio denoising for live recordings, yielding superior performance in both objective and subjective evaluations. Adding PaRIRset RIRs improves MSS model performance compared to using real RIRs from Speech Enhancement tasks alone.
AI.conclusion: The proposed datasets effectively bridge the domain gap between studio and live music recordings for MSS, and are released publicly along with code, model weights, and the datasets themselves.

title: S-Avatar: Diffusion-Guided Gaussian Head Avatars from a Single Image
summary: We propose S-Avatar, a novel method for generating photorealistic 3D head avatars from a single image using a diffusion-guided 3D model generation module and strategies for animating 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). While single-image head avatar reconstruction is crucial for lifelike Virtual Reality (VR) applications, existing approaches often struggle to preserve 3D consistency under unseen viewpoints. S-Avatar addresses this limitation through a three-stage pipeline. First, a high-resolution 3DGS is synthesized directly from a single image using a diffusion-based Gaussian splat generation module. Next, the parametric head model FLAME is aligned with the generated 3DGS by optimizing its parameters and spatial transformations. Finally, to adapt the 3DGS to FLAME variations, we construct a binding template that encodes the spatial relationship between the initial splats and FLAME. The dynamic 3D head avatar can then be rendered in real time by deforming the 3DGS with the binding template. By combining diffusion-guided canonical 3DGS generation with FLAME-based control, our method achieves efficient and accurate reconstruction with enhanced 3D consistency. Evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that S-Avatar outperforms state-of-the-art methods in novel-view and expression generation, achieving superior realism and consistency. Consequently, our approach represents a significant advance in accessible avatar creation, applicable to a wide range of VR/AR applications. The project page is available at https://github.com/hailsong/savatar.

AI.tldr: S-Avatar generates photorealistic 3D head avatars from a single image using a three-stage pipeline: diffusion-guided 3DGS generation, FLAME parametric model alignment, and a binding template for real-time animation, achieving superior realism and 3D consistency.
AI.motivation: Single-image head avatar reconstruction is critical for VR applications, but existing approaches struggle to maintain 3D consistency under unseen viewpoints, limiting the realism of generated avatars.
AI.method: The method uses a three-stage pipeline: (1) a diffusion-based Gaussian splatting generation module synthesizes high-resolution 3DGS directly from a single image; (2) the parametric head model FLAME is aligned with the generated 3DGS by optimizing parameters and spatial transformations; (3) a binding template encoding spatial relationships between splats and FLAME enables real-time deformation and animation of the avatar.
AI.result: Evaluations on public datasets show S-Avatar outperforms state-of-the-art methods in novel-view and expression generation, achieving superior realism and consistency in both rendering quality and 3D coherence.
AI.conclusion: S-Avatar represents a significant advance in accessible avatar creation by combining diffusion-guided canonical 3DGS with FLAME-based control, enabling real-time, photorealistic avatar generation applicable to a wide range of VR/AR applications.

title: A Taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork Requirements
summary: Autonomous systems are increasingly deployed in safety- and mission-critical domains where humans and robots must operate as a team to complete complex tasks. Existing requirements for Human-Robot teamwork remain fragmented across disparate sources, with no unified framework that addresses complexities of collaborative Human-Robot tasks. We address this gap by presenting a taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements derived from analysis of (academic and industrial) literature, standards and regulatory guidance. We extracted a construction corpus of 361 requirements from 14 cross-domain sources. Through iterative classification and refinement, we develop a two-level hierarchical taxonomy comprising 6 high-level categories and 21 low-level subcategories that distinguish information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, and foundational system capabilities. We validate the taxonomy through expert evaluation with 5 domain specialists and a utility demonstration on an independently assembled corpus of 448 requirements drawn from 19 sources spanning six HRT domains.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a two-level hierarchical taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements, derived from 361 requirements across 14 cross-domain sources, comprising 6 high-level categories and 21 low-level subcategories covering information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, and foundational system capabilities. The taxonomy is validated through expert evaluation with 5 specialists and a utility demonstration on an independent corpus of 448 requirements from 19 sources.
AI.motivation: Requirements for Human-Robot teamwork are fragmented across disparate academic, industrial, standards, and regulatory sources, with no unified framework addressing the complexities of collaborative human-robot tasks, creating a gap that this work aims to fill.
AI.method: The authors extracted a construction corpus of 361 requirements from 14 cross-domain sources, then applied iterative classification and refinement to develop a two-level hierarchical taxonomy. Validation was conducted through expert evaluation with 5 domain specialists and a utility demonstration on an independent corpus of 448 requirements from 19 sources spanning six HRT domains.
AI.result: The resulting taxonomy comprises 6 high-level categories and 21 low-level subcategories: information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, and foundational system capabilities. The taxonomy was validated through expert evaluation and demonstrated utility on an independently assembled corpus.
AI.conclusion: The proposed HRT requirements taxonomy provides a unified framework to organize and classify human-robot teamwork requirements, addressing the fragmentation across sources and offering a validated structure useful for safety- and mission-critical autonomous system deployment.

title: PlatformBid: An Auto-Bidding Benchmark from a Unified Advertising Platform's Perspective
summary: Real-time bidding is central to computational advertising, comprising three elements: Supply Side Platform (SSP) selling ad impressions, Demand Side Platform (DSP) bidding for advertisers, and Ad Exchange conducting auctions between them. Traditional auto-bidding algorithms focus solely on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions by adjusting bids against competitors. However, current big ad platforms, such as social media and e-commerce companies, now integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions internally. From such ad platforms' perspective, the goal of the auto-bidding algorithms is not only to maximize the advertisers' conversions, but also the total revenue of the platform. Given the lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks and the pressing need to advance auto-bidding research, we propose PlatformBid - the first comprehensive benchmark designed from a unified ad platform's perspective. To accurately reflect the real-world auto-bidding scenarios, we define three representative settings: (1) homogeneous competition with identical algorithms across advertisers, (2) heterogeneous competition with diverse algorithmic strategies, and (3) promotional competition where some advertisers surge budgets for boosting sales during promotional events like Black Friday. We systematically evaluate a broad spectrum of existing auto-bidding methods across these settings, encompassing classical control methods, RL-based methods, and recent generative methods. Besides these methods, we further propose a novel auto-bidding method based on flow-matching, termed BidFlow, which leverages the flow-matching method's expressive policy representation to effectively handle dynamic competitive environments. Online experiments on Kuaishou further show a +0.68\% improvement in target cost, providing deployment evidence for the offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

AI.tldr: PlatformBid is the first comprehensive benchmark for auto-bidding in computational advertising designed from a unified ad platform's perspective (integrating SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange), covering three competitive settings (homogeneous, heterogeneous, and promotional). The paper also proposes BidFlow, a flow-matching-based auto-bidding method, validated by online experiments on Kuaishou showing +0.68% improvement in target cost.
AI.motivation: Traditional auto-bidding algorithms focus solely on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions against competitors. However, modern ad platforms integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange internally, so their goal is to maximize both advertiser conversions and total platform revenue. There is a lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks for auto-bidding research, motivating the creation of a comprehensive benchmark from the unified ad platform's perspective.
AI.method: The paper proposes PlatformBid, a benchmark defining three representative real-world auto-bidding settings: (1) homogeneous competition with identical algorithms, (2) heterogeneous competition with diverse algorithmic strategies, and (3) promotional competition with budget surges during events like Black Friday. It systematically evaluates existing methods (classical control, RL-based, and generative methods) and introduces BidFlow, a novel flow-matching-based auto-bidding method leveraging expressive policy representation for dynamic competitive environments.
AI.result: The benchmark systematically evaluates a broad spectrum of existing auto-bidding methods across the three settings. BidFlow, the proposed flow-matching-based method, demonstrates effective handling of dynamic competitive environments. Online experiments on Kuaishou show a +0.68% improvement in target cost, providing deployment evidence for offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.
AI.conclusion: PlatformBid serves as the first comprehensive platform-centric benchmark for auto-bidding, filling the gap in evaluation frameworks for unified ad platforms. BidFlow demonstrates the effectiveness of flow-matching methods in auto-bidding, and its successful online deployment on Kuaishou validates the offline-online consistency of the benchmark.

title: Bunraku: Turning a Single Illustration into an Editable Live2D Character
summary: Live2D is the dominant 2D character-animation format for anime characters and virtual avatars, representing each character as a stack of RGBA layers driven by per-layer mesh deformation. Despite its wide use in virtual streaming, mobile games, and interactive characters, authoring a Live2D model still demands weeks of manual layer separation, occlusion completion, mesh placement, and keyframing, and no prior generative method produces such a structured asset end-to-end. We present the first system that, from a single illustration, generates all the structured information a Live2D runtime consumes: ordered RGBA layers, a deformation mesh per layer, and the parameter-driven keypose vertex offsets that make the character move. Stage 1 casts layered decomposition as a layered diffusion process under a Live2D-aware organ-level taxonomy, producing an ordered RGBA stack with hidden-region completion. Stage 2 builds a content-conforming triangle mesh for each layer from its alpha channel alone, then predicts the keypose displacement field of all layers jointly: every vertex of every layer is one token, self-attention spans layer boundaries, and each displacement is factorised into a bounded direction and a log-magnitude. Joint rather than independent prediction is what makes the result a coherent character instead of separately plausible parts, and is our largest gain; scaling the network 112x yields none. On 50 held-out characters, under true generation with no teacher forcing, Stage 2 attains a per-vertex direction cosine of 0.768 (median 0.828). Because a layer's mesh derives from its alpha channel, a clothing layer can be re-textured from a natural-language instruction while the mesh and predicted animation are reused byte-for-byte. We further contribute Live2D-Bench, the first standardized benchmark for the task, and an 8,884-model Live2D corpus with layer and animation supervision.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first end-to-end system that generates a complete, runtime-ready Live2D character animation asset (ordered RGBA layers, deformation meshes, and parameter-driven keypose offsets) from a single input illustration. It introduces a two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 uses a layered diffusion process under an organ-level taxonomy for layer decomposition with hidden-region completion; Stage 2 builds content-conforming meshes from alpha channels and jointly predicts keypose displacement fields across all layers (with each vertex as a token, bounded direction + log-magnitude factorization) to produce coherent character motion. The paper also contributes Live2D-Bench, the first benchmark, and an 8,884-model corpus. Key findings: joint prediction is the largest gain (scaling model 112x yields none), and re-texturing is possible via natural language while reusing mesh and animation.
AI.motivation: Live2D is the dominant 2D character-animation format for anime characters and avatars, but authoring a model manually takes weeks of layer separation, occlusion completion, mesh placement, and keyframing. No prior generative method produces such a structured asset end-to-end, motivating the first fully automatic pipeline from a single illustration to a complete Live2D model.
AI.method: The system comprises two stages. Stage 1 formulates layered decomposition as a layered diffusion process under a Live2D-aware organ-level taxonomy, yielding an ordered RGBA stack with hidden-region completion. Stage 2 constructs a content-conforming triangle mesh per layer from its alpha channel, then predicts the keypose displacement field jointly across all layers using a token-based self-attention model where every vertex is a token (attention spans layer boundaries) and each displacement is factorized into a bounded direction and a log-magnitude. A large-scale corpus of 8,884 Live2D models with layer and animation supervision was collected.
AI.result: On 50 held-out characters under true generation with no teacher forcing, Stage 2 achieves a per-vertex direction cosine of 0.768 (median 0.828). Joint prediction across layers is the largest performance contributor, while scaling the network 112x yields no further gain. Additional capabilities include natural-language-based re-texturing of a clothing layer while reusing the mesh and predicted animation byte-for-byte.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers the first end-to-end generative system for complete Live2D assets from a single illustration, demonstrating that joint, cross-layer displacement prediction is essential for coherent character motion. It also introduces benchmarks (Live2D-Bench) and corpus resources to standardize and advance future research in this task.

title: Asymmetric Collapse in Model Merging: When Refusal Over- writes Recognition
comment: Accepted into COLM AIW, waiting decision for AdvML-Frontiers x CoTMA and HAIPS
summary: Model merging is often used to combine capabilities from separately fine-tuned models without additional training, but it is unclear whether standard merging methods preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously. We study this question through a controlled case study using two Gemma-3-1B-IT finetunes on two complementary safety objectives: CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal. We merge the two fine-tunes using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES, and evaluate the merged models on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. Across all four methods, attack resistance transfers significantly more than classification accuracy: merged models retain 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates while CARES accuracy falls to at most 12.9%. Weight-space measurements suggest that this asymmetry is not caused by strongly opposing task-vector directions: the two task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011). Instead, the refusal fine-tune induces consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive methods to favor refusal updates. These results show that standard model merging can collapse safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether standard model merging methods preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously by merging two Gemma-3-1B-IT finetunes on complementary safety objectives (CARES harm classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal). Across Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES merging, attack resistance transfers significantly better (81-85% jailbreak refusal) than classification accuracy (≤12.9% CARES accuracy). The asymmetry stems not from opposing task-vector directions (nearly orthogonal, cosine 0.011) but from consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes in the refusal finetune, causing magnitude-sensitive merging to favor refusal updates and collapse safety recognition into broad refusal.
AI.motivation: Model merging combines capabilities from separately fine-tuned models without retraining, but it is unclear whether standard merging methods preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously. This work systematically studies whether safety capabilities—harm classification and adversarial refusal—can be jointly preserved through standard merging.
AI.method: A controlled case study merges two Gemma-3-1B-IT finetunes on complementary safety objectives (CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal) using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES merging. Merged models are evaluated on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. Task-vector geometry (cosine similarity and per-layer magnitudes) is also analyzed.
AI.result: All four merging methods preserve attack resistance substantially better than classification accuracy: merged models retain 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates while CARES classification accuracy drops to at most 12.9%. The two task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011), ruling out opposing directions as the cause; instead, the refusal finetune produces consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, so magnitude-sensitive merging methods favor refusal updates.
AI.conclusion: Standard model merging can collapse safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale, even when their directions are not in conflict. This highlights a previously underappreciated failure mode for merging safety-aligned models.

title: Integrating Contextual Embeddings into Evaluation of Expressive MIDI Piano Performances
summary: Objective evaluation of expressive MIDI piano performances typically relies on attribute statistics such as timing, velocity, and duration of individual notes. However, these methods often disregard dependencies between notes, which poses a potential limitation in assessing the similarity between two sets of performances. In generative applications, the wide variety of expressive attributes makes it difficult to aggregate them into a single scalar metric for model selection. In this work, we reexamine attribute-scoped metrics and explore the perceptual properties of contextual embeddings from self-supervised symbolic music models, Aria and CLaMP3. Results from our listening study indicate that these models can be used as perceptual proxies, showing agreement with per-sample human ratings on par with traditional metrics. To measure conditional distributional similarity, we adapt Kernel Audio Distance to the symbolic music domain. Unlike Pearson correlation and reconstruction error, kernel-based methods on contextual embeddings do not require note alignment and are sensitive to contextual perturbations. To facilitate reproducibility, we release Pereval, an open-source library that integrates performance evaluation utilities, including both attribute-scoped and deep feature metrics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new evaluation framework for expressive MIDI piano performances using contextual embeddings from self-supervised symbolic music models (Aria, CLaMP3) as perceptual proxies, and adapts Kernel Audio Distance to symbolic music for measuring conditional distributional similarity without note alignment. They release Pereval, an open-source evaluation library.
AI.motivation: Traditional evaluation metrics rely on attribute statistics (timing, velocity, duration) of individual notes and ignore dependencies between notes. Additionally, the wide variety of expressive attributes makes it hard to aggregate them into a single scalar for model selection in generative applications.
AI.method: Reexamines attribute-scoped metrics; explores perceptual properties of contextual embeddings from self-supervised symbolic music models (Aria and CLaMP3); adapts Kernel Audio Distance (KAD) to the symbolic music domain for conditional distributional similarity; validates via listening study comparing per-sample human ratings with model predictions; releases Pereval, an open-source library integrating both attribute-scoped and deep feature metrics.
AI.result: Listening study results show that Aria and CLaMP3 embeddings can serve as perceptual proxies with agreement with per-sample human ratings on par with traditional metrics. Kernel-based methods on contextual embeddings do not require note alignment and are sensitive to contextual perturbations, unlike Pearson correlation and reconstruction error.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised symbolic music model embeddings offer a viable perceptual proxy for evaluating expressive performances, and kernel-based distributional metrics provide alignment-free, context-sensitive evaluation. The released Pereval library facilitates reproducibility.

title: SIGIL: Compiling Agent Skills into Typed Harnesses
summary: AI-Integrated agents increasingly acquire capability from skills: prose procedure files loaded into a model's context and run by a tool-calling loop. A skill is described to the runtime but never encoded in it, so the model re-derives its control flow on every run and may skip mandated verification. Across 30 skills and two model generations, a prose agent performs only 56% of the steps its own skill mandates, while producing artifacts that pass output checks. The remedy is known: write a harness, in which the procedure is program structure. However, hand-writing harnesses is tedious and discards the authoring surface that made skills succeed. To address this limitation, we introduce Skill Compilation, realized in SIGIL, which compiles a prose skill into an executable harness. At its center is AG-IR, a typed agentic intermediate representation separating model-owned cognition from code-owned mechanism. Compiled harnesses perform 86% of mandated steps, complete the full procedure 2.3x as often, and require 0.58x the tokens. Notably, the guarantee is model-independent: the harness holds at 86% across two model generations while prose swings from 56% to 68%.

AI.tldr: Prose-based AI agent skills are unreliable—agents execute only 56% of mandated steps while passing output checks. The authors introduce Skill Compilation realized in SIGIL, which compiles prose skills into executable harnesses via AG-IR, a typed agentic intermediate representation separating model cognition from code mechanism. Compiled harnesses achieve 86% step compliance, complete procedures 2.3x more often, use 0.58x tokens, and provide model-independent guarantees across model generations.
AI.motivation: AI agents gain capability from prose skill files loaded into context, but these skills lack formal encoding—the model re-derives control flow on each run and often skips mandated verification steps. Hand-writing executable harnesses fixes this but is tedious and loses the accessible authoring surface of prose.
AI.method: The paper introduces Skill Compilation, realized in a system called SIGIL, which compiles prose skills into executable harnesses. At the core is AG-IR, a typed agentic intermediate representation that separates model-owned cognition from code-owned mechanism.
AI.result: Across 30 skills and two model generations, compiled harnesses perform 86% of mandated steps (vs 56% for prose), complete the full procedure 2.3x more often, and require 0.58x the tokens. The guarantee is model-independent: harnesses hold at 86% across model generations while prose performance swings from 56% to 68%.
AI.conclusion: Compiling prose skills into executable harnesses offers a promising middle ground: retaining the authoring ease of prose while delivering near-worst reliability guarantees independent of underlying model capabilities. This addresses the reliability gap in prose-driven agent skills without requiring tedious manual harness development.

title: Beyond KV Reconstruction: Functional Reconstruction for MLA Draft Models in Speculative Decoding
summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) is increasingly important for long-context LLM inference because compact latent states replace the growing key-value (KV) cache and reduce decoding memory traffic. Yet most capable open checkpoints use multi-head or grouped-query attention (MHA/GQA), so conversion is needed to obtain MLA's cache efficiency without retraining from scratch. Speculative decoding offers complementary acceleration, but its speedup depends on agreement between draft proposals and target verification. We find that direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion can sharply reduce this agreement: low-rank factorization and RoPE handling introduce attention-function errors that may be tolerable for standalone generation but substantially lower draft-token acceptance. We therefore formulate MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. Our end-to-end (E2E) method optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states. This converter-agnostic post-conversion procedure preserves the converted cache and inference graph and requires neither verifier logits nor verifier supervision. We evaluate 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations spanning four Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA, HF and vLLM, and four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance, Functional Reconstruction materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, leaves 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreases one. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/swyhahaha/FunctionalMLA.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the problem that direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion for long-context LLM inference introduces attention-function errors that significantly reduce draft-token acceptance in speculative decoding. The authors propose a converter-agnostic post-conversion method called Functional Reconstruction (E2E), which optimizes each converted MLA module to reproduce the original attention module's post-output-projection response on calibration hidden states. Evaluated across 192 configurations spanning various model pairs, converters, backends, and tasks, the method materially improves draft acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells while leaving 26 practically unchanged.
AI.motivation: MLA is important for long-context inference due to compact latent state replacing growing KV cache, but most capable open checkpoints use MHA/GQA, requiring conversion. Direct conversion harms speculative decoding because the introduced attention-function errors drastically lower draft-token acceptance even though standalone generation remains acceptable. Existing approaches treat conversion as cache compression, overlooking the need to preserve functional behavior for downstream acceleration techniques like speculative decoding.
AI.method: The method frames MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. It performs end-to-end post-conversion optimization on each converted MLA attention module to replicate the post-output-projection response from the original MHA/GQA module using calibration hidden states. The approach is converter-agnostic, preserves the converted cache and inference graph, and requires no verifier logits or supervision.
AI.result: Evaluated on 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations spanning four Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, two converters (TransMLA and MHA2MLA), two backends (HF and vLLM), and four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance, Functional Reconstruction materially improved acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, left 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreased one.
AI.conclusion: Functional Reconstruction effectively recovers draft-token acceptance in converted MLA models used for speculative decoding, improving performance across the majority of evaluated configurations with minimal downside, thereby enabling practical adoption of MLA cache efficiency for existing MHA/GQA checkpoints without retraining.

title: Shared Semantic Codebook Distillation for Unpaired Cross-Modal Medical Classification
summary: Cross-modal knowledge distillation can transfer diagnostic knowledge from a strong but costly teacher modality to a cheaper and more deployable student modality. In medical image analysis, however, the two modalities are often unpaired: they are collected from different patient cohorts and occupy geometrically incompatible feature spaces. This makes instance-level distillation invalid and direct feature matching unreliable. To address these challenges, we propose Shared Semantic Codebook Distillation (SSCD), which compares teacher and student representations through a shared discrete codebook. Each image is represented as a distribution over a common, modality-agnostic vocabulary, and knowledge is transferred by aligning these distributions across modalities, both globally and class-conditionally, without requiring paired samples or directly comparable raw features. The codebook is evolved online by exponential moving average and kept diverse through entropy regularization and dead-code restart. At inference, all teacher-side and codebook modules are discarded, leaving only the student encoder and classifier. On two heterogeneous unpaired settings, OCT-to-fundus retinal disease classification and CT-to-chest-X-ray pneumonia classification, SSCD improves the student from 64.5 to 70.2 macro-F1 and from 73.8 to 76.3 macro-F1, respectively, outperforming all evaluated distillation baselines on both settings. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/DillanImans/SSCD-unpaired-distillation

AI.tldr: SSCD proposes a shared discrete codebook approach for cross-modal knowledge distillation when teacher and student modalities are unpaired, representing each image as a distribution over a common modality-agnostic vocabulary and aligning these distributions globally and class-conditionally. It improves student performance from 64.5 to 70.2 macro-F1 (OCT-to-fundus) and 73.8 to 76.3 macro-F1 (CT-to-chest-X-ray), outperforming all distillation baselines.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal knowledge distillation is valuable in medical imaging where a costly modality (e.g., OCT/CT) can teach a cheaper one (e.g., fundus/chest-X-ray), but modalities are often unpaired—collected from different patient cohorts with geometrically incompatible feature spaces—making instance-level distillation and direct feature matching infeasible.
AI.method: SSCD compares teacher and student representations through a shared discrete codebook, where each image is represented as a distribution over a common modality-agnostic vocabulary. Knowledge transfer is achieved by aligning these distributions across modalities both globally and class-conditionally, without needing paired samples or directly comparable raw features. The codebook is evolved online via exponential moving average and kept diverse with entropy regularization and dead-code restart.
AI.result: On two unpaired heterogeneous settings—OCT-to-fundus retinal disease classification and CT-to-chest-X-ray pneumonia classification—SSCD improves the student from 64.5 to 70.2 and 73.8 to 76.3 macro-F1 respectively, outperforming all evaluated distillation baselines. At inference, only the student encoder and classifier remain; teacher and codebook modules are discarded.
AI.conclusion: SSCD demonstrates that a shared discrete codebook enables effective cross-modal knowledge distillation under unpaired, geometrically incompatible medical imaging modalities, providing a deployable student model while outperforming existing distillation methods.

title: Divergence Decoding: Training-Free Capability Fusion
summary: While large language models excel in reasoning, these generalists often lack knowledge for specialized scientific domains. Conversely, domain models~(specialists), while knowledgeable, suffer from specialization side-effects including diminished logic and reduced robustness.To address this dilemma, we introduce Divergence Decoding, a training-free framework for capability fusion. It reconstructs the "draft-and-verify" skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. The core is using Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor the distributional disagreement between the two models at each token. When the specialist exhibits significant divergence, our method identifies it as a potential reasoning risk and instantaneously routes control to the generalist. This allows the dynamic injection of general reasoning while preserving domain expertise, achieving inference-time policy composition of the generalist and the specialist.We evaluate Divergence Decoding across diverse model families (Qwen and Llama series) on challenging scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench). Experimental results demonstrate that Divergence Decoding outperforms both the domain-specialized and general-purpose models, effectively surpassing the performance of most single-model baseline. This suggests that Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration.

AI.tldr: Divergence Decoding is a training-free framework that fuses the capabilities of a generalist LLM and a domain-specialist model by repurposing speculative decoding's draft-and-verify mechanism into an adaptive routing scheme. Using Jensen-Shannon divergence to detect token-level distributional disagreement, it routes control to the generalist when the specialist shows potential reasoning risk, dynamically injecting general reasoning while preserving domain expertise. Experiments on GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench across Qwen and Llama families show it outperforms both specialist and generalist models.
AI.motivation: Large language models face a dilemma: generalists excel at reasoning but lack specialized domain knowledge, while domain specialists possess expertise but suffer from specialization side-effects like diminished logic and reduced robustness. The paper aims to fuse both capabilities without training.
AI.method: Divergence Decoding reconstructs the draft-and-verify skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. It uses Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor distributional disagreement between the specialist (draft) and generalist at each token. When significant divergence is detected, it identifies a potential reasoning risk and instantly routes control from the specialist to the generalist, achieving inference-time policy composition.
AI.result: Evaluated on Qwen and Llama model families across GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench scientific benchmarks, Divergence Decoding outperforms both domain-specialized and general-purpose models, surpassing most single-model baselines.
AI.conclusion: Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration, effectively resolving the generalist-specialist dilemma.

title: Teffic-Audio: Tell Fact from Fiction
comment: 16 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Technical report. Project page: https://tefficlabs.com/teffic-audio
summary: Speech deepfake detection has expanded in scope with increasingly heterogeneous spoofing mechanisms, including speech synthesis, voice conversion, vocoder reconstruction, and neural-codec resynthesis. The resulting spoofing artifacts can be further shaped by variability in source speech, recording environments, and transmission channels. This variability makes robust generalization across heterogeneous conditions a central requirement for practical detection systems. This report presents Teffic-Audio, a general speech deepfake detection system designed for comprehensive evaluation environment. Teffic-Audio adopts a straightforward detector architecture consisting of a Conformer-based speech encoder, multi-head attentive statistics pooling, and a binary classifier. Rather than relying on additional architectural complexity, the system improves generalization through its training recipe, which integrates multi-source data, attack- and source-balanced sampling, and diverse audio augmentation. Trained only with open-source data, Teffic-Audio achieves a pooled EER of 1.454% on the 14 test sets of Speech-DF-Arena, outperforming all currently public systems on the leaderboard. It also obtains the lowest EER on five individual test sets and shows a favorable performance-complexity trade-off compared with larger leading systems. Overall, Teffic-Audio provides a strong and practical reference system for general speech deepfake detection.

AI.tldr: Teffic-Audio is a speech deepfake detection system using a Conformer encoder with attentive statistics pooling, achieving 1.454% pooled EER on Speech-DF-Arena's 14 test sets—outperforming all public systems—through a training recipe focused on multi-source data, balanced sampling, and diverse augmentation rather than architectural complexity.
AI.motivation: Speech deepfake detection must generalize across heterogeneous spoofing mechanisms (synthesis, voice conversion, vocoder reconstruction, neural-codec resynthesis) and variable conditions (source speech, environments, channels), making robust generalization a central requirement for practical detectors.
AI.method: A straightforward detector architecture combining a Conformer-based speech encoder, multi-head attentive statistics pooling, and a binary classifier. Generalization is achieved primarily through the training recipe: multi-source open-source data integration, attack- and source-balanced sampling, and diverse audio augmentation, rather than architectural sophistication.
AI.result: Achieves 1.454% pooled EER on 14 test sets of Speech-DF-Arena, beating all public leaderboard systems. Also obtains the lowest EER on five individual test sets and demonstrates a favorable performance-complexity trade-off relative to larger leading systems.
AI.conclusion: Teffic-Audio provides a strong, practical reference system for general speech deepfake detection, showing that effective training strategies can deliver state-of-the-art performance with a simple architecture trained solely on open-source data.

title: TrustChain-Review: A Risk-Adaptive Blockchain and Game-Theoretic Framework for Trustworthy AI-Assisted Code Review
summary: Context: AI-assisted software development can speed up coding and review, but it also makes accountability harder to establish. Developers may submit insufficiently verified code, reviewers may approve changes with limited inspection, and centralized reputation records may be difficult to audit. Objectives: This study introduces TrustChain-Review, a framework that combines verifiable evidence, strategic incentives, and risk-sensitive governance to support more trustworthy code review. Methods: The framework includes a blockchain-based evidence layer, a three-player game-theoretic model for developers, reviewers, and the platform, and a rule that applies stronger governance when the expected benefit justifies its cost. The evaluation uses a controlled simulation calibrated with the Diff Quality Estimation dataset. Six governance configurations are compared over 30 independent runs using reputation accuracy, trust convergence, malicious-review detection, superficial-review detection, net platform utility, governance cost, and cost-efficiency. Results: The full-evidence configuration produces the strongest reputation, trust, and detection results, but it also has the highest governance cost. The risk-adaptive configuration lowers this cost and improves cost-efficiency by applying stronger controls selectively, although its trust and detection results are lower than those of the full-evidence setting. Conclusion: Strong evidence-based governance is most appropriate for high-risk or audit-sensitive changes. For routine or lower-risk contributions, selective governance offers a more practical balance between trustworthiness and operational cost.

AI.tldr: TrustChain-Review is a framework combining blockchain-based evidence, game-theoretic incentives, and risk-sensitive governance to improve code review trustworthiness. Evaluated via simulation on the Diff Quality Estimation dataset, the full-evidence configuration yields the strongest reputation/detection but highest cost, while the risk-adaptive configuration offers a better cost-efficiency trade-off for routine changes.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted software development accelerates coding and review but undermines accountability—developers may submit insufficiently verified code, reviewers may approve with limited inspection, and centralized reputation records are hard to audit. There is a need for a framework that restores verifiable trust in the code review process.
AI.method: The framework integrates three components: (1) a blockchain-based evidence layer for auditable records, (2) a three-player game-theoretic model covering developers, reviewers, and the platform, and (3) a risk-sensitive governance rule that applies stronger controls only when expected benefit justifies cost. Evaluation uses a controlled simulation calibrated with the Diff Quality Estimation dataset, comparing six governance configurations over 30 independent runs across metrics including reputation accuracy, trust convergence, malicious/superficial-review detection, net platform utility, governance cost, and cost-efficiency.
AI.result: The full-evidence configuration achieves the best reputation, trust, and detection outcomes but incurs the highest governance cost. The risk-adaptive configuration lowers cost and improves cost-efficiency by applying stronger controls selectively, though its trust and detection results are somewhat lower than the full-evidence setting.
AI.conclusion: Strong evidence-based governance is appropriate for high-risk or audit-sensitive changes, while selective governance offers a more practical balance between trustworthiness and operational cost for routine or lower-risk contributions.

title: RLPF: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Code Generation
summary: Code models are increasingly trained with execution feedback, but most training signals still stop at correctness. This leaves an important gap for systems code: two programs can pass the same tests while differing greatly in runtime. We study how to train code agents to prefer faster correct implementations, rather than treating efficiency only as an evaluation metric. The key difficulty is that runtime is a fragile reward. It is meaningful only after a program is correct, varies across tasks, and gives little guidance when most sampled programs fail to compile or run. We propose \textbf{RLPF}, reinforcement learning from performance feedback, which turns execution outcomes into a staged reward. Failed programs are ordered by execution progress, while correct programs are ranked by their relative improvement from the baseline toward the expert reference. This gives useful feedback before correctness and performance-sensitive feedback after correctness. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench raises correct-and-runnable solutions from $11.1\%$ to $54.6\%$ and improves relative efficiency from $8.1\%$ to $38.6\%$. The trained model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems, and its optimization behavior transfers modestly to EffiBench-X. Additional studies show that model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision, and that the full composite reward is more reliable than correctness-only or runtime-only baselines. These results suggest that code agents can be trained not only to pass tests, but also to optimize the programs they write.

AI.tldr: RLPF (Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback) trains code agents to prefer faster correct implementations by converting execution outcomes into a staged reward: failed programs are ordered by execution progress, while correct programs are ranked by relative efficiency improvement over a baseline toward an expert reference. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B on PerfCodeBench raises correct-and-runnable solutions from 11.1% to 54.6% and improves relative efficiency from 8.1% to 38.6%, achieving competitiveness with larger open-weight systems with modest transfer to EffiBench-X.
AI.motivation: Code models are trained with execution feedback, but training signals typically stop at correctness, ignoring runtime differences between programs that pass the same tests. This creates a gap in systems code where efficiency matters significantly. The difficulty is that runtime is a fragile reward—only meaningful after correctness, varies across tasks, and offers little signal when most samples fail to compile or run.
AI.method: RLPF converts execution outcomes into a staged reward. Failed programs are ordered by their execution progress, providing useful feedback before correctness is achieved. Correct programs are ranked by their relative improvement from a baseline toward an expert reference, providing performance-sensitive feedback after correctness. This composite reward is used for fine-tuning via reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench raises correct-and-runnable solutions from 11.1% to 54.6% and improves relative efficiency from 8.1% to 38.6%. The model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems, transfers modestly to EffiBench-X, and the full composite reward outperforms correctness-only or runtime-only baselines. Model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision than expert references.
AI.conclusion: Code agents can be trained not only to pass tests but also to optimize the programs they write. RLPF demonstrates that staged, performance-aware rewards enable effective learning of efficiency preferences, suggesting a promising direction for beyond-correctness code generation training.

title: PIE-APT: A Unified Framework for Temporal Planning and Contradiction Hunting via Incremental Direct-Derivation Abduction
summary: Reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs (DKGs) present significant challenges, especially in open-world environments with incomplete information. Existing action formalisms often face decidability issues and the Ramification Problem, while managing incomplete knowledge via structural abduction requires expansive combinatorial search. This paper introduces a unified framework with two integrated modules---\textbf{PIE-Abducer} (incremental direct-derivation abduction) and \textbf{PIE-APT} (Abductive Planning for Temporal KGs)---operating natively on the highly expressive Description Logic. We model state transitions along a linear timeline as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories. Treating the incremental reasoner as a black-box and representing actions natively in OWL without external modal operators preserves logical decidability. To address incomplete knowledge, \textbf{PIE-Abducer} circumvents traditional Minimal Hitting Set (MHS) enumeration. Instead of combinatorial syntactic search, it injects the logical negation of a target goal into a consistent branch and extracts missing premises via direct refutation consequences. \textbf{PIE-APT} then employs a recursive \textit{Generate-and-Test} architecture, interleaving backward-chaining A* search with \textbf{PIE-Abducer} up to a bounded causal depth, followed by strict validation via forward-chaining Temporal Projection. We evaluate four OWL benchmarks stressing semantic abilities absent in classical planning: parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting. Results demonstrate qualitative superiority over classical planners and prove our direct-derivation approach quantitatively outperforms an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified framework for reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs (DKGs) under open-world, incomplete information. It integrates two modules—PIE-Abducer (incremental direct-derivation abduction) and PIE-APT (Abductive Planning for Temporal KGs)—operating natively on Description Logic. The framework models state transitions as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories, preserves logical decidability by treating the reasoner as a black-box with OWL-native action representations, and avoids Minimal Hitting Set enumeration by injecting goal negation and extracting missing premises via direct refutation. PIE-APT uses a recursive Generate-and-Test architecture interleaving backward-chaining A* with abduction up to bounded causal depth, validated by forward-chaining Temporal Projection. Results demonstrate qualitative superiority over classical planners on four OWL benchmarks and quantitative outperformance of a MHS-faithful baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing action formalisms for reasoning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs suffer from decidability issues, the Ramification Problem, and computationally expensive combinatorial search (via structural abduction / MHS enumeration) when handling incomplete knowledge in open-world environments. The authors aim to unify planning and abduction natively on the expressive Description Logic while preserving logical decidability and scalability.
AI.method: The framework models states as deductively closed DL theories updated non-monotonically along a linear timeline. Actions are represented natively in OWL, with an incremental DL reasoner treated as a black-box to preserve decidability. PIE-Abducer performs incremental direct-derivation abduction by injecting the logical negation of a goal into a consistent branch and extracting missing premises via direct refutation consequences, avoiding MHS enumeration. PIE-APT uses a recursive Generate-and-Test architecture combining backward-chaining A* search interleaved with PIE-Abducer up to a bounded causal depth, followed by strict forward-chaining Temporal Projection for validation.
AI.result: Evaluation on four OWL benchmarks—covering parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting—shows qualitative superiority over classical planners and demonstrates that the direct-derivation abduction approach quantitatively outperforms an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PIE framework provides a unified, decidable, and scalable solution for abductive planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs in open-world settings, overcoming the combinatorial bottlenecks of traditional abduction and outperforming classical planners on semantically demanding tasks.

title: RIPPLE: Generating Multi-Channel Phase, Not Recovering It
summary: Generative models synthesize magnitude spectra with high fidelity, while phase is delegated to a recovery module---Griffin--Lim, a vocoder, or a latent decoder---applied independently to each channel. For multi-channel waveforms this delegation is costly: the physical content of spatial audio and three-component seismograms lives in the phase relationships between channels, precisely what channel-independent recovery cannot produce. The cost is also invisible, since the magnitude-based metrics common to both fields barely move when inter-channel phase coherence collapses---so a pipeline can discard the physical information in its output while still scoring well. We argue that phase should be generated, not recovered, and present RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning), which reinterprets Griffin--Lim as a phase **prior** rather than a final estimator: initialized from the source phase, this prior carries the inter-channel structure to be preserved, and a rectified flow refines it toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss. Tested on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation---two physically unrelated domains---RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on the coherence metrics that downstream analyses consume. The seismic case is decisive: across architecturally distinct generators, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the $57.3^\circ$ random expectation, whereas learned phase reduces it to $33.8^\circ$.

AI.tldr: RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning) reinterprets Griffin-Lim as a phase prior rather than a final estimator, using a rectified flow with an explicit inter-channel phase loss to generate (not recover) phase relationships between channels. It outperforms recovery-based pipelines on inter-channel coherence metrics in both first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation, reducing S-wave polarization error from the 57.3° random expectation to 33.8°.
AI.motivation: Generative models synthesize magnitude spectra with high fidelity but delegate phase recovery to channel-independent modules (Griffin-Lim, vocoders, or latent decoders). This delegation is costly for multi-channel waveforms because the physical content of spatial audio and three-component seismograms lives in inter-channel phase relationships, which channel-independent recovery cannot produce. Moreover, this cost is invisible since magnitude-based metrics barely change when inter-channel phase coherence collapses, allowing pipelines to discard physical information while still scoring well. The authors argue phase should be generated, not recovered.
AI.method: RIPPLE reinterprets Griffin-Lim as a phase prior rather than a final estimator. It is initialized from the source phase, which carries the inter-channel structure to be preserved, and a rectified flow refines this prior toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss.
AI.result: Tested on two physically unrelated domains (first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation), RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on coherence metrics that downstream analyses consume. In the seismic case across architecturally distinct generators, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the 57.3° random expectation, whereas learned phase generation reduces it to 33.8°.
AI.conclusion: Phase should be generated rather than recovered for multi-channel waveform synthesis, as RIPPLE demonstrates that learning inter-channel phase structure substantially improves physical coherence metrics that recovery-based pipelines fail to capture, particularly in seismic polarization analysis.

title: PROGRESS: Property-Guided Regression Search for Semantic Falsification
summary:
Search-based regression-test generation effectively explores complex program structures, yielding high structural coverage, but its oracles are derived from the system under test: faults already present are recorded as expected behavior rather than exposed. Property-based testing offers independent semantic oracles, but depends on high-quality properties and gives little guidance for reaching deep states or satisfying selective preconditions.
  We present PROGRESS (PROperty-Guided REgression Search for Semantic Falsification), integrating intent-driven properties into coverage-guided, search-based evolutionary test generation to reach deep program states and detect violations of intended behavior. PROGRESS (1) extracts intent-bearing code context and uses a language-model pipeline to generate executable jqwik properties while limiting implementation leakage; (2) extends EvoSuite's DynaMOSA with a search objective and property-aware fitness function per property, rewarding progress through preconditions and prioritizing falsifying executions; and (3) binds property parameters and uses jqwik-provided generators to connect quantified inputs to evolving test sequences, steering generation toward coverage and bug-detection goals.
  We evaluate PROGRESS on 25 large-scale Java systems against regression-test generation, standalone property-based testing, and context ablations. PROGRESS detects 328/562 current-version bugs (58%) versus none for regression-test generation, and satisfies all preconditions for 70/150 hard-to-reach properties versus 18 for standalone jqwik. Ablations show documentation and caller/callee context are key to generating valid executable properties. PROGRESS preserves structural exploration while exposing faults missed by regression-derived assertions; we release a comprehensive artifact package.

AI.tldr: PROGRESS is a search-based regression-test generation framework that integrates intent-driven properties from language models with coverage-guided evolutionary search, enabling detection of semantic bugs that traditional regression-test generation misses while reaching deep program states.
AI.motivation: Regression-test generation achieves high structural coverage but derives oracles from the system under test, so existing faults are recorded as expected behavior rather than exposed. Property-based testing offers independent semantic oracles but depends on high-quality properties and provides little guidance for reaching deep states or satisfying selective preconditions. Neither approach alone effectively bridges structural exploration with semantic fault detection.
AI.method: PROGRESS integrates three key components: (1) an intent-driven language-model pipeline that extracts documentation and caller/callee context to generate executable jqwik properties while limiting implementation leakage; (2) an extension of EvoSuite's DynaMOSA with a property-aware fitness function that rewards progress through preconditions and prioritizes falsifying executions; and (3) binding property parameters to jqwik-provided generators to connect quantified inputs to evolving test sequences, steering generation toward both coverage and bug-detection objectives.
AI.result: On 25 large-scale Java systems, PROGRESS detects 328/562 current-version bugs (58%) compared to zero for regression-test generation, and satisfies all preconditions for 70/150 hard-to-reach properties versus only 18 for standalone jqwik. Ablations confirm documentation and caller/callee context are critical for generating valid executable properties, and PROGRESS preserves structural exploration while exposing faults missed by regression-derived assertions.
AI.conclusion: Integrating intent-driven semantic properties into coverage-guided search-based test generation significantly improves bug detection without sacrificing structural coverage. The approach demonstrates that combining LLM-generated properties with evolutionary search is a practical and effective strategy for semantic falsification in large-scale Java systems.

title: SDO: Structure-Aware Data Organization for Efficient LLM Post-Training
summary: Post-training of large language models is expensive, and existing efficiency improvements mainly focus on selecting informative samples or designing training schedules. However, data organization itself is usually treated as a static preprocessing step: embedding-based grouping methods construct fixed partitions before training and cannot adapt to the evolving sample exposure during optimization. As a result, all samples receive similar exposure despite their different optimization needs, leading to redundant updates for some samples while leaving others under-optimized. To address this problem, we propose SDO (Structure-Aware Data Organization), a plug-and-play data organization framework with an exposure-driven feedback mechanism that organizes mini-batch composition and sample exposure according to representation-space structure. SDO operates epoch by epoch on frozen external embeddings, avoiding model warm-up training overhead: within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal; across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling records per-sample participation and reduces the sampling probability of over-exposed samples to preserve long-term coverage. Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence, with the largest gains observed in the early-to-mid phase, producing more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.

AI.tldr: SDO (Structure-Aware Data Organization) is a plug-and-play framework that organizes mini-batch composition and sample exposure in language model post-training using representation-space structure and an exposure-driven feedback mechanism, improving convergence across SFT, DPO, and GRPO.
AI.motivation: Existing post-training efficiency improvements focus on sample selection or training schedules, but data organization is treated as a static preprocessing step. Fixed embedding-based partitions cannot adapt to evolving sample exposure during optimization, causing redundant updates for some samples and under-optimization for others.
AI.method: SDO operates epoch by epoch on frozen external embeddings. Within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal. Across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling records per-sample participation and reduces sampling probability of over-exposed samples to preserve long-term coverage.
AI.result: Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence with the largest gains in the early-to-mid training phase, producing more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.
AI.conclusion: SDO addresses the static data organization limitation in LLM post-training by dynamically adapting sample exposure based on representation-space structure, achieving faster convergence and more balanced performance without permanently discarding any training samples.

title: VideoCoCo: Code-as-CoT for Physically-Consistent Video Generation via an Agentic Dual-Engine System
summary: Text-to-video models have achieved remarkable visual quality, yet they still struggle to generate physically consistent dynamics because the temporal evolution of a scene must be inferred implicitly from a highly compressed text prompt. Existing chain-of-thought approaches introduce intermediate plans or visual states, but these representations are typically non-executable or temporally sparse, limiting their ability to instantiate and control the complete spatiotemporal process. To address this limitation, we introduce VideoCoCo, an agentic dual-engine framework in which executable Blender code serves as a process-level chain of thought. Given a text prompt, a coding agent synthesizes a Blender program that explicitly specifies the scene and its temporal evolution. The executable simulation engine runs the program to produce a deterministic spatiotemporal draft, which is subsequently transformed into a photorealistic video by a generative video engine through draft-conditioned editing. This decomposition separates process-level reasoning from high-fidelity visual realization. To adapt the video editor to simulated drafts, we construct VideoCoCo-3K, a curated dataset of draft-instruction-target triplets. VideoCoCo improves the OmniWeaving baseline from 0.475 to 0.558 on PhyGenBench and from 52.18 to 77.88 on VBench-2.0, achieving the best average score on both benchmarks. These results demonstrate that executable code provides an effective, controllable, and inspectable intermediate representation for physically consistent video generation.

AI.tldr: VideoCoCo is an agentic dual-engine framework that uses executable Blender code as a process-level chain of thought for text-to-video generation. A coding agent synthesizes Blender programs that explicitly define scene and temporal evolution, which are then rendered as deterministic spatiotemporal drafts and transformed into photorealistic videos via draft-conditioned editing, achieving substantial improvements on PhyGenBench and VBench-2.0.
AI.motivation: Text-to-video models struggle to generate physically consistent dynamics because temporal scene evolution must be inferred implicitly from compressed text prompts. Existing chain-of-thought approaches provide intermediate plans or visual states that are either non-executable or temporally sparse, limiting their ability to instantiate and control the complete spatiotemporal process.
AI.method: VideoCoCo employs a dual-engine architecture: (1) a coding agent synthesizes executable Blender code from text prompts that explicitly specifies the scene and its temporal evolution (process-level chain of thought), (2) an executable simulation engine runs the Blender program to produce a deterministic spatiotemporal draft, and (3) a generative video engine transforms the draft into photorealistic video via draft-conditioned editing. The decomposition separates process-level reasoning from high-fidelity visual realization. A curated dataset, VideoCoCo-3K, provides draft-instruction-target triplets to adapt the video editor to simulated drafts.
AI.result: VideoCoCo improves the OmniWeaving baseline from 0.475 to 0.558 on PhyGenBench and from 52.18 to 77.88 on VBench-2.0, achieving the best average score on both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Executable code provides an effective, controllable, and inspectable intermediate representation for physically consistent video generation, demonstrating that explicit process-level reasoning via executable simulations improves physical consistency over implicit text-to-video generation.

title: PAUSE: A User-Centric Benchmark for Personal AI Assistants in Unified Service Environments
summary: Personal AI assistants are increasingly deployed as task-oriented, tool-augmented agents that operate within unified service environments to support everyday user activities. In realistic settings, such assistants must reason over persistent user state, respect user-specific configurations and permissions, and sustain long-horizon, constraint-aware interactions across multiple services. Existing benchmarks, however, often fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic service settings. We introduce PAUSE, a user-centric benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments. PAUSE captures core challenges of real-world assistant deployment by requiring agents to coordinate actions across heterogeneous user-owned resources while maintaining consistency with environment state, authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions. The benchmark incorporates explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation, enabling evaluation beyond static tool execution. To support principled and reproducible evaluation, PAUSE adopts a multi-regime evaluation framework aligned with task characteristics. Open-ended service management tasks are assessed using semantic and trajectory-level behavioral metrics, while constraint-intensive tasks admit deterministic, state-based verification. Benchmark results show that even state-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness, revealing consistent and interpretable failure patterns. Finally, we present a user-centric synthesis pipeline that enables scalable generation of coherent service environments, user configurations, and reliably annotated tasks, supporting benchmark extensibility and future research.

AI.tldr: PAUSE is a user-centric benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments, revealing that even state-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic service settings where assistants must reason over persistent user state, respect user-specific configurations and permissions, and sustain long-horizon constraint-aware interactions.
AI.method: PAUSE introduces a benchmark capturing core challenges of real-world assistant deployment via: (1) coordination across heterogeneous user-owned resources with consistency to environment state and authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions; (2) explicit user-agent interaction through realistic user simulation; (3) a multi-regime evaluation framework where open-ended service management tasks use semantic and trajectory-level behavioral metrics while constraint-intensive tasks use deterministic state-based verification; (4) a user-centric synthesis pipeline for scalable generation of coherent service environments, user configurations, and reliably annotated tasks.
AI.result: State-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness, showing consistent and interpretable failure patterns.
AI.conclusion: PAUSE provides a principled, reproducible, and extensible benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in realistic stateful service environments, with a scalable synthesis pipeline supporting future expansion and research.

title: From Backlog Items to Security Guidance: Towards Continuous Security Compliance
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026), Industry Showcase track
summary: Continuous software engineering in regulated domains requires engineering teams to address security throughout the development lifecycle. Yet making security requirements explicit in backlog items is still problematic. Engineers must instead infer security relevance of backlog items from brief, free-form descriptions and often lack timely guidance on applicable requirements. We present an NLP-based backlog enrichment system that detects security-relevant backlog items and links them to relevant security requirements. The approach combines a security-relevance classifier with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline over security requirements documents. The approach was developed and evaluated in the context of a large enterprise in highly regulated domains. We present three contributions. First, we release a dataset of 288 backlog items labeled for security relevance by nine security practitioners, with substantial agreement (Fleiss' $κ=0.787$). Second, a recall-oriented classifier achieving $F2=0.774$ in-distribution and mean zero-shot G-measure $\approx 0.65$ across five established benchmarks, matching or outperforming most published classical-ML and open-source GPT baselines. Third, we preliminarily evaluated a four-stage security requirements document-grounded RAG pipeline with two practitioners on industrial backlogs using company-internal security policies and CIS Benchmarks. Of the retrieved 24 clauses, 12 were rated at least 4/5 for relevance. Our findings provide first indicators that NLP-based product backlog enrichment can support engineers in identifying security requirements early in the development process. With this work we aim to facilitate continuous security compliance through proactive introduction of security requirements in continuous software engineering.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an NLP-based backlog enrichment system that detects security-relevant product backlog items and links them to relevant security requirements via a security-relevance classifier combined with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline.
