Evaluated in a large enterprise in regulated domains, the work contributes a labeled dataset of 288 backlog items (Fleiss' κ=0.787), a recall-oriented classifier (F2=0.774 in-distribution, ~0.65 zero-shot G-measure), and a preliminary four-stage RAG pipeline evaluation showing 12 of 24 retrieved clauses rated ≥4/5 for relevance.
AI.motivation: In continuous software engineering within regulated domains, security requirements are rarely made explicit in backlog items. Engineers must infer security relevance from brief, free-form descriptions without timely guidance on applicable requirements, creating a gap between development and security compliance.
AI.method: The system combines (1) a security-relevance classifier trained on a newly released dataset of 288 backlog items labeled by nine security practitioners, and (2) a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline over security requirements documents (company-internal security policies and CIS Benchmarks) with a four-stage grounding approach. The classifier was evaluated in-distribution and in zero-shot settings across five benchmarks.
AI.result: The classifier achieved F2=0.774 in-distribution and mean zero-shot G-measure ≈0.65 across five benchmarks, matching or outperforming most published classical-ML and open-source GPT baselines. The RAG pipeline retrieved 24 clauses, of which 12 were rated at least 4/5 for relevance by two practitioners.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide first indicators that NLP-based product backlog enrichment can support engineers in identifying security requirements early in the development lifecycle, facilitating continuous security compliance through proactive introduction of security requirements in continuous software engineering.

title: Rethinking EEG-Based Disease Diagnosis: Decoupling Instance Representation Learning from Subject-Level Supervision
summary: EEG-based disease diagnosis requires one prediction per subject, yet common pipelines segment recordings into short instances, inherit the subject label for every instance, and train instance-level classifiers. This assumes that all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence. Multiple instance learning (MIL) avoids inherited labels by treating each subject as a bag. However, EEG datasets contain far fewer subjects than instances, which can limit the quality of the representations learned by end-to-end MIL. We propose BridgeMIL, a two-stage framework that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags. Variance and covariance regularization prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject predictions, and limits representation drift through feature retention. Across three EEG disease datasets and five representative backbones, BridgeMIL attains the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings and an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater performance sensitivity to subject scarcity than to instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved separation between diagnostic classes. Together, these findings underscore the importance of aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances.

AI.tldr: BridgeMIL is a two-stage multiple instance learning framework for EEG-based disease diagnosis that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains an encoder using self-supervised alignment of temporally nearby windows and within-subject sub-bags with variance/covariance regularization, and Stage 2 transfers it to an attention-based MIL aggregator with subject-level supervision and representation drift control. It achieves 76.57% mean accuracy across three EEG datasets and five backbones, surpassing the strongest baseline by 4.28 percentage points.
AI.motivation: EEG-based disease diagnosis needs one prediction per subject, but standard pipelines segment recordings into instances with inherited subject labels, wrongly assuming all instances carry equally reliable diagnostic evidence. While MIL avoids inherited labels by treating subjects as bags, EEG datasets have far fewer subjects than instances, limiting representation quality in end-to-end MIL.
AI.method: BridgeMIL uses a two-stage framework: (1) Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags, using variance and covariance regularization to prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs; (2) Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject predictions, and limits representation drift through feature retention.
AI.result: BridgeMIL attains the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings across three EEG disease datasets and five backbones, with an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Analyses reveal substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater sensitivity to subject scarcity than instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved class separation.
AI.conclusion: The findings underscore the importance of aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances.

title: IGME: Efficient Chained Method Ensemble for Transferable Semantic Segmentation Attacks
summary: Semantic segmentation models are vulnerable to transferable adversarial perturbations, yet evaluating transfer attacks on dense prediction models can be computationally expensive. Existing ensemble attacks often rely on multiple surrogate models, increasing the computation cost, even harder for segmentation. This paper studies an efficient single-source alternative for transferable attacks on semantic segmentation. We formulate transferable attack composition as a chained computation over differentiable attack components, allowing the expensive source-model gradient computation to be shared. To reduce the update instability introduced by chained composition, we further use an integrated-gradient-style path-averaged direction as an empirical stabilization heuristic. Experiments on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes evaluate the resulting transferability efficiency trade-off across CNN- and transformer-based segmentation models. IGME achieves competitive transferability compared with single-source baselines and favorable runtime compared with model-ensemble attacks, while requiring access to only one source model.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes IGME, a single-source efficient transferable adversarial attack for semantic segmentation. It formulates transferable attack composition as chained computation over differentiable attack components with shared gradient computation, and uses integrated-gradient-style path-averaged direction to stabilize updates. Experiments on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes show competitive transferability versus single-source baselines and favorable runtime versus ensemble attacks, requiring only one source model.
AI.motivation: Evaluating transfer attacks on dense prediction (semantic segmentation) models is computationally expensive. Existing ensemble attacks require multiple surrogate models, further increasing computation cost. The paper aims to study an efficient single-source alternative for transferable attacks on semantic segmentation.
AI.method: The method formulates transferable attack composition as chained computation over differentiable attack components, allowing the expensive source-model gradient computation to be shared across components. To reduce update instability from chaining, an integrated-gradient-style path-averaged direction is used as an empirical stabilization heuristic. The approach (IGME) requires only one source model.
AI.result: Experiments on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes show IGME achieves competitive transferability compared with single-source baselines and favorable runtime compared with model-ensemble attacks, while requiring access to only one source model.
AI.conclusion: A single-source, efficient transferable attack for semantic segmentation can achieve competitive transferability with reduced computational cost compared to ensemble methods, using chained gradient sharing and path-averaged stabilization.

title: SkillMentor: LLM Agent Self-Evolution via Learning Blind-Spot Diagnosis
summary: Agent self-evolution has primarily focused on learning how to act, while overlooking an equally important capability: learning to discover what an agent does not know. Existing approaches typically assume that failure discovery is given, focusing on how to repair failures once they are identified. We ask whether blind-spot diagnosis itself can be learned. We thus study diagnosis as an agent capability separate from execution, and exclude two alternative sources of progress: executor adaptation and human supervision. Under these constraints, performance cannot improve through executor updates or annotated examples, forcing all improvements to originate from the learned diagnostic capability. We propose SkillMentor, which trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurrent failure modes, and curate them into reusable corrective skills. Across AppWorld and BFCLv3, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%. These results suggest that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability, enabling self-evolution without updating executor weights or relying on human-curated data.

AI.tldr: SkillMentor trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to diagnose an agent's blind spots, generating diagnostic tasks, identifying recurrent failure modes, and curating corrective skills—improving executor performance by 44.2% on average across AppWorld and BFCLv3 without updating executor weights or using human supervision.
AI.motivation: Existing agent self-evolution research focuses on learning how to act (execution) but overlooks learning how to discover what the agent does not know (diagnosis). Most approaches assume failure discovery is given and focus only on repairing identified failures. This paper asks whether blind-spot diagnosis itself can be learned as a separate capability, independent of executor adaptation or human annotated examples.
AI.method: The authors propose SkillMentor, which trains a Mentor policy using reinforcement learning to (1) generate diagnostic tasks that probe the executor agent, (2) identify recurrent failure modes from execution traces, and (3) curate these failures into reusable corrective skills. The experimental setup deliberately excludes executor updates and human supervision so that all performance gains must originate from the learned diagnostic capability.
AI.result: Across AppWorld and BFCLv3 benchmarks, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%, demonstrating that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable and effective capability for agent self-evolution.
AI.conclusion: Blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability in itself, enabling agent self-evolution through learned diagnostics alone—without modifying executor weights or relying on human-curated annotations.

title: SWE-NFI: Studying and Benchmarking Coding Agents for Non-Functional Improvements
summary:
Although coding agents have achieved impressive performance on correctness-oriented benchmarks, their ability to make behavior-preserving non-functional improvements (NFIs) remains underexplored. In real-world software development, developers continuously improve software quality without changing observable behavior, yet existing benchmarks primarily evaluate functional correctness and provide limited support for assessing these non-functional improvements.
  In this paper, we present SWE-NFI, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on NFIs beyond functional correctness. Our benchmark contains 188 tasks constructed from real merged pull requests in open-source Python projects. We operationalize developer-oriented NFIs into 92 executable rules and develop a comprehensive evaluation suite that combines functional correctness testing with rule-based NFI evaluation.
  We evaluate state-of-the-art commercial and open-source coding agents. Although the best-performing agent achieves a 70.0\% functional correctness rate, all evaluated agents generally fall short of human developers in overall NFI capability. The gap is particularly evident for structural code improvements, where agents' NFI scores range from 0.0 to 1.3, compared with 1.5 for the human reference. Our benchmark and findings provide a reproducible foundation for evaluating and advancing coding agents beyond functional correctness.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SWE-NFI, a benchmark with 188 tasks derived from real merged pull requests in open-source Python projects, for evaluating coding agents on non-functional improvements (NFIs). It operationalizes 92 executable rules and uses a combined evaluation suite of functional correctness testing and rule-based NFI assessment. While the best coding agent achieves 70.0% functional correctness, all agents fall short of human developers on NFIs, especially on structural code improvements where agents score 0.0–1.3 versus 1.5 for humans.
AI.motivation: Existing coding agent benchmarks primarily focus on functional correctness and do not adequately assess non-functional improvements such as code quality, maintainability, and structural enhancements, despite these being critical in real-world software development.
AI.method: The authors construct SWE-NFI, a benchmark of 188 NFI tasks from real merged pull requests in open-source Python projects. They operationalize developer-oriented NFIs into 92 executable rules and develop an evaluation suite that combines functional correctness testing with rule-based NFI evaluation.
AI.result: The best-performing coding agent achieves 70.0% functional correctness but all evaluated commercial and open-source agents underperform human developers on overall NFI capability. For structural code improvements, agents' NFI scores range from 0.0 to 1.3, compared to 1.5 for the human reference.
AI.conclusion: SWE-NFI provides a reproducible foundation for evaluating and advancing coding agents beyond functional correctness, revealing a significant gap between current agents and human developers in performing behavior-preserving non-functional improvements.

title: Flat Score, Amplified Failures: How the Error Budget Masks Damage in Quantized LLM Agents
summary: Post-training quantization to 4-bit weights is widely reported to be nearly lossless. We test this claim for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, where it now matters most. On $τ^2$-bench, across two open-weight model families in dense and MoE variants and two domains (eight cells, 456 episodes each, at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weights), quantization indeed looks free on the standard metric. No cell shows a score change that survives multiple-comparison correction, and in the cell that carries the largest process damage, equivalence testing bounds the change within $\pm$7.5 points. The process tells a different story. Quantization amplifies the failure the model already exhibits at full precision (tool-name hallucination in telecom, with the same directional trend in retail entity errors) by up to 2.5$\times$ in volume (+17.6 points per task), while creating essentially no new failures. The failure set is the same at every precision (rank correlation $\geq$ 0.94, 0.18% novel events). The score stays flat because the benchmark's ten-error budget absorbs the extra failures. Shrinking the budget to two errors re-exposes a score gap of 17 points, and it does so only in the one cell where quantization added error volume, exactly as the masking account predicts. A targeted error-repair prompt, run for five telecom models at every precision, removes the damage exactly and only where it lives. Both diagnostics, the per-channel error rate and success under a shrinking budget, come from logs benchmarks already collect; we suggest reporting them alongside task reward.

AI.tldr: 4-bit post-training quantization appears nearly lossless on standard metrics for multi-turn tool-calling agents, but this is an artifact of the benchmark's ten-error budget masking amplified failure volumes (up to 2.5x). Shrinking the budget to two errors re-exposes a 17-point score gap, and a targeted repair prompt removes the damage exactly where it lives. The paper proposes reporting per-channel error rates and success under shrinking budgets alongside task reward.
AI.motivation: 4-bit quantization is widely claimed to be nearly lossless, but existing claims may be misleading for multi-turn tool-calling agents where subtle behavioral changes can have outsized consequences. The authors test this claim rigorously on τ²-bench to uncover whether standard metrics hide real degradation in agentic task performance.
AI.method: The study evaluates two open-weight model families (dense and MoE variants) across two domains on τ²-bench, totaling eight cells with 456 episodes each, at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weight precisions. They use standard score metrics, multiple-comparison correction, equivalence testing, rank correlation of failure sets, error-budget manipulation (shrinking from ten to two errors), and a targeted error-repair prompt as a diagnostic intervention across five telecom models.
AI.result: On the standard metric, no cell shows a score change surviving multiple-comparison correction; equivalence testing bounds the largest process damage within ±7.5 points. However, quantization amplifies pre-existing failures (tool-name hallucination in telecom and retail entity errors) by up to 2.5x in volume (+17.6 points per task) while creating essentially no new failure types. The failure set is identical across precisions (rank correlation ≥0.94, only 0.18% novel events). The flat score is explained by the ten-error budget absorbing extra failures; shrinking to two errors re-exposes a 17-point gap only in the cell with added error volume. A targeted repair prompt removes damage exactly and only where it lives.
AI.conclusion: Standard task reward metrics can mask meaningful degradation from quantization in agentic systems; quantization amplifies existing failure modes rather than creating new ones. Benchmarks should additionally report per-channel error rates and success under shrinking error budgets, both derivable from logs already collected, to reveal masked damage.

title: ProgFormer: Hierarchical Voxel Diffusion Transformer for Longitudinal Brain MRI Prediction
summary: Predicting future structural MRI of a brain is challenging because longitudinal changes are often subtle and confined to specific anatomical regions, while most subject-specific brain structure remains stable over time. An effective model should therefore preserve global brain structural consistency while remaining sensitive to fine-grained disease progression. Existing latent-space-based methods improve computational efficiency, but suffer from information loss during their compression-reconstruction procedure. In contrast, direct voxel-space methods avoid latent reconstruction but commonly use a unified prediction pathway to model brain structure and progression-related changes. Subtle local changes may therefore be overshadowed by the dominant stable brain structure. To address these challenges, we propose ProgFormer, a hierarchical voxel-space Diffusion Transformer for longitudinal brain MRI prediction. ProgFormer uses a coarse pathway to perform the primary volumetric prediction from 3D patch tokens. This pathway models overall brain structure and longitudinal context. The fine pathway then uses the coarse representations as spatio-temporal grounding for voxel-level refinement within individual patches. The two pathways jointly estimate a velocity field directly in voxel space through conditional flow matching, enabling end-to-end prediction without a separately learned image autoencoder. The predicted future scan is then generated from Gaussian noise by integrating the estimated velocity field over a sequence of Euler steps. Extensive experimental results on three widely used benchmarks, ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS, under both pairwise and trajectory settings demonstrate favourable performance compared against several state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: ProgFormer is a hierarchical voxel-space Diffusion Transformer for longitudinal brain MRI prediction that uses a coarse pathway for overall brain structure modeling and a fine pathway for voxel-level refinement, jointly estimating a velocity field via conditional flow matching for end-to-end prediction without a separate image autoencoder.
AI.motivation: Existing latent-space methods suffer from information loss during compression-reconstruction, while direct voxel-space methods use a unified prediction pathway where subtle local disease-related changes are overshadowed by dominant stable brain structure. A model must preserve global structural consistency while remaining sensitive to fine-grained disease progression.
AI.method: ProgFormer is a hierarchical voxel-space Diffusion Transformer with two pathways: (1) a coarse pathway performs primary volumetric prediction from 3D patch tokens, modeling overall brain structure and longitudinal context; (2) a fine pathway uses coarse representations as spatio-temporal grounding for voxel-level refinement within patches. The two pathways jointly estimate a velocity field in voxel space through conditional flow matching, and future scans are generated from Gaussian noise by integrating the velocity field over Euler steps.
AI.result: Experiments on three benchmarks (ADNI, AIBL, OASIS) under both pairwise and trajectory settings demonstrate favorable performance compared to several state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The coarse-to-fine hierarchical design in voxel space effectively addresses the trade-off between preserving global brain structure and capturing subtle longitudinal changes, achieving state-of-the-art performance without reliance on latent-space compression.

title: Beyond the Bidirectional Promise: Re-evaluating the Robustness of Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive (AR) generation by enabling bidirectional context and iterative refinement. However, their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored. To address this, we systematically evaluate DLM robustness and calibration against AR baselines, using two parameter-matched pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. This paired design effectively isolates architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors. We find a nuanced robustness profile: while highly stochastic DLM loss landscapes naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes, they provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise, proving that everyday robustness is weight-dependent rather than inherently architectural. Furthermore, DLMs exhibit systematic overconfidence, presenting a practical deployment hazard. Most crucially, mechanistic probing reveals that all models perfectly encode input corruption, isolating behavioral fragility entirely to a decoder routing failure. Consistent with this diagnosis, we show that surface-level prompt patching fails to improve over noisy baselines. Ultimately, DLM robustness cannot be patched on; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates the robustness and calibration of Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) versus autoregressive (AR) baselines using two parameter-matched model pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B, Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B), testing across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. Findings show DLMs resist gradient-based attacks via stochastic loss landscapes but remain vulnerable to natural noise, exhibit systematic overconfidence, and reveal that behavioral fragility stems from decoder routing failure despite perfect input encoding—concluding that DLM robustness must be integrated into the iterative decoding loop rather than patched at the surface.
AI.motivation: While Diffusion Language Models offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation via bidirectional context and iterative refinement, their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored, motivating a systematic evaluation of their robustness and calibration.
AI.method: The study uses two parameter-matched model pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) to isolate architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors, and evaluates them across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses.
AI.result: DLMs exhibit naturally high stochastic loss landscapes that resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes but provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise, indicating everyday robustness is weight-dependent rather than architectural. DLMs also show systematic overconfidence, and mechanistic probing reveals all models perfectly encode input corruption, isolating behavioral fragility to a decoder routing failure, with surface-level prompt patching failing to improve over noisy baselines.
AI.conclusion: DLM robustness cannot be achieved through surface-level patching; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop itself.

title: LimICE: Integrating LLM into ICE Framework for Efficient Loop Invariant Inference
summary: Loop invariant synthesis is a fundamental problem in program verification, yet the inherent undecidability makes it highly challenging. Recent studies have increasingly employed various machine learning techniques to generate loop invariants. However, most of these methods adopt a monolithic approach. Due to the inability to strictly constrain the learning process, learning-based methods struggle to simultaneously consider all necessary conditions and generate complete invariants when tackling complex problems. In fact, a loop invariant is often an ordered sequence of lemmas, rather than a single invariant formula. This motivates us to propose Incremental ICE, a novel learning framework for incremental synthesis. Our framework integrates the incremental philosophy of IC3 into the general invariant learning framework ICE. By defining a lemma-specific learning objective and introducing a counterexample filtering mechanism, we can achieve sound incremental learning. Under this framework, we instantiate a loop invariant synthesis tool, LimICE, which leverages LLMs to generate the ordered sequence of lemmas and incorporates ICE-DT as a fallback mechanism to complement the lemma sequence. Experiments on 367 linear benchmarks and 50 nonlinear benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. LimICE solves 349 (out of 367) linear problems on an average of 15.2 seconds and 47 (out of 50) nonlinear problems on an average of 8.8 seconds. Compared to the state-of-the-art LLM-based baseline, our approach solves 12-24% more instances while running 36-63% faster across linear and nonlinear benchmarks. LimICE also consistently outperforms strong non-LLM baselines and solves at least 86 and 27 additional instances on the linear and nonlinear benchmarks, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Incremental ICE, a novel learning framework for incremental loop invariant synthesis that integrates the IC3 incremental philosophy into the ICE framework. It defines lemma-specific learning objectives and a counterexample filtering mechanism for sound incremental learning, instantiated as the tool LimICE which uses LLMs to generate ordered sequences of lemmas with ICE-DT as a fallback. Experiments on 367 linear and 50 nonlinear benchmarks show LimICE solves 349 and 47 instances respectively, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by 12-24% more solved instances while running 36-63% faster.
AI.motivation: Learning-based loop invariant synthesis methods typically adopt a monolithic approach and struggle to simultaneously consider all necessary conditions due to the inability to strictly constrain the learning process. However, a loop invariant is often an ordered sequence of lemmas rather than a single formula, motivating the need for an incremental synthesis framework.
AI.method: The framework integrates IC3's incremental philosophy into the ICE invariant learning framework. It defines a lemma-specific learning objective and introduces a counterexample filtering mechanism to achieve sound incremental learning. The instantiated tool, LimICE, leverages LLMs to generate ordered lemma sequences and incorporates ICE-DT as a fallback mechanism to complement the lemma sequence.
AI.result: On 367 linear benchmarks, LimICE solves 349 instances in an average of 15.2 seconds; on 50 nonlinear benchmarks, it solves 47 instances in an average of 8.8 seconds. It solves 12-24% more instances than the state-of-the-art LLM-based baseline while running 36-63% faster, and outperforms non-LLM baselines by solving at least 86 and 27 additional instances on linear and nonlinear benchmarks respectively.
AI.conclusion: The Incremental ICE framework effectively addresses the limitations of monolithic learning-based invariant synthesis by decomposing invariants into ordered lemma sequences generated incrementally, demonstrating clear performance advantages over both LLM-based and non-LLM baselines across linear and nonlinear benchmarks.

title: The Kinetics of Training: A Driven-Nucleation Rate Law for Emergence, Plasticity Loss, and Circuit Control in Language Models
summary:
A capability appears in a language model when the last parts of its circuit align in one stochastic attempt, and getting all but one right is worth nothing. We show this no-partial-credit joint alignment is the rate-limiting step of capability formation. Two fingerprints: in a shortcut-free apparatus a five-part circuit missing three waits as long as a three-part circuit missing three (1.19-1.37), so the wait counts missing parts, not size; and on Pythia across seven capabilities and three scales, ablating one part leaves a median 17% of the capability in 32 of 32 discriminating cells, where partial credit predicts 50-83% (p = 2e-10), while a random non-part head leaves 100%.
  One rare event whose barrier grows with missing parts yields a rate equation -- sites x attempts x drive x exp(-beta*K), minus destruction -- read three ways, each preregistered with frozen constants. Forward: a capability flat at baseline ignites at a step of our choosing once the mix passes a concentration floor (10/10 above, 0/12 below), and while still flat its arrival is datable from its precursor to 5% median error on six held-out models. Backward: the delay to learn a withheld capability grows with waiting until, past a critical step, it never ignites -- yet validation loss falls smoothly throughout, so standard monitors are blind to it. We locate the damage (heads commit to the base data) and isolate the cure: re-initializing only the query-key slices restores learnability (6/6) while the value slices do nothing (0/6). We prove the mechanism in a controlled gated-attention model: occupation forces a deadline whose consequences need no mixing assumption. Completed: SGD's noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test, so we install one and anneal, melt and pin circuits on schedule. Scope: conjunction circuits in transformers to 1.4B.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies that a capability forms in a language model only when all parts of its circuit align successfully in one stochastic attempt — no partial credit is given for getting most parts right. This joint alignment is the rate-limiting step. The authors present two empirical fingerprints, a rate equation for capability formation, controlled intervention experiments showing capabilities can be ignited, delayed, or destroyed by adding/removing missing parts, evidence that standard validation loss is blind to capability loss, and a mechanistic account supported by a gated-attention model and targeted re-initialization of query-key (but not value) slices.
AI.motivation: To explain why capabilities appear abruptly in language models through a joint-alignment mechanism rather than gradual partial formation, and to provide a predictive, controllable account of capability formation and loss that standard monitors (e.g., validation loss) fail to detect.
AI.method: Combines two empirical fingerprints (shortcut-free five-part vs three-part circuits missing three parts; ablating one circuit part across seven capabilities/three Pythia scales), a rate equation (sites x attempts x drive x exp(-beta*K) minus destruction) read in forward and backward directions with preregistered frozen constants, a gated-attention controlled model to prove the mechanism involving occupation-driven deadlines, a fluctuation-dissipation test on SGD's noise with an installed anneal/melt/pin schedule, and targeted re-initialization experiments isolating query-key vs value slice effects.
AI.result: The wait time for capability formation counts the number of missing parts, not circuit size. Ablating one part leaves a median 17% of the capability (vs 50-83% predicted by partial credit, p=2e-10) while random non-part heads leave 100%. The rate equation predicts ignition at a chosen step once a concentration floor is crossed (10/10 above, 0/12 below) and forward-dates arrival from precursors to 5% median error on six held-out models. Backward delay grows until a critical step where the capability never ignites while validation loss falls smoothly throughout. Re-initializing query-key slices restores learnability (6/6); value slices do not (0/6). SGD noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test, so a corrective schedule is installed.
AI.conclusion: Capability formation is governed by a joint no-partial-credit alignment that is the rate-limiting step, formalized by a rate equation whose predictions are confirmed across forward and backward directions. Capability loss is invisible to validation loss but traceable to heads committing to base data, and curable by re-initializing only query-key slices. The mechanism is proven in a controlled gated-attention model, with scope over conjunction circuits in transformers up to 1.4B parameters.

title: Drawing-Recode: Annotation Grounding for Parametric CAD Code Generation from Raster 2D CAD Drawings
summary: Recovering Parametric CAD sequences from raster-format 2D Computer-Aided Design (CAD) drawings accumulated prior to digital transformation is important for part reproduction and manufacturing process automation. However, existing studies either process only vector drawings or are limited to specific domains, and fail to explicitly connect dimensional annotations to geometric information, limiting their use of dimensional information for 3D Parametric CAD sequences recovery. We propose Drawing-Recode, a framework that generates Parametric CAD sequences as CAD code from raster 2D CAD drawings. Drawing-Recode extracts geometric features via an image encoder and recognizes annotations through a separate text recognition module, then explicitly grounds annotations to geometric information using cross-attention and our proposed Annotation Grounding Loss (AGL). The resulting features are fed into a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate CAD code in the Structured Parametric CAD Code (SPCC) format. Experiments show that Drawing-Recode outperforms existing baselines and remains robust on scanned drawings resembling industrial conditions. We expect Drawing-Recode contributes to digitizing raster 2D CAD drawings in industrial settings and to part reproduction and manufacturing automation.

AI.tldr: Drawing-Recode is a framework that converts raster-format 2D CAD drawings into parametric CAD sequences (as code) by extracting geometric features via an image encoder, recognizing dimensional annotations via a text recognition module, and explicitly grounding annotations to geometry using cross-attention and a proposed Annotation Grounding Loss (AGL), then feeding these features into an LLM to generate CAD code in the Structured Parametric CAD Code (SPCC) format.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for recovering parametric CAD sequences either handle only vector drawings or are restricted to specific domains, and critically fail to explicitly connect dimensional annotations to geometric information, limiting the use of dimensional information for 3D parametric CAD recovery from raster drawings.
AI.method: Drawing-Recode uses an image encoder to extract geometric features, a separate text recognition module for annotation recognition, and cross-attention plus a novel Annotation Grounding Loss (AGL) to explicitly ground annotations to geometric information. These combined features are fed into an LLM to generate parametric CAD sequences as code in the SPCC format.
AI.result: Drawing-Recode outperforms existing baselines and remains robust on scanned drawings that resemble industrial conditions.
AI.conclusion: Drawing-Recode is expected to contribute to digitizing raster 2D CAD drawings in industrial settings, facilitating part reproduction and manufacturing automation.

title: Bridging Inference-Time Scaling and Episodic Memory with Action-Centric Graphs
summary: Recent advancements in inference-time scaling have significantly unlocked the complex reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models~(LLMs). However, for agents, these approaches suffer from a critical inefficiency, operating in a stateless manner and engaging in redundant search processes. Existing memory mechanisms largely rely on the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, leading to prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, \textit{GAMER}~(Graph-based Action-centric Memory with Episodic Reasoning), that bridges the gap between inference scaling and episodic memory. Our approach models historical reasoning as a dynamic \textit{Action-Centric Graph}. By decoupling the memory mechanism from LLMs, our method can save token/money usage by providing less memory context than memory mechanism baselines. To extract knowledge from the graph effectively, we use a dual-stream Temporal Difference learning mechanism to estimate the positive~(suggestion) and negative~(avoidance) value of action nodes based on past successes and failures. During the inference phase, this learned value function optimizes decision-making bi-directionally, so that positive values provide action suggestions, while negative values indicate high-risk actions. By performing efficient searches on the graph, our method significantly improves the efficiency of inference scaling. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that \textit{GAMER} achieves superior performance by \textbf{20.81\%/6.17\%} for success/progress rate compared to vanilla baselines.

AI.tldr: GAMER is a novel framework that bridges inference-time scaling and episodic memory for LLM agents by modeling historical reasoning as a dynamic Action-Centric Graph, decoupling memory from the LLM to save costs, and using dual-stream Temporal Difference learning to estimate positive and negative action values for bi-directional decision-making during inference.
AI.motivation: Inference-time scaling approaches for LLM agents suffer from critical inefficiency because they operate in a stateless manner and engage in redundant search processes. Existing memory mechanisms heavily rely on LLM reasoning capabilities, leading to prohibitive computational costs.
AI.method: GAMER models historical reasoning as a dynamic Action-Centric Graph and decouples the memory mechanism from the LLM. It uses a dual-stream Temporal Difference learning mechanism to estimate both positive (suggestion) and negative (avoidance) values of action nodes based on past successes and failures. During inference, the learned value function optimizes decision-making bi-directionally: positive values provide action suggestions while negative values indicate high-risk actions, enabled by efficient graph searches.
AI.result: GAMER achieves superior performance on multiple benchmarks with 20.81% improvement in success rate and 6.17% improvement in progress rate compared to vanilla baselines, while also saving token/money usage by providing less memory context than memory mechanism baselines.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling memory from the LLM and leveraging an action-centric episodic graph with learned value functions, GAMER significantly improves the efficiency of inference scaling for LLM agents, demonstrating that structured memory combined with TD learning can outperform both stateless scaling approaches and memory mechanisms that rely on LLM reasoning.

title: Not as Sweet by Another Name: An Empirical Study of Format Robustness in LLM Document Workflows
comment: 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: LLM-driven software systems are rapidly evolving from plain-text conversations to document-centric end-to-end workflows, where the same semantic content can be delivered in diverse document formats (e.g., CSV) through file upload interfaces. Yet existing testing work focuses on the robustness and reliability of models and systems whose input is a single prompt string, leaving a critical question unanswered: Can these document workflows maintain robust behaviors when the same content arrives in a different document format? To fill the gap, in this paper, we propose a format-aware metamorphic testing framework with three metamorphic relations to comprehensively evaluate the format robustness of end-to-end LLM document workflows. Based on this framework, we conduct a large-scale empirical study spanning four representative LLM workflows, four real-world tasks, and four document formats, comprising a total of 48,000 workflow executions. Our findings reveal that format variation poses a systematic and serious threat. Merely switching formats can cause accuracy to drop by up to 53.63% and trigger decision drifts in over 41% of instances. We further design lightweight mitigation strategies from the users' perspective that recover up to 44.21% of format-induced decision drift without model retraining. Our study demonstrates that document format is not a neutral wrapper but a critical factor affecting the reliability of LLM software systems, calling for corresponding testing and safeguards in the deployment in real-world high-stakes scenarios.

AI.tldr: Proposes a format-aware metamorphic testing framework to evaluate the robustness of end-to-end LLM document workflows across different document formats (e.g., CSV), finding that format variation causes accuracy drops up to 53.63% and decision drifts in over 41% of instances, with lightweight user-side mitigations recovering up to 44.21% of induced drift.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven systems are shifting from single-prompt conversations to document-centric end-to-end workflows where semantic content can arrive in diverse formats (e.g., CSV) via file upload. Existing testing focuses on prompt-string robustness, leaving the question of whether document workflows maintain robust behavior when the same content arrives in a different format unanswered.
AI.method: Introduces a format-aware metamorphic testing framework with three metamorphic relations. Conducts a large-scale empirical study spanning four LLM workflows, four real-world tasks, four document formats, and 48,000 total workflow executions. Also proposes lightweight user-perspective mitigation strategies without model retraining.
AI.result: Format variation systematically threatens LLM document workflows: merely switching formats can cause accuracy to drop by up to 53.63% and trigger decision drifts in over 41% of instances. The proposed mitigation strategies recover up to 44.21% of format-induced decision drift without model retraining.
AI.conclusion: Document format is not a neutral wrapper but a critical factor affecting the reliability of LLM software systems, calling for corresponding testing and safeguards in real-world high-stakes deployment scenarios.

title: Benchmarking the Residual: What Long-Horizon Evaluations Add Beyond Matched Short-Task Performance
summary: Long-horizon benchmarks often show that agents fail more as tasks become longer. This observation is useful for deployment, but it does not by itself explain why failure occurs. More stages create more opportunities for ordinary errors to compound; longer tasks may also contain harder individual decisions or become harder as conversation history, tool outputs, and environment changes accumulate. We use trajectory-induced degradation to mean this last possibility: earlier execution makes later work harder. When the harmful accumulation is specifically the text visible to the model, it is often called context rot. In this position paper, we argue that to claim a "long-horizon failure", benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages. We call the log-ratio between this prediction and actual success the horizon residual. The comparison must use the same agent configuration and specify in advance how stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets will be chosen. The residual shows that the full rollout differs from the chosen baseline; targeted experiments are still needed to explain why.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a rigorous definition for "long-horizon failure" in AI agent benchmarks, introducing the concept of a "horizon residual"—the log-ratio between actual full-task success and a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages. This residual distinguishes genuine long-horizon degradation from the mere compounding of ordinary stage-level errors, enabling more precise diagnosis of why agents fail on long tasks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon benchmarks show agents fail more as tasks lengthen, but this observation alone does not explain why. The authors argue that multiple competing causes exist: compounding of ordinary errors across stages, harder individual decisions in longer tasks, and trajectory-induced degradation (earlier execution making later work harder, e.g., context rot). Distinguishing these causes is essential for meaningful benchmarking and agent improvement.
AI.method: The paper proposes a position/methodology: to claim a "long-horizon failure", benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction derived from short, individual stages using the same agent configuration, with stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets specified in advance. The horizon residual is defined as the log-ratio between this predicted baseline success and the actual full-task success.
AI.result: The horizon residual quantifies the deviation of the full rollout from the chosen stage-based baseline. A large positive residual indicates genuine long-horizon degradation (e.g., trajectory-induced degradation or context rot), while a small residual suggests failures stem from compounding of ordinary stage-level errors rather than horizon-specific factors.
AI.conclusion: The residual framework alone shows whether the full rollout differs from the baseline; it does not by itself explain why. Targeted experiments are still required to attribute the cause (e.g., context rot vs. harder decisions), making this a foundational definitional contribution for rigorous long-horizon agent evaluation.

title: Inference-Time Agentic Decision Rules Beat Longer Evolving Search for Multi-Image Medical Reasoning
comment: Presented at the CVPR 2026 Workshop on Multi-Modal Reasoning for Agentic Intelligence
summary: Multi-image medical VQA is not merely a prompt-length problem; it is a fundamental challenge of agentic decision-making. Medical vision-language agents must aggregate evidence across ordered images, remain robust to answer-order perturbations, and avoid overfitting to noisy search-time feedback. We study MedFrameQA through a controlled comparison of five inference-time agentic strategies, optimized using the same high-budget ShinkaEvolve configuration and evaluated on a reproducible internal frozen split (1,331 evolution, 665 holdout, 855 final test). Across five independent repeated runs, the strongest method emerges as the simplest robust aggregator: the \textbf{order-vote} policy achieves $57.89 \pm 0.65\%$ final-test accuracy, significantly outperforming the fixed baseline ($52.73 \pm 0.42\%$) and the more complex, albeit brittle, order-rerank variant ($55.79 \pm 0.43\%$). Paired bootstrap analysis confirms these significant gains. Extending the evolutionary search budget from 50 to 100 generations yields no generalization benefit: while holdout performance marginally increases, final-test accuracy drops from $57.89\%$ to $56.02\%$. Our findings suggest that for multi-image medical reasoning, defining the correct agentic decision rule is substantially more impactful than expanding the optimization search budget.

AI.tldr: Multi-image medical VQA is framed as an agentic decision-making problem rather than a prompt-length issue. Comparing five inference-time agentic strategies, the simple order-vote policy achieves the best final-test accuracy (57.89±0.65%), significantly outperforming both a fixed baseline (52.73±0.42%) and a more complex order-rerank variant (55.79±0.43%). Extending evolutionary search from 50 to 100 generations gives no generalization benefit—final-test accuracy actually drops from 57.89% to 56.02%—indicating that the choice of agentic decision rule matters more than search budget.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether multi-image medical VQA is fundamentally limited by the inference-time decision strategy rather than by prompt length or optimization budget, and to identify which agentic strategy is most robust and generalizable.
AI.method: A controlled comparison of five inference-time agentic strategies optimized under the same high-budget ShinkaEvolve configuration, evaluated on a reproducible internal frozen split (1,331 evolution / 665 holdout / 855 final test). The study includes five independent repeated runs, paired bootstrap analysis for statistical significance, and a comparison of 50 vs. 100 evolutionary generations.
AI.result: The order-vote policy achieved the highest final-test accuracy at 57.89±0.65%, significantly beating the fixed baseline (52.73±0.42%) and the order-rerank variant (55.79±0.43%). Extending the evolutionary search from 50 to 100 generations increased holdout performance marginally but decreased final-test accuracy from 57.89% to 56.02%.
AI.conclusion: For multi-image medical reasoning, defining the correct agentic decision rule is substantially more impactful than expanding the optimization search budget. Simpler robust aggregators (order-vote) outperform more complex but brittle strategies, and over-optimization can lead to overfitting.

title: Dimensionality and Measurement Precision in HLE's Multiple-Choice Subset
summary: Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) is widely used to evaluate frontier language models. HLE organizes its questions into eight subject-domain categories, whose subscores are often interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities. However, no study has assessed whether these labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs, nor whether the benchmark effectively differentiates between models of similar ability. We evaluate 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE ($J = 428$ items) and apply psychometric methods to assess both the dimensionality of the benchmark and the distribution of its measurement precision. Fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model, we find convergent evidence that HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: McDonald's $ω_h = 0.998$, domain labels explain only 3.5\% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's $d = 0.016$), and domain-specific ability estimates are near-redundant with the total score ($r \geq 0.81$). A separate analysis of the test information function reveals that measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above $θ= 0$, where frontier models sit. These findings suggest that HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations and that the benchmark's ability to discriminate among the strongest models is limited.

AI.tldr: This paper applies psychometric methods (IRT modeling) to the text-only multiple-choice subset of Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) and finds that HLE measures a single general reasoning factor rather than eight distinct domain abilities, and that its measurement precision is concentrated at moderate ability levels, making it poorly suited to discriminate among the strongest frontier models.
AI.motivation: HLE's eight subject-domain categories are widely used to interpret subscores as evidence of distinct model capabilities, yet no study has verified whether these labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs or whether the benchmark can differentiate models of similar ability.
AI.method: Evaluated 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE (J=428 items) and applied psychometric methods including a two-parameter logistic IRT model to assess dimensionality (via McDonald's omega_h, domain label variance explanation, residual correlations, and domain-specific ability estimates) and the test information function to examine measurement precision distribution.
AI.result: HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: McDonald's ω_h = 0.998, domain labels explain only 3.5% of item response variance, between- and within-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's d = 0.016), and domain-specific ability estimates correlate with total score at r ≥ 0.81. Measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above θ = 0, where frontier models sit.
AI.conclusion: HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations, and the benchmark's ability to discriminate among the strongest models is limited.

title: Can Large Language Models Resolve Real Java Merge Conflicts? An Evaluation with a Calibrated LLM-as-Judge
summary: Merge conflicts are a recurring cost of collaborative software development, and the traditional structured and semi-structured merge tools that address them frequently abstain: when their heuristics do not apply, they leave the conflict unresolved. Large language models (LLMs) can instead produce a candidate resolution for almost any conflict, but measuring whether those resolutions are actually good at scale is hard, because obtaining human desirability judgments for every model output does not scale. We study both problems together on real Java merge conflicts from ConflictBench. We first build an LLM solver as a generate-validate-retry agent that uses only inference-time signals (conflict markers, a Java parser, and duplicate-declaration checks) and never sees the developer's answer. We then evaluate its resolutions with a two-metric suite: (1) a developer-match LLM-as-judge implemented as a G-Eval metric and, crucially, calibrated against ConflictBench's human labels before use, and (2) a deterministic structural-validity check that uses no LLM. On a meta-evaluation of 292 human-labeled cases, the judge reaches 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall, so every acceptance is trustworthy and every downstream rate is a conservative lower bound. Under this validated judge, LLM solvers match the developer's own resolution on about 55% of true conflicts (conservative floor), and under a coverage-fair comparison the LLMs (55-59%) beat the strongest traditional tool (AutoMerge, 36.7%) by roughly 18-22 points; the edge comes almost entirely from coverage, not raw accuracy, since the tools abstain on 20-90% of conflicts while the LLM under forced resolution abstains on none. Finally, the LLM judge accepted 4 of the 5 resolutions that fail the deterministic structural check, evidence that structural correctness must not be delegated to an LLM.

AI.tldr: This paper studies LLM-based merge conflict resolution on real Java conflicts from ConflictBench. The authors build an LLM solver as a generate-validate-retry agent using only inference-time signals (never seeing the developer's answer), and evaluate it with a two-metric suite: a calibrated LLM-as-judge (G-Eval) for developer-match and a deterministic structural-validity check. The judge achieves 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall on 292 human-labeled cases. LLM solvers match the developer's resolution on ~55% of true conflicts, beating the best traditional tool (AutoMerge, 36.7%) by 18-22 points, with the edge coming almost entirely from coverage since LLMs abstain on none while tools abstain on 20-90% of conflicts. Crucially, the LLM judge accepted 4/5 resolutions failing the deterministic structural check, showing structural correctness must not be delegated to an LLM.
AI.motivation: Merge conflicts are a recurring cost in collaborative development. Traditional structured/semi-structured merge tools frequently abstain (leave conflicts unresolved) when their heuristics fail, while LLMs can propose resolutions for nearly any conflict but lack scalable ways to measure resolution quality. The authors study both problems together to build a trustworthy and scalable LLM-based merge conflict solver and evaluation pipeline.
AI.method: The paper builds an LLM solver as a generate-validate-retry agent that uses only inference-time signals (conflict markers, a Java parser, duplicate-declaration checks) and never sees the developer's answer. Evaluation uses a two-metric suite: (1) a developer-match LLM-as-judge implemented via G-Eval, calibrated against ConflictBench human labels before use, and (2) a deterministic structural-validity check that uses no LLM.
AI.result: On meta-evaluation of 292 human-labeled cases, the judge reaches 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall. LLM solvers match developer resolutions on ~55% of true conflicts (conservative floor), and under coverage-fair comparison LLMs (55-59%) beat AutoMerge (36.7%) by ~18-22 points. The edge is almost entirely from coverage, not raw accuracy. The LLM judge accepted 4 of 5 resolutions failing the deterministic structural check.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based solvers substantially outperform traditional tools on merge conflicts, with the advantage coming primarily from coverage (never abstaining) rather than raw accuracy. While the calibrated LLM-as-judge provides trustworthy acceptance signals (100% precision), structural correctness must not be delegated to an LLM since it accepted 4/5 structurally invalid resolutions. A hybrid approach combining LLM judging with deterministic checks is necessary.

title: TIER-MoE: Trust-Informed Expert Routing via Conditional Modality Risk for Multimodal Fusion in Biomedical Classification
summary: The promise of multimodal fusion lies in combining complementary sources of evidence, yet more evidence does not always yield a better prediction. Recent multimodal models have advanced fusion through richer cross-modal interaction and sample-adaptive fusion. However, the influence assigned to a modality during fusion does not reveal whether that source is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to a specialized expert. To address this limitation, we introduce TIER-MoE, a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model that defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss its unimodal predictor is expected to incur. This risk is learned from out-of-fold predictions generated by models that were not trained on the corresponding sample. TIER-MoE combines the estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while an always-active shared path preserves multimodal complementarity. We evaluate TIER-MoE on four public multimodal biomedical datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease status, skin-lesion malignancy, and retinal classification. Results demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

AI.tldr: TIER-MoE is a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model for multimodal fusion that defines modality reliability as the expected prediction loss of unimodal predictors, learned from out-of-fold predictions. It combines this risk with subspace compatibility for sparse routing, alongside an always-active shared path. It outperforms SOTA on four biomedical datasets with better Macro-F1, Brier score, and zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: Multimodal fusion assumes more evidence yields better predictions, but not all modalities are reliable, redundant, or well-matched to specialized experts. Existing models lack a principled way to determine whether a modality's assigned influence during fusion reflects its actual reliability, motivating a mechanism to identify unreliable, redundant, or mismatched modalities.
AI.method: TIER-MoE estimates sample-specific modality reliability as the expected prediction loss of unimodal predictors, derived from out-of-fold predictions of models not trained on the corresponding sample. This estimated risk is combined with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while an always-active shared path preserves multimodal complementarity.
AI.result: Evaluated on four public multimodal biomedical datasets (Alzheimer's disease, skin-lesion malignancy, retinal classification), TIER-MoE outperforms state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent Macro-F1 and Brier score improvements and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.
AI.conclusion: TIER-MoE demonstrates that risk-guided routing based on learned modality reliability provides a more effective and better-calibrated alternative to traditional fusion weights, particularly in biomedical applications where unreliable or redundant modalities can degrade predictions.

title: Objective-Aligned Direct Answer SFT for Robust Multi-Frame Medical VQA
comment: Presented at the CVPR 2026 Workshop on Multimodal Foundation Models for Biomedicine: Challenges and Opportunities
summary: Multi-frame medical VQA appears to reward increasingly complex adaptation: controller-style inference, localization-aware reranking, static hard-negative mixing, and staged continuation all appear plausible from first principles. We test a simpler competing hypothesis on MedFrameQA: methods that remain tightly aligned with the benchmark's final answer objective should be the strongest \emph{robust} adaptation family once evaluation is controlled across fixed splits, matched budgets, repeated seeds, and calibration. We compare controller-based methods, scaffold evolution, static mixed supervision, continuation-heavy variants, and direct answer-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The strongest robust family is direct decoder-only answer SFT on MedGemma-1.5-4B. Empirically, this family yields substantial improvements in held-out report accuracy over frozen baselines while remaining remarkably stable across repeated seeds and matched controls, ensuring our claims reflect true family-level robustness rather than an isolated hyperparameter peak. Furthermore, post-hoc calibration effectively repairs confidence estimation without compromising accuracy, and the core approach transfers consistently to secondary backbones like Qwen2.5-VL-3B. The main result is therefore not that a complex auxiliary mechanism wins, but that objective-aligned direct answer SFT is the strongest robust adaptation family we found for MedFrameQA. By establishing this strong, minimalist baseline, we hope to redirect community focus toward fundamentally robust optimization rather than architectural complexity.

AI.tldr: On MedFrameQA, direct decoder-only answer SFT with MedGemma-1.5-4B outperforms complex multi-frame medical VQA adaptations (controller-based, scaffold evolution, static mixed supervision, continuation) in robustness and accuracy, with stable results across seeds and transfers to Qwen2.5-VL-3B.
AI.motivation: Multi-frame medical VQA has seen increasingly complex adaptation methods (controller-style inference, localization-aware reranking, static hard-negative mixing, staged continuation) that are plausible from first principles but may not be necessary. The authors hypothesize that methods tightly aligned with the benchmark's final answer objective should be the strongest robust adaptation family once evaluation is properly controlled.
AI.method: Controlled comparison of several adaptation families on MedFrameQA: controller-based methods, scaffold evolution, static mixed supervision, continuation-heavy variants, and direct answer-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Evaluation is controlled across fixed splits, matched budgets, repeated seeds, and calibration. Primary backbone is MedGemma-1.5-4B with transfer testing on Qwen2.5-VL-3B.
AI.result: Direct decoder-only answer SFT is the strongest robust family, yielding substantial gains in held-out report accuracy over frozen baselines while remaining stable across seeds and matched controls. Post-hoc calibration repairs confidence estimation without hurting accuracy, and the approach transfers to Qwen2.5-VL-3B.
AI.conclusion: Objective-aligned direct answer SFT, not complex auxiliary mechanisms, is the strongest robust adaptation family for MedFrameQA. The authors advocate for focusing community efforts on fundamentally robust optimization rather than architectural complexity, positioning their minimalist baseline as a reference point.

title: Leveraging Trajectory Graphs for Pre-Execution Error Diagnosis in Agentic LLM Systems
summary: Large Language Model~(LLM)-based agents have demonstrated exceptional performance across a wide range of complex interactive tasks. However, they often struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks common in domains, such as embodied AI. The complexity and vast action spaces in these settings lead to compounding errors, where a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory, causing the agent to exhaust its limited step budget on inefficient or unrecoverable paths. To overcome this without costly fine-tuning, we draw inspiration from software debugging, where execution logs are analyzed to preemptively catch errors. We propose \textit{Trajectory Graph Copilot}, a novel framework that acts as a ``copilot'' for LLM agents by diagnosing potential action errors before they are executed. At its core,\textit{Graph Debugger} models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure. Functioning as a proactive diagnostic sandbox, our method provides early warnings on potentially flawed actions, prompting the agent to self-correct. This pre-action error diagnosis prevents costly mistakes, significantly enhancing the agent's ability to complete long-horizon tasks successfully. The extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a $14.69\%$ pass ratio improvement on average.

AI.tldr: Trajectory Graph Copilot is a framework that acts as a copilot for LLM-based agents by diagnosing potential action errors before execution. It models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify failure-prone sequential action patterns, providing early warnings so agents can self-correct. This achieves a 14.69% average pass ratio improvement across four benchmarks with three LLM agents.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks (e.g., embodied AI) due to compounding errors from complex action spaces, where a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory and exhaust the limited step budget. Fine-tuning to address this is costly, so a lightweight, inference-time intervention is needed.
AI.method: The framework introduces a Graph Debugger component that models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and employs a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure. Acting as a proactive diagnostic sandbox, it provides early warnings on potentially flawed actions before execution, prompting the agent to self-correct via pre-action error diagnosis.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a 14.69% pass ratio improvement on average.
AI.conclusion: Pre-action error diagnosis prevents costly mistakes and significantly enhances LLM agents' ability to complete long-horizon interactive tasks, without requiring costly fine-tuning.

title: A comparative analysis of automated techniques for security bug report identification
summary:
Timely identification of security-related bug reports is essential to minimize the window of vulnerabilities in software systems. Manually screening incoming bug reports to identify security-related issues is time-consuming, error-prone, and non-scalable for large-scale software systems. Thus, a variety of automatic techniques, including traditional machine learning (ML) techniques and large language models, have been proposed to facilitate this task. However, the literature remains fragmented. Most studies introduce or optimize a particular technique and evaluate it against a limited set of baselines, often under different experimental setups. As a result, it is difficult to compare their results and draw reliable conclusions about the effectiveness of existing approaches, leaving researchers and practitioners without clear guidance on which techniques are most suitable for the task.
  To address this gap, we conducted a comparative analysis of several promising automated techniques to identify security-related bug reports using benchmark datasets. We evaluated Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, OpenAI's GPT-5.2, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and SetFit (a state-of-the-art few-shot learning framework).
  Our results indicate that SetFit achieves the best overall performance, achieving an F1-score of 0.80 and outperforming other techniques on three of the four datasets. RoBERTa performs competitively and approaches SetFit in some projects, while traditional ML techniques, particularly Logistic Regression, remain a strong baseline in certain contexts. In contrast, GPT-5.2 performs poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. In addition, cross-project experiments demonstrate that transfer learning can improve performance for projects with limited data, but may degrade results for projects with strong project-specific characteristics.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of automated techniques for identifying security-related bug reports, evaluating traditional ML methods (Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest) alongside modern approaches (GPT-5.2, BERT-base, RoBERTa, SetFit) across benchmark datasets. SetFit achieves the best overall performance (F1=0.80), while GPT-5.2 performs poorly, and cross-project transfer learning shows mixed benefits depending on data availability and project specificity.
AI.motivation: The literature on automated security-related bug report identification is fragmented—studies introduce or optimize individual techniques under disparate experimental setups, making results incomparable and leaving no clear guidance on which methods are most effective for the task.
AI.method: The authors conducted a comparative analysis of seven automated techniques—Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, GPT-5.2, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and SetFit—evaluated on benchmark datasets. Both within-project and cross-project experiments were conducted to assess performance and transfer learning effectiveness.
AI.result: SetFit achieves the best overall performance with an F1-score of 0.80, outperforming other techniques on three of four datasets. RoBERTa is competitive and approaches SetFit on some projects. Traditional ML, particularly Logistic Regression, remains a strong baseline in certain contexts. GPT-5.2 performs poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. Cross-project transfer learning improves performance for data-limited projects but can degrade results for projects with strong project-specific characteristics.
AI.conclusion: SetFit is identified as the most suitable technique overall for security-related bug report identification, with RoBERTa as a viable alternative. The findings underscore that technique selection should consider project context, and that cross-project transfer learning requires careful consideration of project-specific characteristics.

title: EvoCause: LLM-Guided Evolution of Causal Graphs for Root Cause Analysis
summary: Modern telecommunication, cloud, and microservice systems emit correlated alarm cascades when components fail. Root cause analysis (RCA) aims to identify the small set of alarms that initiate each cascade. A common approach learns a causal graph from observational logs and predicts all zero-in-degree alarms in each incident-induced subgraph. However, the learned graph remains fixed and cannot benefit from expert diagnoses of historical incidents. We close this loop with EvoCause. Expert labels constrain which alarms should be source nodes but do not specify the edge edits needed to satisfy those constraints. EvoCause uses a large language model (LLM) to propose semantically plausible graph edits, while deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity and retains the best graph on a labeled alignment set. At test time, the refined graph alone produces transparent predictions without an LLM call. We also release TeleRCA, an expert-annotated benchmark from a production telecommunication network containing $485{,}681$ alarm events spanning $194$ alarm types over $5{,}621$ resources. On synthetic data, EvoCause initialized with the PC causal discovery algorithm outperforms the unrefined PC baseline, raising Node F1, Case EM, and Graph F1 by $11.59$, $9.40$, and $4.59$ percentage points, respectively, while reducing nSHD by $0.2379$. On TeleRCA, replacing human-readable alarm titles with anonymous identifiers lowers Node F1 and Case EM by $6.12$ and $8.04$ percentage points, respectively, indicating that alarm-name information contributes to graph refinement.

AI.tldr: EvoCause is a framework that closes the loop between root cause analysis (RCA) and expert feedback by using LLMs to propose semantically plausible edits to an initial causal graph, with deterministic code validating and retaining the best graph based on labeled alignment data. On synthetic data, it improves over the PC causal discovery baseline across multiple metrics, and on TeleRCA (a new expert-annotated telecommunication benchmark) it demonstrates that alarm-name semantics contribute substantially to graph refinement quality.
AI.motivation: Existing RCA approaches learn a static causal graph from observational logs and identify zero-in-degree alarms as root causes. However, these learned graphs remain fixed and cannot incorporate expert diagnoses of historical incidents, which carry valuable constraints about which alarms should be root-cause (source) nodes but not the specific edge edits needed to satisfy those constraints.
AI.method: EvoCause uses a large language model (LLM) to propose semantically plausible graph edits based on expert labels, while deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity. The best refined graph is retained based on performance on a labeled alignment set. At test time, the refined graph alone produces transparent predictions without requiring any LLM call. The approach is evaluated on synthetic data initialized with the PC causal discovery algorithm, and on TeleRCA, a newly released expert-annotated benchmark from a production telecommunication network.
AI.result: On synthetic data, EvoCause outperforms the unrefined PC baseline by +11.59 points in Node F1, +9.40 points in Case EM, and +4.59 points in Graph F1, while reducing nSHD by 0.2379. On TeleRCA, replacing human-readable alarm titles with anonymous identifiers lowers Node F1 by 6.12 and Case EM by 8.04 percentage points, demonstrating that alarm-name semantic information contributes to graph refinement.
AI.conclusion: EvoCause effectively integrates expert knowledge into causal graph learning for RCA via an LLM-guided refinement loop, improving root cause identification accuracy while keeping test-time predictions transparent and LLM-free. The release of TeleRCA provides a valuable expert-annotated benchmark for future research in telecommunication alarm RCA.

title: ZMIS-SAM: Segment Anything Model Enhanced with Wavelet Transform for Zooplankton Microscopy Image Instance Segmentation
summary: As primary consumers in the marine food chain, zooplankton play a crucial role in maintaining marine ecological balance. However, the Segment Anything Model (SAM) exhibits limited performance in microscopic image instance segmentation due to its lack of zooplankton-specific domain knowledge. To address these challenges, we propose a novel instance segmentation model based on SAM and wavelet transform (ZMIS-SAM), effectively tackling issues such as inaccurate classification, discontinuous segmentation of slender appendages, and incomplete boundary segmentation. Our framework incorporates three core innovations: ZM-ViT enhances SAM's capability to model zooplankton morphology and image intensity distributions through two lightweight adapters, the Neighboring Feature Aggregation Module (NFAM) improves continuous segmentation of semi-transparent slender appendages by integrating general-purpose and domain-specific features, and the Wavelet-based Multi-scale Multi-directional Feature Enhancement (WM2FE) module effectively recovers high-frequency details to refine boundary segmentation completeness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ZMIS-SAM achieves state-of-the-art instance segmentation performance on the zooplankton dataset and exhibits strong generalization capability across multiple public cross-domain datasets.

AI.tldr: ZMIS-SAM is a novel instance segmentation model combining Segment Anything Model (SAM) with wavelet transform techniques, specifically designed for zooplankton microscopic image segmentation.
