It addresses SAM's limitations in zooplankton-specific tasks through three innovations: ZM-ViT adapters for morphology/intensity modeling, NFAM for continuous segmentation of slender appendages, and WM2FE for boundary refinement via high-frequency detail recovery. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on zooplankton datasets with strong cross-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Zooplankton are critical primary consumers in the marine food chain, but the Segment Anything Model (SAM) performs poorly on microscopic zooplankton image instance segmentation due to its lack of domain-specific knowledge. Existing SAM-based approaches fail to accurately classify, segment discontinuous slender appendages, and produce incomplete boundary segmentation.
AI.method: The proposed ZMIS-SAM framework incorporates three core innovations: (1) ZM-ViT, which enhances SAM's zooplankton morphology and intensity distribution modeling via two lightweight adapters; (2) Neighboring Feature Aggregation Module (NFAM), which integrates general-purpose and domain-specific features to improve continuous segmentation of semi-transparent slender appendages; and (3) Wavelet-based Multi-scale Multi-directional Feature Enhancement (WM2FE) module, which recovers high-frequency details to refine boundary segmentation completeness.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that ZMIS-SAM achieves state-of-the-art instance segmentation performance on the zooplankton dataset and exhibits strong generalization capability across multiple public cross-domain datasets.
AI.conclusion: The integration of wavelet transform with SAM-based adaptation effectively overcomes the domain gap in microscopic zooplankton segmentation, providing a robust and generalizable solution for marine ecological monitoring applications.

title: VAmoS Bench: Voice Agent Simulation Bench
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Agent implementations: https://github.com/veris-ai/riley-agent
summary: Production voice agents span cascaded, speech-to-speech, and hybrid architectures. Voice-agent benchmarks typically measure component quality and conversational properties such as word error rate, latency, naturalness, and turn-taking. Fewer measure whether the agent handled a phone call correctly on its own. Contact centers refer to this as ``containment'': the share of phone calls the automated system resolves without handing off to a human. On some phone calls the right outcome is refusal or a redirect. To address this gap, we introduce VAmoS Bench, the Voice Agent Simulation Bench. It measures complete voice-agent systems end to end in a stateful customer-support task. The agent is Riley, a credit-card support representative for a fictional bank who can freeze, cancel, replace, or activate a card. Each of 100 scenarios supplies a simulated caller with a private goal and a seeded PostgreSQL backend. The platform uses each scenario to populate and activate an isolated simulation in which the caller reaches Riley over audio; roughly one-third apply adversarial pressure. The agent can use five tools that execute real SQL against the backend. Each scenario also defines binary assertions. A grader evaluates them against the complete trace of what the caller and agent said and what the agent did, including tool invocations, arguments, and returned rows. This catches an agent that claims to have changed a card without updating the database, as well as one that makes the right database change while disclosing protected information. This first benchmark version focuses on financial services. Its evaluation protocol supports an evolving leaderboard: additional voice agents can be evaluated on the same version, while later versions can expand the tasks and scenarios.

AI.tldr: VAmoS Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating complete voice-agent systems end-to-end in a stateful customer-support task. It creates 100 isolated simulations where a simulated caller interacts with an agent (Riley) over audio, with the ability to execute real SQL tools against a seeded backend. Binary assertions graded against the full trace (conversation and tool actions) assess whether calls are correctly contained—resolved without human handoff, including cases where refusal or redirect is the correct outcome.
AI.motivation: Existing voice-agent benchmarks focus on component-level metrics (word error rate, latency, naturalness, turn-taking) but rarely evaluate whether the agent correctly handled a phone call end-to-end on its own—what contact centers call "containment." This gap means no standardized way to measure complete agent correctness in real task execution.
AI.method: The benchmark provides 100 scenarios set in a credit-card customer-support domain (a fictional bank). Each scenario supplies a simulated caller with a private goal and a seeded PostgreSQL backend; the platform instantiates isolated simulations where the caller reaches the agent over audio. Roughly one-third of scenarios apply adversarial pressure. The agent has five tools that run real SQL against the backend. Each scenario defines binary assertions evaluated against the complete trace of speech and tool invocations/arguments/returned rows, catching both false claims (e.g., claiming a change without updating the DB) and privacy violations (correct database change while disclosing protected info). The protocol supports an evolving leaderboard: new agents can be evaluated on the same version, and later versions can expand tasks and scenarios.
AI.result: The paper introduces the benchmark version focusing on financial services but does not present benchmark results in the abstract; it establishes the evaluation protocol, scenario design, and grader mechanism as the core contribution.
AI.conclusion: VAmoS Bench addresses the missing measurement of end-to-end voice-agent correctness and containment. By combining realistic audio simulation, live database state, adversarial scenarios, and trace-based binary assertions, it provides a protocol for evaluating and comparing complete voice-agent systems, with a forward-compatible leaderboard design.

title: The Case for Vibe Modeling: A Missing Step in AI-Based Trustworthy Software Development
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate software artifacts from natural language prompts. While this enables rapid prototyping and lowers the barrier to software creation, it also introduces challenges related to understanding, validation, traceability, and trust. In this paper, we argue that current AI-based development practices focus too heavily on the direct generation of code and insufficiently on intermediate representations that preserve human intent and support reasoning about system behavior. We argue for vibe modeling as a lightweight intermediate abstraction between natural language interaction and code generation. To explore its potential, we present a student survey study that examines perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling across several AI-assisted development scenarios. Our results are intended to inform future studies for trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering via vibe modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper argues for "vibe modeling" as a lightweight intermediate abstraction between natural language prompts and code generation in AI-assisted software development, and presents a student survey study examining perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust, and the usefulness of vibe modeling across development scenarios.
AI.motivation: Current AI-based development practices over-emphasize direct code generation and under-invest in intermediate representations that preserve human intent and support reasoning about system behavior, leading to challenges in understanding, validation, traceability, and trust of LLM-generated artifacts.
AI.method: The paper proposes vibe modeling as an intermediate abstraction between natural language and code, and conducts a student survey study to investigate perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust, and perceived usefulness of vibe modeling in various AI-assisted development scenarios.
AI.result: The survey results provide insights into how users perceive understanding, validation effort, and trust in LLM-generated outputs, along with the perceived value of vibe modeling, intended to inform future research.
AI.conclusion: Vibe modeling holds promise as an intermediate representation to support trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering, and the results aim to guide future studies in this direction.

title: THGFM: Dual-Branch Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Fusion Model
summary: Temporal heterogeneous graphs offer a natural abstraction for dynamic relational systems in which diverse node and relation types co-exist and evolve over time. Learning on such graphs requires jointly modeling cross-type structural heterogeneity and the temporal dynamics of interactions, yet existing methods still struggle to reconcile parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and typically inject time only as additive features outside the attention kernel. We propose \textbf{THGFM}, a web-scale temporal heterogeneous graph fusion model that addresses both limitations within a unified dual-path architecture. THGFM couples a \textit{Shared-Space Temporal Attention} branch for parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with a \textit{Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention} branch for relation-aware specialization, and integrates them through \textit{Dual-Path Relational--Shared Fusion}, instantiated with \textit{Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion}: a adaptive mechanism that assigns independent, type-conditioned feature-wise gates to the shared and specialized branches, allowing both to be amplified or suppressed without zero-sum competition. To directly incorporate relative time into the attention score, THGFM further introduces \textit{Rotary Temporal Attention}, which rotates queries and keys by half-phases of relative time before matching. THGFM consistently outperforms baseline graph transformer models on academic graphs benchmarks, delivering a $+3.25\%$ six-task mean gain, with peak relative gains of $+12.37\%$ on OAG-CS PV, $+4.87\%$ on PF-$L_2$, and $+1.18\%$ on PF-$L_1$, and $+4.24\%$, $+3.73\%$, and $+4.61\%$ on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP, respectively.

AI.tldr: THGFM is a web-scale temporal heterogeneous graph fusion model with a dual-path architecture combining shared-space and relation-type-partitioned temporal attention branches, fused via type-conditioned non-competitive gated sum, and using rotary temporal attention to inject relative time directly into the attention kernel. It achieves +3.25% mean six-task gain over baseline graph transformers.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal heterogeneous graph learning methods struggle to reconcile parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and typically inject time only as additive features outside the attention kernel.
AI.method: THGFM uses a dual-path architecture: (1) Shared-Space Temporal Attention for parameter-efficient cross-type transfer, (2) Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention for relation-aware specialization. These are fused via Dual-Path Relational–Shared Fusion with Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion, which assigns independent type-conditioned feature-wise gates to each branch without zero-sum competition. Additionally, Rotary Temporal Attention rotates queries and keys by half-phases of relative time before matching to directly incorporate time into attention scoring.
AI.result: THGFM achieves +3.25% mean gain across six tasks on academic graph benchmarks, with peak gains of +12.37% on OAG-CS PV, +4.87% on PF-L2, +1.18% on PF-L1, and +4.24%, +3.73%, +4.61% on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP respectively, consistently outperforming baseline graph transformers.
AI.conclusion: THGFM demonstrates that jointly modeling cross-type structural heterogeneity and temporal dynamics through dual-path architecture with non-competitive gated fusion and rotary temporal attention in the kernel is an effective and scalable approach for temporal heterogeneous graph learning at web scale.

title: Skill Use or Skill Theater? Evaluating the Reasoning Backroom in Skill-Augmented Language Agents
summary: Reusable skills are becoming a standard interface for extending language agents with task procedures. Yet evaluators usually infer skill use from visible reasoning or the agent's own attribution. These signals show what the agent appears to use, not whether the skill changed its decision. We ask whether skill-augmented agents exhibit a \textbf{Reasoning Backroom}, a systematic gap between stated skill use and intervention-measured influence. We introduce BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework that pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual, intervenes on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and elicits attribution only after the answer is committed. We instantiate the framework as BACKROOMBench, a verified testbed spanning controlled logic and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single-agent and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive provenance failure. Across models and domains, stated skill use often remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing both silent uptake and performative use. Behavioral effects follow procedural content more reliably than displayed skill identity, whereas stated attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. Observational detectors based on direct skill-use claims, text mentions, trace similarity, and an LLM judge do not identify which decisions actually depend on the skill. In multi-agent systems, skill influence can survive communication even after its source is lost, while no-skill teams still name skills and sources that were never supplied. These findings establish the Reasoning Backroom as a general AI provenance problem whose audit requires intervention.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "Reasoning Backroom" — a systematic gap between stated skill use and intervention-measured influence in skill-augmented language agents. The authors present BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework pairing skill-conditioned answers with matched no-skill counterfactuals and intervening on skill aspects (meaning, wording, identity, content, assignment), plus BACKROOMBench, a testbed spanning logic and competition math across single and multi-agent settings. Results reveal pervasive provenance failure: stated skill use often diverges from causal reliance, attribution is driven by artifact availability rather than genuine dependency, and observational detectors fail to identify which decisions actually depend on the skill.
AI.motivation: Current evaluators infer skill use from visible reasoning or agent self-attribution, which only captures what agents appear to use, not whether the skill actually changed their decisions. The authors aim to expose and measure the gap between stated skill use and intervention-measured influence — a general AI provenance problem.
AI.method: The authors introduce BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework that: (1) pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual, (2) intervenes on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and (3) elicits attribution only after the answer is committed. This is instantiated as BACKROOMBench, a verified testbed spanning controlled logic and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single-agent and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families.
AI.result: The evaluation reveals a pervasive provenance failure across models and domains. Stated skill use often remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing silent uptake and performative use. Behavioral effects follow procedural content more reliably than displayed skill identity, while stated attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. Observational detectors (direct claims, text mentions, trace similarity, LLM judge) fail to identify which decisions depend on the skill. In multi-agent systems, skill influence can survive communication even after source is lost, and no-skill teams still name skills and sources never supplied.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish the Reasoning Backroom as a general AI provenance problem whose audit requires intervention-based evaluation rather than observational inference. Stated skill attribution cannot be trusted as evidence of actual influence, necessitating counterfactual and interventional methods for reliable provenance auditing.

title: Specification-Guided Synthesis of Deadlock-Free Communication Protocol Refinements with Large Language Models
summary: Ensuring behavioural correctness in communication protocols is a central challenge in distributed software systems, as subtle inconsistencies can lead to deadlocks. In such settings, protocol refinement - the safe substitution of a protocol that preserves correctness and compatibility with other components - is essential. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and program synthesis, yet lack mechanisms to reliably produce outputs with correct behaviour. Formal specification approaches, such as multiparty session types (MPST), offer rigorous guarantees, including deadlock freedom, but provide limited support for automatically constructing protocol refinements. In this paper, we present Syntropy, a framework for synthesising protocol refinements guided by MPST specifications and LLMs. It incorporates refinement constraints directly into the generation process, ensuring the generated variants satisfy these guarantees. Our comprehensive evaluation indicates that Syntropy achieves 95.6%-99.5% validity while maintaining high syntactic correctness, and produces diverse, non-trivial refinements across multiple LLMs.

AI.tldr: A framework called Syntropy that combines multiparty session types (MPST) with large language models (LLMs) to synthesise protocol refinements that preserve behavioural correctness, achieving 95.6%-99.5% validity across multiple LLMs.
AI.motivation: Protocol refinement is essential for safely substituting protocols in distributed systems while preserving correctness and compatibility. LLMs lack mechanisms to reliably produce behaviourally correct outputs, and formal specification approaches like MPST offer rigorous guarantees but limited support for automatically constructing protocol refinements.
AI.method: Syntropy is a framework that integrates refinement constraints directly into the LLM generation process, guided by MPST specifications, ensuring generated protocol variants satisfy deadlock freedom and other correctness guarantees.
AI.result: The framework achieves 95.6%-99.5% validity while maintaining high syntactic correctness, and produces diverse, non-trivial refinements across multiple LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Combining formal MPST specifications with LLMs provides an effective approach to synthesising behaviourally correct protocol refinements, overcoming the limitations of each technique in isolation.

title: Position, Not Provenance: Separating Reasoning Mediation from Sycophancy in Medical Vision-Language Models
summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) generate chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning before answering clinical questions, but whether this reasoning causally influences predictions remains unclear. We present CoT-Mediate, a behavioral framework that perturbs a single clinically meaningful attribute within a model's own generated reasoning and measures whether the resulting prediction follows the edited reasoning. Our framework combines a dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence with prefix-forced continuation, together with a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to disentangle reasoning mediation from sycophancy. We evaluate LLaVA-Med and MedGemma on 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each. Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting, while the provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Across both models, removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning, whereas laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute. These results show that the mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness and that contextual position, rather than stated provenance, is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning.

AI.tldr: CoT-Mediate is a behavioral framework that tests whether chain-of-thought reasoning in medical VLMs causally influences predictions by perturbing single clinical attributes in the model's own reasoning. Using dual-arm comparison (re-prompting vs. prefix-forced continuation) and provenance-controlled interventions on LLaVA-Med and MedGemma across 1,000 VQA-RAD samples, the study finds prefix-forcing yields higher mediation faithfulness, contextual position (not stated provenance) is the primary determinant of reasoning use, and laterality is the least faithfully tracked attribute.
AI.motivation: Medical vision-language models generate chain-of-thought reasoning before answering clinical questions, but whether this reasoning actually causally influences their final predictions remains unclear. Understanding this causal relationship is crucial for ensuring reliable clinical decision support.
AI.method: The paper introduces CoT-Mediate, a behavioral framework combining (1) a dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence versus prefix-forced continuation, and (2) a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to disentangle reasoning mediation from sycophancy. Evaluation is conducted on LLaVA-Med and MedGemma using 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each.
AI.result: Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting. Provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning across both models, and laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute.
AI.conclusion: The mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness. Contextual position, rather than stated provenance, is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning, highlighting that where reasoning is placed matters more than how it is attributed.

title: MPIE-Bench: Benchmarking Anatomically Plausible Multi-Person Interaction Editing
summary: Text-to-image and personalized editing models now synthesize high-fidelity single-subject images with ease. Yet placing multiple named people into shared contact actions such as embrace, carry, or grapple still exposes major failures: fused limbs, invented extremities, and interpenetrating bodies. Existing evaluations largely overlook these anatomical and geometric issues, and VLM-as-a-judge checklists often saturate on Interaction while the errors remain obvious to humans. We introduce MPIE-Bench, a 2,500-sample benchmark of video-mined editing triplets spanning 405 scenes, 14 interaction categories, and four contact densities (C0-C3). We also propose MPIE-Eval, whose two new axes score contact-time geometry from a frozen public multi-person mesh reconstruction. Anatomy asks whether every human-like mass is explained by a complete set of reconstructed bodies, and Interaction asks whether the penetration and surface distance between those bodies match the contact the instruction asked for. Across ten editors, mesh Anatomy tops out at 0.65 and mesh Interaction at 0.72 on two different models, so no single editor is strong on both, while VLM checklists rate the same images above 0.95. A five-rater study confirms that both axes track human judgement more closely than a zero-shot VLM judge, and the rankings hold under ablation of every weight and threshold.

AI.tldr: Introduces MPIE-Bench and MPIE-Eval, a benchmark and evaluation framework for multi-person image editing with physical contact. MPIE-Bench contains 2,500 video-mined editing triplets across 405 scenes, 14 interaction categories, and 4 contact densities. MPIE-Eval uses a frozen public multi-person mesh reconstruction to score two new axes—Anatomy and Interaction—revealing that existing editors fail on anatomical/geometric fidelity while VLM judges saturate and overestimate quality.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-image and personalized editing models generate high-fidelity single-subject images but fail badly on multi-person contact scenarios (fused limbs, invented extremities, interpenetrating bodies). Current benchmarks and VLM-as-a-judge checklists overlook these anatomical and geometric errors, often saturating on the Interaction axis while human viewers easily notice the defects.
AI.method: Constructs MPIE-Bench, a 2,500-sample benchmark of video-mined editing triplets spanning 405 scenes, 14 interaction categories, and four contact densities (C0-C3). Proposes MPIE-Eval with two new scoring axes computed from a frozen public multi-person mesh reconstruction: Anatomy (whether every human-like mass is explained by a complete set of reconstructed bodies) and Interaction (whether penetration and surface distance between reconstructed bodies match the contact specified by the instruction).
AI.result: Across ten editors, mesh Anatomy tops out at 0.65 and mesh Interaction at 0.72 on two different models, showing no single editor excels on both axes, while VLM checklists rate the same images above 0.95. A five-rater study confirms both axes track human judgment more closely than a zero-shot VLM judge, and the rankings remain stable under ablation of every weight and threshold.
AI.conclusion: Multi-person contact editing remains unsolved; existing editors fail anatomically and geometrically on contact scenes despite high VLM scores. MPIE-Bench and MPIE-Eval provide a more reliable, human-aligned evaluation paradigm that exposes these hidden failures.

title: INCLAIR: Inception-Based Longitudinal Clinical Anomaly Detection with Informed Reasoning
summary: Detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles is clinically important but difficult: abnormal evidence is often sparse, patient histories have unequal length, and expert explanations are costly. We propose INCLAIR, a framework that scores each observation against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision. Under stated within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the complete mean subsequence score takes an order-$l$ U-statistic form, yielding a variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation that controls combinatorial inference cost independently of profile length. The same analysis shows that mean aggregation attenuates localized anomalies by a factor set by the anomaly support and profile length, motivating validation-selected top-$k$ pooling. Across three clinical datasets, INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We further validate practical relevance through a case study on longitudinal steroid profiles, comparing INCLAIR's predictions and explanations against domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis. The results show that INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision.

AI.tldr: INCLAIR is a framework for detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles that scores observations against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision, using U-statistic theory for efficient computation and top-k pooling to mitigate attenuation of localized anomalies.
AI.motivation: Detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles is clinically important but difficult because abnormal evidence is often sparse, patient histories have unequal length, and expert explanations are costly to obtain.
AI.method: INCLAIR scores each observation against multiple historical contexts, then aggregates evidence at the profile level and generates grounded natural-language explanations. Under within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the complete mean subsequence score takes an order-l U-statistic form, enabling a variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation that controls combinatorial inference cost independently of profile length. The analysis shows mean aggregation attenuates localized anomalies, motivating validation-selected top-k pooling.
AI.result: Across three clinical datasets, INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. A case study on longitudinal steroid profiles validates predictions and explanations against domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis, demonstrating clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision.
AI.conclusion: INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection with efficient computation, robust detection of localized anomalies via top-k pooling, and grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision.

title: Advancing Awkward Arrays for High-Performance CPU and GPU Processing
summary: Awkward Array is a Python library for representing and processing nested, variable-length data that is widely used in high-energy physics. As HL-LHC analyses increasingly rely on accelerator hardware, efficient execution of irregular workloads has become essential. While dense numerical arrays map naturally to GPUs, nested and variable-length data structures remain significantly more difficult to accelerate because they require indirect indexing, segmented operations, and irregular memory access patterns. We present recent developments in the Awkward Array GPU backend, including CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CUDA Core Compute Libraries (CCCL), optimized memory management, and segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays. These developments preserve the existing Python programming model while substantially improving GPU throughput on irregular workloads. We describe the backend architecture, automated validation framework, and benchmark results comparing CPU, CuPy, and CUDA implementations.

AI.tldr: The paper presents recent developments in the Awkward Array GPU backend, including CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CCCL, optimized memory management, and segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays, which improve GPU throughput on irregular/nested data workloads while preserving the existing Python programming model.
AI.motivation: HL-LHC analyses increasingly rely on accelerator hardware, and efficient execution of irregular workloads (nested, variable-length data) on GPUs is essential but difficult due to indirect indexing, segmented operations, and irregular memory access patterns.
AI.method: The authors present CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CUDA Core Compute Libraries (CCCL), optimized memory management techniques, and segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays, along with an automated validation framework.
AI.result: Benchmark results show substantial improvements in GPU throughput on irregular workloads when comparing CPU, CuPy, and CUDA implementations.
AI.conclusion: The developments preserve the existing Python programming model while substantially improving GPU performance for nested and variable-length data structures used in high-energy physics.

title: ZUNA1.1: A more flexible EEG foundation model for Denoising and Super-resolution
summary: We introduce ZUNA1.1, a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction. ZUNA1.1 is capable of reconstructing variable length sequences of up to 30s, with an arbitrary number of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels in addition to reconstructing entire channels. We demonstrate that ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with our earlier ZUNA1 model, while being far more flexible and capable of handling a wide range of reconstruction tasks. ZUNA1.1 continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods such as spherical spline interpolation, which is ubiquitously deployed in the MNE package. The ZUNA1.1 model is released open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ZUNA1.1, a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction. It handles variable-length sequences up to 30 seconds, arbitrary numbers of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels. It performs at least on par with the earlier ZUNA1 model while being far more flexible, and substantially outperforms standard EEG denoising methods like spherical spline interpolation.
AI.motivation: To develop a more flexible EEG reconstruction model that can handle variable-length sequences, arbitrary channel configurations, and partial temporal intervals, while maintaining or exceeding the performance of the previous ZUNA1 model and standard EEG reconstruction methods.
AI.method: A 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder architecture designed for flexible EEG signal reconstruction, capable of handling variable-length sequences up to 30 seconds, arbitrary channel numbers/locations, and arbitrary temporal interval reconstruction within channels.
AI.result: ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with ZUNA1 while being significantly more flexible, and substantially outperforms standard EEG denoising/reconstruction baselines such as spherical spline interpolation from the MNE package.
AI.conclusion: ZUNA1.1 is released open source under the Apache 2.0 license, providing a flexible and high-performing solution for EEG reconstruction across a wide range of tasks.

title: MedXplore: Towards Reliable and Unbiased Generalized Category Discovery in Medical Imaging
summary: Deep learning has shown strong potential in medical image analysis, but most existing methods rely on large-scale annotations and a closed-world assumption that rarely holds in clinical practice. Although Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) has advanced rapidly on natural images, it remains underexplored in medical imaging. To address this issue, we propose MedXplore, a unified framework for reliable and unbiased medical GCD, optimizing from both perceptual and decision levels. Specifically, at the perceptual level, taking a frequency domain perspective, Frequency-SNR Adaptive Attention and Consistency (FAAC) performs learnable full-spectrum filtering and global-local energy contrast activation to not only highlight local abnormal signals relative to the global context, but also provide reliable semantic anchors for patch consistency learning. At the decision level, Adaptive Cosine-Angular Margin (ACAM) adjusts angular margins using semantic difficulty and feature confidence to balance intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. Together, the two modules improve lesion-sensitive representation learning and mitigate old-class bias. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show an average \textbf{8.5\%} gain in \textit{All} accuracy over the strongest competing methods. On Kvasir, MedXplore reduces false-old errors from 14.50\% to 0.80\%, demonstrating strong robustness under severe old-new ambiguity.

AI.tldr: MedXplore is a unified framework for Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) in medical imaging, addressing the limitations of existing methods that rely on large-scale annotations and closed-world assumptions. It optimizes both perceptual and decision levels using Frequency-SNR Adaptive Attention and Consistency (FAAC) and Adaptive Cosine-Angular Margin (ACAM), achieving an average 8.5% gain in All accuracy over competing methods and drastically reducing false-old errors.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning methods in medical image analysis depend on large-scale annotations and assume a closed-world setting, which rarely holds in clinical practice. While Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) has advanced in natural images, it remains underexplored in medical imaging, motivating the need for a reliable and unbiased medical GCD framework.
AI.method: MedXplore optimizes from two levels: (1) Perceptual level via Frequency-SNR Adaptive Attention and Consistency (FAAC), which performs learnable full-spectrum filtering and global-local energy contrast activation to highlight local abnormal signals relative to global context and provide semantic anchors for patch consistency learning; (2) Decision level via Adaptive Cosine-Angular Margin (ACAM), which adjusts angular margins using semantic difficulty and feature confidence to balance intra-class compactness and inter-class separability.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show an average 8.5% gain in All accuracy over the strongest competing methods. On the Kvasir dataset, MedXplore reduces false-old errors from 14.50% to 0.80%, demonstrating strong robustness under severe old-new ambiguity.
AI.conclusion: The two proposed modules improve lesion-sensitive representation learning and mitigate old-class bias, making MedXplore a reliable and unbiased solution for medical Generalized Category Discovery in practical clinical settings.

title: MedLLM: An Open Medical Language Model at the Sub-Billion Scale
summary: Open medical language models have converged on a single scale: every widely used system runs at 7B parameters or more, leaving the sub-billion regime uncharacterized. We present MedLLM, an open 0.1B-parameter medical language model trained through a fully open three-phase pipeline: general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb, a reference-guided medical corpus we release that is selected from general web data by embedding similarity to medical question-answering (QA) data, and preference-aligned fine-tuning combining SFT with direct preference optimization (DPO). Across medical benchmarks, MedLLM shows a pattern visible only at sub-billion scale: medical competence does not degrade uniformly under compression but splits by task type. On context-grounded QA it comes within $2.9$pp of a medically adapted 7B model and surpasses the instruction-tuned and general-purpose 7B baselines; on knowledge-recall QA it stays near the task floor on clinical-vignette MedQA yet significantly exceeds every 7B and sub-7B baseline on MedMCQA, indicating that where recall fails the constraint is model capacity rather than adaptation. This dissociation is masked at 7B, where both capabilities are present, and surfaces only when capacity is scarce.

AI.tldr: MedLLM is an open 0.1B-parameter medical language model trained via a three-phase pipeline (curriculum pretraining, domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb, and preference-aligned fine-tuning with SFT+DPO). At sub-billion scale, medical competence splits by task type: context-grounded QA nearly matches a 7B medically adapted model, while knowledge-recall QA shows divergent performance (near floor on MedQA but exceeding all baselines on MedMCQA), revealing a capacity-vs-adaptation dissociation masked at 7B scale.
AI.motivation: Existing open medical language models all cluster at 7B+ parameters, leaving the sub-billion parameter regime entirely uncharacterized. The authors aim to explore whether smaller models can be viable in medical domains and to understand how medical capabilities behave under extreme parameter compression.
AI.method: A fully open three-phase pipeline: (1) general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, (2) domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb, a reference-guided corpus selected by embedding similarity between general web data and medical QA data, and (3) preference-aligned fine-tuning combining supervised fine-tuning with direct preference optimization (DPO).
AI.result: On context-grounded QA, MedLLM comes within 2.9 percentage points of a medically adapted 7B model and surpasses both instruction-tuned and general-purpose 7B baselines. On knowledge-recall QA, it stays near the task floor on MedQA but significantly exceeds all 7B and sub-7B baselines on MedMCQA, demonstrating a task-dependent dissociation between context-grounded and recall-based medical competence.
AI.conclusion: Medical competence does not degrade uniformly under compression; it splits by task type. The dissociation between context-grounded and knowledge-recall capabilities is masked at 7B scale (where both exist) and only surfaces when model capacity is scarce, indicating that recall failures at small scale stem from model capacity limits rather than training adaptation issues.

title: Integrating AI into Requirements Quality Learning in Software Engineering Education: A TPACK-Guided Empirical Study
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables, presented in the 38th CSEE&T in Florence, Italy, from July 20-22, 2026
summary: The rapid adoption of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in software engineering (SE) practice creates a need for pedagogically grounded approaches to AI integration in SE education, especially in conceptually intensive subjects such as requirements engineering (RE). This study examines a TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level RE assignment on requirements quality analysis. Using a mixed-methods design (N=100; 72 submissions analysed), we examine how structured assignment design shaped students' AI use, affected their understanding of user story quality criteria, and influenced their perceptions of AI's benefits and limitations. Results show that students used the AI tool selectively, mainly as support for analysis and evaluation rather than automation. Alignment improvements were most evident for structurally concrete requirements quality dimensions, such as value articulation and testability, while negotiability showed mixed effects. Students reported conditional trust, active refinement, and increased awareness of quality criteria, alongside moderate usability challenges. The findings show that TPACK-guided scaffolding can align AI affordances with pedagogical goals and RE content, offering design guidance for responsible AI integration in RE education.

AI.tldr: This study examines a TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level requirements engineering assignment, using mixed-methods with 100 students (72 submissions). Results show students used AI selectively for analysis and evaluation, with improved alignment on structurally concrete quality dimensions, conditional trust, and increased awareness of quality criteria, demonstrating that TPACK-guided scaffolding can align AI affordances with pedagogical goals.
AI.motivation: The rapid adoption of generative AI in software engineering practice creates a need for pedagogically grounded AI integration approaches in SE education, particularly for conceptually intensive subjects like requirements engineering.
AI.method: Mixed-methods design with N=100 students (72 submissions analyzed) examining a TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level RE assignment focused on requirements quality analysis, assessing student AI usage, understanding of user story quality criteria, and perceptions of AI benefits/limitations.
AI.result: Students used the AI tool selectively (as support for analysis/evaluation rather than automation); alignment improved most for structurally concrete quality dimensions (value articulation, testability) while negotiability showed mixed effects; students reported conditional trust, active refinement, increased quality criteria awareness, and moderate usability challenges.
AI.conclusion: TPACK-guided scaffolding can effectively align AI affordances with pedagogical goals and RE content, offering design guidance for responsible AI integration in requirements engineering education.

title: Modeling Decisions in Blockchain Analytics: A Leakage-Aware Evaluation of Tree-Based vs. Sequential Models
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 23rd International Conference on Modeling Decisions for Artificial Intelligence (MDAI 2026)
summary: Sybil bots are Ethereum actors that imitate legitimate users to extract airdrop rewards or influence governance. Recent Sybil detection methods increasingly use deep learning and treat blockchain activity as a quasi-linguistic sequence. However, complex sequence models are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, and their reported performance may be inflated by label leakage from high-signal smart contracts. We ask whether and how organic users, Sybil bots, and MEV bots differ in the structural complexity of their transaction histories; whether sequential models outperform tree-based tabular models once leakage is reduced; whether transaction order or timing provides the stronger behavioral signal; and whether the resulting models are practical for low-latency deployment. Our approach to leakage-aware Sybil bot detection consists of a Blind-Spot protocol and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. The former eliminates shortcuts associated with high-signal contracts, whereas the latter models wallets using rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. We evaluate this approach on Ethereum actor classification by comparing Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines. We contribute a framework for leakage-aware Ethereum actor classification and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. Our results demonstrate that, under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while providing lower latency and estimated energy use.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a leakage-aware framework for Sybil bot detection on Ethereum, using a Blind-Spot protocol to eliminate label leakage from high-signal smart contracts and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. Under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while offering lower latency and energy consumption.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning-based Sybil detection methods for Ethereum are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring and may have inflated performance due to label leakage from high-signal smart contracts, calling into question whether complex sequence models genuinely outperform simpler baselines.
AI.method: The approach consists of two components: (1) a Blind-Spot protocol that removes shortcuts from high-signal contracts to enable leakage-aware evaluation, and (2) a Transaction Grammar representation that models wallets via rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models are compared against XGBoost and SVM baselines on Ethereum actor classification.
AI.result: Under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models, while providing lower latency and estimated energy use for practical deployment.
AI.conclusion: Complex sequence models do not offer advantages over tree-based tabular models once label leakage is addressed; the paper contributes a leakage-aware framework and Transaction Grammar representation for Ethereum actor classification, demonstrating that simpler models are more practical and equally or more effective.

title: BlindPSNR: A No-Reference Fidelity Predictor for Low-Light Image Enhancement
summary: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) methods involve tunable parameters that are typically fixed, often leading to performance degradation when applied across scenes. Manually selecting the best configuration, however, can be time-consuming and not always practical. Peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) is the natural fidelity criterion for automating parameter selection, yet it requires a ground-truth reference that is typically unavailable. To our knowledge, no learning-based method addresses no-reference PSNR prediction for low-light image enhancement; the natural surrogate, no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA), targets perceptual quality rather than signal fidelity, and all seven baselines we test achieve 0% top-1 selection accuracy on our benchmark. With paired training data, the ground-truth PSNR is analytically computable, providing exact supervision without a separate teacher network. Building on this, we propose BlindPSNR, a lightweight no-reference network that fuses the enhanced image with the degraded low-light input via windowed cross-attention and estimates PSNR through heteroscedastic regression. While a scalar-regression baseline achieves top-1 accuracy of 54.4%, BlindPSNR raises this to 89.5% with regret dropping from 1.62 dB to 0.026 dB, and generalizes to unseen datasets (SRCC = 0.61-0.67).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes BlindPSNR, a lightweight no-reference network that predicts PSNR for low-light image enhancement without ground-truth references. It fuses the enhanced image with the degraded low-light input via windowed cross-attention and uses heteroscedastic regression. BlindPSNR achieves 89.5% top-1 selection accuracy (vs 54.4% for scalar regression baseline) with regret dropping from 1.62 dB to 0.026 dB, and generalizes to unseen datasets (SRCC = 0.61-0.67).
AI.motivation: LLIE methods have tunable parameters that are typically fixed, causing performance degradation across scenes. Manual hyperparameter selection is time-consuming and impractical. PSNR is the natural criterion for automated parameter selection, but it requires a ground-truth reference that is typically unavailable. Existing NR-IQA methods target perceptual quality rather than signal fidelity, and all seven baselines achieve 0% top-1 selection accuracy.
AI.method: BlindPSNR is a lightweight no-reference network that fuses the enhanced image with the degraded low-light input through windowed cross-attention, and estimates PSNR via heteroscedastic regression. With paired training data, the ground-truth PSNR is computed analytically, providing exact supervision without a separate teacher network.
AI.result: BlindPSNR achieves 89.5% top-1 selection accuracy compared to 54.4% for a scalar-regression baseline. The regret (PSNR loss from suboptimal parameter selection) drops from 1.62 dB to 0.026 dB. It also generalizes to unseen datasets with SRCC between 0.61 and 0.67.
AI.conclusion: BlindPSNR effectively addresses no-reference PSNR prediction for LLIE, enabling accurate automatic parameter selection without ground-truth references, significantly outperforming existing NR-IQA baselines (which all fail with 0% top-1 accuracy) and generalizing across datasets.

title: A dataset of rated conceptual arguments
summary: Large language models have improved rapidly on tasks with verifiable answers, such as mathematics and programming. Much less is known about their ability to reason about what we call conceptual questions: questions for which no ground truth is realistically accessible and no widely accepted resolution methodology exists, but on which progress can still be made by debating arguments. Most philosophical questions are of this kind, as are central components of questions in AI safety, decision theory, and social choice. Our approach is based on the view that while bottom-line conclusions on such questions are hard to evaluate, individual contextualized arguments can be evaluated far more reliably. We therefore introduce a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts, spanning topics from AI safety and decision theory to ethics and politics, with 1,458 ratings by six expert raters along dimensions including centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. We propose two scoring functions and benchmark a range of models. Performance tracks general capability rankings.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques across 442 position texts on conceptual questions (philosophy, AI safety, decision theory, social choice), with 1,458 expert ratings, and benchmarks language models using two proposed scoring functions.
AI.motivation: While LLMs have been shown to perform well on verifiable tasks like math and programming, little is known about their ability to reason on conceptual questions where no ground truth exists. Since evaluating bottom-line conclusions on such questions is difficult, but evaluating individual contextualized arguments is more reliable, the authors aim to benchmark LLM reasoning on argumentative critiques of conceptual positions.
AI.method: The authors construct a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts across philosophy, AI safety, decision theory, ethics, and politics. Six expert raters provide 1,458 ratings on dimensions including centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. They propose two scoring functions and benchmark a range of language models against this dataset.
AI.result: Model performance on the conceptual reasoning benchmarks tracks general capability rankings, suggesting that current language model capabilities on verifiable tasks may translate to argumentative reasoning on conceptual questions, though no specific results are detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a benchmark for evaluating LLM reasoning on conceptual questions through argumentative critiques, with results indicating that model performance correlates with general capability rankings.

title: Agentic Metaverse Services: A New As-a-Service Paradigm
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures; Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Web Services (ICWS 2026); Corresponding author: Prof. Xiaofei Xu
summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reconstructing the digital virtual world, upgrading agents through enhancing their abilities in autonomous learning, multi-modal interaction, content generation, and collaborative decision-making. In particular, the shift from conversational chatbots to agentic AI, the most recent significant technical breakthrough of GenAI, has brought a new form of services, agentic services and Agent-as-a-Service (AaaS), in which the agent's abilities are encapsulated, such as perception, decision-making, execution, collaboration, and content generation, to provide the customized agent services to users. The metaverse is a virtual ecosystem for human life, work, creation, and entertainment, supported by the new generation of digital technologies. Through combining agentic services and the metaverse, an Agentic Metaverse Service, denoted as AMServ, is produced for metaverse business processing, as a new form of metaverse service. The AaaS in the metaverse environment, denoted as Meta-AaaS, as an approach to realize AMServ, has become a new paradigm of agentic services and service computing. This paper overviews the evolution and new features of agents and services empowered by GenAI, reveals the roles and principles of agentic services in the metaverse environment, presents the forms, characteristics, and principles of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS, discusses the typical application examples of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS, and finally points out the new tendencies and research directions of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS. The AMServ and the Meta-AaaS will bring great opportunities to human society and services in the AI era, and promote the rapid development of emerging service industries in the future.

AI.tldr: This paper provides an overview of Agentic Metaverse Service (AMServ) and Meta-Agent-as-a-Service (Meta-AaaS), a new paradigm that combines agentic AI services (advanced by Generative AI) with the metaverse, covering their evolution, features, forms, principles, application examples, and future research directions.
AI.motivation: Generative AI has shifted agents from conversational chatbots to agentic AI, creating new forms of services (agentic services and AaaS). The metaverse provides a virtual ecosystem that, when combined with these agentic services, generates a new service paradigm (AMServ/Meta-AaaS) for metaverse business processing. The paper aims to systematically overview this emerging paradigm and its implications.
AI.method: The paper conducts a comprehensive overview: it traces the evolution and new features of GenAI-empowered agents and services, reveals the roles and principles of agentic services in the metaverse, presents the forms, characteristics, and principles of AMServ and Meta-AaaS, discusses typical application examples, and outlines new tendencies and research directions.
AI.result: The paper establishes AMServ as a new form of metaverse service and Meta-AaaS as the realization approach/paradigm of agentic services and service computing, highlighting their potential to bring great opportunities to human society and accelerate the development of emerging service industries in the AI era.
AI.conclusion: AMServ and Meta-AaaS represent a significant new direction in agentic services and service computing, expected to transform metaverse business processing and drive the rapid growth of emerging service industries in the AI era.

title: Compression-Based Behavioral Similarity for Open-World Sybil Discovery on Ethereum
comment: Accepted as a full paper and scheduled for presentation at the European Conference on Advances in Databases and Information Systems (ADBIS 2026)
summary: Sybil attackers are Blockchain actors that adopt the characteristics of regular users to exploit airdrops or influence governance. Current methods of Sybil actor detection include constructing graphs, which requires token transfers between examined wallets. Machine learning algorithms have been employed as well, but they treat the task as a closed-set classification problem, making them vulnerable to frequent changes in attack strategies or evasion tactics. We address the following questions: can compression-based similarity differentiate Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bot wallets without direct financial links? What is the effect of high-signal contracts on the discovery of Sybils, and how robust are behavioral graphs under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations? Our approach synthesizes a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) traces, capturing separately transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. The high-signal contracts are filtered with our own protocol, called the Blind-Spot Protocol. Gzip-based NCD is used to construct a behavioral graph for Sybil discovery. We validate this framework against supervised machine learning baselines, a temporal split, and synthetic camouflage stress tests. Ultimately, we contribute a leakage-aware behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery. Its core NCD primitive requires no supervised training and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links. We position the method as a training-free local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits, rather than as a formal open-set recognition system.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a compression-based (Gzip NCD) behavioral similarity framework for Sybil actor detection in blockchain networks. It synthesizes a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM traces capturing transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent, filters high-signal contracts via a Blind-Spot Protocol, and constructs behavioral graphs for Sybil discovery without requiring token transfers or supervised training.
AI.motivation: Sybil attackers mimic regular user behavior to exploit airdrops or influence governance. Existing methods either rely on token-transfer graph construction (requiring direct financial links between wallets) or supervised machine learning that treats detection as closed-set classification, making them vulnerable to evolving attack strategies and evasion tactics.
AI.method: The framework synthesizes a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM traces, separately capturing transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. High-signal contracts are filtered using a custom "Blind-Spot Protocol." Gzip-based Normalized Compression Distance (NCD) is then used to construct a behavioral graph for Sybil discovery. Validation includes comparisons against supervised ML baselines, a temporal split, and synthetic camouflage stress tests.
AI.result: The framework successfully differentiates Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bot wallets without direct financial links. It is validated against supervised machine learning baselines, temporal drift scenarios, and adversarial camouflage stress tests, demonstrating robustness where closed-set classification approaches fail.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a leakage-aware, training-free behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery. The core NCD primitive requires no supervised training and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links. It is positioned as a local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits rather than a formal open-set recognition system.

title: 4DHumanDiff: Direct Text-to-4DGS Generation for Consistent 360-Degree Dynamic Humans
summary: Generating high-quality 360-degree dynamic human assets from text prompts is challenging. Existing methods usually synthesize monocular or multi-view videos first and then fit a 4D representation, which is expensive and often causes incomplete geometry or view-inconsistent renderings. We present 4DHumanDiff, a diffusion framework that directly generates dynamic humans represented by 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) from text prompts. By modeling the structured 4D representation space end-to-end, 4DHumanDiff avoids video pre-generation and per-scene reconstruction, making it better suited for view-consistent and temporally coherent asset generation. The model uses a 3D U-Net backbone with temporal attention for motion-aware generation. We further construct a large-scale text-to-4DGS dataset with 60,000 high-quality pairs, and introduce 2D regularization and training-free 4D interpolation to improve rendering quality and motion smoothness. Experiments show that 4DHumanDiff generates consistent 360-degree dynamic humans within one minute, achieves better temporal and multi-view consistency, and reduces inference time by more than 10x.

AI.tldr: 4DHumanDiff is a diffusion framework that directly generates 360-degree dynamic human assets as 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) from text prompts, avoiding expensive video pre-generation and per-scene reconstruction. It uses a 3D U-Net with temporal attention, trained on a custom 60,000-pair text-to-4DGS dataset, and achieves consistent dynamic human generation in under one minute with over 10x speedup.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for generating dynamic human assets from text typically synthesize monocular/multi-view videos first and then fit a 4D representation, which is expensive and suffers from incomplete geometry and view-inconsistent renderings. The goal is to directly generate high-quality 4D dynamic human representations from text prompts in an end-to-end manner.
AI.method: 4DHumanDiff is a diffusion framework that models the structured 4D Gaussian Splatting representation space end-to-end. It uses a 3D U-Net backbone with temporal attention for motion-aware generation. The authors construct a large-scale text-to-4DGS dataset with 60,000 pairs and introduce 2D regularization with training-free 4D interpolation to enhance rendering quality and motion smoothness.
AI.result: 4DHumanDiff generates consistent 360-degree dynamic humans within one minute, achieving better temporal and multi-view consistency compared to existing methods, and reduces inference time by more than 10x.
AI.conclusion: Directly generating 4DGS representations from text in an end-to-end diffusion framework is a viable and efficient alternative to video-then-reconstruction pipelines, producing view-consistent and temporally coherent dynamic human assets significantly faster.

title: Automated Transcript Analysis for Detecting Flaws in Agentic Benchmarks
summary: Capabilities of frontier models are often assessed using agentic benchmarks. To trust these results, benchmarks must accurately measure what they claim to and be free from invalidating flaws. Previous manual audits of benchmarks such as SWE-Bench-Verified have uncovered several validity issues in transcripts. However, manual review is difficult to scale, and it is unclear whether automated methods can reliably surface flaws that compromise benchmark validity. In this paper, we developed AI scanners to detect four types of validity issues: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. We produced grading rubrics for each to instruct human labeling, and evaluated the scanners against human labels on a held-out test set of Inspect Evals benchmarks. Our scanners identified several verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. Not all cases were identified, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria and models. We highlight several open challenges to be addressed to improve scanners for stronger quality assurance claims, including broader standardization gaps in the evaluation field that degrade scanner performance. Together, these results serve as a proof of concept for using automated transcript analysis to audit benchmark quality more broadly.

AI.tldr: This paper develops AI-based "scanners" to automatically detect four types of validity issues in agentic benchmark evaluations: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. Evaluated against human labels on Inspect Evals benchmarks, the scanners identified verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, though performance varied substantially. The work serves as a proof of concept for automated transcript analysis to audit benchmark quality at scale.
AI.motivation: Agentic benchmarks are used to assess frontier model capabilities, but their results are only trustworthy if the benchmarks are free from validity flaws. Manual audits (e.g., of SWE-Bench-Verified) have uncovered validity issues, but manual review does not scale. It is unclear whether automated methods can reliably surface flaws that compromise benchmark validity.
AI.method: The authors developed AI scanners targeting four validity issue types: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. They created grading rubrics to guide human labeling, then evaluated the scanners against human labels on a held-out test set from Inspect Evals benchmarks.
AI.result: The scanners identified several verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. However, not all issues were identified, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria, and models. Broader standardization gaps in the evaluation field degraded scanner performance.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a proof of concept for using automated transcript analysis to audit benchmark quality at scale, while highlighting open challenges—including standardization gaps—that must be addressed to strengthen quality assurance claims for benchmark validity.

title: Agentic Method for Deterministic Validation of Legacy Code Migration
summary: Migration of legacy COBOL programs to Java requires extensive testing to ensure correct functionality. This effort is often complicated by the lack of test data and the difficulty of validating all corner cases. In this paper we propose a novel agentic test-synthesis method, the "Locksmith Loop," which is initiated by preparing two runtime environments: the COBOL source and the generated Java target are each instrumented with mocks and executed off-mainframe on commodity hardware, then an iterative agentic loop performs Witness Search over input mocks to penetrate program branches, followed by parity-preserving mutations. When routing boundaries are reached, an analyzer identifies a Locked Paragraph: a condition preventing deeper exploration. Across three COBOL-Java case studies, spanning two open-source programs and one internal production-like COBOL program and ranging from 430 to 4,114 source lines, Locksmith consistently improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus, reaching nearly complete coverage on the two open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on the internal production-like COBOL program. The generated Java matched the COBOL reference under deterministic parity checks in all accepted test cases. Through these findings we demonstrate, to the best of our knowledge, a novel approach for validating agentic coding output using a deterministic oracle.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "Locksmith Loop," an agentic test-synthesis method for validating migrated COBOL-to-Java code. It sets up dual runtime environments (COBOL source and Java target with mocks), then iteratively searches for test inputs using Witness Search and parity-preserving mutations to penetrate program branches, identifying "Locked Paragraphs" when exploration stalls. Results across three case studies (430-4,114 SLOC) show near-complete coverage on open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on an internal production-like COBOL program, with all accepted test cases passing deterministic parity checks against the COBOL reference.
AI.motivation: Testing migrated COBOL-to-Java programs is difficult due to lack of test data and challenges in validating corner cases, making it hard to ensure correct functionality of the migrated code.
AI.method: The method involves: (1) preparing two runtime environments where COBOL source and generated Java target are instrumented with mocks and executed off-mainframe on commodity hardware; (2) running an iterative agentic loop performing Witness Search over input mocks to penetrate branches, followed by parity-preserving mutations; (3) when routing boundaries are reached, an analyzer identifies a "Locked Paragraph"—a condition preventing deeper exploration—to guide further test generation.
AI.result: Across three COBOL-Java case studies (two open-source and one internal production-like, ranging from 430 to 4,114 SLOC), Locksmith consistently improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus. It achieved nearly complete coverage on the two open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on the internal production-like COBOL program. All accepted test cases matched the COBOL reference under deterministic parity checks.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a novel approach for validating agentic coding output using a deterministic oracle, where the original COBOL program serves as the reference for parity checks, enabling rigorous validation of migrated Java code even in the absence of pre-existing test data.

title: Explorative Modeling: Unlocking a Third Pretraining Axis and End-to-End Generation
summary: The deep learning revolution, kicked off by AlexNet, taught us that end-to-end training beats decomposing a problem into hand-designed stages. Generative modeling, however, has remained the exception-despite generative models being remarkably capable, they are still not trained end-to-end. This is because, at its core, generative modeling is about handling distributions with many modes, and existing scalable approaches handle this the same way, by factoring the generation procedure, which prevents end-to-end generation. In this work, we introduce Explorative Modeling, a new paradigm that instead factors the training loop, exploring K candidate matches between model generations and data, and training on the best, so predictions commit to modes rather than blurring them. We find Explorative Models (XMs) useful in two settings. First, increasing exploration adds a third pretraining axis beyond parameters and data for existing generative models-where scaling exploration monotonically improves performance across both continuous and discrete domains (images, video, and language). Notably, gains from exploration increase with scale, climbing from 7% to 36% as data scales and from 13% to 23% as models grow, with efficiency gains more than doubling at 3x the compute. Concretely, exploration improves FLOP efficiency by 4.1x, sample efficiency by 6.2x, parameter efficiency by 47%, lifts the strongest of image-generation recipes to a near-state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance, enables scaling how end-to-end existing models are, and unlocks scaling generalization. Second, XMs enable end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling, matching diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps. Together, these results establish XMs as both a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Explorative Modeling (XM), a new generative modeling paradigm that factors the training loop by exploring K candidate matches between model generations and data, then training on the best match. This allows predictions to commit to modes rather than blurring them, enabling both a new scaling axis for existing generative models (beyond parameters and data) and standalone end-to-end generative modeling. XMs show monotonic performance improvements across images, video, and language, with 4.1x FLOP efficiency, 6.2x sample efficiency, 47% parameter efficiency gains, near-SOTA 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance, and 16-256x fewer inference steps than diffusion on control tasks.
AI.motivation: Unlike the rest of deep learning, generative models are still not trained end-to-end because scalable approaches handle many-moded distributions by factoring the generation procedure. The authors aim to overcome this by introducing a paradigm that factors the training loop instead, enabling end-to-end generation while preserving scalability.
AI.method: Explorative Modeling (XM) factors the training loop by exploring K candidate matches between model generations and data, then training on the best match so predictions commit to specific modes. Exploration can be scaled as a third pretraining axis (alongside parameters and data) for existing generative models across domains, and XMs also enable standalone end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling.
AI.result: Exploration scaling monotonically improves performance across images, video, and language. Gains increase with scale (7% to 36% as data scales, 13% to 23% as models grow). XMs achieve 4.1x FLOP efficiency, 6.2x sample efficiency, 47% parameter efficiency, a 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance (near SOTA), and enable end-to-end reconstructive modeling that matches diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps.
AI.conclusion: Explorative Models serve both as a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and as a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm, establishing exploration as a meaningful scaling dimension in generative modeling.

title: MMOOC: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Out-of-Context Evaluation in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks, but often fail under imperfect or shifted contexts. A reliable MLLM should refuse truly out-of-context (OOC) questions with subject-level context shifts while still answering shifted in-context (Shifted IC) questions with non-subject context shifts. Existing benchmarks mainly target OOC or visually unanswerable questions, but overlook answerable Shifted IC cases and cover limited OOC shifts. To fill this gap, we present MMOOC, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating refusal and robust answering abilities of MLLMs. MMOOC contains over 41K image-question pairs, including answerable Shifted IC cases and unanswerable OOC cases, spanning three question formats, eight shift types and six visual scenarios, with data quality ensured through MLLM-based filtering and human verification. We evaluate model responses using Accuracy and Refusal Rate, and further introduce an LLM-as-a-Judge metric to assess the correctness of model reasoning. Experiments on diverse MLLMs show that current models still struggle to balance answer-ability and refusal under shifted contexts. We further analyze key failure patterns and show that post-training can improve robustness. MMOOC will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MMOOC, a large-scale benchmark (over 41K image-question pairs) for evaluating multimodal LLMs' refusal and robust answering abilities under context shifts, covering both answerable shifted in-context (Shifted IC) and unanswerable out-of-context (OOC) cases across three question formats, eight shift types, and six visual scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs fail under imperfect or shifted contexts. While current benchmarks focus on OOC or visually unanswerable questions, they overlook answerable Shifted IC cases and cover only limited OOC shift types. There is a gap in comprehensively evaluating both refusal (for truly OOC questions) and robust answering (for Shifted IC questions) capabilities.
AI.method: The authors construct MMOOC, a benchmark containing over 41K image-question pairs with answerable Shifted IC and unanswerable OOC cases, spanning three question formats, eight shift types, and six visual scenarios. Data quality is ensured through MLLM-based filtering and human verification. Evaluation uses Accuracy and Refusal Rate, plus an LLM-as-a-Judge metric for reasoning correctness.
AI.result: Experiments on diverse MLLMs show current models still struggle to balance answerability and refusal under shifted contexts. Key failure patterns are identified, and post-training is shown to improve robustness.
AI.conclusion: MMOOC provides a comprehensive benchmark highlighting the unresolved challenge of balancing refusal and robust answering in MLLMs under shifted contexts, and the dataset will be made publicly available.

title: AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge
summary: As generative artificial intelligence becomes one of the most significant systems of knowledge production in our society today, questions relating to who can access and shape that production grow increasingly important in our discourse. This paper argues that the existing frameworks for AI literacy, which are dominated by technical competency and responsible-use principles, are insufficient because they enforce a "consumer" orientation toward AI rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. Based upon Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of AI literacy as a critical practice that equips individuals not just to use AI systems, but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance. The paper further argues that unequal access to AI tools in society recapitulates longstanding epistemic injustices, and that a literacy framework oriented toward empowerment must account for these structural inequities. A three-part framework of AI literacy based on the notions of contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance frames this literacy as a cultivation of epistemic "agents" rather than the training of competent consumers of AI-generated information.
