AI.tldr: This paper proposes a reconceptualization of AI literacy as a critical practice grounded in Foucault's power-knowledge, Freire's critical consciousness, and digital literacy scholarship. It argues that current AI literacy frameworks (focused on technical competency and responsible use) promote a "consumer" orientation rather than genuine epistemic agency. The paper proposes a three-part framework—contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance—to cultivate individuals as epistemic agents who can evaluate, resist, and govern AI systems, while addressing structural inequities that recapitulate epistemic injustices.
AI.motivation: As generative AI becomes a dominant system of knowledge production, current AI literacy frameworks—dominated by technical competency and responsible use—are insufficient because they enforce consumer orientations toward AI rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. This paper addresses the critical gap in how literacy frameworks account for power, access, and governance.
AI.method: The paper draws on theoretical synthesis, combining Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and digital literacy scholarship to reconceptualize AI literacy. It proposes a three-part framework based on contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance.
AI.result: The paper presents a reconceptualized AI literacy framework oriented toward empowerment that accounts for structural inequities and positions individuals as epistemic agents rather than competent consumers of AI-generated information.
AI.conclusion: AI literacy should be reframed as a critical practice that equips individuals not merely to use AI systems, but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance.

title: From Textual Requirements to Microservice Architectures - A Comprehensive Evaluation of LLM-Based Design Synthesis
summary: Microservice architectures have become dominant for modernizing monolithic systems, yet identifying appropriate services remains challenging and largely manual. Existing decomposition approaches are predominantly code-centric, limiting applicability in early design stages where only textual requirements are available. Despite advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), limited empirical evidence exists on their ability to synthesize complete microservice architectures from natural-language requirements, including service definitions and inter-service interactions. This study investigates whether an LLM can bridge requirements engineering and architectural design, generating architectures solely from textual requirements and evaluating structural agreement and perceived quality of results. We conduct a mixed-method study using OpenAI o3 under zero-shot (ZS) and few-shot (FS) prompting across two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic), one execution per system/condition. Architectures are evaluated through (i) comparison with reference architectures using precision, recall, and F1-score for service identification and communication recovery, and (ii) a blinded expert assessment of correctness, completeness, modularity, and plausibility, plus open feedback synthesis. OpenAI o3 identifies services with higher agreement under FS prompting (F1 = 0.79 for ZS versus = 0.97 for FS). Communication recovery is more challenging: ZS produces dense architectures with high recall but low precision (F1 = 0.61), while FS improves agreement, reaching F1 = 0.82 and reducing unsupported dependencies. Expert evaluation corroborates these results, with FS architectures perceived as more modular, coherent, and plausible than ZS outputs. OpenAI o3 shows potential for requirements-driven synthesis when guided by exemplar prompting. Results are model- and context-specific from two small systems, not model-independent proof.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether an LLM (OpenAI o3) can generate complete microservice architectures directly from natural-language requirements, using zero-shot and few-shot prompting across two systems. Few-shot prompting significantly outperforms zero-shot in both service identification (F1=0.97 vs 0.79) and communication recovery (F1=0.82 vs 0.61), with expert evaluation corroborating that few-shot architectures are more modular and plausible. Results are promising but model- and context-specific, limited to two small systems.
AI.motivation: Microservice decomposition remains largely manual and code-centric, limiting applicability during early design stages when only textual requirements exist. Despite advances in LLMs, there is limited empirical evidence on their ability to synthesize complete microservice architectures (services plus inter-service interactions) directly from natural-language requirements.
AI.method: Mixed-method study using OpenAI o3 with zero-shot (ZS) and few-shot (FS) prompting across two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic), one execution per system/condition. Architectures are evaluated via (i) quantitative comparison against reference architectures using precision, recall, and F1-score for service identification and communication recovery, and (ii) blinded expert assessment covering correctness, completeness, modularity, and plausibility, complemented by open feedback synthesis.
AI.result: FS prompting achieves higher service identification agreement (F1=0.97 vs 0.79 for ZS). Communication recovery is more challenging: ZS yields dense architectures with high recall but low precision (F1=0.61), while FS improves agreement to F1=0.82 and reduces unsupported dependencies. Expert evaluation corroborates these findings, with FS architectures perceived as more modular, coherent, and plausible than ZS outputs.
AI.conclusion: OpenAI o3 shows potential for requirements-driven microservice architecture synthesis when guided by exemplar prompting. However, the results are model- and context-specific based on two small systems and do not constitute model-independent proof of capability.

title: The Convergence Behavior of Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise
summary: We establish the first convergence guarantees for the plain vector-form \emph{Adam} optimizer under heavy-tailed stochastic noise. While several Adam variants are known to achieve optimal iteration complexity in bounded-variance nonconvex optimization, little is understood about their behavior when stochastic gradients admit only a bounded $p$-th central moment for some $p \in (1,2]$, a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning. To address this gap, we generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise. Building on this generalized framework, we develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam, without restrictive parameter coupling. Our results show that Adam converges to $(ρ,ε)$-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise. However, it exhibits a suboptimal iteration complexity and $p$-dependent convergence, a suboptimality that persists even in the bounded-variance case ($p=2$). When the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, a standard setup in related literature, the convergence rate improves to match the optimal complexity. These findings provide new theoretical insight into the robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes the first convergence guarantees for plain vector-form Adam optimizer under heavy-tailed stochastic noise (bounded p-th central moment for p∈(1,2]). It generalizes the online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise and shows Adam converges to (ρ,ε)-stationary points, though with suboptimal iteration complexity and p-dependent convergence. When the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, the rate improves to match optimal complexity.
AI.motivation: Adam variants are known to achieve optimal iteration complexity under bounded-variance settings in nonconvex optimization, but their behavior under heavy-tailed stochastic gradients—a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning—is not well understood. This paper addresses this gap by providing the first theoretical convergence guarantees for Adam in this challenging regime.
AI.method: The authors generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise. They then develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam without restrictive parameter coupling, enabling convergence guarantees independent of typical coupling assumptions between hyperparameters.
AI.result: Adam converges to (ρ,ε)-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise, but exhibits suboptimal iteration complexity and p-dependent convergence, which persists even in the bounded-variance case (p=2). When the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, the convergence rate improves to optimal complexity.
AI.conclusion: These findings provide new theoretical insight into the robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes, characterizing a trade-off between its practical popularity and theoretical optimality guarantees depending on the availability of domain information.

title: Learning Color Grading, No Photo Sharing: Federated Aesthetic Preference Learning for Personalized Image Enhancement
summary: Personalized image enhancement should reflect individual aesthetic taste, yet learning such preferences commonly depends on private photos and ratings that are unsuitable for centralized collection. The task must infer preference from sparse, heterogeneous feedback and translate it into natural-looking color transformations on resource-constrained user devices. We introduce FedPAIE, a federated personalized aesthetic image enhancement framework for user-adaptive color grading without centralizing raw photos or ratings. FedPAIE trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer, calibrates it into a personalized scorer on a small local support set, and freezes it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer from unpaired local photographs. Fidelity constraints and an excess-gap penalty regularize scorer-guided adaptation to limit proxy-score over-optimization while preserving content and natural appearance. Training remains lightweight throughout the pipeline: scorer learning updates at most 0.787M parameters, enhancer adaptation updates 0.265M, and inference retains only a 0.293M-parameter personalized enhancer. Experiments on MIT-Adobe FiveK and Flickr-AES demonstrate effective open-world personalization and a favorable balance between user preference and image fidelity. FedPAIE thus connects decentralized preference learning with efficient personalized image transformation without requiring paired user retouches.

AI.tldr: FedPAIE is a federated framework for personalized aesthetic image enhancement (color grading) that infers individual user taste from sparse local feedback without centralizing photos or ratings. It trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer, personalizes it on small local support sets, and uses it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer on unpaired local photos, achieving efficient on-device personalization.
AI.motivation: Personalized image enhancement should reflect individual aesthetic taste, but learning such preferences typically depends on private photos and ratings unsuitable for centralized collection, requiring inference from sparse, heterogeneous feedback while producing natural-looking transformations on resource-constrained devices.
AI.method: FedPAIE trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer, calibrates it into a personalized scorer on a small local support set, then freezes it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer from unpaired local photographs. Fidelity constraints and an excess-gap penalty regularize scorer-guided adaptation to prevent proxy-score over-optimization while preserving content and natural appearance.
AI.result: Scorer learning updates at most 0.787M parameters, enhancer adaptation updates 0.265M, and inference retains only a 0.293M-parameter personalized enhancer. Experiments on MIT-Adobe FiveK and Flickr-AES demonstrate effective open-world personalization and a favorable balance between user preference and image fidelity.
AI.conclusion: FedPAIE connects decentralized preference learning with efficient personalized image transformation without requiring paired user retouches, offering a practical solution for privacy-preserving, on-device aesthetic personalization.

title: Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation
summary: This research evaluates the efficacy of large language models (LLMs) in generating new product ideas. To do so, we compare three pools of ideas for new products targeted toward college students and priced at 50 dollars or less. The first pool of ideas was created by university students in a product design course before the availability of LLMs. The second and third pools of ideas were generated by GPT-4 from OpenAI using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, respectively. We evaluated idea quality using standard market research techniques to predict average purchase intent probability. We used text mining to assess idea similarity and human raters to evaluate idea novelty. We find that AI-generated ideas outperform human-generated ideas in terms of average purchase intent, with few-shot prompting yielding slightly higher intent than zero-shot prompting. However, AI-generated ideas are perceived as less novel and exhibit higher pairwise similarity, particularly with few-shot prompting, indicating a less diverse solution landscape. When focusing on the quality of the best ideas rather than the average ideas, we find that AI-generated ideas are seven times more likely to rank among the top 10 percent of ideas, demonstrating a significant advantage over human-generated ideas. We propose that this seven-to-one advantage is a conservative estimate because it does not account for the greater productivity of AI. Our findings suggest that despite some drawbacks, AI creativity presents a substantial benefit in generating high-quality ideas for new product development.

AI.tldr: This paper compares human-generated product ideas with AI (GPT-4) generated ideas for new products targeting college students. AI ideas outperform human ideas in average purchase intent and are 7x more likely to be top-tier, but are less novel and more similar to each other.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether large language models can effectively generate high-quality new product ideas compared to human designers.
AI.method: Compared three idea pools: (1) student-generated ideas from a pre-LLM product design course, (2) GPT-4 zero-shot ideas, and (3) GPT-4 few-shot ideas. Evaluated ideas using market research techniques for purchase intent, text mining for similarity, and human raters for novelty.
AI.result: AI ideas outperformed human ideas in average purchase intent (few-shot slightly better than zero-shot), but were perceived as less novel with higher pairwise similarity. AI ideas were 7x more likely to rank in the top 10% of ideas.
AI.conclusion: Despite lower novelty and diversity, AI creativity offers substantial advantages in generating high-quality product ideas, with the 7:1 top-quartile advantage being a conservative estimate not accounting for AI's greater productivity.

title: Structural Validation of LLM-Generated Microservice Decompositions Using Source-Code Dependencies
summary: Decomposing monolithic systems into microservices is a key activity in software modernization. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate semantically plausible decompositions from textual requirements, it remains unclear whether these proposals preserve the structural dependencies implemented in the source code. This paper evaluates the structural adherence of microservice decompositions generated by OpenAI o3 for the PetClinic and Bookstore systems. We propose an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis and compare zero-shot and few-shot prompting using dependency preservation (TPD) and dependency violation (TVD) metrics. A robustness analysis was conducted to control for differences in class-to-service mapping coverage. After normalization, both prompting strategies produced equivalent structural adherence, achieving TPD values of 68.0% (PetClinic) and 83.3% (Bookstore). The findings demonstrate that structural evaluations of LLM-generated decompositions should explicitly control for mapping coverage, as apparent differences between prompting strategies may otherwise reflect methodological bias rather than genuine architectural quality.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether microservice decompositions generated by OpenAI o3 preserve structural source-code dependencies, proposing an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis. Comparing zero-shot and few-shot prompting on PetClinic and Bookstore systems, both strategies yield equivalent structural adherence after normalizing for mapping coverage, with TPD values of 68.0% and 83.3% respectively.
AI.motivation: While LLMs can generate plausible microservice decompositions from textual requirements, it remains unclear whether these proposals preserve the structural dependencies actually implemented in the source code—a critical concern for software modernization contexts where architecture must reflect implementation reality.
AI.method: The authors propose an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis. They compare zero-shot and few-shot prompting of OpenAI o3 on two systems (PetClinic and Bookstore), using dependency preservation (TPD) and dependency violation (TVD) metrics. A robustness analysis controls for differences in class-to-service mapping coverage, followed by normalization of results.
AI.result: After normalization for mapping coverage, both prompting strategies produced equivalent structural adherence. TPD values reached 68.0% for PetClinic and 83.3% for Bookstore. Apparent differences between prompting strategies were shown to reflect methodological bias from mapping coverage rather than genuine architectural quality differences.
AI.conclusion: Structural evaluations of LLM-generated decompositions must explicitly control for mapping coverage; otherwise, observed differences between prompting strategies may be artifacts of methodological bias rather than indicators of true architectural quality.

title: FunL2O: LLM-Guided Feature Function Design for Learning to Optimize
summary: Learning-to-optimize (L2O) methods accelerate repeated optimization by training models to predict solutions, warm starts, branching decisions, or other forms of solver guidance. A critical yet largely overlooked component of these pipelines is the feature function that maps problem instances to inputs for machine learning models. Existing L2O methods typically rely on hand-crafted features, making representation design manual and largely fixed across domains. We introduce FunL2O, the first unified framework for automating feature design through LLM-driven program evolution for L2O. In a FunSearch-style loop, an LLM proposes executable feature functions, while a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model and measures downstream optimization performance. We evaluate FunL2O on linear and quadratic programming tasks involving solution prediction and warm-starting, as well as on mixed-integer optimization tasks using GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search. Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks and four LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations. These results establish LLM-driven feature evolution as a general and effective approach to automating representation design in L2O.

AI.tldr: FunL2O is the first unified framework that automates feature design in learning-to-optimize (L2O) pipelines by using LLM-driven program evolution in a FunSearch-style loop. It evolves executable feature functions that map problem instances to ML model inputs, consistently outperforming hand-crafted representations across continuous optimization (LP/QP), mixed-integer optimization (backdoor branching, Predict-and-Search), and four different LLMs.
AI.motivation: L2O methods rely on ML models to accelerate optimization, but the feature function that converts problem instances into model inputs is largely overlooked and manual. Existing approaches depend on hand-crafted features, making representation design domain-specific, inflexible, and suboptimal.
AI.method: FunL2O employs a FunSearch-style iterative loop where an LLM proposes executable feature functions, and a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model to measure downstream optimization performance, using the feedback to guide further evolution. It is evaluated on LP/QP solution prediction and warm-starting, plus mixed-integer optimization with GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search.
AI.result: Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks and four different LLMs, the evolved features from FunL2O consistently outperform hand-crafted representations, demonstrating the effectiveness of LLM-driven feature evolution for L2O.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven feature evolution is a general, automated, and effective approach to representation design in L2O, eliminating the need for manual feature engineering across diverse optimization problem types.

title: Witness Evidence Portfolios: Single-Prefill Risk Detection for Closed Multimodal Answers
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures; includes supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/SouthWinter/WEP
summary: Reliable deployment of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) requires deciding whether a confident visual answer should be trusted, reviewed, or routed to a stronger system. Confidence scores capture candidate margins, but not where the estimated signed visual readouts associated with those margins come from or how they are distributed. We study inference-time risk detection for closed visual answers using the same white-box prefill path that produces the answer. Witness Evidence Portfolios (WEP) first estimates, layer by layer, which visual contributions support or contradict the predicted candidate. It summarizes these contributions through two interpretable route families: question-related evidence provenance and signed evidence concentration. Nested grouped validation chooses the more reliable family and a sparse top-k route portfolio, which is fused with candidate confidence. WEP needs no image perturbation, decoding change, backward pass, or external verifier. Across three MLLMs and four binary-answer benchmarks, WEP improves mean error AP by 0.134. All 12 model--dataset gains are positive, and image-cluster bootstrap intervals are strictly positive on 10 pairs. WEP targets white-box closed-answer systems and uses a labeled calibration slice.

AI.tldr: WEP is a white-box inference-time risk detection method for multimodal LLMs that estimates layer-by-layer which visual contributions support or contradict a predicted answer, summarizes them into interpretable route families (question-related evidence provenance and signed evidence concentration), and fuses them with candidate confidence via nested grouped validation to decide whether a visual answer should be trusted, reviewed, or routed to a stronger system.
AI.motivation: Reliable deployment of MLLMs requires deciding whether a confident visual answer should be trusted, reviewed, or routed to a stronger system. Existing confidence scores capture candidate margins but not where the signed visual readouts associated with those margins come from or how they are distributed, motivating a method that uses the same white-box prefill path that produces the answer to estimate risk.
AI.method: WEP estimates layer-by-layer which visual contributions support or contradict the predicted candidate, then summarizes these via two interpretable route families: question-related evidence provenance and signed evidence concentration. Nested grouped validation selects the more reliable family and a sparse top-k route portfolio, which is fused with candidate confidence. It requires no image perturbation, decoding change, backward pass, or external verifier.
AI.result: Across three MLLMs and four binary-answer benchmarks, WEP improves mean error AP by 0.134. All 12 model-dataset gains are positive, and image-cluster bootstrap intervals are strictly positive on 10 pairs.
AI.conclusion: WEP effectively improves inference-time risk detection for closed visual answers in white-box MLLM systems, using only the prefill path and a labeled calibration slice, with consistently positive gains across models and benchmarks.

title: Evaluating Agentic Bioinformatics through Function, Evidence, and Validation
summary: Large language model agents increasingly plan, execute, and interpret biological analyses, yet fluent responses, successful tool calls, and benchmark performance alone do not establish scientific credibility. Existing reviews primarily organize biological agents by application, architecture, and agentic capability, but do not jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. We address this gap by treating the inspectable workflow trajectory, rather than architecture or final output alone, as the primary unit of analysis. We introduce the Function--Evidence--Validation (FEV) framework, which separates demonstrated workflow operations, traceable support for actions and claims, and use-case-specific validation. Using FEV, we map 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark or evaluation resources, representing 128 unique publications across genomics, single-cell and spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation. Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. We therefore argue that agentic bioinformatics should be assessed through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. FEV provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Function-Evidence-Validation (FEV) framework to assess the scientific credibility of LLM-based bioinformatics agents by analyzing inspectable workflow trajectories rather than final outputs alone. It maps 109 agentic systems and 28 evaluation resources across 128 publications, finding that planning and tool execution have outpaced provenance, replayability, and rigorous scientific validation.
AI.motivation: LLM agents for biological analysis can produce fluent responses and pass benchmarks, yet neither of these guarantees scientific credibility. Existing reviews organize agents by application, architecture, or capability but fail to jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. A gap exists in treating the workflow trajectory itself as the primary unit of assessment.
AI.method: The authors propose the Function-Evidence-Validation (FEV) framework, which separates (1) demonstrated workflow operations (function), (2) traceable support for actions and claims (evidence), and (3) use-case-specific validation. Using FEV, they systematically map 109 agentic/agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark/evaluation resources across 128 publications covering genomics, single-cell/spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation.
AI.result: Across all surveyed domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. The analysis reveals a systematic imbalance in maturity between execution capabilities and credibility-related properties of agent workflows.
AI.conclusion: Agentic bioinformatics should be evaluated through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. The FEV framework provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

title: Demystifying Solana Bots: From GitHub Blueprints to On-Chain Fingerprints
summary: Solana is an emerging blockchain platform designed for high throughput and low transaction fees, making it inexpensive to submit transactions at scale and, consequently, increasing exposure to bot spamming and related financial exploitation. Solana bots are typically off-chain software systems that operate in a competitive on-chain execution environment by constructing and submitting transactions, and the bot-related transactions on the decentralized exchanges exceed 250 million dollars in daily trading volume in January 2026. Prior studies on Solana have examined system performance, smart-contract security, and specific on-chain phenomena. However, we still lack a systematic understanding of what Solana bots implement in practice and how these implementations manifest as observable on-chain execution fingerprints. To address this gap, we performed a large-scale empirical study of Solana bots from two complementary views: (i) 586 bot repositories collected from GitHub, and (ii) 200 bot addresses on Solana, with over 44 million on-chain transactions. Our study derives an implementation-grounded taxonomy of Solana bots comprising 15 categories grouped into five domains (e.g., Trading Operations, MEV, and On-chain Analytics), identifies a largely shared five-stage operational pipeline manifested in bot implementations, and uncovers systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors of Solana bots across diverse trading platforms and assets. Based on our findings, we highlight future research directions, and provide recommendations for building and operating bots on the Solana blockchain.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study of Solana bots, combining 586 GitHub repositories and 200 on-chain bot addresses with over 44 million transactions, to derive an implementation-grounded taxonomy (15 categories across 5 domains), identify a shared five-stage operational pipeline, and uncover systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors.
AI.motivation: Solana's high throughput and low fees make it vulnerable to bot spamming and financial exploitation, yet there is no systematic understanding of what Solana bots implement in practice or how these implementations manifest as observable on-chain execution fingerprints.
AI.method: A two-view empirical study: (i) a static analysis of 586 bot repositories from GitHub, and (ii) an on-chain analysis of 200 bot addresses totaling over 44 million transactions on Solana.
AI.result: Derived a taxonomy of 15 bot categories across 5 domains (e.g., Trading Operations, MEV, On-chain Analytics), identified a largely shared five-stage operational pipeline in bot implementations, and uncovered systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors across trading platforms and assets.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a systematic view of Solana bot implementations and their on-chain fingerprints, highlighting future research directions and offering recommendations for building and operating bots on the Solana blockchain.

title: ECG-InterpBench: Benchmarking the Interpretability of ECG Foundation Models with Matched-Scale Sparse Autoencoders
comment: Research paper. Includes supplementary material and publicly available source code
summary: Existing benchmarks for electrocardiogram foundation models primarily evaluate downstream predictive performance, providing limited insight into whether their internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses. We introduce ECG-InterpBench, a benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations. ECG-InterpBench uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments and matches their capacity across models to enable controlled comparisons. We evaluate six frozen ECG foundation models across five standardized encoder depths, five matched dictionary widths, and three random seeds, producing a 450-cell interpretability atlas comprising 75 exactly matched six-model comparison blocks. The benchmark evaluates complementary dimensions of representation interpretability, including sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility and coverage of 49 clinically meaningful ECG measurements, and cross-seed feature reproducibility. The evaluation further quantifies patient-sampling uncertainty, depth- and seed-dependent variation, and sensitivity to the sparsity parameterization. The benchmark reveals that ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles. A matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms that reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. The benchmark is accompanied by executable evaluation code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits. ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled and reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability.

AI.tldr: ECG-InterpBench is a benchmark for systematically evaluating the interpretability of ECG foundation models using sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments, producing a 450-cell interpretability atlas across six models, five encoder depths, five dictionary widths, and three seeds, evaluating sparse reconstruction fidelity, clinical feature accessibility/coverage, and cross-seed reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Existing ECG foundation model benchmarks only measure downstream predictive performance, providing no insight into whether internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses. A dedicated interpretability benchmark is needed.
AI.method: The benchmark uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments with capacity matched across models. It evaluates six frozen ECG foundation models across five encoder depths, five dictionary widths, and three seeds, yielding a 450-cell interpretability atlas with 75 matched six-model comparison blocks. It measures sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility and coverage of 49 clinical ECG measurements, and cross-seed feature reproducibility, while quantifying patient-sampling uncertainty, depth/seed variation, and sparsity-parameter sensitivity.
AI.result: ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles. A matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG shows that reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models, indicating these dimensions are complementary and not interchangeable.
AI.conclusion: ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled, reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability. The benchmark is released with executable code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits.

title: JigShape: Evaluating Visual-Geometric Reasoning in VLMs through Jigsaw Puzzles
summary: Jigsaw puzzle solving requires jointly reasoning about visual content and geometric constraints, yet existing benchmarks use rectangular cuts that create ambiguous ground truth in texture-repeated regions. We introduce \textit{\ours{}}, a benchmark with tab-and-blank interlocking pieces where geometric constraints provide strong local compatibility requirements that, combined with visual content, yield unambiguous ground truth. Across 95K instances at four grid densities (4$\times$4 to 16$\times$16), we find that \textbf{zero-shot VLMs largely lack geometric reasoning}: only one of five frontier models (GPT-5.5) exceeds random baseline on 4$\times$4 puzzles, while all others perform at chance level. While supervised fine-tuning achieves $>$97\% on 4$\times$4, \textbf{all models collapse on larger grids}: GPT-5.5 drops from 70\% to near-random on 8$\times$8, and even fine-tuned models fall below 5\% on 12$\times$12. This ``scaling cliff'' suggests current architectures cannot maintain consistent constraint satisfaction as the number of pieces increases. \ours{} establishes scalable geometric reasoning as an open challenge for vision-language models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark for jigsaw puzzle solving with tab-and-blank interlocking pieces that provide unambiguous ground truth via geometric constraints. Across 95K instances at grid densities from 4x4 to 16x16, the authors find that zero-shot VLMs largely lack geometric reasoning (only GPT-5.5 exceeds random baseline on 4x4), and all models collapse on larger grids—a "scaling cliff" that establishes scalable geometric reasoning as an open challenge.
AI.motivation: Existing jigsaw puzzle benchmarks use rectangular cuts that create ambiguous ground truth in texture-repeated regions, failing to properly evaluate geometric reasoning in vision-language models. A benchmark with unambiguous ground truth is needed to assess whether models truly reason about geometric constraints.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark with tab-and-blank interlocking puzzle pieces, where geometric constraints provide strong local compatibility requirements combined with visual content to yield unambiguous ground truth. The benchmark spans 95K instances across four grid densities (4x4 to 16x16). They evaluate five frontier zero-shot VLMs and supervised fine-tuned models.
AI.result: Only one of five frontier zero-shot VLMs (GPT-5.5) exceeds random baseline on 4x4 puzzles; all others perform at chance level. Supervised fine-tuning achieves >97% on 4x4, but all models collapse on larger grids: GPT-5.5 drops from 70% to near-random on 8x8, and fine-tuned models fall below 5% on 12x12.
AI.conclusion: The "scaling cliff" observed indicates current architectures cannot maintain consistent constraint satisfaction as piece count increases, establishing scalable geometric reasoning as an open challenge for vision-language models.

title: DeepResearch Agent System
summary: The DeepResearch Agent System is a large language model system engineered for deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks. Built upon a sparse activation architecture with 30 billion total parameters of which only 3 billion are activated per token, the system achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple agent search benchmarks while delivering 3.2 times faster inference compared to dense counterparts of equivalent scale. The system supports a 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention mechanisms that yield 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements over standard long-context approaches. A dual-mode reasoning engine provides both a ReAct paradigm for basic multi-step problem solving and an IterResearch mode for high-performance iterative research with up to 20 reasoning steps, collectively delivering a 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines. Multi-tool coordination integrates retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing modules to achieve 92.1% tool-use accuracy. A reinforcement learning optimization framework based on the GRPO algorithm provides token-level policy gradients that improve training stability by 35% and accelerate convergence by 42%. An automated data synthesis pipeline with seed-based expansion achieves a 92.5% usability rate. Benchmark results include 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA. The system is fully open-sourced, including data synthesis, training, and inference code, and supports applications in academic research, business analysis, R&D support, and education.

AI.tldr: The DeepResearch Agent System is a sparse-activation LLM-based agent (30B total/3B active parameters) designed for deep information retrieval and autonomous research, achieving state-of-the-art results on agent search benchmarks with 3.2x faster inference than dense models, 128K context with hierarchical attention, dual-mode reasoning (ReAct and IterResearch), multi-tool coordination, GRPO-based RL optimization, and an automated data synthesis pipeline, all fully open-sourced.
AI.motivation: To build a large language model system capable of deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks that outperforms existing agent systems in accuracy, efficiency, and long-context handling, while remaining open-source and widely applicable.
AI.method: The system employs a sparse activation architecture (30B total, 3B active per token) with hierarchical attention for a 128K context window; a dual-mode reasoning engine combining a ReAct paradigm for basic multi-step problems and an IterResearch mode supporting up to 20 iterative reasoning steps; multi-tool coordination across retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing; GRPO-based reinforcement learning with token-level policy gradients for training stability and faster convergence; and an automated data synthesis pipeline using seed-based expansion.
AI.result: Achieves 3.2x faster inference than dense counterparts; 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements in long-context tasks; 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines; 92.1% tool-use accuracy; 35% training stability improvement and 42% faster convergence via GRPO; 92.5% data usability rate; benchmark scores of 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA.
AI.conclusion: The DeepResearch Agent System demonstrates that sparse activation combined with hierarchical attention, dual-mode reasoning, and RL-based optimization can deliver state-of-the-art agentic research performance with computational efficiency. As a fully open-sourced system covering data synthesis, training, and inference, it is positioned for broad applications in academic research, business analysis, R&D support, and education.

title: Emerging Challenges in Threat Modeling for GenAI-Augmented Systems: A View from the Trenches
comment: Accepted at the 2026 International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM)
summary: Threat modeling remains a central task in secure software engineering, as it enables the identification of security issues from system architectures. As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly pervasive across software systems, traditional threat modeling methods (e.g., STRIDE) are insufficient to assess emerging GenAI-specific risks. In this work, we present the first results from an exploratory assessment of GenAI-aware threat modeling methods in a Small and Medium Enterprise (SME) setting. For this, we conducted a rapid literature review to select relevant techniques and systematically applied three shortlisted methods to an industrial case study involving a GenAI-augmented system. The results highlight differences in the threats identified by each technique and reveal limited support for certain GenAI-specific risk categories, particularly those related to software supply chains and human-centered security issues. We further report practitioners' perceptions of the usability and integration of these methods in SME development workflows, including their perceived effort and adoption challenges.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an exploratory assessment of GenAI-aware threat modeling methods applied in a Small and Medium Enterprise (SME) setting. Three selected methods were systematically applied to an industrial case study of a GenAI-augmented system, revealing differences in identified threats and limited coverage of GenAI-specific risk categories such as software supply chain and human-centered security issues. Practitioner feedback highlighted usability concerns and adoption challenges within SME workflows.
AI.motivation: Traditional threat modeling methods like STRIDE are insufficient for assessing emerging GenAI-specific security risks, yet GenAI systems are becoming increasingly pervasive. There is a need to evaluate whether existing GenAI-aware threat modeling techniques are suitable for industrial practice, particularly in resource-constrained SME environments where such methods might be adopted.
AI.method: The study conducted a rapid literature review to select relevant GenAI-aware threat modeling techniques, then systematically applied three shortlisted methods to an industrial case study of a GenAI-augmented system in an SME context. Findings were supplemented by collecting practitioners' perceptions on usability, integration, perceived effort, and adoption challenges.
AI.result: The assessment revealed differences in the threats identified by each technique, and highlighted limited support for certain GenAI-specific risk categories—particularly software supply chain risks and human-centered security issues. Practitioners reported varying perceptions of usability and integration of these methods in SME development workflows, along with concerns about effort and adoption barriers.
AI.conclusion: Existing GenAI-aware threat modeling methods have gaps in covering critical GenAI-specific risk areas (supply chain and human-centered security). While these methods can be applied in SME settings, adoption is hindered by perceived effort and integration challenges, indicating a need for more tailored threat modeling approaches for GenAI-augmented systems in small enterprises.

title: Context-Informed Ship Trajectory Prediction via Conditional Attention
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 29th International Conference on Information Fusion (IEEE FUSION)
summary:
Long-term ship trajectory prediction is a fundamental capability for maritime safety and autonomous navigation. While recent Transformer-based architectures have improved forecasting horizons, they predominantly rely on historical kinematic states, treating vessel motion as an isolated system. In reality, maritime navigation is profoundly modulated by extrinsic factors like weather and constrained by static vessel characteristics. Existing multimodal approaches fundamentally model the joint distribution over states and contexts, treating environmental variables as peer features rather than encoding the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions.
  In this work, we propose the Conditional Informer, a novel encoder-decoder architecture that formulates trajectory prediction as a conditional generation task. We employ a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where the vessel state explicitly queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates - but is not generated by - vessel dynamics. Furthermore, to address the intermittency of real-world data, we introduce a Modality Masking training strategy to prevent catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback. Extensive experiments on AIS and ERA5 data demonstrate that our approach outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Crucially, Modality Masking prevents shortcut learning, reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Conditional Informer, an encoder-decoder architecture for long-term ship trajectory prediction that formulates the task as conditional generation, explicitly encoding the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental contexts (weather) via a Conditional Attention mechanism, along with a Modality Masking training strategy to handle sensor data intermittency.
AI.motivation: Existing Transformer-based trajectory prediction methods treat vessel motion as an isolated system, relying only on historical kinematic states. Multimodal approaches that incorporate environmental variables treat them as peer features rather than encoding the directional physical dependence—weather modulates vessel dynamics but is not generated by them. Additionally, real-world sensor data is intermittent, causing catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback.
AI.method: The Conditional Informer uses a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where the vessel state explicitly queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates vessel dynamics. A Modality Masking training strategy is introduced to prevent shortcut learning and mitigate performance degradation during sensor fallback, addressing intermittency in real-world data.
AI.result: On AIS and ERA5 data, the approach outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Modality Masking reduces fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.
AI.conclusion: Encoding the causal/directional physical dependence between environmental contexts and vessel dynamics improves long-term trajectory prediction accuracy, and explicit masking-based training robustness is necessary to avoid shortcut learning and maintain performance during sensor unavailability.

title: RefineSVG: Visual Feedback-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Image-to-SVG Generation
comment: 17 pages, 5 main-paper figures. Accepted at the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026). Includes the complete supplementary material
summary: We propose RefineSVG, a single-step closed-loop visual feedback framework that enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perform high-fidelity image-to-SVG generation through self-correction. Existing MLLM-based approaches rely on single-pass open-loop inference, where the model receives visual input only once and must generate thousands of SVG code tokens without intermediate verification. This paradigm inevitably leads to geometric drift, error accumulation, and visual hallucination on complex images. RefineSVG overcomes this limitation by invoking an external rendering engine after an initial SVG generation pass to compare the rendered output against the target image. The comparison yields a multi-dimensional visual residual map (Diff-Map) that is fed back to the model as a ReAct-style correction signal, driving a targeted correction step. To support this render-observe-correct interaction, we further introduce an SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary that compresses token sequences by over 52%. A progressive training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampling cold-start data construction, and end-to-end agentic reinforcement learning aligns the model with closed-loop visual correction. Extensive experiments show that RefineSVG consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity, structural accuracy, and code efficiency.Code is available at https://github.com/liuxiaobo66/RefineSVG.

AI.tldr: RefineSVG is a single-step closed-loop visual feedback framework that enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perform high-fidelity image-to-SVG generation through self-correction. It uses an external rendering engine to compare rendered output against the target image, generating a multi-dimensional visual residual map (Diff-Map) fed back to the model as a ReAct-style correction signal. The framework introduces an SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary compressing token sequences by over 52%, and a progressive training pipeline (supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampling cold-start data construction, and end-to-end agentic reinforcement learning) aligns the model for closed-loop visual correction. It consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity, structural accuracy, and code efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM-based image-to-SVG generation approaches rely on single-pass open-loop inference, where the model receives visual input once and generates thousands of SVG code tokens without intermediate verification. This leads to geometric drift, error accumulation, and visual hallucination on complex images.
AI.method: RefineSVG adopts a closed-loop render-observe-correct interaction: (1) an initial SVG generation pass; (2) an external rendering engine compares the rendered output against the target image to produce a multi-dimensional visual residual map (Diff-Map); (3) the Diff-Map is fed back to the model as a ReAct-style correction signal to drive a targeted correction step. A new SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary compresses token sequences by over 52%. A progressive training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampling cold-start data construction, and end-to-end agentic reinforcement learning supports this framework.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show RefineSVG consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity, structural accuracy, and code efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The closed-loop visual feedback paradigm with Diff-Map-based self-correction effectively mitigates the limitations of open-loop MLLM-based SVG generation, delivering higher-fidelity results. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/liuxiaobo66/RefineSVG.

title: What makes prompts a graph: necessary and sufficient conditions for prompt graph engineering
summary: Prompts stopped being isolated strings some time ago. In real systems, one model call feeds another, retrieval interleaves with generation, routers branch, and aggregators merge parallel results. Practice converged on a single structure to hold this together: the graph. Frameworks such as LangGraph, DSPy, and Prompt Flow expose it openly, and research systems already optimize it automatically. The vocabulary, however, lags behind. Graph names, variously, a reasoning topology inside one sampling strategy, a multi-agent conversation, or an orchestration artifact, while prompt engineering still evokes writing one good string. What is missing is a reference definition treating prompts as nodes of an explicit, executable, improvable graph. We build that definition through conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers, complemented by primary grey literature. We reconstruct the genealogy of the idea, from dataflow graphs and build systems, through prompt chaining and the thought topologies (chain, tree, graph), to graphs compiled and optimized as artifacts. We then propose a constitutive definition of prompt graph engineering, state its four conditions (explicit structure, separation between structure and prompt content, executable semantics, and the graph as a first-class engineering artifact), and operationalize them as an inclusion and exclusion test. We draw the boundary against six neighboring concepts and apply the test to six real systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, and Claude Code subagents); it includes and excludes consistently. We close with a research agenda organized along four design tension axes. The contribution is an operational definition and a shared vocabulary for a practice that industry already exercises daily without naming precisely.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a constitutive definition of "prompt graph engineering" — treating prompts as nodes of an explicit, executable, improvable graph — backed by four operational conditions (explicit structure, structure/prompt content separation, executable semantics, and the graph as a first-class engineering artifact), validated via an inclusion/exclusion test against six real systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, Claude Code subagents) and contrasted with six neighboring concepts.
AI.motivation: While industry practice has converged on graph-structured prompt orchestration (e.g., LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow) and research systems already optimize such graphs automatically, the vocabulary lags behind: "prompt engineering" still evokes writing a single string, and the term "graph" is used inconsistently across reasoning topologies, multi-agent conversations, and orchestration artifacts. A precise reference definition is missing.
AI.method: The paper performs conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers, supplemented by primary grey literature. It reconstructs the genealogy of the idea (from dataflow graphs and build systems, through prompt chaining and thought topologies like chain/tree/graph, to compiled and optimized graphs), then proposes a constitutive definition of prompt graph engineering with four conditions (explicit structure, separation of structure from prompt content, executable semantics, and the graph as a first-class engineering artifact), operationalized as an inclusion/exclusion test. The test is applied to six neighboring concepts and six real systems.
AI.result: The four-condition definition consistently includes and excludes the six candidate systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, Claude Code subagents) and cleanly draws boundaries against six neighboring concepts. The paper delivers an operational definition and shared vocabulary, closing with a research agenda organized across four design tension axes.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is an operational, testable definition and a shared vocabulary for a practice that industry already exercises daily without naming precisely. This foundational framing aims to bring conceptual clarity and enable further research on graph-based prompt engineering.

title: CoGate: Confidence-Gated Co-Decoding for Secure Code Generation
summary: Large language models are widely used for code generation, but they can also produce insecure programs due to patterns learned from their pretraining data. Decoding-time steering has become an important solution to this problem: a small expert model is combined with the target model at each step to generate more secure code, which is referred to as co-decoding. However, the acceptance rule for existing co-decoding approaches does not consider the expert model's confidence. When the security expert is unconfident due to unseen patterns or out-of-distribution (OOD) contexts, its guidance can therefore be misleading. To address the challenge, we propose CoGate, a confidence-gated co-decoding approach that controls the expert's influence on the co-decoding process based on its confidence. We implement our approach and evaluate it across multiple LLM backends (CodeGen, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen-Coder, StarCoder) on several code generation benchmarks (HumanEval, security suite, and CWEval). Our approach outperforms existing co-decoding methods (CoSec+) across multiple benchmarks, achieving up to a 12.6% gain of Func-Sec@10 on CWEval.

AI.tldr: CoGate is a confidence-gated co-decoding approach for secure code generation that controls a security expert model's influence based on its confidence, outperforming existing co-decoding methods like CoSec+ by up to 12.6% on Func-Sec@10.
AI.motivation: Large language models can generate insecure code due to patterns learned from pretraining data. While co-decoding (combining a small security expert with the target model at each decoding step) has become a key solution, existing acceptance rules do not account for the expert model's confidence. When the expert is unconfident due to unseen or out-of-distribution contexts, its guidance can be misleading.
AI.method: CoGate proposes a confidence-gated co-decoding approach that modulates the expert model's influence on the co-decoding process based on its confidence level, preventing the expert from providing misleading guidance when it is uncertain.
AI.result: Evaluated across multiple LLM backends (CodeGen, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen-Coder, StarCoder) on benchmarks including HumanEval, security suite, and CWEval. CoGate outperforms existing co-decoding methods (CoSec+), achieving up to a 12.6% gain on Func-Sec@10 for CWEval.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-gating the expert model's influence in co-decoding improves secure code generation, demonstrating that accounting for expert uncertainty leads to better and safer generated code across various LLM backends.

title: Good Rankers, Bad Objectives: Bilinear Contrastive Critics under Expressive Policy Search
summary: Good action rankings do not make a contrastive critic safe to maximize. These critics increasingly act as value-like objectives for best-of-$K$ selection, planning, and critic-guided generation. Unbounded bilinear scores can let large embedding norms inflate off-support values, but cosine bounding does not remove the failure. A controlled support decomposition attributes most raw bilinear regret to norm drift. Cosine and hybrid critics nevertheless select off-support actions from most pools and incur comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile across four OGBench navigation tasks, and they fail to order fixed-query actions by value. Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds, including in a parameter-matched function-class control. Realized costs depend on the task: simulator rollouts reveal single-step selection costs on PointMaze and the exact-$Q^*$ toy but well-powered nulls on AntMaze and HumanoidMaze, where the controller can self-correct. A training/readout decomposition traces the lost ordering to the cosine training objective; raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization. Candidate maximization can therefore exploit false positives caused by norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics remain useful compatibility rankers on navigation and manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar.

AI.tldr: Contrastive critics (bilinear or cosine-bounded) are unsafe to maximize as value-like objectives for action selection; their top-score selections are often off-support or misordered. Bellman-trained TD-Q preserves value calibration, while norm drift, score saturation, and in-support misranking explain the failures.
AI.motivation: Despite contrastive critics being increasingly used for best-of-K selection, planning, and critic-guided generation, no prior analysis establishes whether maximizing such critics is safe—i.e., whether their scores are value-calibrated and can reliably rank actions by expected return.
AI.method: The authors perform a controlled support decomposition separating raw bilinear regret into norm drift and in-support components, compare cosine-bounded and hybrid critics against Bellman-trained TD-Q, evaluate on four OGBench navigation tasks plus PointMaze, AntMaze, HumanoidMaze, and an exact-Q* toy, and run simulator rollouts to measure realized costs. They also probe a training/readout decomposition by renormalizing raw-trained embeddings at inference time.
AI.result: Norm drift accounts for most raw bilinear regret; cosine bounding does not fix failure and hybrid critics still select off-support actions with comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top decile across tasks and fail to order actions by value, whereas TD-Q succeeds under matched function classes. Realized costs vary by environment: single-step selection hurts on PointMaze and the toy, but AntMaze/HumanoidMaze show well-powered nulls because the controller self-corrects. Raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering only after inference-time normalization, implicating the cosine training objective.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive critics cannot be safely maximized for action selection because norm drift, score saturation, and in-support misranking create exploitable false positives. They remain useful as compatibility rankers for navigation/manipulation, but value-calibrated scalar objectives like TD-Q are required for action selection.

title: Calibrate Before Reason: Robust Visual Token Reduction against Semantic Drift in VLMs
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) suffer from prohibitive inference overhead due to long sequences of visual tokens. However, existing visual token reduction methods mainly improve efficiency by pruning or compressing redundant tokens without examining whether the resulting representation remains semantically consistent with the original representation. Mapping the original N-token visual sequence to K tokens may discard, dilute, or misassign critical visual cues, triggering severe semantic drift that deviates the VLM's understanding. In this paper, we first introduce the principle of 'Calibrate Before Reason' to visual token reduction and propose CaRe, a training-free robust framework that calibrates compact visual representations before reasoning to preserve semantic fidelity in VLMs. CaRe consists of two mutually complementary modules: 1) Perturbation-Robust Calibration Anchoring, which identifies calibration anchors with stable model-side influence under multi-directional perturbations; 2) Confidence-Gated Token Calibration, which extracts reliable calibration signals from unselected tokens and injects them into anchors. Extensive evaluations across diverse VLM architectures and benchmarks verify that CaRe outperforms state-of-the-art token reduction baselines. While pruning 94.4% of visual tokens, our method retains 96.4% of the original full-token performance, delivering up to 2.30 times faster end-to-end inference speed relative to unpruned vanilla models.

AI.tldr: CaRe is a training-free framework for visual token reduction in Large Vision-Language Models that calibrates compact visual representations before reasoning to preserve semantic fidelity, achieving 96.4% of full-token performance while pruning 94.4% of visual tokens and delivering up to 2.30x faster inference.
AI.motivation: Existing visual token reduction methods improve efficiency by pruning or compressing redundant tokens but do not verify that the resulting representations remain semantically consistent with the original, which can cause semantic drift by discarding, diluting, or misassigning critical visual cues.
AI.method: CaRe introduces the principle of 'Calibrate Before Reason' and consists of two mutually complementary modules: 1) Perturbation-Robust Calibration Anchoring, which identifies calibration anchors with stable model-side influence under multi-directional perturbations; 2) Confidence-Gated Token Calibration, which extracts reliable calibration signals from unselected tokens and injects them into these anchors.
AI.result: CaRe outperforms state-of-the-art token reduction baselines across diverse VLM architectures and benchmarks. It retains 96.4% of original full-token performance while pruning 94.4% of visual tokens, and delivers up to 2.30 times faster end-to-end inference speed relative to unpruned vanilla models.
AI.conclusion: Calibrating compact visual representations before reasoning, rather than relying solely on pruning, is an effective training-free strategy to preserve semantic fidelity and improve inference efficiency in VLMs, enabling aggressive token reduction with minimal performance loss.

title: From Minds to Models: The Intersection of Psychology and LLM Behaviours
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are often compared with the human mind because their decision-making is complex, non-linear and difficult to interpret. Psychological methods developed to investigate unobservable mental processes may therefore help examine LLM behaviour, particularly in government and healthcare. Building on prompt-based adaptations of the Implicit Association Test, this study tested whether ChatGPT produced sentiment differences across racial conditions in open-ended text. Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, producing 126 prompts. Each was submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4 and GPT-4T, yielding 378 responses. Sentiment scores were derived from categorical labels and source scores: positive labels retained the source score, negative labels were assigned its negative, and neutral responses were coded zero. A two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition, F(8, 351) = 2.04, p = .042, partial-eta squared = .044, but no effect of model, F(2, 351) = 0.07, p = .933, and no interaction, F(16, 351) = 0.23, p = .999. However, the effect was not retained in a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis, F(8, 351) = 1.53, p = .145, and Tukey-corrected comparisons found no significant pairwise differences. An uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant, but was selected post hoc and is reported only as hypothesis-generating. Evidence for sentiment differences was therefore weak and analysis-dependent. Sentiment scoring also cannot distinguish evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by a prompt. We outline design changes needed to address these limitations and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.
  Keywords: Implicit Bias, Psychological Research Methods, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Large Language Models, Sentiment Analysis

AI.tldr: This study adapts the Implicit Association Test to examine whether ChatGPT produces sentiment differences across racial conditions in open-ended text. Using 126 prompts across eight racial categories and a control, submitted to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, and GPT-4T (378 responses), a two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition (partial-eta squared = .044, p = .042), but this was not retained in rank-transformed sensitivity analysis, and no significant pairwise differences survived Tukey correction. Evidence for sentiment differences was weak and analysis-dependent, and the authors outline design changes and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit complex, non-linear decision-making that is difficult to interpret. The authors propose that psychological methods developed to investigate unobservable mental processes in humans may help examine LLM behaviour, particularly in high-stakes domains like government and healthcare where potential bias could have serious consequences.
AI.method: Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, producing 126 prompts, each submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, and GPT-4T (378 responses). Sentiment scores were derived from categorical labels and source scores: positive labels retained the source score, negative labels were assigned its negative, and neutral responses were coded zero. A two-way ANOVA was conducted, followed by rank-transformed sensitivity analysis and Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons.
AI.result: A two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition, F(8, 351) = 2.04, p = .042, partial-eta squared = .044, but no effect of model and no interaction. The effect was not retained in rank-transformed sensitivity analysis (p = .145), and no significant pairwise differences survived Tukey correction. An uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant but was selected post hoc.
AI.conclusion: Evidence for sentiment differences across racial conditions in LLM outputs is weak and analysis-dependent. Sentiment scoring cannot distinguish evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by a prompt. The authors outline design changes to address these limitations and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.

title: PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks
comment: Accepted at the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: SWE-bench-like benchmarks are widely used for evaluating LLM's issue resolution capability. They typically follow a common construction pipeline: each PR (Pull Request) is paired with its linked issue by extracting issue references from the PR description; the issue description is used as the problem statement, and the PR patch serves as the test oracle. However, due to the inherent complexity of developing and maintaining large repositories, such PR-Issue pairings are often misaligned in practice. In this work, we systematically study SWE-bench Verified instances, finding that 13.6% exhibit misalignment across five patterns in eleven fine-grained scenarios. To enable reliable and scalable construction of those benchmarks in the future, we propose PAIChecker, a multi-agent system for checking PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks. Specifically, PAIChecker adopts a three-phase design that combines specific pattern identification, cross-agent label synthesis, and code-level validation, thereby enabling more accurate, generalizable, and progressively verified detection. Experiments on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual show that PAIchecker achieves the best performance across all four LLM backbones, reaching up to 92.12% and 91.67% binary accuracy, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces PAIChecker, a multi-agent system for detecting PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks. The authors find 13.6% of SWE-bench Verified instances exhibit misalignment across five patterns and eleven fine-grained scenarios. PAIChecker uses a three-phase design combining pattern identification, cross-agent label synthesis, and code-level validation, achieving up to 92.12% and 91.67% binary accuracy on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual respectively.
AI.motivation: SWE-bench-like benchmarks are widely used to evaluate LLM issue resolution but often contain misaligned PR-Issue pairings due to the complexity of large repository development and maintenance. This misalignment undermines benchmark reliability and validity, motivating the need for systematic detection and correction.
AI.method: The paper first conducts a systematic study of SWE-bench Verified instances, identifying five misalignment patterns across eleven fine-grained scenarios affecting 13.6% of instances. It then proposes PAIChecker, a multi-agent system with a three-phase architecture: (1) specific pattern identification, (2) cross-agent label synthesis, and (3) code-level validation, enabling more accurate, generalizable, and progressively verified detection.
AI.result: Experiments on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual show PAIChecker achieves the best performance across all four LLM backbones, reaching up to 92.12% and 91.67% binary accuracy on the two benchmarks respectively.
AI.conclusion: PAIChecker provides a reliable and scalable approach for constructing future SWE-bench-like benchmarks by detecting and mitigating PR-Issue misalignment, improving the overall quality of LLM issue resolution evaluation.

title: SE(3)-MeanFlow: Few-Step Protein Backbone Generation on Lie Groups
summary: Generative modeling of protein backbones promises the de novo design of proteins with prescribed structural and functional properties. Existing diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality backbones on SE(3)^N, but inference requires numerically integrating an ODE over hundreds of network evaluations, each involving a Lie group exponential map - a bottleneck for high-throughput design campaigns. We introduce SE(3)-MeanFlow, a few-step generative framework that extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to the Lie group geometry of protein frames. Working natively in the Lie algebra so(3) and in R^3, we derive closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations, giving simulation-free training targets. We further introduce an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that removes the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch and serves as a warm-up stage, after which training switches to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss that is used for the remainder of pretraining and for rectification-based post-training. In protein backbone generation, SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps, and its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification lets it lead at every matched budget - at a modest cost in diversity.

AI.tldr: SE(3)-MeanFlow is a few-step generative framework extending MeanFlow to SE(3) for protein backbone generation, using closed-form average-velocity identities in the Lie algebra to enable simulation-free training, achieving quality on par with or exceeding flow-matching baselines while using fewer sampling steps.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion and flow-matching models for protein backbone generation produce high-quality structures on SE(3)^N, but inference requires numerically integrating an ODE over hundreds of network evaluations with expensive Lie group exponential maps, creating a bottleneck for high-throughput design campaigns.
AI.method: The authors extend MeanFlow from Euclidean space to the Lie group geometry of protein frames, working natively in the Lie algebra so(3) and R^3. They derive closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations (simulation-free training targets), introduce an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that removes the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch as a warm-up stage, then switch to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss for pretraining and rectification-based post-training.
AI.result: In protein backbone generation, SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps. Its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification enables it to lead at every matched sampling budget, at a modest cost in diversity.
AI.conclusion: SE(3)-MeanFlow provides an efficient few-step alternative to standard flow-matching for protein backbone design, substantially reducing inference cost while maintaining or improving generation quality, with a minor trade-off in structural diversity.

title: PrintAnything: Learning an Intermediate Representation for 3D printing G-code Generation
summary: Point clouds are one of the most fundamental and widely used 3D representations, serving as the most basic geometric representation of 3D shapes. Nevertheless, most existing 3D printing pipelines require a watertight mesh as input, preventing the direct use of point clouds for fabrication. A common workaround is to reconstruct meshes from point clouds; however, the resulting meshes often contain geometric artifacts, such as incorrect faces or topological inconsistencies, that are difficult to repair and may lead to printing failures. To overcome these limitations, we propose PrintAnything, a novel framework that learns to produce executable 3D printing G-code directly from 3D point clouds without requiring mesh reconstruction. To enable point clouds to serve as direct input for slice-wise toolpath generation, we introduce a slice-wise point projection strategy that transforms unstructured 3D point clouds into slice-aligned 2D representations consistent with layer-by-layer nature of fused deposition modeling in 3D printing. To eliminate mesh dependency and provide a unified representation that bridges point clouds and G-code, we propose Geometric plan (G-plan) map, a compact 2D representation composed of occupancy, region, and flow maps that encode the geometric and extrusion properties required for toolpath synthesis in 3D printing. As a result, our proposed method accurately generates printable G-code directly from point clouds, enabling a practical and fully mesh-free pipeline for 3D printing.
