It accumulates policy gradients derived from a temporary behavioral objective over a small set of rollouts or demonstrations to construct a removable task vector that can be added to (or subtracted from) the model's activations at inference time.
AI.result: PGS demonstrates calibration and reversibility in a two-route gridworld environment. On chess puzzles, independently fitted PGS vectors work both in isolation and combination, with compatible tactical objectives accumulating constructively. In competitive football, PGS alters specific team behaviors and its effects transfer across opponents.
AI.conclusion: Policy gradients provide a natural interface for constructing temporary, composable behavioral adaptations in LLMs across diverse decision-making domains, overcoming the limitations of current steering methods.

title: EEG-EditBench: Probing Visual Information in EEG-Image Retrieval Models with Controlled Image Edits
comment: Main paper with supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/XiaoZhangYES/EEG-EditBench. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/xiaozgg/EEG-EditBench
summary: Recent EEG-to-image retrieval models have achieved strong performance in identifying viewed images from semantically diverse candidates. Yet such success does not reveal what visual information supports the match. A model may readily identify a cheetah among tools, plants, and vehicles, but can it still distinguish the viewed cheetah from the same scene with the cheetah replaced by a dog? Motivated by this question, we introduce EEG-EditBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines this question through controlled edits of object identity, attributes, background, and object presence. Built from the 200 THINGS-EEG2 test images, EEG-EditBench contains 2,137 quality-controlled edits and evaluates eight representative EEG visual decoding models. Our results show that strong standard retrieval does not consistently transfer to edit-based evaluation, with fine-grained attribute changes presenting the greatest challenge. EEG-EditBench reveals model behavior hidden by aggregate retrieval accuracy and provides a controlled basis for studying what visual information EEG-image models preserve. The code and complete dataset are publicly available.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces EEG-EditBench, a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating whether EEG-to-image retrieval models can distinguish subtly edited versions of viewed images (e.g., object identity, attributes, background, presence changes), revealing that strong standard retrieval performance does not transfer to fine-grained edit-based evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG-to-image retrieval benchmarks only evaluate identification among semantically diverse candidates, which masks what specific visual information models actually preserve. A model may succeed at coarse-level retrieval without retaining fine-grained visual details, so a controlled edit-based benchmark is needed to diagnose this.
AI.method: The authors build EEG-EditBench from 200 THINGS-EEG2 test images, containing 2,137 quality-controlled edits across four dimensions: object identity, attributes, background, and object presence. They evaluate eight representative EEG visual decoding models on this benchmark.
AI.result: Strong standard retrieval performance does not consistently transfer to edit-based evaluation. Fine-grained attribute changes present the greatest challenge to existing models, and the benchmark reveals model behavior that aggregate retrieval accuracy hides.
AI.conclusion: EEG-EditBench provides a controlled and publicly available diagnostic framework for studying which visual information EEG-image models actually preserve, going beyond aggregate retrieval accuracy to expose hidden model limitations.

title: Baikal: Structured Search for Deep Research over Data Lakes
summary: Deep research over data lakes requires an LLM agent to investigate evidence across thousands of heterogeneous tables and passages to synthesize a report. Existing methods perform iterative retrieval and generation, letting accumulated context determine what to investigate next, which can overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget. To address this, we cast deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem and present Baikal - a framework that clusters heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions, then searches over them adaptively to balance exploration and exploitation. Within each selected region, Baikal generates and investigates region-grounded subquestions, using finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates and guide search under policies ranging from random and LLM-guided selection to Bayesian $ε$-greedy and UCB. We evaluate Baikal on 15 queries each over HybridQA and TAT-QA data lakes containing 10,993 and 2,757 tables, respectively, together with 227K Wikipedia passages and 13K financial report passages. We assess research quality with a new rubric covering groundedness, relevance, diversity, and utility, and use GPT-5-mini to score Baikal and strong baselines, including DeepSearcher and an OpenCode research agent with retrieval and clustering variants. Across both data lakes, Baikal performs strongly under several region-selection policies; its best configuration improves report scores over the strongest baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Our analyses attribute these gains to organizing and exploring semantic evidence regions, which improves groundedness and diversity and yields more useful findings under the same subquestion budget. These results demonstrate the value of structured semantic exploration for systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes.

AI.tldr: Baikal is a framework that treats deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem, clustering heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions and adaptively balancing exploration and exploitation via policies like Bayesian ε-greedy and UCB. It outperforms strong baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA using a new rubric covering groundedness, relevance, diversity, and utility.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents for deep research over data lakes use iterative retrieval and generation where accumulated context determines what to investigate next. This leads to overexploiting locally promising evidence and failing to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget, resulting in incomplete and biased research reports.
AI.method: Baikal (1) casts deep research as a budgeted search problem, (2) clusters heterogeneous evidence (tables and passages) into semantic regions, (3) searches over regions adaptively to balance exploration and exploitation using policies from random and LLM-guided selection to Bayesian ε-greedy and UCB, and (4) generates region-grounded subquestions within selected regions, using finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates. A new rubric (groundedness, relevance, diversity, utility) scored by GPT-5-mini is used for evaluation.
AI.result: On 15 queries over HybridQA (10,993 tables, 227K Wikipedia passages) and TAT-QA (2,757 tables, 13K financial passages), Baikal's best configuration improves report scores over the strongest baselines (DeepSearcher, OpenCode research agent with retrieval and clustering variants) by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Analyses show gains come from organizing and exploring semantic evidence regions, improving groundedness and diversity, and yielding more useful findings under the same subquestion budget.
AI.conclusion: Structured semantic exploration over evidence regions is valuable for systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes, enabling better coverage of distinct semantic regions and higher quality research reports under constrained budgets.

title: MUGEN: A Unified Framework for Efficient Motion Understanding and Generation
summary: Grounding human motion in language, and language in motion, is a central step toward physical AI systems that can understand, generate, and communicate human behavior. Unified motion--language systems first coupled the two directions through a shared discrete motion codebook, but quantization limits generation quality. The strongest generators buy quality back at growing cost: stacked residual codebooks enlarge the representation; masked decoding stages, long autoregressive rollouts, and denoising chains of tens to hundreds of steps stretch inference; even the continuous-latent designs among them reach their latent only through an iterative diffusion head; and none of this decoding machinery serves understanding. We therefore propose MUGEN, a unified motion--language framework that pays neither cost: no codebook, one draw. A single adaptive-length autoencoder compresses any-length motion into a few continuous latent slots, the system's only motion representation: the language model generates them for text-to-motion and reads them back for motion understanding. Depth-routed hidden states let each slot read from the transformer depth it needs, and a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, so a single draw carries the text-conditional, cross-slot variation a description permits. At a decoding cost of K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass, MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D while raising retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen.

AI.tldr: MUGEN is a unified motion-language framework that eliminates the quantization and iterative decoding costs of prior systems by using a single adaptive-length autoencoder that compresses motion into continuous latent slots, generated or read back by a language model in a single draw with one decoder pass, achieving state-of-the-art results on HumanML3D and SnapMoGen.
AI.motivation: Prior unified motion-language systems either suffer from quantization limits on generation quality or pay growing computational costs (stacked codebooks, long autoregressive rollouts, denoising chains, iterative diffusion heads) to buy back quality—and none of this decoding machinery serves the understanding direction. The goal is a unified framework that achieves high-quality generation and understanding without these costs.
AI.method: MUGEN uses a single adaptive-length autoencoder that compresses any-length motion into a few continuous latent slots as the sole motion representation. A language model generates these slots for text-to-motion and reads them back for motion understanding. Depth-routed hidden states allow each slot to read from the transformer depth it needs, and a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set so a single draw captures text-conditional, cross-slot variation. Decoding costs K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass.
AI.result: MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D, raises retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen.
AI.conclusion: MUGEN demonstrates that a unified motion-language framework can achieve strong generation quality and understanding without codebooks or iterative decoding machinery, showing that a single latent representation and single-draw decoding suffices for both directions of motion-language grounding.

title: Learning to Understand Body Language from Flight through Robust 3D Avatar Placing
summary: Perceiving human motion and intent at long range is a prerequisite for socially intelligent aerial robots, yet the data to learn it barely exists. We introduce Drones2BodyLanguage, a dataset grounding human motion in real UAV footage: avatars manifesting ten communicative intents are placed into unmodified 4K drone scenes with metrically correct position, scale and orientation, maintained over hundreds of frames of camera motion. Enabling it is a lightweight geometric world model of the local scene - semantically selected anchors lifted to 3D through streaming monocular depth - in which a placement point is predicted as an affine anchor combination with provably rigid-invariant weights, and re-rendered under an SVD-fitted ground rotation. Across twelve architectures on scene- and motion-disjoint splits, training on placed data lifts mean intent accuracy by a wide margin for real, retargeted and generated motion alike, with gains confirmed on two in-the-wild scenes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Drones2BodyLanguage, a dataset of avatars displaying ten communicative intents placed into unmodified 4K drone footage with metrically correct position, scale, and orientation maintained over hundreds of frames, enabling long-range human motion and intent perception for aerial robots.
AI.motivation: Perceiving human motion and intent at long range is a prerequisite for socially intelligent aerial robots, yet the data required to learn this behavior barely exists.
AI.method: A lightweight geometric world model of the local scene is used, with semantically selected anchors lifted to 3D via streaming monocular depth. A placement point is predicted as an affine anchor combination with provably rigid-invariant weights, and re-rendered under an SVD-fitted ground rotation to maintain metric accuracy over hundreds of camera frames.
AI.result: Across twelve architectures on scene- and motion-disjoint splits, training on placed data lifts mean intent accuracy by a wide margin for real, retargeted, and generated motion alike, with gains confirmed on two in-the-wild scenes.
AI.conclusion: The Drones2BodyLanguage dataset significantly improves long-range human intent recognition for aerial robotics, with robust generalization demonstrated across multiple architectures and diverse motion types.

title: VeriSkill: A Self-Evolution Framework for Program Verification Skills
summary: Automating program verification with LLM agents requires generating specifications, annotations, auxiliary lemmas, and tool invocations, all of which depend on reusable skills. A natural remedy is skill self-evolution: distilling skills from trajectories and refining them through feedback. However, existing evolution methods struggle with program verification tasks because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback. In this paper, we propose VeriSkill, a self-evolution framework built for program verification. It attributes verification failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills, admitting only revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics. Experiments show that VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.

AI.tldr: VeriSkill is a self-evolution framework for program verification with LLM agents that attributes verification failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills—admitting only revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics. It outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.
AI.motivation: LLM-agent-based program verification relies on reusable skills for generating specifications, annotations, auxiliary lemmas, and tool invocations. Skill self-evolution is a natural remedy, but existing evolution methods fail in program verification because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback.
AI.method: VeriSkill attributes verification failures to specific skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills. It only admits revisions that demonstrably improve verification performance while preserving program semantics.
AI.result: VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.
AI.conclusion: A self-evolution framework that reliably identifies skill-specific failures and extracts actionable signals from verifier feedback can effectively enable skill improvement in program verification, surpassing existing baselines in robustness and generality.

title: Prox: Training-Free FFN Activation Sparsity via Approximate Intermediate-Channel Salience in LLMs
summary: Feed-forward networks (FFNs) dominate memory traffic and computation in large language model (LLM) inference, making them a primary target for activation sparsification. However, existing training-free methods suffer substantial model-quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in their channel-selection strategies. We observe that the SwiGLU intermediate state provides a highly effective channel-selection signal, but obtaining it requires costly dense computation. To address this, we present \emph{Prox}, a two-stage training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs. Prox hinges on the key insight: sparse execution requires only the channel mask induced by the intermediate state, which can be constructed from the magnitude ranking of its entries rather than their exact values. Specifically, Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared mask; Stage 2 computes the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections. Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieves up to a $1.99\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup at 70\% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.

AI.tldr: Prox is a two-stage training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs in LLM inference that constructs channel masks from the magnitude ranking of the intermediate state (using input sparsity and quantized proxy weights) rather than computing exact values, enabling up to 1.99x end-to-end decoding speedup at 70% FFN sparsity while outperforming training-free baselines across ten LLMs.
AI.motivation: FFNs dominate memory traffic and computation in LLM inference, and activation sparsification is a key optimization target. However, existing training-free sparsification methods suffer severe model-quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in their channel-selection strategies. Although the SwiGLU intermediate state provides an excellent channel-selection signal, obtaining it requires costly dense computation that defeats the purpose of sparsification.
AI.method: Prox is a two-stage training-free framework. It exploits the insight that sparse execution only needs the channel mask induced by the intermediate state, which can be derived from the magnitude ranking of its entries rather than exact values. Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared mask; Stage 2 computes the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three FFN projections (i.e., the two gate/up projections and the down projection).
AI.result: Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieves up to 1.99x end-to-end decoding speedup at 70% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.
AI.conclusion: Prox effectively decouples channel-mask construction from exact intermediate-state computation, enabling high-quality activation sparsification without training while maintaining compatibility with other efficiency techniques like quantization and sparse attention.

title: DECODE: Tackling Representation and Decision Degradation in Continual AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: As generative models continue to evolve, AI-generated image detectors must incrementally adapt to emerging generative domains while preserving knowledge acquired from previous ones. This continual learning setting is particularly challenging because forensic traces are often subtle and generator-specific, making detectors highly vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. Existing methods primarily address this problem by stabilizing feature representations, implicitly treating forgetting as a representation-level issue. In this paper, we show that this perspective is incomplete. We demonstrate that even when feature representations remain discriminative, the decision boundary can progressively drift as the classification head is continually optimized on new domains. These two effects jointly give rise to a compound failure mode, termed Dual Degradation. To overcome this challenge, we propose DECODE, a decoupled continual detection framework that jointly mitigates representation- and decision-level forgetting. Specifically, we introduce Subspace Diversity Regularization (SDR) to preserve diverse forensic representations and Closed-Form Decision Alignment (CDA) to recalibrate the shared classification head after each adapter merge without manual hyperparameter tuning. Extensive experiments on 19 generative domains show that DECODE achieves an average accuracy of 99.36% with only 0.39% forgetting, while further generalizing to 11 unseen generators with 95.36% accuracy.

AI.tldr: DECODE is a decoupled continual learning framework for AI-generated image detection that jointly addresses both representation-level and decision-level forgetting (termed Dual Degradation), achieving 99.36% average accuracy across 19 generative domains with only 0.39% forgetting, and generalizing to 11 unseen generators with 95.36% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing continual learning methods for AI-generated image detection only stabilize feature representations, implicitly treating catastrophic forgetting as purely a representation-level problem. The authors show this perspective is incomplete: even when representations remain discriminative, the classification head's decision boundary drifts as it is continually optimized on new domains, creating a compound failure mode (Dual Degradation) that existing methods fail to address.
AI.method: DECODE is a decoupled continual detection framework with two key components: (1) Subspace Diversity Regularization (SDR) to preserve diverse forensic representations across generative domains, and (2) Closed-Form Decision Alignment (CDA) to recalibrate the shared classification head after each adapter merge without manual hyperparameter tuning. The framework decouples representation-level and decision-level forgetting mitigation.
AI.result: On 19 generative domains, DECODE achieves 99.36% average accuracy with only 0.39% forgetting. It further generalizes to 11 unseen generators, achieving 95.36% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: DECODE demonstrates that effectively addressing continual AI-generated image detection requires jointly tackling both representation-level and decision-level forgetting, not just feature stabilization alone. The decoupled approach yields state-of-the-art performance with minimal forgetting and strong generalization to unseen generators.

title: SpecCal: Ambiguity-Aware Candidate Calibration for Infrared Spectrum-Based Molecular Structure Reconstruction
summary: Inferring molecular structures from infrared (IR) spectra is a fundamental yet challenging problem. A key difficulty is that an IR spectrum provides limited structural information: different molecules may share similar functional groups and local vibrational patterns, leading to highly similar spectral responses. Thus, even when an observed spectrum has a unique underlying structure, reconstructing it from the spectrum remains ambiguous. Existing IR-to-molecule models usually generate a ranked set of candidate molecules, but this set is largely determined by the model's learned generation preference and may not fully capture the structures that best satisfy the observed spectral constraints. To address this limitation, we propose SpecCal, a training-free candidate calibration framework for IR-to-molecule prediction. SpecCal operates on the candidate outputs of existing base models and improves the prediction set by re-ranking current candidates while introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency. The framework is plug-and-play and model-agnostic, requiring no parameter updates for integration with diverse base models. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models. Further analyses demonstrate that calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity provides a practical way to improve molecular reconstruction from IR spectra. The code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SpecCal-B18A.

AI.tldr: SpecCal is a training-free, model-agnostic candidate calibration framework that improves IR-to-molecule prediction by re-ranking existing candidates and introducing structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency, consistently improving top-k reconstruction across benchmarks and base models.
AI.motivation: Existing IR-to-molecule models generate a ranked set of candidate molecules, but this set is largely determined by the model's learned generation preference and may not fully capture the structures that best satisfy the observed spectral constraints, due to the inherent ambiguity of IR spectra where different molecules can share similar functional groups and vibrational patterns.
AI.method: SpecCal operates on candidate outputs of existing base models and improves the prediction set by (1) re-ranking current candidates and (2) introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency. It is plug-and-play and model-agnostic, requiring no parameter updates for integration with diverse base models.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models. Further analyses demonstrate that calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity provides a practical way to improve molecular reconstruction from IR spectra.
AI.conclusion: Calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity is a practical and effective approach to improve molecular reconstruction from IR spectra, and SpecCal provides a general, training-free solution applicable to diverse base models.

title: Compliance2LoRA: On-Demand Safety Alignment on Arbitrary Policy Subsets via Hypernetwork-Generated LoRA Adapters
summary: Post-training alignment in large reasoning models (LRMs) has significantly improved their adaptability to diverse safety compliance settings. However, as LRMs personalization for downstream users takes center stage, the demand for varying levels of policy compliance grows as different user-specific LRMs must adhere to distinct subsets of safety policies. Training a separate LRM for each policy subset introduces severe combinatorial overhead. While in context learning methods overcome this combinatorial overhead, they introduce additional computational challenges associated with long context generation. To address this challenge, we propose \ours, a unified adaptive hypernetwork-based framework for multi-policy compliance. In our framework, safety policies serve as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator, which learns to produce policy compliant LoRA weights for downstream LRM. When added to the LRM these weights enable the generation of responses compliant with the specified policy subsets. In this work, we demonstrate that training such a hypernetwork enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance across reasoning models of different sized and different evaluation datasets. This highlights the effectiveness and practicality of adaptive hypernetwork based alignment in LRMs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an adaptive hypernetwork-based framework for multi-policy compliance in large reasoning models (LRMs). The framework takes safety policies as inputs to a LoRA adapter generator, producing policy-compliant LoRA weights that enable on-demand adjustment of a single LRM to adhere to different subsets of safety policies without combinatorial retraining overhead or long-context computational costs.
AI.motivation: As LRMs are personalized for different downstream users, they need to comply with distinct subsets of safety policies. Training a separate LRM per policy subset incurs severe combinatorial overhead, while in-context learning methods avoid this but introduce computational challenges due to long context generation.
AI.method: The proposed framework uses an adaptive hypernetwork where safety policies serve as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator. The generator learns to produce policy-compliant LoRA weights that are added to a single base LRM, enabling compliance with specified policy subsets.
AI.result: The framework enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance across reasoning models of different sizes and across different evaluation datasets.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive hypernetwork-based alignment is effective and practical for multi-policy compliance in LRMs, providing a scalable solution to personalized safety policy adherence without combinatorial training or long-context inference overhead.

title: Unifying Adversarially Robust Model Experts in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, posing a serious problem for real-life applications and deployment. Adversarial fine-tuning emerges as a prominent defense method; however, different fine-tuning strategies often produce specialized models with distinct robustness characteristics. Each fine-tuned model in turn thrives in some evaluation settings but falters on others, limiting their defensive capabilities. We refer to these specialized fine-tuned models as robust model experts and propose a collaborative adversarial fine-tuning framework: CARE - Collaborative Adversarial Robustness fine-tuning using Embedding alignment. CARE maintains multiple experts during training, enables knowledge exchange through embedding-space harmonization, and consolidates the learned knowledge into a single unified robust model. Experts benefit from one another while preserving their individual specializations, enabling the final model to inherit complementary robustness properties. In this paper, we demonstrate CARE on two different adversarial fine-tuning strategies with complementary robustness behaviors. Extensive experiments on classic image classification and downstream vision-language tasks display the effectiveness of our approach, with CARE being able to outperform individually learned model experts. The results suggest that collaborative learning across model experts is a promising direction for improving adversarial robustness.

AI.tldr: CARE is a collaborative adversarial fine-tuning framework that maintains multiple robust model experts, enables knowledge exchange through embedding-space harmonization, and consolidates their complementary robustness properties into a single unified robust model, outperforming individually trained experts across image classification and downstream vision-language tasks.
AI.motivation: Adversarial fine-tuning of VLMs like CLIP produces specialized robust models that each excel in some evaluation settings but falter in others. Since no single fine-tuning strategy yields comprehensive robustness, there is a need to combine complementary robustness properties from different experts into one unified model.
AI.method: CARE (Collaborative Adversarial Robustness fine-tuning using Embedding alignment) maintains multiple robust model experts during training, facilitates knowledge exchange via embedding-space harmonization across experts, and consolidates the collectively learned knowledge into a single unified robust model that preserves each expert's specialization while benefiting from complementary robustness.
AI.result: CARE outperforms individually learned model experts on classic image classification and downstream vision-language tasks, demonstrating that collaborative learning across model experts effectively improves adversarial robustness.
AI.conclusion: Collaborative learning across model experts is a promising direction for improving adversarial robustness in vision-language models, enabling a single unified model to inherit complementary robustness properties that no individual fine-tuning strategy can achieve alone.

title: Annotating Topical Legal Insights from Case Proceedings
summary: In this paper, we mainly concentrate on finding concepts or topics from the legal case proceedings, since adopting a structured representation for legal documents, as opposed to a mere bag-of-words flat text representation, can significantly enhance processing capabilities. To achieve this objective, we put forward a set of diverse concepts for legal case proceedings. With this motivation, we propose LeDA, a system for Legal Data Annotation. The system offers the generic functionality of annotating and adjudicating entities or concepts within documents via a web-based interface. A novel feature of our system is that it allows to dynamic create new tags for annotation, which is a particularly useful provision for situations where there exists no pre-defined ontology for the entities (concepts) that need to be annotated - these being rather discovered by annotators as they continue examining more documents. The system that we demonstrate is currently in use to annotate a set of concepts from legal documents to construct semantic representations of documents as bags of concepts that can then be used for several downstream tasks, such as prior case retrieval, judgment prediction, and so on. Along with the system features in general, we also describe how LeDA was used by 3 assessors to annotate and adjudicate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.

AI.tldr: LeDA is a web-based system for annotating legal data that allows users to dynamically create new concept tags during annotation. It was used by 3 assessors to annotate legal concepts from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings, constructing bags of concepts for downstream tasks like prior case retrieval and judgment prediction.
AI.motivation: Legal documents benefit from structured representations over flat bag-of-words representations since structured concepts significantly enhance processing capabilities. There is a need to identify and annotate concepts in legal case proceedings, but in many domains no pre-defined ontology exists for these entities.
AI.method: The authors propose LeDA, a system for Legal Data Annotation, offering web-based annotation and adjudication of entities/concepts. Its novel feature allows dynamic creation of new annotation tags, enabling annotators to discover concepts as they examine documents. The system was used by 3 assessors to annotate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.
AI.result: The system successfully enables annotation of legal documents as bags of concepts and was demonstrated in use for annotating Indian Supreme Court case proceedings with 3 assessors.
AI.conclusion: LeDA provides a flexible annotation platform for legal documents, particularly valuable when no pre-defined ontology exists, and enables construction of semantic document representations for downstream legal tasks.

title: Back from the Future: Key-Value Cache Management by Counter-Causal Surprise
summary: Key-value (KV) cache management through compression and eviction strategies has emerged as an important research direction in recent years. Computational demands of large language models (LLMs) and their multi-modal variants during output generation can be partially alleviated by caching previous key and value calculations needed by subsequent scaled dot-product attention operations. However, this leads to another problem: the size of the resulting KV cache grows linearly with context length and quickly consumes all available GPU memory when either the prompt or the generated output are long. KV cache management periodically prunes entries from the cache thereby reducing its memory footprint while attempting to retain sufficient information for accurate generation. A by-product is faster inference speed. We propose a simple yet effective KV eviction scheme motivated by the insight that past tokens which can be well-predicted from more recent tokens are redundant and their associated keys and values can be removed from the cache. To score entries for eviction we run the model on the tokens in their original order, reusing the key and value representations already stored in the KV cache, and applying a counter-causal attention mask so that each position attends only to its future context. This is in-distribution, tied directly to the actual cache contents, and requires no additional training. To further reduce cost, we additionally propose a fast single-layer approximation that restricts the counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer, achieving a significant speedup per refresh cycle at marginal accuracy cost. We evaluate our strategy on various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets showing competitive or improved performance over other state-of-the-art methods. Reference code is available at https://github.com/metacognitionai/counter_causal.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a KV cache eviction scheme for LLMs that removes redundant entries by identifying past tokens that can be well-predicted from more recent tokens, using a counter-causal attention pass (with a fast single-layer approximation) to score cache entries for eviction.
AI.motivation: KV cache size grows linearly with context length and quickly exhausts GPU memory for long prompts or generated outputs. Existing cache management reduces memory but often loses important information, motivating a principled eviction strategy that retains sufficient information for accurate generation while improving inference speed.
AI.method: The method scores KV cache entries for eviction by running the model on tokens in original order, reusing existing key/value representations in the cache, and applying a counter-causal attention mask so each position attends only to future context. Tokens well-predicted from more recent tokens are deemed redundant and evicted. A fast single-layer approximation restricts the counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer for speed. No additional training is required.
AI.result: The proposed eviction strategy achieves competitive or improved performance over other state-of-the-art KV cache management methods across various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: Counter-causal KV eviction is an effective, training-free cache management strategy that identifies redundant entries in-distribution using actual cache contents, balances memory reduction with generation accuracy, and offers a fast approximation variant at marginal accuracy cost.

title: CoRE-UIR: Prior-guided common and residual experts for efficient all-in-one remote sensing image restoration
comment: Accepted by ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
summary: Remote sensing images acquired by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and satellites are often degraded by adverse weather, illumination variation, and imaging artifacts, which may co-occur and jointly induce global distribution shifts and local structural corruption. Although All-in-One image restoration offers an appealing unified alternative to task-specific pipelines, existing methods still suffer from weak or implicit degradation cues and parameter redundancy caused by full-rank multi-expert designs with overlapping restoration behaviors. We propose CoRE-UIR (Common and Residual Experts for Universal Image Restoration), a prior-guided global-local framework centered on the Common-and-Residual Expert Block (CoRE). CoRE explicitly decomposes restoration capacity into a common dense expert for degradation-invariant restoration and low-rank residual experts for degradation-specific compensation, enabling adaptive specialization without redundant expert replication. Built on this design, Degradation Prior Embedding (DPE) adapts frozen CLIP features into an explicit restoration-oriented prior, while Global Feature Modulation (GFM) aligns global feature statistics before local residual compensation. We also construct MDVD-108K (Multi-Degradation VisDrone), a large-scale UAV restoration dataset covering both single and compound degradations, together with a real-world test set. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets show that CoRE-UIR improves the overall average PSNR by 1.05 dB while running 11.83$\times$ faster and reducing peak memory by 85.3% relative to the strongest baseline, BaryIR, thereby maintaining a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. Evaluations on downstream tasks and unseen degradation also validate the generalizability of CoRE-UIR. The code and dataset will be released at https://github.com/zzaiyan/CoRE-UIR.

AI.tldr: CoRE-UIR is a unified all-in-one image restoration framework using a Common-and-Residual Expert Block (CoRE) that decomposes restoration capacity into a common dense expert for degradation-invariant restoration and low-rank residual experts for degradation-specific compensation, achieving 1.05 dB PSNR improvement over the strongest baseline while being 11.83x faster and using 85.3% less peak memory.
AI.motivation: Existing all-in-one image restoration methods suffer from weak or implicit degradation cues and parameter redundancy caused by full-rank multi-expert designs with overlapping restoration behaviors, especially when multiple degradations (weather, illumination, artifacts) co-occur in UAV and satellite imagery.
AI.method: Proposes CoRE-UIR with three key components: (1) Common-and-Residual Expert Block (CoRE) that explicitly decomposes restoration capacity into a common dense expert for degradation-invariant restoration and low-rank residual experts for degradation-specific compensation; (2) Degradation Prior Embedding (DPE) that adapts frozen CLIP features into an explicit restoration-oriented prior; (3) Global Feature Modulation (GFM) that aligns global feature statistics before local residual compensation. Also constructs MDVD-108K, a large-scale UAV restoration dataset with single and compound degradations plus a real-world test set.
AI.result: Improves overall average PSNR by 1.05 dB while running 11.83x faster and reducing peak memory by 85.3% relative to the strongest baseline (BaryIR). Downstream task evaluations and unseen degradation tests validate the generalizability of the approach.
AI.conclusion: CoRE-UIR achieves a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off in universal image restoration, demonstrating that explicit decomposition of restoration capacity into common and residual experts effectively handles co-occurring degradations without redundant expert replication.

title: MemeBench: What LVLMs Miss When Interpreting Culture-Dependent Memes
summary: Large vision-language models have improved at describing visual content, but accurate descriptions do not ensure interpretation when meaning depends on knowledge beyond the pixels. Memes expose this gap because they rely on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions. Most meme benchmarks reduce interpretation to labels or holistic scores, obscuring where an explanation breaks down. We introduce MemeBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes with human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations, centered on anime, comics, games, and adjacent online subcultures. Its VIKR schema decomposes explanations into Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, and Reasoning mechanisms. Across 26 LVLMs, every model covers visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed to interpret it, and even the strongest retains a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. To test whether this diagnosis can guide improvement, we introduce KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase. Across four controlled models, KAR raises VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% and, compared with generic retrieval, repairs more answers and breaks fewer. Yet both retrieval conditions improve Identity and Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage in every comparison. MemeBench reveals whether an interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills the diagnosed gap.

AI.tldr: MemeBench is a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes with human-written references and VIKR annotations (Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, Reasoning mechanisms) revealing that all LVLMs cover visible content better than the background knowledge needed to interpret memes. A new entity-guided retrieval baseline (KAR) raises VIKR Success by 3.6–7.4% across four controlled models, though retrieval generally improves Identity/Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage.
AI.motivation: Accurate descriptions by large vision-language models do not ensure correct interpretation of memes, whose meaning depends on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions. Existing meme benchmarks reduce interpretation to labels or holistic scores, obscuring where explanation breaks down.
AI.method: The paper introduces MemeBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes centered on anime, comics, games, and adjacent online subcultures, with human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations. The VIKR schema decomposes explanations into Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, and Reasoning mechanisms. They evaluate 26 LVLMs and introduce KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase, tested across four controlled models.
AI.result: Every evaluated model covers visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed to interpret it; the strongest model still retains a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. KAR raises VIKR Success by 3.6–7.4% compared with generic retrieval, repairing more answers and breaking fewer. However, both retrieval conditions improve Identity and Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage in every comparison.
AI.conclusion: MemeBench provides a diagnostic tool that reveals whether an interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills the diagnosed gap—demonstrating both the persistent Visual-Knowledge gap in LVLMs and the partial benefit of targeted retrieval.

title: Kalman Meets Curriculum: Efficient Dynamic Prompt Selection for Adaptive RL Finetuning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet its effectiveness critically depends on selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty for the current policy. This is challenging because prompt difficulty evolves throughout training. Existing online methods therefore face a trade-off: evaluation-based approaches are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based approaches are efficient but typically assume stationary difficulty, making them ill-suited to RL's non-stationary training dynamics. To address these issues, we propose a Kalman-Guided Prompt Selection method (KGPS), which reformulates prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem rather than static difficulty prediction. KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model, with process noise coupled to the magnitude of policy updates so that uncertainty increases when the policy changes more substantially. A Kalman filter then maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty, and prompts are selected by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while naturally revisiting uncertain ones. The resulting procedure is adaptive to policy drift and requires no additional rollouts beyond standard policy training. Extensive experiments across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks, as well as multiple RL algorithms, show that KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines, establishing state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods. For example, on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while even improving the average performance by 0.12 point across six math reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: KGPS reformulates RL prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem using a Kalman filter over each prompt's latent success rate in logit space, enabling accurate and efficient difficulty-aware prompt selection that adapts to non-stationary policy updates without extra rollouts.
AI.motivation: RL finetuning of LLMs requires selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty, but prompt difficulty evolves throughout training. Existing methods face a trade-off: evaluation-based approaches are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based approaches are efficient but assume stationary difficulty, which fails under RL's non-stationary training dynamics.
AI.method: KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model, with process noise coupled to policy update magnitude. A Kalman filter maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty, and prompts are selected by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while revisiting uncertain ones.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks, and multiple RL algorithms, show KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines, establishing state-of-the-art among online prompt selection methods. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while improving average performance by 0.12 point across six math reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: KGPS demonstrates that treating prompt selection as dynamic state estimation rather than static difficulty prediction effectively handles RL's non-stationary training dynamics, delivering superior accuracy and efficiency without requiring additional rollouts beyond standard policy training.

title: One Patch Is Enough: Reinforcement-Optimized Visual Token Grounding for MLLM-Based Scene Text Spotting
comment: 15 pages, 11 figures. Accepted to ACM Multimedia 2026
summary: Scene text spotting requires high-precision alignment between textual recognition and spatial localization. While visual-token grounding has emerged as a promising formulation for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), the previous multi-patch paradigm often introduces redundant noise and localization ambiguity, particularly for dense or small text instances. To address this, we propose Single-Patch Text Spotting (SPaTS), a vision-centric framework that routes each text instance through a single anchor visual token and then recovers geometry via full-image refinement. To accurately identify this anchor without oracle labels, we introduce Single-Patch Selective Optimization (SPaSO), a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes discrete visual-token selection using patch-level rewards. To further improve representation robustness and localization precision, we introduce Directional Embedding Alignment (DEA) to suppress unstable norm bias by decoupling feature magnitude and direction, and Patch-Enhanced Decoding (PED) to fuse the routed anchor with language semantics and cross-attend over the full-image feature map for geometry-aware boundary regression beyond coordinate-space surrogates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPaTS consistently and significantly outperforms both frontier closed-source MLLMs and OCR MLLMs. Code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: SPaTS is a vision-centric single-patch text spotting framework for MLLMs that routes each text instance through a single anchor visual token, using reinforcement learning (SPaSO) for anchor selection, Directional Embedding Alignment (DEA) for robust embeddings, and Patch-Enhanced Decoding (PED) for geometry-aware boundary regression, outperforming frontier closed-source and OCR MLLMs.
AI.motivation: Scene text spotting with MLLMs requires precise alignment between textual recognition and spatial localization. Previous multi-patch visual-token grounding paradigms introduce redundant noise and localization ambiguity, especially for dense or small text instances, motivating a cleaner single-anchor-token routing approach without oracle labels.
AI.method: SPaTS routes each text instance through a single anchor visual token and recovers geometry via full-image refinement. It introduces: (1) SPaSO, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes discrete visual-token selection using patch-level rewards; (2) DEA, which decouples feature magnitude and direction to suppress unstable norm bias; and (3) PED, which fuses the routed anchor with language semantics and cross-attends over the full-image feature map for geometry-aware boundary regression.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPaTS consistently and significantly outperforms both frontier closed-source MLLMs and OCR MLLMs across benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The single-patch vision-centric paradigm with selective optimization and geometry-aware decoding provides a superior alternative to multi-patch grounding for scene text spotting in MLLMs.

title: STEREODISCO: Discovering Stereotypicality in LLMs
summary: LLMs encode, convey, and perpetuate stereotypes. Prior computational research focuses on a small set of semantic axes investigated in social psychology, and operates on word embeddings produced by language models, leaving open which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs and how LLMs internally represent such axes. We introduce STEREODISCO, a framework that adapts the semantic differential method (Osgood et al., 1957) to the systematic study of stereotypes in LLM internal representations. STEREODISCO constructs approx. 2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via probing, and identifies stereotypical axes via a statistical test over concept projections. As a case study, we apply STEREODISCO to social group stereotypes with LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT. We find that the two LLMs agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans, suggesting that LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from that documented in social psychology. We also discover stereotypical axes not investigated in prior work -- including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which human annotators independently confirm.

AI.tldr: STEREODISCO is a framework that adapts the semantic differential method to systematically discover and identify stereotype-carrying semantic axes in LLM internal representations. Applied to LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT, it finds LLMs diverge from human-documented stereotypes and uncovers novel stereotypical axes (e.g., humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, cowardly vs. brave) confirmed by human annotators.
AI.motivation: Prior computational research on stereotypes in LLMs is limited to a small set of semantic axes from social psychology and operates on word embeddings, leaving unknown which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations and how LLMs internally represent these axes.
AI.method: STEREODISCO constructs ~2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via probing, and identifies stereotypical axes via a statistical test over concept projections. It is applied as a case study to social group stereotypes in two instruction-tuned LLMs.
AI.result: The two LLMs agree more with each other than with humans on social group ratings, indicating LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from social psychology literature. The framework discovered novel stereotypical axes not previously studied, including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which were independently confirmed by human annotators.
AI.conclusion: STEREODISCO enables systematic, scalable discovery of stereotypes in LLM internal representations, revealing that LLMs encode a broader and different set of stereotypical associations than those documented in prior work, highlighting the importance of studying internal representations rather than just embeddings.

title: Real-Time Hard Peak Age-of-Information Safety with No-Regret Learning
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE Real-Time Systems Symposium (RTSS)
summary: Safety-critical IoT systems such as industrial closed-loop control, V2X coordination, and remote teleoperation require every sensor's peak Age of Information (peak AoI, also abbreviated PAoI) to stay below a hard per-slot deadline, not merely an average bound. Existing approaches meet this requirement only under restrictive assumptions: stochastic channels for Whittle-index AoI, simulator rollouts for deep reinforcement learning, or sublinear cumulative violation for long-term constrained online convex optimization. Under adversarial coefficients, OCO-PAoI-Hard guarantees zero per-slot violation of the modeled AoI state under one-step viability and O(sqrt(T)) regret against any static safe comparator; packet-level safety requires stronger service assumptions. Our key observation is that the fractional peak-AoI deadline collapses exactly to an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, turning hard real-time scheduling into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility through one Euclidean projection per slot, the gradient step preserves no-regret behavior, and the classical virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate. We establish closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds, a matching Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant against execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio. On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAoI-Hard attains zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds, while four representative baselines miss between 1.65 percent and 64.0 percent of slots, and the empirical normalized regret stays below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OCO-PAoI-Hard, a framework that converts hard per-slot Age of Information (peak AoI) deadline constraints in safety-critical IoT systems into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set, achieving zero per-slot violations of the modeled AoI state with O(sqrt(T)) regret and closed-form bounds, validated on adversarial simulations.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical IoT applications (industrial control, V2X, teleoperation) require hard per-slot peak-AoI deadlines, not merely average bounds. Existing methods (Whittle-index, deep RL, long-term constrained OCO) only work under restrictive assumptions such as stochastic channels, simulator rollouts, or sublinear cumulative violations, and cannot guarantee zero per-slot violations under adversarial conditions.
AI.method: The paper observes that the fractional peak-AoI deadline maps exactly to an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, reformulating hard real-time scheduling as time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility via one Euclidean projection per slot, while the gradient step maintains no-regret behavior; the virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate.
AI.result: Closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds, a matching Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant robust to execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio are established. On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAoI-Hard achieves zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds, while four baselines miss 1.65-64.0% of slots; empirical normalized regret stays under the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.
AI.conclusion: OCO-PAoI-Hard offers the first framework guaranteeing zero per-slot modeled-AoI deadline violations under adversarial coefficients with optimal O(sqrt(T)) regret, providing a rigorous and practical solution to hard real-time scheduling in safety-critical IoT systems.

title: ARD-REFSM: Enhancing Reflection Symmetry Detection with Asymmetric Denoising and Rotation Equivariance
summary: Reflection symmetry detection remains challenging due to interference from asymmetric regions and arbitrary orientations of symmetric patterns. Asymmetric regions introduce background clutter that disrupts symmetric pattern matching, whereas conventional convolutional neural networks lack rotation equivariance, leading to inconsistent feature representations under rotational transformations. To address these issues, we propose an Asymmetric Region Denoising (ARD) module and a Rotation Equivariant Feature Similarity Matching (REFSM) module. The ARD module suppresses asymmetric interference to refine symmetric patterns, while the REFSM module enhances rotation equivariance through feature similarity matching between original and rotated images. Specifically, our dual-input REFSM framework leverages rotation loss to maximize consistency between the score maps of original and rotated images, thereby enabling precise prediction of rotation-equivariant symmetry axes. Furthermore, we introduce GMSYM, a new benchmark dataset that categorizes images into diverse scenarios and incorporates various interferences to address the limitations of existing reflection symmetry detection benchmarks. Extensive experiments on four standard datasets (DENDI, NYU, LDRS, SDRW) and our proposed GMSYM dataset demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and robustness.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an asymmetric region denoising (ARD) module and a rotation equivariant feature similarity matching (REFSM) module for reflection symmetry detection, along with a new benchmark dataset GMSYM. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on four standard datasets and the proposed benchmark.
AI.motivation: Reflection symmetry detection is challenged by asymmetric background clutter that disrupts symmetric pattern matching, and conventional CNNs lack rotation equivariance, producing inconsistent feature representations under rotation. These limitations hinder accurate detection of arbitrarily oriented symmetric patterns.
AI.method: The proposed method consists of two modules: (1) an Asymmetric Region Denoising (ARD) module that suppresses asymmetric interference to refine symmetric patterns, and (2) a Rotation Equivariant Feature Similarity Matching (REFSM) module with a dual-input framework that leverages rotation loss to maximize consistency between score maps of original and rotated images for precise rotation-equivariant symmetry axis prediction. Additionally, a new benchmark dataset (GMSYM) is introduced with diverse scenarios and various interferences.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four standard datasets (DENDI, NYU, LDRS, SDRW) and the proposed GMSYM dataset demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and robustness.
AI.conclusion: The combination of asymmetric region denoising and rotation equivariant feature matching effectively addresses both background clutter and rotation inconsistency, achieving superior reflection symmetry detection across standard and newly proposed benchmarks.

title: Sign Language Question Answering: A New Task, Benchmark, and Baseline for Sign Language Understanding
summary: Recent advances in sign language (SL) understanding (SLU) have led to remarkable progress in tasks such as continuous SL recognition and SL translation. However, these tasks are designed with predefined objectives, requiring models to learn a fixed mapping from sign videos to glosses or spoken-language sentences. As a result, they provide only a limited assessment of whether a model truly understands the semantic content of SL videos. To address this limitation, \textbf{we first propose a new task, Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA)}, which evaluates SL understanding by requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. Unlike previous SLU tasks, SLQA provides a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses multiple reasoning capabilities beyond recognition and translation. To facilitate this task, \textbf{we further construct two SignQA benchmarks} based on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily by automatically generating question-answer pairs from existing gloss and sentence annotations using carefully designed templates. The resulting datasets cover five complementary question categories, including position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, and translation understanding. \textbf{Finally, we propose a simple yet effective baseline model} equipped with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy, enabling effective knowledge transfer from existing SLU tasks while enhancing question-aware temporal feature modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all question categories, establishing a strong benchmark for future research on SLQA. Datasets are available at:{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hulala/SignQA-2026}.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA), a new task that evaluates SL understanding by requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about sign language videos. The authors construct two SignQA benchmarks (based on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily) with five question categories, and propose a baseline model with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and in-domain knowledge transfer, which outperforms representative vision-language models.
AI.motivation: Existing sign language understanding (SLU) tasks such as continuous SL recognition and SL translation are limited by predefined objectives that only learn fixed mappings from sign videos to glosses or spoken sentences. These tasks do not adequately assess whether a model truly understands the semantic content of SL videos, motivating a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework that tests multiple reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: The authors (1) propose SLQA, a new task requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos; (2) construct two SignQA benchmarks from PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily by automatically generating question-answer pairs via carefully designed templates from existing gloss and sentence annotations, covering five question categories (position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, translation understanding); and (3) propose a baseline model with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy for question-aware temporal feature modeling.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that the proposed baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all five question categories, establishing a strong benchmark for future SLQA research.
AI.conclusion: SLQA provides a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework for sign language understanding, and the proposed baseline, along with the two SignQA benchmarks, sets a strong foundation for future research in this new task. Datasets are publicly available.

title: First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization Over Distributed Networks for Robust Coreset Selection
summary: With the rapid advancement of the Internet of Things (IoT), massive amounts of data are generated across distributed edge networks. Training models on full data incurs significant computational overhead and storage bottlenecks, rendering coreset selection a critical paradigm. Furthermore, given the privacy-sensitive nature of local data and the escalating demand for model robustness in real-world deployments, developing an effective distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection is vital, yet remains largely unexplored. To this end, this work first characterizes the hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning, and formulates the distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints. Furthermore, to effectively solve the trilevel problem in a distributed manner, the \underline{F}ederated \underline{F}irst-order \underline{C}onstrained \underline{T}rilevel \underline{O}ptimization (F$^2$CTO) is proposed, which synergistically integrates a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation and a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, F$^2$CTO is the first method developed for distributed robust coreset selection, as well as the first distributed optimization approach for trilevel optimization problems with level-wise constraints. Additionally, we prove that the proposed method achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-3/2})$ for finding an $ε$-stationary point. Extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed F$^2$CTO.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses distributed robust coreset selection for IoT edge networks, formulating it as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints. The authors propose F²CTO (Federated First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization), which integrates a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation with a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm. F²CTO achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(ε^{-3/2}) for finding an ε-stationary point, and is the first method for distributed robust coreset selection and the first distributed optimization approach for constrained trilevel problems.
AI.motivation: With the growth of IoT, massive data is generated across distributed edge networks, making full-data model training computationally expensive and storage-intensive. Coreset selection becomes critical, but local data is privacy-sensitive and real-world deployments demand model robustness. An effective distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection is vital yet remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The problem is first characterized as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints, capturing hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning. To solve it distributedly, the F²CTO algorithm is proposed, synergistically integrating a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation and a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm.
AI.result: F²CTO is proven to achieve a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(ε^{-3/2}) for finding an ε-stationary point. Extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method.
AI.conclusion: F²CTO represents the first distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection and the first distributed approach for trilevel optimization with level-wise constraints, offering both theoretical convergence guarantees and empirical validation in continual learning settings.

title: LAST: The Last Query Token Guides Visual Token Pruning for Edge-Cloud Collaborative MLLM Inference
summary: Multimodal foundation models are reshaping edge-cloud visual intelligence from task-specific feature pipelines into token-based interfaces, where edge devices encode visual inputs into tokens for a general-purpose cloud MLLM. However, dense visual-token sequences increase cloud-side inference costs. Existing pruning methods mainly target centralized inference: vision-driven methods can operate before cloud execution but are typically query-agnostic, whereas query-guided methods often rely on internal states of the target MLLM and cannot determine token relevance before transmission. Compact guidance models offer an alternative, but existing designs may require costly attention aggregation or auxiliary generation. We propose LAST, a training-free framework for query-dependent visual token pruning in edge-cloud collaborative MLLM inference. LAST uses a compact edge-side VLM as a guidance proxy and derives a lightweight importance signal from the last query token's attention to visual tokens. Under causal attention, the last query token can attend to the full visual sequence and the entire query context, enabling query-aware pruning without cloud-model access, autoregressive generation, or costly aggregation over multiple query positions. LAST then retains a diverse set of query-relevant visual tokens under a fixed token budget. We evaluate LAST on 11 multimodal benchmarks under multiple token budgets against pruning methods with different guidance strategies. Experiments show that LAST consistently achieves the strongest performance, preserving 95.4% of the full-token accuracy while retaining only 12.5% of the visual tokens, with low edge-side selection overhead and reduced cloud-side computation.

AI.tldr: LAST is a training-free framework for query-dependent visual token pruning in edge-cloud collaborative multimodal LLM inference, using a compact edge-side VLM as a guidance proxy to leverage the last query token's attention to visual tokens. It retains diverse query-relevant visual tokens under a fixed budget, achieving 95.4% of full-token accuracy with only 12.5% of visual tokens across 11 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Multimodal foundation models are moving edge-cloud visual intelligence toward token-based interfaces, but dense visual-token sequences increase cloud-side inference costs. Existing pruning methods are limited: vision-driven methods are query-agnostic, query-guided methods rely on internal states of the target MLLM (unsuitable before transmission), and compact guidance models often require costly attention aggregation or auxiliary generation.
AI.method: LAST employs a compact edge-side VLM as a guidance proxy and derives a lightweight importance signal from the last query token's attention to visual tokens. Under causal attention, the last query token can attend to the full visual sequence and entire query context, enabling query-aware pruning without cloud-model access, autoregressive generation, or costly multi-position aggregation. LAST then retains a diverse set of query-relevant visual tokens under a fixed token budget.
AI.result: Evaluated on 11 multimodal benchmarks under multiple token budgets, LAST consistently achieves the strongest performance compared to pruning methods with different guidance strategies, preserving 95.4% of full-token accuracy while retaining only 12.5% of visual tokens, with low edge-side selection overhead and reduced cloud-side computation.
AI.conclusion: LAST demonstrates that query-aware visual token pruning is feasible at the edge without cloud-model access by leveraging a compact guidance VLM and the causal attention property of the last query token, achieving strong performance with significant computation savings.

title: MemTxn: A Transaction Boundary for Source-Supported Updates and Complete-State Recovery in Agent Memory
summary: Persistent memory lets long-running large language model agents reuse information across sessions and tasks. Yet errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems improve storage and retrieval, but they do not provide a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery. We therefore propose MemTxn, a governance layer outside the answer model. MemTxn verifies whether an update is supported by its source. It also selects the visible version when facts conflict and restores the application-visible state after a fault. The system uses Ordered PatchTest to validate writes, a Temporal Resolver to select versions, and a durable snapshot journal to recover state. On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo states, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the actual physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, MemTxn achieves the highest average F1 across all twelve answer-model configurations. It outperforms Dense by 17.06--24.07 points in five representative settings.

AI.tldr: MemTxn is a governance layer for persistent memory in LLM agents that provides transaction boundaries—verifying updates against sources, resolving version conflicts, and recovering state after faults—achieving perfect audit accuracy and state restoration while outperforming baselines on memory benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Persistent memory allows long-running LLM agents to reuse information, but errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems improve storage and retrieval but lack a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery.
AI.method: MemTxn implements a governance layer outside the answer model with three components: Ordered PatchTest for validating writes, a Temporal Resolver for selecting visible versions under conflict, and a durable snapshot journal for fault recovery.
AI.result: On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the actual physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, it achieves the highest average F1 across all twelve answer-model configurations, outperforming Dense by 17.06–24.07 points in five representative settings.
AI.conclusion: MemTxn demonstrates that adding a transactionally reliable governance layer to persistent memory can prevent corruption, ensure consistency, and significantly improve memory consolidation performance across diverse answer models.

title: Certifying when decision-time information justifies adaptive experimentation
summary: Adaptive laboratories choose measurements during experiments, yet most methods begin after adaptation is permitted. We introduce Opportunity-aware Policy Authorization for Laboratories (\OPAL{}), a framework that decides whether adaptation should be enabled at all. \OPAL{} uses a precommitted contract to require non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk and positive executed value after cost. We establish an impossibility boundary: source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and derive a target-calibrated recovery.
