Applied to an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities and achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion; its 5.18\% false-activation upper bound remained below a 7.5\% limit. Among six methods, only \OPAL{} combined non-zero activation with this risk control. Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability, establishing authorization as a distinct layer for safe adaptive science.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OPAL (Opportunity-aware Policy Authorization for Laboratories), a framework that decides whether adaptive experimentation should be enabled at all, using a precommitted contract requiring non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk, and positive executed value after cost. Applied to an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, it selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities, achieved strictly positive executed value, and maintained a 5.18% false-activation upper bound below its 7.5% limit. It establishes authorization as a distinct safety layer for adaptive science.
AI.motivation: Most adaptive laboratory methods assume adaptation is already permitted and focus on measurement selection during experiments. This work motivates addressing the earlier, foundational question of whether adaptation should be enabled at all, adding an authorization layer before experimentation begins.
AI.method: OPAL uses a precommitted contract to require non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk, and positive executed value after cost. It establishes an impossibility boundary showing source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and derives a target-calibrated recovery.
AI.result: On an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities, and achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion, with a 5.18% false-activation upper bound below the 7.5% limit. Among six methods, only OPAL combined non-zero activation with this risk control.
AI.conclusion: Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability, establishing authorization as a distinct and necessary layer for safe adaptive science, separate from the adaptation policy itself.

title: FiRE: Enhancing MLLMs with Fine-Grained Context Learning for Complex Image Retrieval
summary: Due to their strong generalizable multimodal processing and reasoning capabilities, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated significant potential as universal image retrievers, effectively addressing diverse real-world image retrieval tasks. Nevertheless, pioneering studies, while promising, overlook the potential of fine-grained context modeling and disentangled fine-tuning objectives in enhancing MLLMs' retrieval performance, particularly for complex tasks such as long-text-to-image retrieval, visual dialog retrieval, and composed image retrieval (CIR). Therefore, in this work, we propose an automated fine-grained multimodal quintuple dataset construction pipeline and a novel two-stage fine-grained multimodal fine-tuning strategy. The dataset generation pipeline produces a comprehensive CIR dataset with fine-grained image captions and modification text, facilitating fine-grained context modeling. Beyond the previously entangled fine-tuning paradigm, our approach separates the fine-tuning process into two distinct stages: (1) fine-grained context reasoning-oriented fine-tuning and (2) fine-grained retrieval-oriented fine-tuning. These stages aim to sequentially enhance the model's context understanding and query-target alignment capabilities, thereby improving retrieval performance. Extensive experiments across five datasets encompassing diverse and complex image retrieval tasks demonstrate the remarkable superiority of our method over existing approaches in zero-shot retrieval settings, even with a more lightweight MLLM backbone compared to those methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an automated fine-grained multimodal quintuple dataset construction pipeline and a novel two-stage fine-grained fine-tuning strategy for MLLMs to improve complex image retrieval tasks (long-text-to-image, visual dialog retrieval, CIR), demonstrating superior zero-shot retrieval performance over existing methods even with a lighter backbone.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM-based retrieval approaches overlook the potential of fine-grained context modeling and disentangled fine-tuning objectives, particularly struggling with complex retrieval tasks like long-text-to-image retrieval, visual dialog retrieval, and composed image retrieval (CIR).
AI.method: The method consists of two components: (1) an automated pipeline that constructs a comprehensive CIR dataset with fine-grained image captions and modification text using multimodal quintuples; (2) a two-stage fine-tuning strategy that separates fine-grained context reasoning-oriented fine-tuning from fine-grained retrieval-oriented fine-tuning, sequentially enhancing context understanding and query-target alignment.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across five datasets spanning diverse complex image retrieval tasks show the proposed method significantly outperforms existing approaches in zero-shot retrieval settings, even when using a more lightweight MLLM backbone.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained context modeling coupled with disentangled two-stage fine-tuning effectively improves MLLM-based image retrieval performance on complex tasks, achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot results with a more efficient backbone.

title: Crossing the Margin Cliff: Toward Relearn-Robust LLM Unlearning via Margin Calibration
summary: Large language model unlearning is consistently fragile under relearn attacks. On TOFU, fine-tuning on twenty forget examples substantially recovers held-out forget-set ROUGE for every method we evaluate, and we trace this fragility to optimization geometry. The per-token answer margin of fourteen post-hoc methods spanning gradient, preference, and distillation families converges into a narrow band above the retain reference in 41 of 42 method--size cells, a regularity we call the margin cliff. We prove that this cliff follows whenever the retain coupling holds the diagnostic log-odds of forget content above a floor, a condition that token-saturating losses induce at stationarity and that we verify directly on 34 of 42 cells. Margin Calibration (\textsc{MC}) is a plug-in polish adding a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference's per-token margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus, restoring forget-side pressure where the native loss saturates. Under a stated gradient-dominance condition, whose on-trajectory gradient signature we measure by instrumenting the polish, its stationary set lies on the cliff-crossing side, yielding an attack-budget upper bound on the relearn margin lift. Across TOFU (three Llama-3 sizes, three forget tiers), MUSE-News on Llama-2-7B-hf, and a Phi-3.5 panel, a single frozen configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells (panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L $0.41$ to $0.18$) and lowers raw membership AUC on 13/14, with reduced retain-side utility as the main cost. A deployment variant matches these gains without a retain-trained reference.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies that LLM unlearning is fragile under relearn attacks (fine-tuning on a few forgotten examples restores forget-set knowledge), traces this to a "margin cliff" where post-hoc unlearning methods converge to a narrow margin band. The authors prove this cliff arises from token-saturating losses and propose Margin Calibration (MC), a plug-in polish with a non-saturating margin hinge and KL probe, which restores forget-side pressure and consistently outperforms baselines across TOFU, MUSE-News, and Phi-3.5 benchmarks with a single frozen configuration.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM unlearning methods are vulnerable to relearn attacks—fine-tuning on a handful of forget examples recovers forgotten content. The authors aim to understand the systematic cause of this fragility and develop a method that resists such attacks.
AI.method: The paper analyzes 14 post-hoc unlearning methods (gradient, preference, distillation) and identifies a "margin cliff" where per-token answer margins converge into a narrow band. They prove the cliff follows from the retain coupling and token-saturating loss stationarity. They propose Margin Calibration (MC): a plug-in polish with a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus. Under a gradient-dominance condition (measured via on-trajectory gradient instrumentation), its stationary set lies on the cliff-crossing side, enabling an attack-budget upper bound on relearn margin lift.
AI.result: Across TOFU (three Llama-3 sizes, three forget tiers), MUSE-News, and Phi-3.5, a single frozen MC configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells (panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L drops from 0.41 to 0.18), lowers raw membership AUC on 13/14 settings, with reduced retain-side utility as the main cost. A deployment variant achieves similar gains without a retain-trained reference.
AI.conclusion: The margin cliff explains widespread unlearning fragility, and Margin Calibration provides a robust, plug-in solution that resists relearn attacks across diverse models and benchmarks, at the cost of some retain-side utility. The deployment variant makes the approach practical without needing a retain-trained reference model.

title: Evaluation Protocols and Cross-Subject Generalization in EEG Emotion Recognition
comment: 41 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables including supplementary information. Submitted to Applied Intelligence
summary: Reported accuracy in electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition depends on the complete evaluation procedure, not only the classifier. We separate the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule, then use one archived dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) pathway on SEED and SEED-IV as an illustrative case. In a protocol-matched subject-dependent check, the SEED result was within 1.47 percentage points of the public reference value; the 3.40-point SEED-IV difference remained unresolved. Across 30 matched SEED subject-session trajectories, checkpoint selection based on repeated test-set evaluation increased mean window accuracy from 0.7855 at epoch 80 to 0.8892. Under five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation, validation-selected checkpoints achieved training-participant trial accuracies of 0.9990 on SEED and 0.9920 on SEED-IV. Accuracy for entirely held-out participants was 0.5348 (95% conditional subject-level bias-corrected and accelerated [BCa] interval [0.4667, 0.5985]) on SEED. The SEED-IV estimate was 0.3954 ([0.3343, 0.4648]) and is reported only as secondary sensitivity evidence because its protocol-matched compatibility check remained unresolved. The observed train-to-held-out-subject gaps are inconsistent with simple optimization underfitting, but they do not isolate subject identity from implementation, preprocessing, representation, or distributional factors. Supporting analyses further showed that participant rankings depended on representation and time scale, while a development-selected tail-risk ensemble did not establish a positive gain in a separate final evaluation. Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results should therefore be reported as answers to different questions.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that reported EEG emotion recognition accuracy depends on the full evaluation procedure (target quantity, development, and reporting rule), not just the classifier. Using an archived DGCNN pipeline on SEED and SEED-IV, the authors show large performance gaps between subject-dependent, validation-selected, and held-out-subject evaluations, concluding these should be reported as answers to different questions.
AI.motivation: To disentangle the components of the evaluation procedure in EEG emotion recognition and demonstrate that reported accuracy is procedure-dependent, not solely classifier-dependent. The authors want to expose how checkpoint selection and evaluation protocol can inflate performance estimates and obfuscate generalization.
AI.method: The authors separate the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule. They use one archived dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) pathway on SEED and SEED-IV. They perform protocol-matched subject-dependent checks, 30 matched subject-session trajectories with repeated test-set checkpoint selection, five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation with validation-selected checkpoints, and final evaluation on entirely held-out participants with BCa confidence intervals. Supporting analyses include participant rankings across representations/time scales and a development-selected tail-risk ensemble.
AI.result: Subject-dependent SEED accuracy was within 1.47 percentage points of the public reference; SEED-IV differed by 3.40 points and remained unresolved. Test-set checkpoint selection increased mean window accuracy from 0.7855 (epoch 80) to 0.8892. Validation-selected checkpoints achieved 0.9990 (SEED) and 0.9920 (SEED-IV) training-participant accuracy, but held-out participant accuracy dropped to 0.5348 on SEED (BCa [0.4667, 0.5985]) and 0.3954 on SEED-IV ([0.3343, 0.4648]). The train-to-held-out gap is inconsistent with simple optimization underfitting. Participant rankings depended on representation/time scale; the tail-risk ensemble showed no positive gain in final evaluation.
AI.conclusion: EEG emotion recognition results must be reported with explicit specification of the evaluation protocol. Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results answer different questions and should not be conflated. The large held-out-subject performance drop suggests that reported high accuracies often reflect within-participant memorization rather than genuine cross-subject generalization, though subject identity cannot be fully isolated from other factors.

title: FootprintNet: State-Transition-Guided Dynamic Footprint Learning for Multi-temporal Remote Sensing Change Detection
summary: Despite substantial progress in remote sensing multi-temporal change detection (MTCD), most existing MTCD methods still represent the dynamic process at each spatial location over the entire observation period using a single change category associated with the final observation. This implicit single-change assumption limits their ability to characterize regions of recurrent change closely related to human activities. To address this limitation, we introduce Urban Building Dynamics Detection (UBDD), which identifies building-change dynamic footprints, i.e., the temporal intervals in which changes occur, from multi-temporal imagery and produces pixel-wise classification masks. For regions undergoing two or more changes, UBDD introduces an independent multi-change class for unified representation, thereby enabling unified modeling of single- and multi-change processes. Furthermore, we propose FootprintNet, which abstracts building-change processes as interactions between latent states and actions, and imposes state-action transition constraints to guide the learning of causally coherent change trajectories. It further exploits temporal change-boundary cues to enhance feature contrast across boundary sides, thereby improving the discrimination among different dynamic footprints and enabling accurate detection of dynamic footprints. Moreover, we introduce the Building Change Dynamics Score (BCDS) to address the inability of conventional metrics to reflect the temporal proximity between predicted footprints and labels. It evaluates predictions according to their preservation of change semantics and temporal offsets from the corresponding labels. Extensive experiments on TSCD, MUDS, and WUSU demonstrate that FootprintNet outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/zmoka-zht/FootprintNet.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Urban Building Dynamics Detection (UBDD) and FootprintNet for detecting building-change dynamic footprints from multi-temporal imagery. It addresses the single-change assumption in existing MTCD methods by introducing an independent multi-change class, using state-action transition constraints for causally coherent change trajectories, temporal change-boundary cues for feature contrast, and a new metric (BCDS) for evaluating temporal proximity. FootprintNet achieves state-of-the-art results on TSCD, MUDS, and WUSU datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-temporal change detection methods assume each spatial location undergoes a single change category associated with the final observation, which fails to characterize regions of recurrent change closely related to human activities.
AI.method: The paper proposes (1) UBDD task formulation that detects building-change dynamic footprints (temporal intervals of change) with an independent multi-change class for regions with two or more changes; (2) FootprintNet which models building-change processes as latent state-action interactions with state-action transition constraints, and exploits temporal change-boundary cues to enhance feature contrast; (3) BCDS metric that evaluates predictions based on change semantics preservation and temporal offsets.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on TSCD, MUDS, and WUSU datasets demonstrate that FootprintNet outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dynamic footprint detection paradigm with unified single/multi-change modeling, coupled with the causality-aware network architecture and the temporally-aware evaluation metric, advances the capability of remote sensing change detection for recurrent change characterization.

title: Virtual Process Dossier: A Process-Aware Data Catalogue
summary: We propose the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that also captures workflow provenance. We developed VPD for multi-stage manufacturing use-cases where downstream AI-based optimization tasks require to distinct between datasets generated during individual workflow steps. VPD provides these datasets in a FAIR manner and makes both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance explicit. Our contributions are: (1) the VPD ontology that serves as the catalogue's semantic core; (2) the VPD provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation into the production environment; and (3) the VPD user interface that provides human-centered interaction with the VPD Knowledge Graph. The ontology and code are available at https://github.com/kubeluk/VirtualProcessDossier .

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that captures workflow provenance for multi-stage manufacturing, providing FAIR datasets with explicit prospective and retrospective provenance. It contributes an ontology, a provenance framework for integrating ontology instantiation into production, and a user interface for human-centered interaction.
AI.motivation: Downstream AI-based optimization tasks in multi-stage manufacturing require the ability to distinguish between datasets generated during individual workflow steps, which demands a data catalogue that not only organizes data but also captures workflow provenance in a FAIR manner.
AI.method: The VPD is built as a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue with three key components: (1) the VPD ontology as the semantic core, (2) a provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation into the production environment, and (3) a user interface for human-centered interaction with the Knowledge Graph. Both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance are made explicit.
AI.result: The paper presents the complete VPD system including its ontology, provenance framework, and user interface. The ontology and code are publicly available on GitHub, enabling reproducibility and further adoption.
AI.conclusion: VPD provides a FAIR, Knowledge Graph-based solution for managing and distinguishing datasets across workflow steps in multi-stage manufacturing, with explicit provenance tracking to support AI-based optimization tasks.

title: Looped Transformers with Source-Centered State Evolution
summary: Looped Transformers create a useful train- and test-time compute axis by reusing the same Transformer block over recurrent depth, increasing effective depth at a fixed parameter count. However, that shared block must then govern an entire trajectory of varying hidden states over trained and extrapolated depths. Furthermore, in additive-injection looped Transformers, an input-conditioned signal is reintroduced at every recurrent step, so applying the shared transition at an input-conditioned reference can still move the hidden state. In this paper, we propose Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE), which is designed to reconcile input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence. Specifically, SCSE retains input dependence through its learned anchor and initial deviation, allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance through its zero-deviation mask. The designated anchor is thereby a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias is the next deviation produced from the anchor itself and vanishes in SCSE, while nonzero deviations remain active and support state-dependent recurrent computation. Our theory shows that the zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom whose task effect can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial; SCSE resolves this choice in favor of exact anchor invariance by setting the bias to zero. Across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier. Ablation studies identify the learned anchor and the anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as the primary contributors to the gain, and a trained-model case study grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

AI.tldr: SCSE proposes a design for looped Transformers that reconciles input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence by making the learned anchor a one-step fixed point, improving recurrent quality across multiple language modeling benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers reuse a single shared block over recurrent depth, but this block must govern many varying hidden states at both trained and extrapolated depths. In additive-injection variants, an input-conditioned signal is reintroduced each step, so applying the shared transition at an input-conditioned reference can still move the hidden state, breaking reference preservation.
AI.method: SCSE retains input dependence via a learned anchor and initial deviation; nonzero deviations drive recurrent computation while zero deviation maps to zero; a zero-deviation mask ensures exact anchor invariance, making the anchor a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias (the next deviation from the anchor itself) is set to zero, while nonzero deviations remain active to support state-dependent recurrent computation.
AI.result: Theory shows the zero-deviation forcing bias is a degree of freedom whose task effect can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial; SCSE resolves this in favor of exact anchor invariance. Across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier. Ablations identify the learned anchor and anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as primary contributors; a case study grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.
AI.conclusion: SCSE improves looped Transformer performance by enforcing exact anchor invariance with a zero-deviation mask, turning the anchor into a designed fixed point while keeping nonzero deviations active—yielding gains across multiple benchmarks and highlighting the learned anchor and anchor-coordinate recurrence as key mechanisms.

title: Now You Have My Healthy Attention: A U-DiT for Brain-MRI Inpainting
summary: The ASNR-MICCAI BraTS Local Synthesis (Inpainting) task asks for the anatomically plausible completion of healthy brain tissue within a masked region of a T1-weighted MRI, providing a tumor-free anatomical reference for downstream analysis. As the task is scored by distortion metrics (SSIM, PSNR, MSE), we build a deterministic regression model and focus on giving it inductive biases tailored to inpainting. Our network follows the U-DiT principle of performing self-attention on a downsampled token grid: a volumetric encoder-decoder imports long-range context through a downsampled global self-attention block with three-dimensional rotary position embeddings, while convolutions and skip connections preserve high-frequency detail. Two ideas drive our results. First, we constrain the attention so that occluded ("void") tokens attend only to known-healthy tokens of the same volume, with a learned bias toward each query's contralateral homologue, forcing the completion to be inferred from observed anatomy rather than from other unknown regions. Second, we add a contralateral-symmetry input that supplies the mirrored healthy hemisphere as a patient-specific prior; since the brain is approximately bilaterally symmetric and lesions are typically unilateral, this prior improves the distortion metrics at matched structural similarity. On the official BraTS-2026 validation leaderboard our submission reaches a mean healthy-region SSIM of $0.864$, PSNR of $24.7$\,dB and MSE of $4.6{\times}10^{-3}$ over $219$ cases. We further analyse the residual smoothness inherent to distortion-optimal regression and discuss its implications for anatomical realism.

AI.tldr: The authors present a deterministic regression model for the BraTS-2026 Inpainting task, combining a U-DiT architecture with three-dimensional rotary position embeddings, a constrained attention mechanism where void tokens only attend to known-healthy tokens (with a learned contralateral bias), and a mirrored-hemisphere input as a patient-specific prior. The model achieves a mean healthy-region SSIM of 0.864, PSNR of 24.7 dB, and MSE of 4.6×10⁻³ on the official validation leaderboard across 219 cases.
AI.motivation: The task requires anatomically plausible completion of healthy brain tissue within masked regions of T1-weighted MRI to provide tumor-free anatomical references. Since scoring is based on distortion metrics, the authors aim to build a deterministic regression model with inductive biases specifically tailored to the inpainting problem.
AI.method: The network follows the U-DiT principle: a volumetric encoder-decoder with self-attention on a downsampled token grid, using 3D rotary position embeddings. Convolutions and skip connections preserve high-frequency detail. Two key ideas: (1) masked ("void") tokens attend only to known-healthy tokens within the same volume, with a learned bias toward the contralateral homologue; (2) a contralateral-symmetry input provides the mirrored healthy hemisphere as a patient-specific prior exploiting approximate bilateral brain symmetry.
AI.result: On the official BraTS-2026 validation leaderboard over 219 cases, the submission achieves a mean healthy-region SSIM of 0.864, PSNR of 24.7 dB, and MSE of 4.6×10⁻³.
AI.conclusion: The authors discuss the residual smoothness inherent to distortion-optimal regression and its implications for anatomical realism, acknowledging a trade-off between metric-optimal performance and visually/structurally realistic completions.

title: Simplifying Neural Networks During Training
summary: Understanding and exploiting the training dynamics of overparameterized deep neural networks remains a central challenge in modern machine learning. Recent evidence on Neural Collapse (NC) shows that class representations and classifiers exhibit highly structured geometry, while the Tunnel Effect suggests that only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction. We combine these two perspectives and propose an NC-inspired training framework for simplifying deep networks during training. Our method monitors representation dynamics through the Inverse Fisher Criterion, a stable and efficient proxy for the variability collapse behavior, to identify both the split point between feature extraction and classification and the training stage at which simplification becomes viable. We then replace the trailing layers with a lightweight classification head and continue training the reduced model. Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures show that the proposed method achieves substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to that of the full model. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at: https://github.com/LorenzoSciandra/NNS.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an NC-inspired training framework that uses the Inverse Fisher Criterion to monitor neural collapse dynamics, identifying when and where to replace trailing layers of a deep network with a lightweight classification head, achieving substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Understanding training dynamics of overparameterized deep networks remains challenging. Recent findings on Neural Collapse and the Tunnel Effect suggest that only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction, motivating a principled framework to simplify networks during training.
AI.method: The method monitors representation dynamics via the Inverse Fisher Criterion (a stable, efficient proxy for variability collapse) to determine (1) the split point between feature extraction and classification layers and (2) the training stage at which simplification is viable. The trailing layers are then replaced with a lightweight classification head, and training continues on the reduced model.
AI.result: Experiments on image classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures demonstrate substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to the full model.
AI.conclusion: The NC-inspired approach effectively simplifies deep networks during training by exploiting neural collapse dynamics, achieving parameter efficiency without sacrificing accuracy across multiple architectures.

title: Understanding Submodular Information Measure Based Objectives for Representation Learning: A Variance and Separation Perspective
summary:
Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for representation learning and multimodal learning. In particular, the SCORE framework~\cite{majee2024score} demonstrated that SIMs can serve as effective objectives for supervised contrastive learning. Despite their empirical success, however, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood.
  In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition. We show that Total Information (TI) objectives characterize intra-class structure: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, and Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation that emphasizes rare and confusable classes. We further show that Mutual Information (MI) objectives capture complementary notions of inter-class structure: Graph Cut MI is closely related to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation through Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap.
  We validate these theoretical characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap. Across all settings, the empirical behavior closely matches the proposed theory. Our results provide the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures and offer principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first unified theoretical framework connecting Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition, showing that Total Information objectives characterize intra-class structure while Mutual Information objectives capture inter-class structure, validated through controlled synthetic experiments.
AI.motivation: While SIMs and the SCORE framework have shown empirical success in supervised contrastive learning, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood, creating a gap between empirical usage and theoretical understanding.
AI.method: The authors develop a unified theoretical framework that maps specific SIM objectives (Graph Cut, LogDet, Facility Location) under both Total Information and Mutual Information formulations to classical concepts such as within-class variance, generalized variance, centroid separation, Fisher-style discrimination, Mahalanobis distance, and nearest-mode overlap. They validate these characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap.
AI.result: The paper establishes precise theoretical correspondences: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation emphasizing rare and confusable classes; Graph Cut MI relates to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation via Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap. Empirical results from synthetic experiments closely match these theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures, offering principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

title: ViP-Rig: Visual-Prompted Controllable Rigging
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Zihan Qin and Mingze Sun contributed equally. Xianming Liu is the corresponding author
summary: Rigging is inherently task-dependent because the same mesh may require different skeletons and deformation behaviors across animation tasks. In practice, artists often inspect an initial rig and repeatedly edit its skeletal structure and deformation behavior to meet specific animation requirements. Existing automatic methods primarily generate a plausible rig from geometry, offering limited explicit control over the resulting skeleton and deformation behavior. In this work, we present ViP-Rig, a visual-prompted framework that supports both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing by injecting features extracted from user-drawn or edited 2D skeletal and rigidity prompts into frozen pretrained backbones. Specifically, ViP-Rig consists of two stages, Skeleton Generation and Skinning Prediction. In the first stage, the skeletal sketch is processed by the Dense-to-Compact Visual Prompt Encoding to produce compact, fixed-length conditioning tokens. The resulting tokens are injected into a frozen pretrained autoregressive generator through gated adapters to control joint placement and branching structure while preserving the generator's geometric prior. In the second stage, the rigidity map is processed using the same visual encoding design, while the pretrained skinning backbone remains frozen. The resulting tokens are symmetrically injected into the point and joint streams to modulate point-joint compatibility and the resulting skinning weights. Experiments on Articulation-XL2.0 and zero-shot evaluation on ModelsResource show that ViP-Rig more accurately recovers target skeletons and skinning weights than geometry-conditioned baselines under prompt-guided evaluation. Qualitative results further demonstrate explicit and localized control in both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing.

AI.tldr: ViP-Rig is a visual-prompted framework for mesh rigging that injects features from user-drawn 2D skeletal and rigidity prompts into frozen pretrained backbones, supporting both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing to give users explicit control over skeleton structure and deformation behavior.
AI.motivation: Rigging is task-dependent, and artists often need to repeatedly edit an initial rig to meet specific animation requirements. Existing automatic methods only generate plausible rigs from geometry with limited explicit control over the resulting skeleton and deformation behavior.
AI.method: ViP-Rig comprises two stages: (1) Skeleton Generation, where a Dense-to-Compact Visual Prompt Encoding converts user-drawn skeletal sketches into compact conditioning tokens injected into a frozen pretrained autoregressive generator via gated adapters to control joint placement and branching; (2) Skinning Prediction, where rigidity map tokens are symmetrically injected into frozen point and joint streams of the pretrained skinning backbone to modulate point-joint compatibility and skinning weights.
AI.result: Experiments on Articulation-XL2.0 and zero-shot evaluation on ModelsResource show that ViP-Rig recovers target skeletons and skinning weights more accurately than geometry-conditioned baselines under prompt-guided evaluation. Qualitative results demonstrate explicit and localized control in both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing.
AI.conclusion: Visual prompting with user-drawn 2D skeletal and rigidity prompts enables explicit, localized control over rig generation while preserving the priors of frozen pretrained backbones, outperforming geometry-only conditioning.

title: Back to All-Entity Ranking: Sampler-Dependent Evaluation in Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs
summary:
Next-destination prediction in continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs) commonly ranks an observed interaction against sampled negative destinations. The resulting score is conditional on both the negative distribution and the number of candidates chosen by the researcher. We show that a non-uniform negative distribution changes the Bayes-optimal ranking, while even a finite candidate set drawn uniformly can destabilize model rankings and measured module effects.
  Time-varying source-destination history membership and model operations that use this information directly transmit the sampler's influence to the evaluation score. We examine this mechanism using a factorial evaluation of repeated and new positives against seen and unseen negatives, a minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership, and controlled representation interventions. Across six models on LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, and Wikipedia, at least one model pair changes relative order between the expected Uniform-20 metric and the full catalog on three of the four datasets. The measured effect of the same module also changes in magnitude and direction with the candidate-set size and training objective.
  These results establish that model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the stated candidate configuration. All-entity ranking evaluates every destination in a fixed catalog, eliminating negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining the original CTDG scorer. We therefore recommend all-entity ranking as the primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with an enumerable, fixed destination catalog.

AI.tldr: In continuous-time dynamic graph (CTDG) link prediction, ranking against sampled negative destinations yields evaluation scores that depend on the choice of negative distribution and candidate-set size. This paper shows these sampling choices can alter model rankings and measured module effects across multiple datasets, and recommends all-entity ranking (evaluating every destination in a fixed catalog) as the primary evaluation method for architecture comparisons.
AI.motivation: Standard sampled-negative benchmarks introduce a free parameter—the negative sampling distribution and candidate count—that may confound model comparisons. The authors demonstrate that ranking scores are conditional on these choices, meaning conclusions about model superiority and ablation effects may be artifacts of the sampling configuration rather than genuine model capabilities.
AI.method: The authors analyze the mechanism by which sampler influence propagates through time-varying source-destination history membership into evaluation scores. They run a factorial evaluation contrasting repeated/new positives against seen/unseen negatives, employ a minimal scorer based purely on pair-history membership, and perform controlled representation interventions. They test six models across LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, and Wikipedia datasets.
AI.result: Across the four datasets, at least one model pair changes relative order between the expected Uniform-20 metric and the full catalog on three datasets. The measured effect of the same module changes in both magnitude and direction depending on candidate-set size and training objective. A non-uniform negative distribution changes the Bayes-optimal ranking, and even uniformly drawn finite candidate sets can destabilize model rankings.
AI.conclusion: Model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the candidate configuration. The authors recommend all-entity ranking—evaluating every destination in a fixed catalog—as the primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with an enumerable, fixed destination catalog, as it eliminates negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining the original scorer.

title: FedOGL: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Federated Open-World Multimodal Graph Learning
summary: Federated graph learning enables collaborative training over decentralized graph data without sharing raw graph information. As such risks evolve, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams, retain historical categories, and reject samples outside the known class space. In this setting, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting samples outside the current known class space. The core challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which in federated multimodal graphs is not merely a classifier-level failure: old knowledge can be erased through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedOGL}, a semantic-structural memory preservation framework. On the client side, FedOGL preserves historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation, while protecting graph-propagation memory via projection onto a globally shared structure basis. On the server side, FedOGL maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to facilitate cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with the best-performing baselines, FedOGL reduces performance degradation caused by catastrophic forgetting by \textbf{42.67\%}, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: FedOGL is a semantic-structural memory preservation framework for federated graph learning that addresses catastrophic forgetting in open-world multimodal graph streams, reducing forgetting degradation by 42.67% over the best baselines.
AI.motivation: In federated graph learning over multimodal graph streams, clients must learn new classes while retaining old ones and rejecting out-of-distribution samples. Catastrophic forgetting in this setting is not merely classifier-level but spans modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation, a challenge not adequately addressed by existing methods.
AI.method: FedOGL consists of client-side and server-side mechanisms. Client-side: replay and task-start distillation preserve historical decision behavior, while graph-propagation memory is protected via projection onto a globally shared structure basis. Server-side: compact category prototypes are maintained and transferred across clients to enable knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show FedOGL reduces catastrophic forgetting performance degradation by 42.67% compared to the best-performing baselines while maintaining or improving downstream task performance.
AI.conclusion: FedOGL effectively addresses catastrophic forgetting in federated multimodal graph learning by jointly preserving semantic and structural memory, demonstrating significant improvements in forgetting mitigation and downstream task performance.

title: Deep learning-based hierarchical insect classification using camera trap imagery
summary: Declining insect populations make reliable biodiversity monitoring increasingly urgent, yet monitoring of insect biodiversity is hampered by a lack of standardised data and by costly and time-consuming manual identification by expert entomologists. Deep learning-based image classifiers, processing data from automated non-lethal camera traps, have the potential to transform and scale insect biodiversity monitoring. However, challenges remain in acquiring expert-annotated datasets, developing model architectures that generalise well across diverse taxonomic levels and training models on highly imbalanced data. Hierarchical data also benefits from designing models that default to higher-confidence, coarser-level predictions, when uncertain about finer taxonomic levels. In this paper we address these challenges with a deep learning-based hierarchical classification model. First, we present a manually curated, long-tailed dataset of around one million images of insects, extracted from 1,801 camera-trap video recordings and annotated with a five-level, 34-class hierarchy. Further, we adapt a hierarchical classification model architecture to a five-level variable-depth hierarchy, with class-balanced weighting. Our model improves on non-hierarchical classifiers by leveraging biological taxonomy to extract granularity-specific visual features and makes hierarchy-consistent predictions to the deepest taxonomic level that meets a confidence threshold (T = 0.6). Our model achieved a per-level accuracy of 80-99% on test data, across five levels of hierarchy. Furthermore ...

AI.tldr: This paper presents a deep learning-based hierarchical classification model for automated insect biodiversity monitoring from camera-trap images, using a manually curated dataset of ~1 million images with a five-level, 34-class taxonomy. The model leverages biological hierarchy for granularity-specific feature extraction and makes hierarchy-consistent predictions with a confidence threshold, achieving 80-99% per-level accuracy.
AI.motivation: Declining insect populations require reliable biodiversity monitoring, but current methods are hampered by lack of standardized data and costly manual identification by experts. Deep learning on camera-trap images could scale monitoring, yet challenges remain in acquiring expert annotations, generalizing architectures across taxonomic levels, and handling imbalanced data.
AI.method: The authors curate a long-tailed dataset of ~1 million insect images from 1,801 camera-trap video recordings, annotated with a five-level, 34-class hierarchy. They adapt a hierarchical classification model architecture to a variable-depth hierarchy with class-balanced weighting, enabling granularity-specific visual feature extraction and hierarchy-consistent predictions to the deepest taxonomic level meeting a confidence threshold (T=0.6).
AI.result: The model achieves a per-level accuracy of 80-99% on test data across all five levels of the hierarchy, improving on non-hierarchical classifiers.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical deep learning classification leveraging biological taxonomy, combined with confidence-based depth selection, offers an effective and scalable approach to automated insect biodiversity monitoring from camera-trap imagery.

title: Orca: Neural Operators for Causal Reasoning in Continuous Time
summary: Structural causal models are the standard language for reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, but they describe static variables, typically measured once, and usually forbid cyclic dependencies. Many systems we care about, such as patients, climates, and economies, instead evolve continuously in time, are observed at irregular time points, and contain feedback loops. We argue that neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in this setting, and propose Orca, a framework in which each node of the causal graph is a function of time and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces. We extend existing neural operator architectures to express causal mechanisms: a mechanism computes the function value of a node from its parent nodes by taking several parent functions as input, respects the arrow of time, and treats latent exogenous noise as a function that can be inferred and reused for counterfactuals. We formalize the model class and demonstrate counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples. Code is available at https://github.com/gerritgr/orca

AI.tldr: Orca is a framework extending structural causal models to continuous-time settings using neural operator learning, where causal graph nodes are functions of time and mechanisms are learned maps between function spaces, enabling counterfactual reasoning in dynamic systems with feedback loops and irregular observations.
AI.motivation: Structural causal models are limited to static variables and typically forbid cyclic dependencies, yet many real-world systems (patients, climates, economies) evolve continuously in time, are observed irregularly, and contain feedback loops. The paper argues that neural operator learning provides a natural foundation to extend causal reasoning to this dynamic setting.
AI.method: Orca extends neural operator architectures to express causal mechanisms, where each node in the causal graph is a function of time and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces. A mechanism computes a node's function value from its parent functions, respects the arrow of time, and treats latent exogenous noise as an inferable function reusable for counterfactuals.
AI.result: The paper formalizes the model class and demonstrates counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples, with code made publicly available.
AI.conclusion: Neural operator learning is a promising foundation for causal reasoning in continuous-time dynamical systems, overcoming limitations of static structural causal models by enabling feedback loops, irregular observations, and function-valued counterfactuals.

title: Tight Sample Complexity for Low-Rank Adaptation: Matching Bounds and Rank Selection
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard mechanism for fine-tuning large pretrained models, yet its statistical properties remain only partially understood. Existing generalization results provide upper bounds of the form O~(sqrt(rd/n)) or O~(rd/n), but a matching lower bound is missing, and the question of how to choose the LoRA rank r has no formal answer. Both gaps are closed here. A local Rademacher argument establishes an upper bound of O~(rd/n) on the excess risk of the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA, whenever the target adaptation has rank at most r. A matching minimax lower bound of Omega(rd/n) is then proved via a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of R^{d x d}; the bound applies to any estimator whose output lies in the rank-r LoRA class. Combining the two yields a rank-selection dichotomy. For the constrained empirical risk minimizer, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r*, and over-ranking strictly hurts. For adaptive estimators of the nuclear-norm-then-truncate type, over-ranking is harmless and the rate saturates at Theta~(r* d / n) regardless of r. Taken together, the three results characterize the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning within the well-specified locally quadratic regime, and identify the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty as a property of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than of the LoRA class itself. Predictions of the theory are verified on a synthetic trace-regression benchmark and on real LoRA fine-tuning across three (model, task) configurations covering DistilBERT and RoBERTa on SST-2 and MRPC. All configurations exhibit the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with two showing statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p = 0.016).

AI.tldr: This paper provides matching upper and lower bounds (O(rd/n)) on the excess risk of rank-r LoRA fine-tuning, proving a rank-selection dichotomy: constrained empirical risk minimization (ERM) has an optimal rank equal to the intrinsic rank r* where over-ranking hurts, while nuclear-norm-then-truncate adaptive estimators are robust to over-ranking with rates saturating at Theta(r* d/n). The theory is verified on synthetic trace regression and real LoRA fine-tuning on DistilBERT/RoBERTa across SST-2 and MRPC, showing predicted U-shaped validation loss.
AI.motivation: LoRA is the standard fine-tuning method, but its statistical properties are only partially understood. Existing upper bounds lack matching lower bounds, and there is no formal guidance on selecting the LoRA rank r. The paper aims to close both gaps by providing a complete statistical characterization of LoRA fine-tuning.
AI.method: The paper uses three main techniques: (1) a local Rademacher complexity argument to establish the O(rd/n) upper bound on excess risk for the constrained ERM over rank-r LoRA; (2) a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of R^{dxd} to prove a matching minimax lower bound of Omega(rd/n) applicable to any estimator whose output lies in the rank-r LoRA class; (3) combining the bounds to derive a rank-selection dichotomy between constrained ERM and adaptive nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators. Empirical validation uses synthetic trace-regression benchmarks and real fine-tuning on DistilBERT and RoBERTa for SST-2 and MRPC.
AI.result: The upper and lower bounds match at Theta(rd/n) in the well-specified locally quadratic regime. For constrained ERM, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r*, and over-ranking strictly hurts. For nuclear-norm-then-truncate adaptive estimators, over-ranking is harmless with rate saturation at Theta(r* d/n) regardless of r. Real experiments across three (model, task) configurations exhibit the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with two configurations showing statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p = 0.016).
AI.conclusion: The paper fully characterizes the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning, showing that the over-parameterization penalty observed empirically is a property of unregularized ERM rather than inherent to the LoRA class itself. This provides formal guidance for rank selection and distinguishes when over-ranking is harmful (constrained ERM) versus harmless (adaptive estimators).

title: Beyond Classification: Pathology Foundation Models as Detection Encoders for Mitotic Figures
summary: Pathology foundation models (FMs) are models trained on vast amounts of typically unlabeled data and have been shown to yield regularized latent spaces that can be used effectively in downstream classification tasks. This is also true for the classification of mitotic figures vs. other cells. However, it is so far unclear if the latent space of current FMs provides features that are discriminant and spatially suitably resolved to also serve as a backbone for dense object detection paradigms. In this work, we investigate this question for common current pathology FMs (UNI, UNI2-h, Virchow, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, H-optimus-1) and compare their performance against a fully end-to-end trained baseline based on a ResNet50 architecture. We combine FM backbones with representatives of single stage, dual stage and self-attention-based detectors (RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, Deformable DETR respectively) on the multi-domain MIDOG++ dataset, and on the TUPAC16 dataset as an out-of-domain case. We show that the H-optimus-0 and Virchow models yielded competitive performance, indicating that the latent spaces of current FMs, all trained on image-level self-supervision, are suitable for direct mitotic figure detection and may be slightly more robust on our out-of-domain test case. All code is made available publicly at https://github.com/DeepMicroscopy/FM4MFdet.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether pathology foundation models (UNI, UNI2-h, Virchow, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, H-optimus-1) can serve as backbones for dense object detection for mitotic figure classification, comparing them against a fully end-to-end ResNet50 baseline across three detector types (RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, Deformable DETR) on MIDOG++ and TUPAC16 datasets. H-optimus-0 and Virchow achieve competitive performance with improved out-of-domain robustness.
AI.motivation: Pathology foundation models produce regularized latent spaces effective for classification, but it is unclear whether these latent spaces contain features that are sufficiently discriminant and spatially resolved to serve as backbones for dense object detection paradigms, such as mitotic figure detection.
AI.method: The authors evaluate six current pathology FMs (UNI, UNI2-h, Virchow, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, H-optimus-1) as backbones combined with three detector types—RetinaNet (single-stage), Faster R-CNN (dual-stage), and Deformable DETR (self-attention-based)—on the MIDOG++ dataset and the TUPAC16 out-of-domain dataset, benchmarking against a fully end-to-end ResNet50 baseline.
AI.result: H-optimus-0 and Virchow models achieved competitive performance comparable to the end-to-end baseline for mitotic figure detection, and demonstrated slightly better robustness on the out-of-domain TUPAC16 test case.
AI.conclusion: The latent spaces of current pathology FMs, trained via image-level self-supervision, are suitable as direct backbones for dense mitotic figure detection, suggesting they can be effectively reused beyond classification tasks. All code is publicly released.

title: Search as Computation Allocation
summary: Many algorithms spend an internal resource before returning a decision and are evaluated only by the quality of that terminal output. We formalize such procedures as terminal computation-allocation problems: costly computations produce observations, update beliefs about a latent environment, and matter only through terminal decision loss. Bellman equations characterize optimal allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. We then relate value of computation (VOC) to information. Mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, whereas under simple regret VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity; moreover, information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly, although it gives a one-sided upper bound on VOC. Bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions illustrate the same model under different computation topologies. Finally, under an explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model, maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases. The theory identifies a shared decision problem without asserting that one acquisition rule is universally optimal.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes terminal computation-allocation problems, where algorithms spend internal computational resources (producing observations and updating beliefs) that matter only through terminal decision loss. Bellman equations characterize optimal allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. The value of computation (VOC) is related to information: mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, while simple regret yields a knowledge-gradient quantity. The framework unifies bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions under different computation topologies, and recovers weighted A* as a special case.
AI.motivation: Many algorithms allocate computational resources internally before producing a final decision, yet evaluation typically focuses only on the terminal output quality. There is no unified formal framework for understanding how computation should be allocated when intermediate computations matter exclusively through the terminal decision.
AI.method: The authors formalize terminal computation-allocation problems, derive Bellman equations for optimal allocation under varied settings (fixed budgets, priced computation, exact certification), and establish formal relationships between value of computation and information-theoretic quantities. They demonstrate the framework across diverse computation topologies (bandit pulls, tree simulations, node expansions) and show that maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A* with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases under an explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model.
AI.result: Mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss; under simple regret, VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity. Information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly relative to VOC, though it provides a one-sided upper bound on VOC. The framework unifies several algorithm families and recovers weighted A* as an instantiation of approximate VOC maximization.
AI.conclusion: The theory identifies a shared decision problem underlying diverse algorithms without asserting any single acquisition rule is universally optimal, providing a principled lens for reasoning about computation allocation across different problem structures.

title: Event-Structured Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Differentiable Critical Clearing Boundaries
summary: Transient-stability assessment determines whether a power system can recover after a disturbance and is therefore essential to preventing generator trips and cascading outages. A key metric is the critical clearing time (CCT), which specifies the maximum time available to clear a fault before synchronism is lost. Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because complicated fault-clearing dynamics require repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times. We propose an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) that aligns its representation with the pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics and enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces. A smooth trajectory-induced stability margin defines a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, enabling accurate boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction through a distilled readout. We further prove a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate, in which exact event chaining eliminates separate state-interface defect terms. Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show that ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) for transient-stability assessment and critical clearing time (CCT) estimation in power systems. It aligns the network with pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing dynamics, enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces, and uses a smooth trajectory-induced stability margin for differentiable CCT boundary approximation. The method outperforms neural-surrogate baselines on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems.
AI.motivation: Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because fault-clearing dynamics require repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times. Traditional approaches are computationally expensive, and existing neural surrogates lack physics-informed structure that aligns with the piecewise event-driven nature of fault dynamics.
AI.method: ES-PINN is an event-structured PINN that: (1) aligns its representation with pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics; (2) enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces; (3) uses a smooth trajectory-induced stability margin for differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary; (4) provides a distilled readout for direct CCT prediction; and (5) establishes a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate with exact event chaining eliminating separate state-interface defect terms.
AI.result: Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses demonstrate effectiveness and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ES-PINN framework provides a computationally efficient and physically consistent approach for transient-stability assessment and CCT estimation, with theoretical guarantees via the residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error bound, making it a promising alternative to repeated simulation-based approaches for power system stability analysis.

title: ENCORE: Event-Assisted Complementary Motion Refinement for Learned Video Compression
summary: Learned video compression relies on accurate temporal modeling to remove redundancy between adjacent frames. However, most existing codecs infer motion solely from discretely sampled RGB frames, making their estimates vulnerable to fast motion, blur, occlusion, weak texture, low illumination, and abrupt brightness changes. Event cameras asynchronously capture fine-grained intensity changes between RGB timestamps and therefore provide complementary evidence about inter-frame dynamics. We propose ENCORE, an Event-Assisted Complementary Motion Refinement framework for learned video compression. ENCORE first employs Complementary Motion Representation (CMR) to decompose aligned RGB-event features into common and modality-specific motion representations. Spatial Energy and Redundancy-Informed Calibration (SERIC) then identifies event-specific responses that are active and novel relative to RGB, suppresses weak or redundant evidence, and predicts a candidate flow correction. Finally, Energy-Aware Routing (EAR) determines where and how strongly the correction should refine the RGB flow. Events serve solely as an auxiliary modality for motion modeling, while RGB remains the only coding and reconstruction target. Experiments on BS-ERGB, HQ-EVFI, and CED demonstrate consistent gains across datasets and GOP lengths. On BS-ERGB, ENCORE achieves up to 20.80% PSNR-RGB and 22.14% MS-SSIM-RGB BD-rate savings, while retaining clear improvements on the other two datasets.

AI.tldr: ENCORE is a learned video compression framework that uses event cameras as an auxiliary modality to refine motion estimation between RGB frames. It decomposes aligned RGB-event features via Complementary Motion Representation, uses Spatial Energy and Redundancy-Informed Calibration to predict candidate flow corrections, and employs Energy-Aware Routing to selectively refine RGB motion. It achieves up to 20.80% PSNR-RGB and 22.14% MS-SSIM-RGB BD-rate savings on BS-ERGB while remaining RGB-only for coding and reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Existing learned video codecs estimate inter-frame motion solely from discretely sampled RGB frames, making them vulnerable to fast motion, blur, occlusion, weak texture, low illumination, and abrupt brightness changes. Event cameras asynchronously capture fine-grained intensity changes between RGB timestamps, providing complementary evidence about inter-frame dynamics that can improve motion estimation robustness.
AI.method: ENCORE comprises three components: (1) Complementary Motion Representation (CMR) decomposes aligned RGB-event features into common and modality-specific motion representations; (2) Spatial Energy and Redundancy-Informed Calibration (SERIC) identifies active and novel event-specific responses, suppresses weak or redundant evidence, and predicts a candidate flow correction; (3) Energy-Aware Routing (EAR) determines where and how strongly the correction should refine the RGB flow. Events serve only as an auxiliary modality for motion modeling while RGB remains the sole coding and reconstruction target.
AI.result: Experiments on BS-ERGB, HQ-EVFI, and CED demonstrate consistent gains across datasets and GOP lengths. On BS-ERGB, ENCORE achieves up to 20.80% PSNR-RGB and 22.14% MS-SSIM-RGB BD-rate savings, with clear improvements retained on the other two datasets.
AI.conclusion: Event-assisted complementary motion refinement is an effective and general strategy for improving learned video compression under challenging conditions, with consistent rate-distortion gains achieved without compromising the RGB-only coding/reconstruction pipeline.

title: An Empirical Study of Coordination Mode as the First-Class Citizen in From-Scratch Multi-Agent Coding
summary:
Multi-agent vibe coding promises to accelerate software development, yet existing benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion. We introduce multi-agent from-scratch evaluation benchmark, MSEval, evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world tasks. Grounded in 10 authentic, full-stack projects across 10 domains, MSEval scores performance using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics.
  Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate via periodic sync intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. Concurrently, the automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Across 100 runs, MSEval reveals that organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed--cost--quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying the topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, whereas heavy managerial oversight degrades performance. Ultimately, MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software. The benchmark is released at https://github.com/robinren03/MSEval.

AI.tldr: MSEval is a new benchmark for evaluating multi-agent vibe coding on real-world full-stack tasks, featuring authentic projects, hierarchical requirement scoring, 10 collaboration topologies tested via the LegoGent execution engine, and an automated grader (TAgent) that measures functional success, latency, and token cost. Experiments across 100 runs show that organizational topology significantly impacts the speed-cost-quality trade-off, even rivaling model capability.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent coding benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical costs (time and money), conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion. There is a need for a benchmark grounded in realistic software development scenarios that captures the true speed-cost-quality trade-offs of multi-agent systems.
AI.method: MSEval is constructed using 10 authentic full-stack projects across 10 domains, scored via hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics. The LegoGent execution engine tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate via periodic sync intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. The automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost.
AI.result: Across 100 runs, organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed-cost-quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, while heavy managerial oversight degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software, addressing the gap between synthetic benchmarks and real-world engineering practice.

title: NMINE: Normalized Mutual Information Neural Estimation
summary:
Mutual information is a general measure of statistical dependence that captures both linear and nonlinear relationships between random variables. For continuous and multidimensional variables For continuous multidimensional variables, mutual information must be estimated from samples. Because mutual information is unbounded, its values are not directly comparable across datasets, dimensions, or applications. Normalized mutual information addresses this limitation by converting mutual information into a normalized dependency score. Recent work has demonstrated the practical value of normalized mutual information in applications such as molecular dynamics {arXiv:2405.04980} and interpretable machine learning {arXiv:2409.16768}, but existing estimators remain sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability {arXiv:2410.07642}.
  In this paper, we propose a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables. The proposed approach combines a MINE-based neural mutual information estimator {arXiv:1801.04062} with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators {arXiv:1905.12957}. Mutual information is estimated using the Donsker--Varadhan representation, while marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution, from which entropy is recovered. The resulting estimator provides a neural alternative to k-nearest-neighbor-based normalized mutual information estimation {arXiv:2405.04980}.
  Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show that the proposed estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline. These results indicate that neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables, combining a MINE-based mutual information estimator with neural marginal entropy estimators to provide a more accurate alternative to k-nearest-neighbor-based methods.
AI.motivation: Mutual information is difficult to compare across datasets due to its unbounded nature, and existing normalized mutual information estimators remain sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability issues. A more robust estimator is needed for continuous multidimensional settings.
AI.method: The proposed approach combines a MINE-based neural mutual information estimator (using the Donsker-Varadhan representation) with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators. Marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference, from which entropy is recovered.
AI.result: Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show that the proposed neural estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline.
AI.conclusion: Neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings, offering improved accuracy over existing k-nearest-neighbor-based baselines.

title: Split and Drive: Dual-Axis Disentanglement for Real-Time Gaussian Head Avatars
summary: Creating photorealistic animatable head avatars from a single image remains a fundamental challenge in digital human synthesis. While recent 3D Gaussian Splatting methods have achieved promising results, they rely on external tracking pipelines whose latency is excluded from inference measurements. Furthermore, they adopt unified representations that entangle geometrically distinct facial regions, limiting both expressiveness and rendering fidelity. We propose SpiD (Split and Drive), a single-image Gaussian head avatar framework built on two disentanglement axes. The compute axis internalizes per-frame driving, eliminating external tracking dependency at inference. The feature axis decomposes the avatar into three specialized Gaussian branches, each modeling a geometrically distinct facial domain. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistently strong performance against state-of-the-art methods while achieving the fastest inference speed among all compared methods on a single GPU with the complete driving pipeline included.

AI.tldr: SpiD is a single-image Gaussian head avatar framework that disentangles computation (internalizing per-frame driving to eliminate external tracking) and features (decomposing into three specialized Gaussian branches for geometrically distinct facial regions), achieving state-of-the-art performance with the fastest inference speed including the full driving pipeline.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting head avatar methods depend on external tracking pipelines whose latency is excluded from inference measurements, and they use unified representations that entangle geometrically distinct facial regions, limiting expressiveness and rendering fidelity.
AI.method: SpiD (Split and Drive) builds on two disentanglement axes: (1) a compute axis that internalizes per-frame driving to remove external tracking dependency at inference, and (2) a feature axis that splits the avatar into three specialized Gaussian branches, each modeling a geometrically distinct facial domain.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show consistently strong performance against state-of-the-art methods while achieving the fastest inference speed among all compared methods on a single GPU with the complete driving pipeline included.
AI.conclusion: The disentangled design across both compute and feature axes enables high-fidelity, expressive, and efficient single-image head avatars without relying on external tracking infrastructure.

title: Not All Tokens Deserve Equal Credit: Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation for Long-CoT Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is central to improving long-CoT reasoning in large language models.
