Critic-free methods such as GRPO convert response-level rewards into advantages and uniformly broadcast them across tokens, overlooking their unequal contributions to the final outcome. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) instead provides dense distributional supervision by minimizing the forward KL divergence between an unprivileged policy and a privileged self-teacher, implicitly assuming that the resulting likelihood shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information. We test this premise by fixing each sampled trajectory and re-scoring it under two opposing outcome conditions, one asserting correctness and the other incorrectness. Most affected tokens shift in the same direction under both conditions, with few sign reversals and substantial overlap in the induced optimization signals. Large shifts also concentrate on highly substitutable surface-form tokens, whereas tokens carrying problem-specific reasoning content are less sensitive. These findings show that privileged shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions, while their magnitudes primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. Based on these observations, we propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a simple extension of GRPO that reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve both the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction. On long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO baseline with the same number of policy updates. Targeted ablations further corroborate our diagnosis: privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the premise underlying on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) for RLVR in long-CoT reasoning, finding that privileged self-teacher shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions. The authors propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a simple GRPO extension that reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes advantages, achieving consistent improvements over GRPO on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Critic-free RLVR methods like GRPO broadcast response-level rewards uniformly across tokens, ignoring unequal token contributions. OPSD attempts to provide dense supervision via privileged self-distillation, but its implicit assumption—that likelihood shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information—has not been rigorously tested. The authors aim to validate or refute this premise and design a credit allocation method grounded in counterfactual sensitivity.
AI.method: The authors conduct a diagnostic study by fixing sampled trajectories and re-scoring them under two opposing outcome conditions (correct vs. incorrect) to measure token-level shift behavior. They then propose CSCR, which extends GRPO by downweighting credit for highly counterfactually sensitive tokens and renormalizing token-level advantages to preserve both the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction. Targeted ablations test intermediate weighting and modulation strength.
AI.result: Most affected tokens shift in the same direction under both correctness conditions, with few sign reversals and substantial overlap in optimization signals. Large shifts concentrate on substitutable surface-form tokens rather than problem-specific reasoning content. CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO on long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks with equal policy updates. Ablations show moderate downweighting is most effective and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.
AI.conclusion: Privileged shift magnitudes primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value, making OPSD-style directions unreliable. CSCR offers a lightweight, principled correction by reallocating credit away from highly sensitive tokens, demonstrating that counterfactual sensitivity is a practical signal for improving RLVR credit assignment.

title: VESTIGE: A Knowledge-Guided Masking Strategy for Corruption-Aware Fine-Tuning of Genomic Transformers, Validated on Ancient DNA Reconstruction
summary: Standard masked-language-model fine-tuning applies a uniform masking probability across every token position, assuming reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic. When the degradation process is characterised and concentrated at predictable positions, this assumption fails: at peak damage sites the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor. We introduce VESTIGE, a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns the masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile. We apply it to ancient DNA (aDNA) reconstruction, where cytosine deamination produces a position-dependent C-to-T / G-to-A gradient quantified per-position by mapDamage2. Rescaling so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15% - identical to standard MLM - isolates spatial redistribution as the sole variable, with model, data, seed, and hyperparameters held fixed across both DNABERT-2 runs on a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes). Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE leads standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions (three genes) even under damage amplified 10-30x beyond authentic PMD rates. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier returns AUC = 0.935 and clears 98.2% of reconstructed windows, the 1.76% remainder attributable to reference-genome features, not reconstruction artefacts. The principle is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile - FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore - substitutes directly for the PMD array, making VESTIGE a knowledge-guided training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

AI.tldr: VESTIGE is a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns the masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile. Applied to ancient DNA reconstruction, it outperforms standard MLM across all tested settings (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), reduces validation cross-entropy by 13%, and produces high-quality protein reconstructions (TM-score > 0.95) even under amplified damage, while remaining domain-agnostic for other degradation processes.
AI.motivation: Standard MLM fine-tuning assumes reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic by applying uniform masking probability across all token positions. This assumption fails when degradation is concentrated at predictable positions (e.g., peak damage sites in ancient DNA), where the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor. The authors identify this gap and propose aligning masking distribution with actual corruption profiles.
AI.method: VESTIGE replaces the standard MLM collator by rescaling the masking distribution to match an empirically measured per-position corruption profile (from mapDamage2 for aDNA). Masking rates are rescaled so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15%, identical to standard MLM, isolating spatial redistribution as the only variable. All other factors (model, data, seed, hyperparameters) are held fixed across DNABERT-2 runs on a mammoth CDS corpus.
AI.result: Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE outperforms standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), reduces validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions even under 10-30x amplified damage. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier returns AUC = 0.935 and clears 98.2% of reconstructed windows, with the remainder attributable to reference-genome features, not reconstruction artefacts.
AI.conclusion: VESTIGE demonstrates that knowledge-guided, position-aware masking significantly improves reconstruction on degraded sequence data. The principle is domain-agnostic—applicable to FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore corruption profiles—making it a generalizable training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

title: TongueReenact: Geometry-Anchored Tongue Synthesis for Face Reenactment
summary: Modern face reenactment systems achieve impressive pose and expression transfer using geometry-driven representations. However, they largely ignore tongue dynamics, leading to anatomically inconsistent mouth interiors during speech and expressive motions. We introduce the first framework for cross-identity tongue dynamics transfer in face reenactment. We propose a foundation-model-assisted bootstrapping pipeline that produces a dedicated tongue segmentation model for in-the-wild reenactment without curated annotations. We further introduce a spatially constrained latent masked diffusion model for realistic tongue synthesis, with adaptive mask dilation for seamless mouth boundary transitions. Extensive experiments demonstrate improvements of more than two times over all baselines on every tongue-specific metric. We additionally propose a VLM-based evaluation protocol that replicates expert annotation at scale, confirming perceptual superiority across all ablation variants.

AI.tldr: A novel framework for cross-identity tongue dynamics transfer in face reenactment, using a foundation-model-assisted bootstrapping pipeline to build a tongue segmentation model, a spatially constrained latent masked diffusion model for realistic tongue synthesis, and a VLM-based evaluation protocol, achieving >2x improvement over baselines on all tongue-specific metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing face reenactment systems excel at pose and expression transfer via geometry-driven representations but ignore tongue dynamics, resulting in anatomically inconsistent mouth interiors during speech and expressive facial motions. This is the first work to address cross-identity tongue dynamics transfer in face reenactment.
AI.method: (1) A foundation-model-assisted bootstrapping pipeline that produces a dedicated tongue segmentation model for in-the-wild reenactment without curated annotations; (2) a spatially constrained latent masked diffusion model for realistic tongue synthesis with adaptive mask dilation for seamless mouth boundary transitions.
AI.result: Improvements of more than two times over all baselines on every tongue-specific metric. A VLM-based evaluation protocol replicates expert annotation at scale and confirms perceptual superiority across all ablation variants.
AI.conclusion: Tongue dynamics can be faithfully transferred across identities in face reenactment, and the proposed framework sets a new state-of-the-art for anatomically consistent mouth interiors, with validation supported by both quantitative metrics and scalable VLM-based perceptual evaluation.

title: Dynamic Spectral Filtering for Temporal Graph Learning: Learning Evolving Propagation Operators
summary: Temporal graph learning is commonly organized around the evolution of node states or the encoding of interaction histories. We study an underexplored, operator-centric question: should the graph propagation mechanism itself evolve over time? We introduce Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), which represents propagation at snapshot t by a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. DSF explicitly treats these compact multi-order coefficients as recurrent temporal states. A recurrent branch proposes updates, while multiplicative global and order-specific gates regulate their magnitude. The temporal state is independent of the number of nodes. On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF runs attain AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860, respectively, with 93K to 133K trainable parameters, 68 to 182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6 to 2.1 seconds of training per epoch. Against the closely related DEFT baseline, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3 to 8.6 times fewer parameters, 25 to 33 times less GPU memory, and 5 to 19 times less time per epoch. Relative to all measured alternatives, it uses 3.3 to 38.6 times less GPU memory. These results support direct spectral-response evolution as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), a temporal graph learning method where the graph propagation mechanism itself evolves over time via time-dependent Chebyshev polynomial filter coefficients treated as recurrent states. DSF achieves competitive link-prediction accuracy on MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit benchmarks while being dramatically more parameter-efficient and computationally cheaper than comparable baselines.
AI.motivation: Temporal graph learning typically focuses on evolving node states or encoding interaction histories, but the question of whether the propagation mechanism itself should evolve over time remains underexplored. The authors investigate this operator-centric perspective as a potentially useful temporal inductive bias.
AI.method: DSF represents the propagation operator at each snapshot t as a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. These compact multi-order coefficients are explicitly treated as recurrent temporal states. A recurrent branch proposes coefficient updates, and multiplicative global and order-specific gates regulate their magnitude. The temporal state is node-count independent.
AI.result: On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, DSF achieves AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860 with only 93K to 133K parameters, 68 to 182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6 to 2.1 seconds per training epoch. Compared to the DEFT baseline, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3-8.6x fewer parameters, 25-33x less GPU memory, and 5-19x less time per epoch. It uses 3.3-38.6x less GPU memory than all measured alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Direct spectral-response evolution serves as a useful temporal inductive bias, particularly when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement. The findings support the value of evolving the propagation mechanism itself over time.

title: Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules
summary: Modern deep learning typically keeps the batch size static throughout training, thus overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on the training dynamics. In this paper, we study the deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization and derive a joint characterization of loss in terms of both schedules, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This characterization yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule, and further leads to joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static batch size baselines, highlighting the significance of dynamic batch size schedule in large language model training.

AI.tldr: The paper studies deep learning dynamics through convex optimization, deriving a joint characterization of loss in terms of both learning rate and batch size schedules. This yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any given learning rate schedule, and joint scaling laws that outperform static batch size baselines in large language model training.
AI.motivation: Modern deep learning keeps batch size static during training, overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on training dynamics. The authors aim to address this gap by studying how these two hyperparameters jointly affect training.
AI.method: The paper derives a joint characterization of loss in terms of both learning rate and batch size schedules through the lens of convex optimization, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This leads to a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule.
AI.result: The joint scaling laws derived from the characterization consistently outperform static batch size baselines, demonstrating the significance of dynamic batch size scheduling in large language model training.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic batch size scheduling is important and beneficial for large language model training; the proposed joint characterization and optimal batch size schedule provide a principled way to improve training efficiency beyond static batch size approaches.

title: Temporal Concentration from Rollout Errors: Implicit Preference Optimization for Text-to-Video Diffusion
summary: Recent advances in preference alignment for diffusion-based video generation, particularly via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), have significantly improved visual quality. However, temporally sparse artifacts such as motion collapse, object flickering, and color oversaturation remain a major barrier to perceptual realism. Existing methods struggle with these issues due to two key limitations: (1) the preference attribution bottleneck, where offline human annotations are costly and fail to accurately capture learning dynamics, while online reward signals are rollout-aware but often unstable and biased; and (2) temporal credit misallocation, where uniformly applied supervision cannot effectively target the brief segments in which artifacts occur. To address these challenges, we propose concentrated Implicit Preference Optimization (cIPO), a post-training framework for video diffusion models. cIPO derives implicit preference signals directly from the denoising process: given a real video, the model adds forward noise and reconstructs it via iterative denoising, treating the original as the preferred sample and the reconstruction as the dispreferred one. This formulation captures inference-time errors without requiring human annotations or external reward models. Moreover, frame-level discrepancies between original and reconstructed videos reveal when failures occur. cIPO leverages this by computing temporal reconstruction errors and concentrating optimization on high-error segments, enabling more precise correction of failure-prone regions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that cIPO consistently enhances video authenticity and temporal coherence across multiple datasets, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of implicit preference with temporally concentrated optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes cIPO (concentrated Implicit Preference Optimization), a post-training framework for video diffusion models that derives implicit preference signals directly from the denoising process—treating the original video as preferred and its forward-noise-then-reconstruct version as dispreferred—and concentrates optimization on high temporal reconstruction error segments to address temporally sparse artifacts like motion collapse, object flickering, and color oversaturation.
AI.motivation: Existing preference alignment methods (e.g., DPO) for video diffusion suffer from two key limitations: (1) preference attribution bottleneck—offline human annotations are costly and fail to capture learning dynamics, while online reward signals are unstable and biased; and (2) temporal credit misallocation—uniform supervision cannot effectively target the brief segments where temporal artifacts occur. These temporally sparse artifacts (motion collapse, flickering, oversaturation) remain a major barrier to perceptual realism.
AI.method: cIPO derives implicit preference signals from the denoising process: given a real video, the model adds forward noise and reconstructs it via iterative denoising, using the original as the preferred sample and the reconstruction as the dispreferred one. This requires no human annotations or external reward models. Additionally, cIPO computes frame-level temporal reconstruction errors between original and reconstructed videos to identify failure-prone segments, and concentrates optimization on high-error regions for precise correction.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that cIPO consistently enhances video authenticity and temporal coherence across multiple datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of implicit preference signals combined with temporally concentrated optimization.
AI.conclusion: Implicit preference signals derived directly from the denoising process, combined with temporally concentrated optimization targeting high-error segments, offer an effective and efficient solution to address temporally sparse artifacts in video diffusion models without relying on human annotations or external reward models.

title: MMHBench: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark for Mental Health Understanding in Long-Form Videos
summary: Mental health understanding in long-form videos requires nuanced reasoning over observable behavior, interpersonal context, and latent psychological states. Existing benchmarks largely reduce this task to coarse-grained classification, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations. To address this limitation, we introduce MMHBench, a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for multi-perspective mental health understanding, comprising 268 long-form videos and 2,184 carefully curated questions. MMHBench organizes the evaluation into two complementary settings: (1) third-person assessment, consisting of 605 questions that focus on the interpretation of observable behaviors and multimodal evidence, and (2) first-person perspective-taking, comprising 1,579 questions that require perspective-conditioned reasoning to identify the interpretation of the mental state supported by the available multimodal evidence. We propose a Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework that simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple perspectives. The generated questions are refined through multi-role feedback and iterative optimization, followed by expert-guided verification to ensure quality and validity. Extensive evaluation of 22 representative multimodal large language models (MLLMs), spanning both open-source and leading closed-source models, demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging.

AI.tldr: MMHBench is a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for multi-perspective mental health understanding in long-form videos, comprising 268 videos and 2,184 curated questions across third-person assessment and first-person perspective-taking settings. Evaluations of 22 MLLMs show the task remains highly challenging.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks reduce mental health understanding in videos to coarse-grained classification, offering limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations. A finer-grained, multi-perspective benchmark is needed.
AI.method: MMHBench introduces two complementary evaluation settings: (1) third-person assessment (605 questions) focusing on observable behavior interpretation and multimodal evidence, and (2) first-person perspective-taking (1,579 questions) requiring perspective-conditioned reasoning. Questions are generated via a Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework that simulates diverse social roles, refined through multi-role feedback, iterative optimization, and expert-guided verification.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation of 22 representative multimodal large language models (open-source and closed-source) demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging, indicating significant gaps in current MLLM capabilities for this task.
AI.conclusion: Long-form video mental health understanding is far from solved, and MMHBench provides a rigorous, multi-perspective evaluation framework to drive future progress in this domain.

title: Improving the Robustness/Accuracy Tradeoff Against Adversarial Attacks Using Information Bottleneck Distillation Through Dual Teachers
summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in classical machine learning problems. However, they are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Countermeasures proposed in the literature, notably Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) introduced by Kuang et al., degrade the classification accuracy on clean inputs while improving the robustness to adversarial inputs. In this work, we extend the IBD framework by introducing an extra teacher model (clean teacher) trained with only clean inputs, into the distillation process from a robust teacher model trained by adversarial training. The features of both clean and robust teachers are transferred to the student through a cross-layer attention matrix. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets show that the proposed method improves classification accuracy on clean samples compared to the original IBD, while maintaining similar accuracy on adversarial samples. Furthermore, our methods are competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, including the recent dual-teacher distillation framework B-MTARD, particularly in terms of the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. We also analyze the impact of different training settings that have different influences on the attention module.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) framework for adversarial robustness by introducing an additional "clean teacher" model (trained only on clean inputs) alongside the robust teacher (trained via adversarial training). Both teachers' features are distilled into a student via a cross-layer attention matrix. Experiments on CIFAR-10/100 show improved clean accuracy over IBD while maintaining adversarial robustness, achieving competitive results with state-of-the-art dual-teacher methods like B-MTARD.
AI.motivation: Adversarial training-based distillation (IBD) improves robustness but degrades clean classification accuracy. The authors aim to address this trade-off by incorporating knowledge from a clean teacher to help the student retain accuracy on clean samples while preserving robustness from the robust teacher.
AI.method: The proposed framework extends IBD by adding a clean teacher model (trained only on clean inputs) to the existing robust teacher (trained via adversarial training). Both teachers' features are transferred to the student through a cross-layer attention matrix that enables feature-level distillation from both sources simultaneously.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, the proposed method achieves higher clean classification accuracy than the original IBD while maintaining similar adversarial accuracy. It is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches including the dual-teacher distillation framework B-MTARD, particularly on the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. The paper also analyzes the impact of different training settings on the attention module.
AI.conclusion: Adding a clean teacher to the IBD distillation framework effectively mitigates the clean accuracy degradation caused by robust distillation, achieving a better balance between clean and adversarial performance. The method is competitive with or better than existing state-of-the-art dual-teacher approaches.

title: Landmark shape spaces with induced metrics
summary: We present a unification of Kendall's landmark shape spaces, where rigid motions are factored out and scale fixed on landmark configurations equipped with Euclidean geometry, with landmark configuration spaces carrying Riemannian metrics descending from right-invariant Sobolev metrics on the diffeomorphism group. The resulting new landmark shape spaces achieve the defining properties of both approaches: The regularity of the descending metric prevents landmarks from colliding, the metric is defined in the ambient space independent of the number of landmarks, local rigid transformations are preserved, global rigid motions are removed, and scale fixed. To achieve this, we define a particular Sobolev-type operator, the screened elasticity operator, whose null-space consists exactly of the rigid motions, we show how this operator descends to achieve the desired geometry, and we present approaches to solving matching problems and computing geodesics numerically. The resulting construction allows the use of landmark configuration spaces with sufficiently regular metrics in applications while retaining the shape invariances that are a hallmark of Kendall's shape spaces.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new landmark shape space that unifies Kendall's shape spaces (where rigid motions are factored out and scale is fixed) with landmark configuration spaces equipped with Riemannian metrics from right-invariant Sobolev metrics on the diffeomorphism group. This is achieved via a "screened elasticity operator" whose null-space consists exactly of rigid motions, enabling collision prevention, ambient metric definition, preservation of local rigid transformations, and removal of global rigid motions with fixed scale.
AI.motivation: To combine the desirable properties of Kendall's shape spaces—where global rigid motions are removed and scale is fixed—with the advantages of Sobolev metric-based landmark spaces, which prevent landmark collisions and define metrics independent of landmark count. A unification provides a geometry that simultaneously offers shape invariances and metric regularity.
AI.method: The authors define a specific Sobolev-type operator called the screened elasticity operator whose null-space is exactly the set of rigid motions. They demonstrate how this operator descends to the quotient space to yield the desired geometry, and present numerical approaches for solving matching problems and computing geodesics on the resulting shape spaces.
AI.result: The construction yields new landmark shape spaces that prevent collision via the regular descending metric, define the metric in the ambient space independent of the number of landmarks, preserve local rigid transformations, remove global rigid motions, and fix scale—all hallmarks of both Kendall's shape spaces and Sobolev metric-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: The resulting landmark shape spaces can be used in applications requiring sufficiently regular metrics while retaining the shape invariances characteristic of Kendall's shape spaces, thus bridging two previously distinct frameworks for landmark-based shape analysis.

title: A Cross-Architecture Audit of Direction-Based Inference-Time Defences in Vision-Language Models
summary: Inference time defences against vision language model jailbreaks often subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream at a chosen decoder layer. We compare five defence candidates across 15 model and layer cells from four architectural families under a magnitude controlled protocol that matches the intervention size for each prompt and pairs every direction with a random control of the same norm. The candidates are the mean image conditioning shift, a CMRM style refusal direction, a ShiftDC style attack specific residual, a prompt instruction to ignore the image, and a random control. No single candidate dominates on both refusal recovery and utility preservation. The image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate whose utility loss remains at the measurement noise floor in every family. The prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL, while the attack specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction specific in 13 of 15 cells, but strongly architecture specific and nontransferable across the only dimension compatible pair, LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. We also connect text only and multimodal refusal geometry. The CMRM direction has positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells, with mean 0.35, range 0.17 to 0.65, 15 to 25 times the random vector null, and a sign test p value of about 3e-5. These results show that the two recipes recover partially overlapping geometry and that direction based defences should be calibrated separately for each language decoder family.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares five inference-time defence directions for vision language model jailbreak prevention across 15 model/layer cells from four architectural families, under a magnitude-controlled protocol. No single candidate dominates; image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B with noise-floor utility loss, prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL, and attack-specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The CMRM refusal direction and image conditioning shift share partially overlapping geometry (positive cosine alignment in all 15 cells), but defences are strongly architecture-specific and not transferable.
AI.motivation: Inference-time defences against VLM jailbreaks typically subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream, yet there is no systematic comparison of candidate directions under fair, controlled conditions. The authors aim to determine which direction candidate best recovers refusal behaviour while preserving utility, and whether these directions transfer across architectures or share common geometric structure.
AI.method: The study uses a magnitude-controlled protocol that matches intervention size per prompt and pairs every defence direction with a random control of equal norm. Five candidates are compared: mean image conditioning shift, CMRM-style refusal direction, ShiftDC-style attack-specific residual, a prompt instruction to ignore the image, and a random control. The evaluation spans 15 model/layer cells across four architectural families (LLaVA 1.5, Pixtral 12B, Qwen2.5 VL, Qwen2 VL 2B), measuring both refusal recovery and utility preservation. Cosine alignment analysis connects text-only refusal geometry to multimodal directions, with sign tests and random-vector null comparisons.
AI.result: No single candidate dominates across all cells. Image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate with utility loss at the measurement noise floor in every family. Prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL; attack-specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction-specific in 13/15 cells but non-transferable across the only architecturally compatible pair. The CMRM direction shows positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells (mean 0.35, range 0.17–0.65), 15–25× the random vector null, with sign-test p≈3e-5.
AI.conclusion: Text-only (CMRM) and multimodal (image conditioning shift) refusal directions recover partially overlapping geometry in the residual stream, confirming shared refusal mechanisms across modalities. However, direction-based defences are highly architecture-specific and must be calibrated separately for each language decoder family; no universal defence direction exists.

title: ROCS: Request-Oriented Compute Sharing for Efficient Large-Scale Recommendation
summary:
Modern recommendation models gain prediction quality by scaling feature-interaction and sequence modules, but production cost constraints cap how far systems can scale.
  In this work, we propose Request-Oriented Compute Sharing (ROCS), a modeling and inference paradigm that exploits a unique property of recommendation inference: each user request is evaluated against many candidates, while request-side features are shared across candidates. ROCS defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates substantial portions of the model once per request rather than once per candidate, significantly improving inference efficiency while maintaining or improving prediction quality. To realize this paradigm, we develop Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, and Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures. To support efficient GPU deployment, we co-design In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) that significantly accelerates ROCS model execution.
  Experiments on public benchmarks show that ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. On production-scale workloads, ROCS achieves up to a 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. ROCS has been deployed across large-scale recommendation systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, and more than two orders of magnitude in inference complexity, delivering significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.

AI.tldr: ROCS is a modeling and inference paradigm for recommendation systems that exploits the fact that user requests share features across many candidate evaluations. By deferring request-candidate interactions and isolating candidate-dependent representations, ROCS evaluates substantial portions of the model once per request instead of once per candidate, improving inference efficiency while maintaining or improving prediction quality. It introduces GLM (Generalized Layer Masking), DCA (Deep Cross Attention), and IKBO (In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization) to realize this paradigm across feature-interaction and sequence architectures, achieving up to 3x QPS improvement on production retrieval models and delivery significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.
AI.motivation: Modern recommendation models improve prediction quality by scaling feature-interaction and sequence modules, but production cost constraints cap scalability. The authors identify an untapped property of recommendation inference—each user request is evaluated against many candidates while request-side features are shared—and propose exploiting this to break the quality-efficiency tradeoff.
AI.method: ROCS defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates substantial portions of the model once per request rather than once per candidate. It is realized via three components: (1) Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, (2) Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures, and (3) In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) for efficient GPU deployment.
AI.result: On public benchmarks, ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. On production-scale workloads, it achieves up to 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation, and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. ROCS has been deployed across large-scale recommendation systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, and more than two orders of magnitude in inference complexity.
AI.conclusion: ROCS demonstrates that exploiting request-side feature sharing in recommendation inference can deliver significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost, establishing a new modeling and inference paradigm that improves both quality and efficiency simultaneously across diverse recommendation workloads.

title: BladeYOLO: Wind Turbine Blade Defect Detection with Limited Annotations and Weak-Saliency Awareness
comment: Accepted to IEEE TGRS, Code: https://github.com/zhangfangtao/BladeYOLO
summary: Wind turbine blade defect detection remains highly challenging in real-world inspection scenarios due to limited on-site data and the subtle visual characteristics of defects. In practice, blade defects are often small-scale, low-contrast, and difficult to distinguish from complex backgrounds, which significantly limits the robustness of existing detectors. To address these challenges, we propose BladeYOLO, a defect detection framework for wind turbine blades. Specifically, we integrate a Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone initialized with DINOv3 self-supervised pre-trained weights into YOLOv12-L, enabling the transfer of large-scale generic visual priors to blade defect detection and improving feature representation under limited training annotations. To enhance the perception of subtle defects, we further develop a Mamba-guided Weak-Defect Enhancement module, which consists of a Detail-Enhanced Multi-scale Branch for preserving high-frequency structural cues and a Cross-Mamba module for progressively propagating high-level semantic guidance to shallow features. In addition, we introduce a lightweight Style-Injector module that captures environment-related style information via Fourier decomposition and injects it into selected ViT self-attention layers, thereby improving robustness against environment-induced appearance variations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BladeYOLO achieves superior performance on the WTBlade-Defect dataset, with additional annotation-budget experiments showing its favorable performance under reduced training annotations. Evaluation on the public Wind Surface Defect dataset further provides supportive evidence for the cross-dataset robustness of BladeYOLO. In particular, on this public dataset, BladeYOLO outperforms the best competing method by 3.5\% in mAP$_{50}$ and 2.5\% in mAP$_{50-95}$.

AI.tldr: BladeYOLO is a defect detection framework for wind turbine blades that integrates a DINOv3-pretrained Vision Transformer backbone into YOLOv12-L, along with a Mamba-guided Weak-Defect Enhancement module and a lightweight Style-Injector, achieving state-of-the-art results on WTBlade-Defect and Wind Surface Defect datasets.
AI.motivation: Real-world wind turbine blade defect detection is challenging due to limited on-site training data, small-scale and low-contrast defects, and difficulty distinguishing defects from complex backgrounds, which limits the robustness of existing detectors.
AI.method: BladeYOLO integrates three key components: (1) a ViT backbone initialized with DINOv3 self-supervised pre-trained weights replacing/merging into YOLOv12-L for transferring generic visual priors; (2) a Mamba-guided Weak-Defect Enhancement module containing a Detail-Enhanced Multi-scale Branch for preserving high-frequency cues and a Cross-Mamba module for propagating semantic guidance to shallow features; (3) a lightweight Style-Injector that captures environment-related style via Fourier decomposition and injects it into ViT self-attention layers for robustness to appearance variations.
AI.result: BladeYOLO achieves superior performance on the WTBlade-Defect dataset with favorable performance under reduced annotation budgets. On the public Wind Surface Defect dataset, it outperforms the best competing method by 3.5% in mAP50 and 2.5% in mAP50-95, demonstrating cross-dataset robustness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed BladeYOLO effectively addresses the challenges of limited data and subtle defect characteristics in wind turbine blade inspection, leveraging self-supervised pre-training and targeted enhancement modules to achieve robust and superior detection performance across datasets.

title: IFHierBench: Hierarchical Instruction Following for Large Language Models
summary: Instruction-following ability is critical for deploying large language models in real-world applications, where downstream components depend on the output satisfying specific constraints. Modern deployments increasingly handle the full task in a single LLM call, with one prompt specifying a layered output whose overall artifact, structural sections, and nested fields must each satisfy concrete constraints. Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat the constraint set as a flat list applied uniformly to the response, so they cannot scope a check to a particular section of the output. We introduce IFHierBench, a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark of 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints, each prompt paired with a deterministic checker that verifies satisfaction at every scope. Evaluating seven leading proprietary and open-weight models, we find that even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy and that accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth grows. Reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, motivating future training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to achieve better instruction-following ability.

AI.tldr: IFHierBench is a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark with 600 prompts spanning four constraint-tree depths and 35 constraints, each with deterministic checkers. Evaluation of seven LLMs shows the best model barely exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy, with sharp degradation as constraint depth increases, revealing that reliable nested constraint following remains a major gap.
AI.motivation: Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat constraints as a flat list applied uniformly to the response, failing to capture real-world scenarios where prompts specify layered outputs (overall artifact, structural sections, nested fields) that must each satisfy scope-specific constraints. This inability to scope checks to particular output sections limits evaluation fidelity.
AI.method: The authors construct IFHierBench with 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints, pairing each prompt with a deterministic checker that verifies constraint satisfaction at every scope level. They evaluate seven leading proprietary and open-weight models on this benchmark.
AI.result: The strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy, and accuracy degrades sharply as constraint-tree depth grows. Current LLMs exhibit a substantial gap in reliably following nested/hierarchical constraints.
AI.conclusion: Reliably following nested constraints remains a significant challenge for current LLMs, motivating future training methods that incorporate constraint adherence at finer granularity to improve instruction-following capability in hierarchical output structures.

title: DAS-PMVC: A Framework for Partial Multi-View Clustering via Dual Alignment and Structure Enhancement
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted by ACM Multimedia 2026
summary: In recent years, multi-view clustering has attracted widespread research interest. However, due to limitations in data collection devices, data across different views often suffer from misalignment, leading to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP). To mitigate the impact of view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, this paper proposes a framework for partial multi-view clustering via dual alignment and structure enhancement (DAS-PMVC), which leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance. Specifically, DAS-PMVC includes three parts: \textbf{anchor graph structure alignment}, where sample joint embedding representations with consistent latent space are derived from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; \textbf{structure-enhanced feature learning}, where the model learns view structure information through pretraining and combines multi-view graph convolutional networks to further extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure to improve the discriminative power of representations; and \textbf{a dual alignment strategy}, where initial alignment is performed through the anchor graph in the pretraining phase, and contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm are introduced in the training phase to further optimize the alignment of latent features. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the DAS-PMVC framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, showcasing its effectiveness and superiority.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DAS-PMVC, a partial multi-view clustering framework that addresses the partial view alignment problem (PVAP) through anchor graph structure alignment, structure-enhanced feature learning using multi-view graph convolutional networks, and a dual alignment strategy combining contrastive learning with the Hungarian algorithm. Experiments show DAS-PMVC outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Multi-view clustering suffers from misalignment across views due to data collection device limitations, causing the partial view alignment problem (PVAP). The asymmetric view structure and irrelevant samples degrade clustering performance, motivating the need for an approach that leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance to mitigate these issues.
AI.method: DAS-PMVC consists of three components: (1) anchor graph structure alignment, which derives sample joint embedding representations with consistent latent space from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; (2) structure-enhanced feature learning, which learns view structure information through pretraining and uses multi-view graph convolutional networks to extract deep latent features from aligned graph structures; (3) a dual alignment strategy that performs initial alignment via anchor graph in pretraining, then uses contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm during training to further optimize latent feature alignment.
AI.result: Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the DAS-PMVC framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, confirming its effectiveness and superiority.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual alignment and structure enhancement framework effectively addresses partial view alignment by combining structure consistency, deep feature extraction, and multi-stage alignment optimization, achieving superior clustering performance compared to existing approaches.

title: mmRadarTwin: A Measurement-Calibrated Signal-Level Digital Twin Platform for Indoor mmWave Radar
summary: Indoor mmWave radar perception is difficult to reproduce because measured range-angle responses depend on scene geometry, material response, multipath, hardware conventions, and signal processing. Existing ray-tracing and digital-twin tools often expose rendering, channel, or path-level quantities, while radar sensing requires complex signal products that can be processed and compared in the same domain as real FMCW measurements. We present mmRadarTwin, a signal-level and path-attributed digital-twin platform for indoor mmWave radar. mmRadarTwin links a real radar measurement branch with an Unreal Engine scene-simulation branch through a shared receive-channel and range-angle processing interface. The simulator writes complex multi-channel receive grids and exports per-path contribution records that identify the actor, material tag, propagation event, and output-bin support of each simulated return. We evaluate mmRadarTwin in an office deployment using a commodity monostatic mmWave radar and mobile scene-capture hardware. Across 154 measured poses spanning 22 radar locations, the current physics-only path-basis simulator recalls 70.8% of measurement-active geometry-supported response regions in the central usable field of view while exposing residuals caused by weak or missing path support, shifted responses, unsupported anchors, and missing physical mechanisms. Rather than claiming complete radar-map reconstruction or cross-room generalization, mmRadarTwin establishes a practical systems workflow for constructing, comparing, and diagnosing indoor radar digital twins.

AI.tldr: mmRadarTwin is a signal-level, path-attributed digital-twin platform for indoor mmWave radar that links real FMCW measurement with Unreal Engine scene simulation through a shared receive-channel and range-angle processing interface. Evaluated across 154 poses over 22 radar locations in an office, it recalls 70.8% of measurement-active geometry-supported response regions, providing a practical workflow for constructing and diagnosing indoor radar digital twins without claiming complete reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Indoor mmWave radar perception is hard to reproduce because range-angle responses depend on scene geometry, materials, multipath, hardware conventions, and signal processing. Existing ray-tracing and digital-twin tools expose rendering/channel/path-level quantities rather than complex signal products comparable to real FMCW measurements, motivating a signal-level platform.
AI.method: mmRadarTwin bridges a real radar measurement branch and an Unreal Engine scene-simulation branch via a shared receive-channel and range-angle processing interface. The simulator produces complex multi-channel receive grids and per-path contribution records that attribute each simulated return to its actor, material tag, propagation event, and output-bin support.
AI.result: In an office deployment using a commodity monostatic mmWave radar and mobile scene-capture hardware, across 154 poses over 22 radar locations, the physics-only path-basis simulator recalls 70.8% of measurement-active geometry-supported response regions in the central usable field of view, while exposing residuals from weak/missing path support, shifted responses, unsupported anchors, and missing physical mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Rather than claiming complete radar-map reconstruction or cross-room generalization, mmRadarTwin establishes a practical systems workflow for constructing, comparing, and diagnosing indoor radar digital twins.

title: One Anchor for All: Unified Multilingual and Multimodal Safety Alignment for LVLMs
summary: As large vision-language models (LVLMs) are deployed globally, the combination of multilingual instructions and visual information makes malicious attacks more covert and sophisticated than ever before. However, existing methods isolate language and modality defenses, which, coupled with the scarcity of safety data and high fine-tuning costs, makes it difficult for models to defend against compound attacks. To address this severe challenge, we propose a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework driven by modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). First, we identify monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful and benign samples, quantifying functional saliency through activation strength and downstream impact. Then, by intersecting these unimodal neurons within each language, we extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) responsive to both visual and textual risks, bridging the safety representation gap between modalities. Furthermore, using English as a semantic anchor, we intersect MS-Neurons across languages to identify modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons), serving as key defenses against compound attacks. Finally, we update only this minimal subset of shared neurons (~0.03% of parameters), transferring English-only safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework (MLS-Neurons) for large vision-language models that identifies modality- and language-shared safety neurons by intersecting monolingual and unimodal safety neurons, then fine-tunes only ~0.03% of parameters to defend against compound multilingual-multimodal attacks while preserving general utility.
AI.motivation: Existing safety defense methods for LVLMs isolate language and modality defenses, making it difficult to counter compound attacks that combine multilingual instructions with visual information. This is exacerbated by scarce safety data and high fine-tuning costs.
AI.method: The framework works in four stages: (1) identify monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful and benign samples using activation strength and downstream impact as functional saliency metrics; (2) intersect unimodal neurons within each language to extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) bridging visual and textual risks; (3) use English as a semantic anchor to intersect MS-Neurons across languages, yielding modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons); (4) fine-tune only this minimal subset (~0.03% of parameters) to transfer English-only safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while maintaining general utility.
AI.conclusion: By discovering and updating only a minimal subset of shared safety neurons, the framework achieves efficient cross-dimensional (language and modality) safety alignment for LVLMs, effectively addressing compound multilingual-multimodal attacks with negligible fine-tuning cost.

title: Train Small, Deploy Large: Zero-Shot GNN Transfer Through Geometric Renormalization
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can operate on large graphs but become infrastructure-sensitive at the scale of millions of nodes and typically require scalable training techniques for even larger graphs. This raises a central question: when can a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica of a graph be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining? We introduce a zero-shot transfer protocol in which a GNN is trained on a graph coarse-grained by geometric renormalization (GR), and the resulting weights are transferred directly to the original network. Across synthetic and real-world networks, training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. We further find that learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales. These findings suggest that structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a zero-shot transfer protocol where GNNs are trained on graphs coarse-grained via geometric renormalization (GR) and the weights are directly transferred to the full-resolution network without retraining. Across synthetic and real-world networks, this approach preserves predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost, and learned representations remain aligned across scales, suggesting structural similarity matters more than network size for GNN transferability.
AI.motivation: GNNs can operate on large graphs but become infrastructure-sensitive at the scale of millions of nodes, requiring scalable training techniques. The central question addressed is when a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica of a graph can be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining, which would dramatically reduce computational costs.
AI.method: The authors propose a zero-shot transfer protocol: train a GNN on a graph that has been coarse-grained using geometric renormalization (GR), then transfer the learned weights directly to the original (full-resolution) graph without any retraining. The approach is evaluated on both synthetic and real-world networks, comparing predictive performance and analyzing learned representations and predictive trajectories across scales.
AI.result: Training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. Learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales in both synthetic and real-world networks.
AI.conclusion: Structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures that can generalize across graph resolutions without retraining.

title: Towards Practical Algorithm Selection for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation in Medical Imaging
summary: Numerous unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) algori-thms exist, but for clinical practice, selecting the best-suited one along with proper hyperparameters often remains unclear, as the unlabeled deployment (target) domain prevents direct evaluation. We propose a label-free criterion that jointly selects the algorithm and hyperparameters for UDA. Given a pool of candidate models from multiple algorithms trained with different hyperparameters, our approach scores each candidate against an agreement reference, and selects the one with the highest score. The agreement reference is constructed in two levels without using target labels. First, we leverage multiple label-free selection signals, using each to nominate a model within every algorithm. Second, the nominated models are aggregated across algorithms to form a reference prediction for each unlabeled target sample. The candidate whose predictions agree most with this reference is then selected for deployment. Experimental results on four brain MRI and four chest X-ray datasets across seven clinically relevant transfer scenarios show that our method achieves better selection performance than other methods and remains effective across different algorithm pools. Our approach takes a step towards practical, label-free algorithm selection for clinical deployment of UDA.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a label-free selection criterion for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) that jointly selects both the best algorithm and hyperparameters for clinical deployment, using a two-level agreement reference constructed without target labels.
AI.motivation: In clinical practice, many UDA algorithms exist but selecting the best one with proper hyperparameters is unclear because the unlabeled target domain prevents direct evaluation/validation.
AI.method: The approach builds a two-level agreement reference without target labels: (1) leverage multiple label-free selection signals to nominate a model within each algorithm, and (2) aggregate nominated models across algorithms to form a reference prediction per target sample. Candidates are scored based on agreement with this reference, and the highest-scoring model is selected.
AI.result: Experiments on four brain MRI and four chest X-ray datasets across seven clinically relevant transfer scenarios show the method achieves better selection performance than others and remains effective across different algorithm pools.
AI.conclusion: The approach advances practical, label-free algorithm selection for clinical deployment of UDA in medical imaging settings.

title: Meta-Task: Turning Terminal Task Synthesis into a Terminal Task for Scalable Agent Training
summary: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories, yet acquiring such data remains a significant challenge. Existing synthesis methods face two key limitations: (1) weak reliability caused by the disconnect between task generation and real execution, and (2) limited diversity and scalability due to dependence on existing repositories. We propose Meta-Task, a framework that redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself: an agent operates within a real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, so that synthesized components are checked for internal consistency and executability within the generation loop itself. Building upon this, we decouple the target task requirements along multiple dimensions, introduce a multi-phase mechanism that dynamically designs novel task specifications before producing the actual tasks, and incorporate optional external material support to enhance diversity and realism. We additionally apply LLM-as-Judge filtering to ensure the quality of the final training data. Experiments on Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.

AI.tldr: Meta-Task is a framework that reformulates terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself, where an agent operates in a real container to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks. This ensures internal consistency and executability within the generation loop. It decouples task requirements across multiple dimensions, uses a multi-phase mechanism for dynamic task specification design, incorporates optional external material support, and applies LLM-as-Judge filtering. Fine-tuning on 3,221 Meta-Task trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B on Terminal-Bench 2.0.
AI.motivation: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories, but acquiring such data is challenging. Existing synthesis methods suffer from weak reliability (disconnect between task generation and real execution) and limited diversity/scalability (dependence on existing repositories).
AI.method: Meta-Task redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task: an agent runs in a real container to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, ensuring internal consistency within the generation loop. It decouples task requirements across multiple dimensions, introduces a multi-phase mechanism to dynamically design novel task specifications before producing tasks, incorporates optional external material support for diversity/realism, and applies LLM-as-Judge filtering for training data quality.
AI.result: Experiments on Terminal-Bench 2.0 show fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.
AI.conclusion: Meta-Task effectively addresses both reliability and diversity limitations of existing task synthesis methods by embedding verification into the generation loop, and demonstrates superior performance with much less training data compared to concurrent approaches.

title: Beyond the Best Teacher: Expanding and Compressing the Reasoning Solution Manifold
summary: A single reinforcement-learning run can produce a strong reasoner yet an incomplete teacher: it often amplifies only a subset of the valid solution modes. We argue that reinforcement learning (RL)-trained policies should therefore be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold, rather than as globally reliable supervisors. Based on this view, we propose an expand-then-compress framework that couples teacher construction with multi-teacher policy distillation. In the expansion stage, Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization and redirects each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. In the compression stage, reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes. For each example, only reliable teachers contribute, and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by their per-example quality. We further introduce Consensus-Residual Decomposition, which preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over its reliable peers, preventing specialist behavior from being suppressed during teacher aggregation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show that the resulting Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, yielding relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while retaining single-model inference. These results establish a simple but powerful principle: stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union.

AI.tldr: RL-trained policies are local probes of a multi-basin reasoning manifold rather than globally reliable teachers. The paper proposes an expand-then-compress framework (RGRPO for teacher expansion + TU-OPD for distillation) that constructs a complementary teacher union and compresses it into a single student model, consistently outperforming any individual teacher across math, code, and instruction-following tasks.
AI.motivation: A single RL run produces a policy that amplifies only a subset of valid solution modes, making it a weak supervisor despite being a strong reasoner. This incomplete-teacher problem limits the quality of student models in policy distillation. The authors challenge the assumption that a single teacher is globally reliable and argue for viewing RL policies as local probes of a multi-basin solution manifold.
AI.method: The framework has two stages: (1) Expansion via Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO), which trains a sequence of teachers from a shared initialization, redirecting later rounds toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. (2) Compression via reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD), where a student learns from its own response prefixes, with reliable teachers contributing per-example weighted token-level OPD losses. A Consensus-Residual Decomposition preserves the winner teacher's excess token preferences over reliable peers, preventing specialist behaviors from being lost during aggregation.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show the Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher in all three domains, with relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while maintaining single-model inference.
AI.conclusion: Stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union. This establishes a simple but powerful principle for teacher-student distillation in RL settings.

title: Face and Voice Cross-modal Association with Learning Convex Feature Embedding
summary: Face-and-voice association learning is one of the most challenging tasks in deep learning. In this paper, we propose a simple but powerful cross-modal feature embedding method for the association of faces and voices. Previous work has studied cross-modal association tasks to establish the correlation between voice clips and facial images. These works have addressed cross-modal discrimination but underestimate the importance of handling heterogeneity in inter-modal features between audio and video, resulting in a lot of false positives and false negatives. To tackle the problem, the proposed method learns the embeddings of cross-modal features by making another feature exist between cross-modal features, facilitating the voice and face features of the same person to be embedded in a convex hull. Moreover, the incorporation of cross-modal attention mechanisms with convex embedding techniques represents a highly effective strategy for the attenuation of false positives and false negatives, accomplished via the minimization of inter-class discrepancies. We exhaustively evaluated our method for cross-modal verification, matching, and retrieval tasks on the large-scale VoxCeleb dataset. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves notable improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a cross-modal feature embedding method for face-voice association learning that uses convex embedding techniques along with cross-modal attention mechanisms. By embedding features such that same-person face and voice features lie in a convex hull, the method reduces false positives and false negatives, achieving state-of-the-art results on the VoxCeleb dataset for verification, matching, and retrieval tasks.
AI.motivation: Previous cross-modal association methods for faces and voices focus on cross-modal discrimination but underestimate inter-modal feature heterogeneity, leading to many false positives and false negatives.
AI.method: The proposed method learns cross-modal feature embeddings by placing an additional feature between cross-modal features so that face and voice features of the same person are embedded within a convex hull. It also incorporates cross-modal attention mechanisms with convex embedding to minimize inter-class discrepancies.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on the large-scale VoxCeleb dataset for cross-modal verification, matching, and retrieval tasks show notable improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: Combining convex embedding with cross-modal attention effectively handles inter-modal heterogeneity, reducing false positives/negatives and advancing face-voice association learning.

title: The Geometric Nature and a Free Proxy for Flow-Matching Uncertainty
summary: Flow matching (FM) has become a popular action head paradigm for modern embodied models. However, as a conditional generative model, it does not explicitly expose its inherent uncertainty, producing faulty action chunks even when it misinterprets the scene or encounters out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. Therefore, determining when an FM-generated action can be trusted is essential for safe deployment, yet existing uncertainty estimation methods on real-time control suffer from several issues: extra training budget, high computational overhead, and low generalization ability. In this work, we provide a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing that uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Building on this observation, we introduce denoising acceleration ($\mathrm{accel}$), a highly-generalizable and cost-free uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that $\mathrm{accel}$ is a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty and further test its utility in online failure detection. Results show that $\mathrm{accel}$ identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or even outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines across settings under realistic deployment budget. Code and demos available at: https://github.com/rrrrrrzy/fm-geometry.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a geometric interpretation of uncertainty in Flow Matching (FM) action heads for embodied models, showing that uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. The authors propose "denoising acceleration" (accel), a cost-free uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of denoising trajectories from a single forward pass—requiring no extra training, model evaluations, or resampling—and demonstrate it matches or outperforms costly baselines in online failure detection.
AI.motivation: FM has become a popular action head for embodied models, but as a conditional generative model, it does not explicitly expose its inherent uncertainty, producing faulty action chunks when it misinterprets scenes or encounters OOD inputs. Determining when FM-generated actions can be trusted is essential for safe deployment, yet existing uncertainty estimation methods on real-time control suffer from extra training budget, high computational overhead, and low generalization ability.
AI.method: The authors provide a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Based on this observation, they introduce denoising acceleration (accel), a highly-generalizable and cost-free uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling.
AI.result: Theoretically and empirically demonstrated that accel is a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty. In online failure detection, accel identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines across settings under realistic deployment budgets.
AI.conclusion: Denoising acceleration (accel) provides an efficient, generalizable, and cost-free uncertainty proxy for Flow Matching-based embodied models, enabling reliable online failure detection without incurring additional computational or training overhead.

title: Collaborative Feature Aggregation for Face Super-Resolution and Robust Re-Identification
summary: We propose a novel collaborative approach for face super-resolution (SR) and robust person re-identification from sequential or multi-view facial images. Traditional SR methods often suffer from blurring and distortion in faces recovered from poor-quality images due to low resolution. Image- and video-based facial SR methods using facial landmarks or segmentation also have similar challenges. To overcome these limitations, we leverage multiple correlated facial observations, across time or viewpoints, by introducing a transformer-based collaborative feature aggregation method that unifies identity features from multi-sequence or multi-view data. This allows faces in multiple sequences of an individual to contribute to accurately estimating common facial features. Furthermore, we propose a cascade SR network to progressively restore the high-resolution image of the target's face with gradual facial feature unification. The unified identity representation is further utilized in person re-identification scenarios, enabling accurate matching even under severe image degradation. The exhaustive experimental results and comparisons show that our method outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating consistent improvements in both face super-resolution and re-identification performance. Our work highlights the effectiveness of joint identity reconstruction and progressive image restoration from multiple facial inputs in enhancing downstream visual recognition tasks.

AI.tldr: A transformer-based collaborative feature aggregation method that jointly performs face super-resolution and person re-identification from multi-sequence or multi-view facial images, unifying identity features across correlated observations and progressively restoring high-resolution faces via a cascade SR network.
AI.motivation: Traditional and landmark/segmentation-based face SR methods suffer from blurring and distortion when recovering faces from low-quality images, and existing approaches do not effectively exploit multiple correlated facial observations across time or viewpoints for joint identity reconstruction and SR.
AI.method: (1) A transformer-based collaborative feature aggregation module that unifies identity features from multi-sequence or multi-view facial data, allowing multiple observations of the same individual to jointly estimate common facial features. (2) A cascade super-resolution network that progressively restores high-resolution target face images with gradual facial feature unification. (3) The unified identity representation is reused for person re-identification under severe image degradation.
