AI.result: Exhaustive experiments show the method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving consistent improvements in both face super-resolution and person re-identification performance.
AI.conclusion: Joint identity reconstruction and progressive image restoration from multiple facial inputs effectively enhances downstream visual recognition tasks, highlighting the value of collaborative multi-view/sequence information for face SR and re-identification.

title: Shapes from Examples: Foundations of Shape Learning in Recursive SHACL
comment: full version of a paper accepted at ISWC26
summary: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, making automatic shape learning essential for knowledge graph applications. We investigate the well-known fitting approach to this task: given sets P and N of positive and negative example nodes from an input graph, compute a shape expression C, possibly using shape names defined in a recursive shape catalogue, that validates at every node in P and none in N. We focus on the case where C is written in a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the Description Logic ELI. For the catalogue, we consider the well-founded, stable, and supported semantics. We address fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems, and obtain polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates automatic SHACL shape learning for knowledge graph validation. It focuses on fitting problems where shape expressions (in an ELI-equivalent core fragment of SHACL) must validate positive example nodes and reject negative ones, examining existence and most-specific fitting under well-founded, stable, and supported catalogue semantics, with tight exponential and polynomial complexity bounds.
AI.motivation: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, but manually authoring shapes is labor-intensive. Automatic shape learning is essential for practical knowledge graph applications, and understanding the computational complexity of the fitting approach is a necessary foundational step.
AI.method: The paper formally defines the shape fitting problem: given positive and negative example node sets (P and N) from an input graph, compute a recursive SHACL shape expression (in a core fragment corresponding to Description Logic ELI) that validates all nodes in P and none in N. It considers three semantics for the shape catalogue—well-founded, stable, and supported—and studies fitting existence and most-specific fitting computation.
AI.result: The paper establishes tight exponential-time upper bounds for both fitting existence and most-specific fitting computation in the general case, and obtains polynomial-time bounds for relevant special cases of the problem.
AI.conclusion: The SHACL shape fitting problem in the ELI fragment is computationally tractable within exponential time in general, with polynomial-time solvability for special cases, providing a complexity-theoretic foundation for automatic shape learning from labelled example nodes.

title: LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO): A Sampling-Time Low-Rank Scaffold for Recovering Reinforcement-Learning Gradient on Zero-Reward Cliff Prompts
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning suffers from a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts-those on which every sampled rollout in a group fails-the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, so GRPO produces no gradient on precisely the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. We introduce LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO), a sampling-time mechanism that recovers this lost gradient. Each RL step, LSPO detects cliff prompts, fits a small low-rank (LoRA) adapter by a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions, re-rolls the cliffs with the base-plus-adapter model, splices the now-successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base alone; the adapter receives only the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins and one exact tie), with gains of up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; averaged over the 16 cells the improvement is +3.8 points.

AI.tldr: LSPO is a sampling-time mechanism that recovers the lost gradient on "cliff" prompts (where all group rollouts fail) in RLVR for mathematical reasoning. It fits a small LoRA adapter via supervised fine-tuning on ground-truth solutions, re-rolls with the base+adapter model, splices successful completions back into the GRPO batch with importance-sampling correction, and discards the adapter after each step. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, LSPO beats DAPO on 15 of 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells with one exact tie, gaining up to +10.7 points on AIME24 and averaging +3.8 points across 16 cells.
AI.motivation: GRPO's group-normalized advantage is identically zero on "cliff" prompts where every sampled rollout in a group fails, meaning no gradient is produced on exactly the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. This structural blind spot limits RLVR's ability to improve on hard problems where the model currently cannot produce any correct answer.
AI.method: LSPO operates at sampling time each RL step: (1) detect cliff prompts; (2) fit a small LoRA adapter with a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions; (3) re-roll the cliff prompts using the base-plus-adapter model; (4) splice the now-successful completions into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction; (5) take a GRPO step on the base-only model, while the adapter receives only supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint. This yields a base-only model at the end.
AI.result: On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step horizon: LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats DAPO on all 16 cells (15 strict wins, one exact tie), with gains of +10.7 points (AIME24/pass@4), +6.7 points (AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16), +2.4 points (MATH500/pass@1), and a +3.8-point average improvement across all 16 cells.
AI.conclusion: LSPO effectively recovers the gradient lost by GRPO on cliff prompts, providing consistent improvements over the DAPO baseline across benchmarks and pass@k settings, while producing a deployable base-only model with no extra adapter at inference time.

title: Convolutional Neural Shading for High-Quality 3D Reconstruction from Multi-View Images
summary: We propose a convolutional neural shading (CNS), a novel pipeline to reconstruct high-quality 3D shapes from multi-view images. Several recent studies have used neural radiance fields and other neural differentiable rendering methods to understand 3D geometry. However, these approaches rely on single-point geometric information, such as positions and normals of the surface, leading to a lack of detailed local geometry. Our approach addresses the inherent limitations of single-point information by leveraging a neural shader to capture variations even in dark and textureless regions with a convolutional neural shader, resulting in far more accurate geometry predictions. Additionally, our method mitigates surface irregularities at image boundaries by introducing a fine-detail displacement network, which utilizes spatial information of surface geometry and learns fine displacement details by correlating neighboring values in the rendering coordinates. Through extensive experiments, our proposed method has demonstrated significant quality improvements in the reconstructed shapes and rendered images over current state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a convolutional neural shading (CNS) pipeline for high-quality 3D shape reconstruction from multi-view images, using a convolutional neural shader to capture local geometric variations beyond single-point information, plus a fine-detail displacement network to smooth surface irregularities at boundaries. The method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in reconstruction and rendering quality.
AI.motivation: Existing neural differentiable rendering methods (e.g., NeRF-based approaches) rely on single-point geometric information such as surface positions and normals, which limits their ability to capture detailed local geometry, particularly in dark and textureless regions.
AI.method: Two key components: (1) a convolutional neural shader that captures local variations using spatial neighborhoods rather than single-point information, improving accuracy in dark/textureless areas; (2) a fine-detail displacement network that uses spatial information of surface geometry and correlates neighboring rendering-coordinate values to reduce surface irregularities at image boundaries.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate significant quality improvements in both reconstructed 3D shapes and rendered images compared to current state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging convolutional (neighborhood-based) shading information instead of single-point information yields substantially more accurate 3D geometry reconstruction, effectively addressing limitations of prior neural differentiable rendering approaches.

title: From Scoring to Acting: Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
summary: Recent work on LLM agents is shifting from external capability elicitation to capability internalization, enabling agents to retain useful skills without retrieval at inference time. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising direction, but many existing methods typically supervise students by scoring actions along student-generated trajectories. Such supervision has two limitations: teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes, and action-level scores underuse information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship. We therefore advocate outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories. Based on this view, we propose Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD). OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, and retains only outcome-verified successful continuations. It then applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence and distills the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales show that OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD), a method for LLM agents to internalize skills by supervising students through outcome-verified teacher feedback and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories, achieving significant success-rate gains on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales.
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) methods supervise students by scoring actions along student trajectories, which has two limitations: teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes, and action-level scores underutilize information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship. The authors advocate for outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories.
AI.method: OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, and retains only outcome-verified successful continuations. It then applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence point and distills the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales show OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.
AI.conclusion: OVCSD demonstrates that outcome-verified teacher supervision combined with comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories is an effective paradigm for capability internalization in LLM agents, offering significant improvements with minimal additional privileged interaction cost.

title: Revisiting Predictive Process Monitoring in the Age of Foundation Models: A Comparative Study of Sequence, Tabular, and LLM Approaches
summary: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) leverages event logs to forecast the future of running process instances, for instance, predicting the next activity, the remaining time until case completion, or the time to the next event. While PPM research in recent years has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, foundation-model approaches---particularly large language models (LLMs)---are increasingly explored for PPM. At the same time, tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities offer a promising alternative but have not yet been systematically benchmarked for PPM. Thus, it remains unclear whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive in this evolving landscape. This paper compares the three modeling paradigms both conceptually and empirically through a controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks. The results show that sequence models consistently perform best for next activity prediction, whereas tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, with LLMs usually lagging behind despite higher cost.

AI.tldr: A controlled benchmark comparing sequence models (e.g., LSTM), tabular foundation models, and LLMs for predictive process monitoring across multiple datasets and tasks. Sequence models perform best on next-activity prediction; tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks; LLMs lag behind despite higher cost.
AI.motivation: PPM is shifting from classical deep sequence models trained from scratch to foundation-model approaches, particularly LLMs. Tabular foundation models with in-context learning offer a promising alternative but have not been systematically benchmarked for PPM, leaving it unclear whether sequence-based models remain competitive.
AI.method: A controlled benchmark comparing three modeling paradigms—sequence models, tabular foundation models, and LLMs—conceptually and empirically across multiple datasets and prediction tasks (e.g., next activity, remaining time, time to next event).
AI.result: Sequence models consistently outperform other paradigms for next-activity prediction. Tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks (remaining time, time to next event). LLMs usually lag behind despite substantially higher computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Classical sequence models remain competitive, especially for categorical/temporal-adjacent predictions, while tabular foundation models offer a viable alternative for temporal tasks; LLMs are currently not cost-effective for PPM.

title: What Makes Deep Learning Work for Traditional Chinese Medicine Tongue Diagnosis? A Comprehensive Ablation Study
summary: Deep learning has shown promise for automated tongue diagnosis in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), yet the design space remains underexplored. We conducted a systematic ablation study spanning 20+ model versions under rigorous 5-fold cross-validation on TongueDx2 (5,109 images, 976 expert-annotated) and a merged dataset of 11,101 samples. We compared six backbone architectures, four loss functions, five augmentation strategies, and six training strategies. The best 976-sample model achieved weighted-F1 of 0.6625 using ConvNeXt-Tiny with restrained augmentation and weak-group ensemble, while the best 11,101-sample model reached weighted-F1 of 0.7761. Six key design principles emerged: (1) ConvNeXt-Tiny offers optimal parameter efficiency; (2) BCE substantially outperforms Asymmetric Loss (+2.7%); (3) restrained color augmentation is critical; (4) weak-group ensemble replacement (+2.1%) outperforms probability averaging; (5) data scaling yielded +20.6% improvement; (6) expanding from 13 to 45 label dimensions caused catastrophic collapse (0.78 to 0.22). These principles are generalizable to multi-label medical image classification with class imbalance.

AI.tldr: A systematic ablation study across 20+ deep learning model versions for automated tongue diagnosis in TCM, evaluating backbones, losses, augmentations, and training strategies. The best models achieve weighted-F1 of 0.6625 (976 samples) and 0.7761 (11,101 samples), yielding six generalizable design principles for multi-label medical image classification.
AI.motivation: Deep learning shows promise for automated tongue diagnosis in TCM, but the design space of models, losses, augmentations, and training strategies remains systematically underexplored.
AI.method: Systematic ablation study spanning 20+ model versions under rigorous 5-fold cross-validation on TongueDx2 (5,109 images, 976 expert-annotated) and a merged dataset of 11,101 samples. Compared six backbone architectures, four loss functions, five augmentation strategies, and six training strategies.
AI.result: Best 976-sample model achieved weighted-F1 of 0.6625 using ConvNeXt-Tiny with restrained augmentation and weak-group ensemble; best 11,101-sample model reached 0.7761. Key findings include BCE outperforming Asymmetric Loss by +2.7%, weak-group ensemble gaining +2.1%, data scaling yielding +20.6%, and expanding labels from 13 to 45 causing catastrophic collapse (0.78 to 0.22).
AI.conclusion: Six key design principles emerged, including ConvNeXt-Tiny as optimal in parameter efficiency, BCE superiority, importance of restrained color augmentation, weak-group ensemble advantage, data scaling benefits, and risks of excessive label expansion. These principles generalize to multi-label medical image classification with class imbalance.

title: MARS-RA: Rank Aggregation for Credit Assignment via Multimodal Comparisons in Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation
summary: Credit assignment is a fundamental challenge in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly in embodied AI settings characterized by limited and delayed feedback as well as dynamically changing numbers of active agents. We propose MARS-RA, a framework that reformulates credit assignment as a rank aggregation problem using contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents generated by large multimodal models. This shift from absolute to relative estimation ensures robustness against noise and dynamic agent participation, converting comparison results into contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping. We provide theoretical justification for the convergence and robustness of the proposed framework, and show that Shapley values can be used as an interpretive reference. Experimental results on challenging tasks of different types indicate that MARS-RA can guide agents toward effective cooperation.

AI.tldr: MARS-RA reformulates credit assignment in cooperative multi-agent RL as a rank aggregation problem using pairwise comparisons from large multimodal models, converting them into contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical results.
AI.motivation: Credit assignment is a fundamental challenge in cooperative multi-agent RL, especially in embodied AI settings with limited/delayed feedback and dynamically changing numbers of active agents. Traditional absolute credit estimation methods are fragile under these conditions, motivating a more robust approach.
AI.method: MARS-RA reformulates credit assignment as a rank aggregation problem, using contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents generated by large multimodal models. It shifts from absolute to relative estimation, converts comparison results into contribution scores, and employs potential-based reward shaping. Theoretical analysis covers convergence, robustness, and interpretation via Shapley values.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates robustness against noise and dynamic agent participation, with experiments on diverse challenging tasks showing that MARS-RA effectively guides agents toward cooperation, outperforming baselines.
AI.conclusion: MARS-RA provides a theoretically grounded and empirically effective approach to credit assignment in cooperative multi-agent embodied AI, leveraging relative comparisons and rank aggregation to overcome the limitations of absolute estimation methods.

title: Learning-Augmented and Randomized Algorithms for Line Aggregation with Delays
summary: This paper studies learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric. We consider advice given as online suggested service lengths, and evaluate the algorithms in terms of robustness and consistency. For each $λ\in (0,1]$, we first propose a deterministic learning-augmented \textsc{Balance} algorithm that is $(4/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(4+λ)$-consistent. We also propose a randomized algorithm for the problem in the classical adversarial model, which is $(e+1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary, improving over the deterministic $5$-competitive \textsc{Balance} benchmark~\cite{bienkowski2013chain}. Notably, this competitive ratio is even lower than the lower bound of $4$ for deterministic online algorithms. Moreover, we establish a lower bound of $e$ on the competitive ratio of randomized online algorithms, improving the previous lower bound of $e/(e-1)$. Besides, we combine the two ideas and obtain a randomized learning-augmented algorithm that is $(e/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(e+λ)$-consistent. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to complement our theoretical analysis and evaluate the empirical performance of our algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper studies online aggregation with delays on a line metric, combining learning-augmented and randomized approaches. It proposes deterministic and randomized learning-augmented Balance algorithms with robustness/consistency guarantees, achieves an (e+1)-competitive randomized algorithm beating the deterministic 5-competitive benchmark and even the lower bound of 4, establishes a lower bound of e for randomized algorithms, and validates results via numerical experiments.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to improve the competitive ratio of online aggregation with delays on a line metric. While the deterministic 5-competitive Balance algorithm was the benchmark, the authors seek to overcome the deterministic lower bound of 4 by leveraging randomness and learning-augmented advice to achieve better performance guarantees.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) a deterministic learning-augmented Balance algorithm with (4/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (4+λ)-consistency; (2) a randomized algorithm in the classical adversarial model achieving (e+1)-competitiveness against an oblivious adversary; (3) a randomized learning-augmented algorithm combining both ideas with (e/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (e+λ)-consistency; and (4) a lower bound proof of e for randomized algorithms.
AI.result: The randomized algorithm achieves (e+1)-competitiveness, which improves upon the deterministic 5-competitive Balance benchmark and beats the deterministic lower bound of 4. The paper also improves the lower bound for randomized algorithms from e/(e-1) to e. Both learning-augmented variants provide tunable robustness-consistency trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that randomness can significantly improve the competitive ratio for online aggregation with delays, breaking the deterministic lower bound. The learning-augmented framework provides flexible performance guarantees, and numerical experiments confirm the theoretical findings empirically.

title: OPLD: On-Policy Latent Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Interleaved multimodal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) improves visual reasoning by incorporating auxiliary visual evidence into intermediate reasoning. However, existing approaches remain constrained by externally defined reasoning traces and visual operations, limiting their ability to develop flexible and abstract visual thinking. Reasoning with latent has recently offered a promising direction by internalizing intermediate computation into continuous representations. Nevertheless, existing visual-latent methods mainly supervise latent states through alignment with compressed auxiliary visual features, treating them as proxies for visual observations rather than active reasoning states. Consequently, they capture the provided evidence but fail to fully internalize the abstract reasoning process induced by multimodal CoT. In this paper, we propose OPLD (On-Policy Latent Distillation), a simple framework that transfers the reasoning capability induced by privileged multimodal CoT into latent reasoning representations. Extensive experiments on diverse multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that OPLD consistently outperforms existing latent reasoning methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. The results suggest that supervising latent representations at the reasoning-process level provides a more effective paradigm for multimodal latent reasoning than conventional feature-level alignment.

AI.tldr: OPLD is a framework that distills multimodal Chain-of-Thought reasoning capabilities into latent representations via on-policy distillation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multimodal benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal latent reasoning methods supervise latent states through alignment with compressed auxiliary visual features, treating them as proxies for visual observations rather than active reasoning states. This fails to internalize the abstract reasoning process induced by multimodal CoT.
AI.method: OPLD (On-Policy Latent Distillation) transfers reasoning capability from privileged multimodal CoT into latent reasoning representations through on-policy distillation.
AI.result: OPLD consistently outperforms existing latent reasoning methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple diverse multimodal benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Supervising latent representations at the reasoning-process level provides a more effective paradigm for multimodal latent reasoning than conventional feature-level alignment.

title: Share the Judge, Learn the Deferral: Where Specialization Helps LLM Evaluation
summary: Agentic systems have widened the gap between producing candidate outputs and reviewing them. This paper asks a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be built into an evaluator's weights, or into the rule that decides when its judgment can be trusted? We study 99,952 public, rubric-conditioned examples. Supplying the correct rubric improves locked-test accuracy by 2.11 points over a response-only control; replacing it with an unrelated rubric costs 2.66 points. Dividing the same training corpus among eight criterion-family LoRA judges, however, loses 10.05 points and cuts audited coverage at a 5% risk target from 24.44% to 5.43%. Matching the bank's stored capacity with one rank-64 adapter does not reproduce this loss. Nor is the result explained by learning rate or optimizer steps. Initializing the family adapters from a shared, trained judge recovers test accuracy to 76.85%, 19.94 points above scratch training at the same learning rate (95% interval 18.88-21.02). The result changes when specialization governs deferral rather than judgment. On RewardBench 2, learned correctness heads route examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade without changing any reward score. Across 20 locked repartitions, the cascade attains 89.40% accuracy, compared with 84.75% for 8B alone, at 0.415 normalized parameter compute. Every run passes an exact one-sided 95% risk audit; margin-based rules remain near 84.8% accuracy while using at least 0.94 compute. These results suggest a qualified design rule: share the learning of judgment until there is enough data to justify a split, and place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary.

AI.tldr: The paper asks whether domain specialization should be built into an evaluator's weights or into the deferral/release rule governing when its judgment can be trusted. Using 99,952 rubric-conditioned examples, the authors find that sharing judgment learning (via a unified adapter or initialization from a shared judge) dramatically outperforms splitting training into family-specific LoRA judges; instead, specialization should be placed in an audited release/deferral boundary. A learned routing cascade on RewardBench 2 achieves 89.40% accuracy vs 84.75% for 8B alone using 0.415 normalized parameter compute.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems have widened the gap between producing candidate outputs and reviewing them, raising a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be embedded in an evaluator's weights or in the rule that decides when its judgment can be trusted?
AI.method: The study compares (1) supplying correct vs. unrelated rubrics to a locked evaluator, (2) splitting a training corpus among eight criterion-family LoRA judges vs. a single rank-64 adapter, (3) initializing family adapters from a shared trained judge, and (4) on RewardBench 2, learning correctness heads that route examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade without changing reward scores, with margin-based deferral rules as baselines. All runs are audited with exact one-sided 95% risk tests.
AI.result: Correct rubrics improve locked-test accuracy by 2.11 points; unrelated rubrics cost 2.66 points. Splitting into eight family LoRA judges loses 10.05 points and cuts audited coverage from 24.44% to 5.43%, not explained by learning rate/optimizer or capacity. Initializing from a shared judge recovers accuracy to 76.85%, 19.94 points above scratch (95% CI 18.88-21.02). The learned cascade attains 89.40% vs 84.75% for 8B alone at 0.415 normalized compute across 20 locked repartitions; margin rules stay ~84.8% using at least 0.94 compute.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose a qualified design rule: share the learning of judgment until sufficient data justifies a split, and place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary (deferral rule) rather than in the evaluator's weights.

title: Contrastive Concept Importance: Explaining Pairwise Class Decisions Through Automatically Extracted Concept Representations
summary:
Concept-based explanations are a prevalent way to explain the decisions of complex black-box methods through semantically meaningful, human-interpretable concepts. To attribute the contribution of such concepts to a model's decisions, feature attribution methods are used to quantify how strongly each concept contributes to a model output. These attributions are typically computed for a single output class and therefore answer a non-contrastive "why P?" question. In many situations, however, such as cases of misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question to ask is "why P rather than Q?".
  We introduce contrastive concept importance (CCI), which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast, or foil, class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. The resulting scores are signed, indicating whether a concept supports the target over the foil or the foil over the target, and can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects. This makes it possible to distinguish globally important concepts from concepts that specifically influence a class-pair distinction, including whether their effect is shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.
  We evaluate the method on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases, insertion and deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy. The results show that contrastive concept importance reveals class-pair-specific model behavior that is not captured by ordinary concept importance alone, and that highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to assess whether they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces contrastive concept importance (CCI), a method for attributing concept contributions to the logit margin between a target class and a contrast (foil) class, enabling "why P rather than Q?" explanations for black-box models. CCI produces signed scores decomposable into target-logit and foil-logit effects, revealing class-pair-specific model behavior beyond what ordinary concept importance captures.
AI.motivation: Existing concept-based feature attribution methods answer non-contrastive questions ("why P?") by computing attributions for a single output class. However, in cases like misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question is contrastive ("why P rather than Q?"), which current methods do not address.
AI.method: The paper introduces CCI, which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a foil class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. The method produces signed scores that can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects, allowing distinction between globally important concepts and those that specifically influence a class-pair distinction (shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive effects).
AI.result: Evaluation on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases shows that CCI reveals class-pair-specific model behavior not captured by ordinary concept importance. Insertion/deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy assessments demonstrate that highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to determine if they affect fine-grained distinctions versus broad category evidence.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive concept importance provides a more nuanced understanding of model decisions by explaining why one class is preferred over another, complementing standard single-class concept attribution. The decomposition into target and foil effects enables distinguishing global concepts from class-pair-specific ones, and reveals model behavior tied to fine-grained distinctions that ordinary concept importance misses.

title: SKIMIX: Multi-Agent Harness-Time Scaling with Skill Mixture for Dynamic Harness Engineering
summary: AI agents increasingly rely on large skill libraries, but selecting, combining, and maintaining skills remains difficult. We propose SKIMIX, a multi-agent framework in which agents with different skill portfolios collaborate through iterative refinement. SKIMIX combines embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution. Across six reasoning benchmarks, multi-agent collaboration substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but offers limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic, and most improvements arise during the first refinement round. These results show that task characteristics determine whether skill-level ensembles help and provide practical guidance for scalable agent design.

AI.tldr: SKIMIX is a multi-agent framework for managing large skill libraries, combining embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution. Evaluations across six reasoning benchmarks show collaborative agents substantially improve open-ended mathematical reasoning but yield limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks, with non-monotonic scaling and most gains from the first refinement round.
AI.motivation: AI agents rely on increasingly large skill libraries, making selection, combination, and maintenance of skills difficult. The goal is to improve how agents leverage large skill portfolios through multi-agent collaboration.
AI.method: SKIMIX is a multi-agent framework where agents with diverse skill portfolios collaborate via iterative refinement. It integrates three components: (1) embedding-based skill retrieval for relevant skill selection, (2) submodular anti-dilution routing to prevent redundant or diluted contributions, and (3) adaptive skill evolution for maintaining and updating the skill library over time.
AI.result: Across six reasoning benchmarks, multi-agent collaboration significantly improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but provides limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic, and the majority of performance improvements occur within the first refinement round.
AI.conclusion: Task characteristics determine whether skill-level ensembles are beneficial. The findings offer practical guidance for designing scalable multi-agent systems, suggesting that collaborative skill aggregation is task-dependent and should be applied selectively.

title: Class-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Counterfactual Explanation Generation
summary: Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) enhance the interpretability of black-box models by generating alternative instances with adjusted feature values that achieve a contrastive outcome. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach for CFE generation, enabling efficient exploration of counterfactual instances while ensuring control over key metrics like validity, sparsity, and proximity. Previous studies have formulated RL states exclusively using features derived from the predictors in the supervised dataset. This study explores the impact of including an instance's predicted class, alongside features derived from the predictors, in the RL state representation for generating CFEs. The hypothesis is that class-awareness enhances exploration efficiency and improves policy optimality. We compare the proposed class-aware RL method with the class-blind RL method, which is similar but excludes the instance's class information from the state representation. The comparison was conducted using seven datasets from diverse domains, varying in size. The results show that during training, class-aware RL offers benefits in terms of convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction. Moreover, it generates significantly more valid CFEs compared to class-blind RL. Finally, the instance's class-based feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in RL's action-selection, as shown by the SHAP and LIME values, underscoring the significance of class-awareness in RL for CFE generation. The impact is heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether incorporating an instance's predicted class into the RL state representation improves counterfactual explanation (CFE) generation. A class-aware RL method is compared against a class-blind variant across seven datasets, showing faster convergence, better reward optimization, shorter episodes, and significantly more valid CFEs. SHAP and LIME analyses confirm the class-based feature is among the most influential predictors in action selection.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning is a promising approach for generating counterfactual explanations, but previous studies formulated RL states exclusively using features from the predictors in the supervised dataset. This study hypothesizes that including the instance's predicted class in the state representation could enhance exploration efficiency and improve policy optimality, a dimension not previously explored.
AI.method: The authors propose a class-aware RL method that includes the instance's predicted class alongside predictor-derived features in the RL state representation for CFE generation. They compare this against a class-blind RL variant (identical but excluding class information) across seven datasets from diverse domains and varying sizes, evaluating training dynamics (convergence speed, reward, episode length), CFE validity, and feature influence via SHAP and LIME.
AI.result: Class-aware RL demonstrates benefits in convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction during training. It generates significantly more valid CFEs than class-blind RL. SHAP and LIME analyses show the instance's class-based feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in the RL agent's action-selection, confirming the importance of class-awareness.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating the predicted class into the RL state representation for CFE generation yields heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets. Class-awareness is a significant and impactful design choice in RL-based CFE generation.

title: Think with Extra-Image: A Farmland Segmentation Agent Driven by Spatio-Temporal Information Gain
summary: Existing farmland remote sensing image (FRSI) segmentation follows a "Think with Intra-Image" paradigm, assuming that the current image contains sufficient visual evidence for reliable segmentation. Yet farmland appearance varies with phenology and spatial context and is often confused with other land-cover, making instantaneous, local observations inadequate. Thus, segmentation ambiguity stems not only from limited model representation, but more fundamentally from the required spatio-temporal information lying beyond the current image. Based on this insight, we redefine FRSI segmentation from an information bottleneck perspective as a dynamic decision process driven by task-relevant extra spatio-temporal information gain. We further propose FarmSeeker, a dynamic FRSI segmentation agent that identifies ambiguous regions, reasons about their causes, and queries extra spatio-temporal information on demand for accurate segmentation. To evaluate FarmSeeker, we construct GSFS-Bench, the first global-scale, high-resolution FRSI segmentation benchmark that supports reasoning-querying. Experiments show that FarmSeeker achieves more stable segmentation performance than existing methods. The project is publicly available at: https://withoutocean.github.io/FarmSeeker/

AI.tldr: FarmSeeker redefines farmland remote sensing image segmentation by treating it as a dynamic decision process that queries extra spatio-temporal information on demand to resolve ambiguity, outperforming existing methods on a new global-scale benchmark (GSFS-Bench).
AI.motivation: Existing FRSI segmentation follows an "Intra-Image" paradigm that assumes the current image alone is sufficient for reliable segmentation. However, farmland appearance varies with phenology and spatial context and can be confused with other land-cover types, meaning the required spatio-temporal information often lies beyond the current image. Segmentation ambiguity thus stems fundamentally from missing information rather than just limited model representation.
AI.method: FarmSeeker is a dynamic FRSI segmentation agent that operates from an information bottleneck perspective. It identifies ambiguous regions, reasons about the causes of ambiguity, and queries task-relevant extra spatio-temporal information on demand to make accurate segmentation decisions. A new benchmark, GSFS-Bench, was constructed as the first global-scale, high-resolution FRSI segmentation benchmark that supports reasoning-querying evaluation.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that FarmSeeker achieves more stable segmentation performance than existing methods on GSFS-Bench.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues that FRSI segmentation should move beyond intra-image reasoning and adopt a dynamic, query-driven paradigm that actively seeks supplementary spatio-temporal evidence, enabled by the new GSFS-Bench benchmark and the FarmSeeker agent.

title: MMLDSum-LLM: Multimodal Long-Document Summarization with Visual-Alignment and Keyword-Aware
summary: Multimodal long documents are core carriers of professional knowledge, where critical evidence is sparsely distributed across paragraphs and modalities. This easily causes key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in summarization by multimodal LLMs. These issues stem from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and gaps in inter-modal alignment. To address this, we introduce MMLDSum-Bench, a high-quality benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions. We further propose MMLDSum-LLM, a reproducible two-stage training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by GRPO with a multi-objective reward (keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control). Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench, comparing against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol - including LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE - demonstrate that our approach significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MMLDSum-Bench, a benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, and MMLDSum-LLM, a two-stage training framework (SFT with visual-alignment and keyword-aware weighted losses, followed by GRPO with multi-objective rewards) that improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency in multimodal summarization.
AI.motivation: Multimodal long documents contain sparsely distributed critical evidence across paragraphs and modalities, causing key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in multimodal LLM summarization. These issues arise from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and gaps in inter-modal alignment.
AI.method: The authors propose MMLDSum-Bench, a high-quality benchmark covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions. They propose MMLDSum-LLM, a two-stage training framework: (1) supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by (2) GRPO with a multi-objective reward incorporating keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench, comparing against leading open/closed-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol (LLM-as-a-judge, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment, and ROUGE), demonstrate significant improvements in key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark and training framework effectively address attention drift and inter-modal alignment gaps in multimodal long-document summarization, leading to better key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency compared to existing multimodal models.

title: S-CEReBrO: Breaking the Memory Barrier in Continuous EEG Monitoring
comment: This is the pre-rebuttal version of a paper accepted at MICCAI 2026. The camera-ready version will be posted following the embargo
summary: Foundation models offer a promising paradigm for Electroencephalography (EEG) analysis, leveraging generalizable representations from vast unlabeled datasets. Yet, Transformer-based architectures face a critical bottleneck: global attention mechanisms couple the attention memory state to the signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. To address this, we introduce S-CEReBrO (Streaming CEReBrO), an evolution of the CEReBrO architecture designed for continuous monitoring. Our novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory as only the active window requires resident attention maps. Empirical scaling analysis confirms that windowed alternating attention can process signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. Compared to low-rank linear attention on long contexts, windowed alternating attention requires 55% of the memory while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. Pre-trained on >25,000 hours of recordings from >12,000 subjects, S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks, with up to 60% fewer parameters. This work represents a significant step toward the realization of efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring. An accompanying code repository is available.

AI.tldr: S-CEReBrO is a streaming evolution of the CEReBrO architecture for continuous EEG monitoring. It introduces a Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism that factorizes attention into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory regardless of signal duration. Pre-trained on >25,000 hours of data from >12,000 subjects, it achieves SOTA on 7 of 11 downstream tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters, while processing signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based EEG foundation models suffer from a critical memory bottleneck: global self-attention couples the attention memory (KV cache) to signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring applications.
AI.method: The paper introduces S-CEReBrO with a novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism that factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows. This guarantees constant KV cache memory since only the active window requires resident attention maps, enabling unbounded streaming.
AI.result: Empirical scaling analysis shows windowed alternating attention processes signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. On long contexts, it uses 55% of the memory of low-rank linear attention while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. Pre-trained on >25,000 hours from >12,000 subjects, S-CEReBrO achieves SOTA on 7 of 11 downstream tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: S-CEReBrO demonstrates that efficient, streaming EEG monitoring is achievable via fixed-size attention windows without sacrificing representational quality, representing a significant step toward practical continuous EEG monitoring with foundation models.

title: Scaling Vision-Language Models Is Not Enough to Mitigate Bias
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as CLIP are now foundational to multimodal systems, yet their robustness to spurious correlations remains poorly understood at scale. We present the first large-scale empirical study of 194 publicly available VLMs, including 16 model families, covering a wide range of model sizes, 24 training datasets, and three evaluation benchmarks, namely ImageNet (overall performance), CelebA (typical single-attribute bias), and UrbanCars (complex multi-attribute biases). Across these settings, the Spearman correlation between model scale and performance weakens as evaluation shifts from ImageNet ($ρ{=}0.68$) to single-attribute ($ρ{=}0.48$) and further to multi-attribute ($ρ{=}0.05$) bias benchmarks. In contrast, properties of the training data (size and quality) show more consistent relationships with worst-group accuracy across both bias benchmarks. Notably, curated datasets yield improvements of up to 25% over uncurated alternatives at a comparable scale. Finally, the effect of architectural choices (e.g., patch size, image resolution) is highly context-dependent, varying with the nature of the benchmark, including the type of bias and its spatial distribution within images.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study of 194 publicly available VLMs (16 families, 24 training datasets) finds that model scale correlates weakly with robustness to spurious correlations, while training data properties (especially curation) matter more. Curated data yields up to 25% gains over uncurated data at comparable scale, and architectural effects are context-dependent.
AI.motivation: VLMs like CLIP are foundational to multimodal systems, yet their robustness to spurious correlations is poorly understood at scale. This work aims to fill that gap with the first large-scale empirical study.
AI.method: Evaluates 194 publicly available VLMs across 16 model families, 24 training datasets, and three benchmarks: ImageNet (overall performance), CelebA (single-attribute bias), and UrbanCars (multi-attribute bias). Computes Spearman correlations between model scale and performance, and analyzes relationships between training data properties and worst-group accuracy.
AI.result: Spearman correlation between model scale and performance drops from 0.68 (ImageNet) to 0.48 (single-attribute bias) to 0.05 (multi-attribute bias). Training data properties (size and quality) correlate more consistently with worst-group accuracy. Curated datasets improve performance by up to 25% over uncurated ones at comparable scale. Architectural choices have context-dependent effects varying with benchmark, bias type, and spatial distribution of bias.
AI.conclusion: Model scaling alone does not guarantee robustness to spurious correlations; training data curation is a more reliable lever for improving worst-group accuracy, and model design choices must be evaluated in context-specific ways.

title: MUL-T: Decoding Spatial Cellular Architecture in Multiplexed Tissue Images
summary: Understanding tissue organisation in multiplexed imaging requires modelling both cellular phenotypes and their spatial context. Existing approaches typically rely on handcrafted features, such as marker intensity statistics or cell-type proportions, which often fail to scale or generalise across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels. We introduce MUL-T, a lightweight transformer framework that reframes tissue architecture as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens. By learning contextualised [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision, the model captures higher-order cellular interactions while remaining computationally efficient. We evaluate MUL-T on several clinically relevant downstream tasks, including core-level tumour pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction. Across tasks, MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines and achieves performance comparable to a foundation ViT model, despite substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost.

AI.tldr: MUL-T is a lightweight transformer framework that reframes tissue architecture analysis in multiplexed imaging as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens, achieving performance comparable to foundation models while being substantially more parameter-efficient.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for modelling tissue organisation in multiplexed imaging rely on handcrafted features like marker intensity statistics or cell-type proportions, which fail to scale or generalise across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels.
AI.method: MUL-T uses a lightweight transformer that performs masked contextual prediction over discrete cell tokens, learning contextualised [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision to capture higher-order cellular interactions efficiently.
AI.result: MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines across core-level tumour pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction, and achieves comparable performance to a foundation ViT model with fewer parameters and lower training cost.
AI.conclusion: MUL-T demonstrates that a lightweight, self-supervised transformer over discrete cell tokens can capture clinically relevant tissue architecture information effectively, offering a scalable and generalisable alternative to handcrafted features or heavy foundation models.

title: Exact Action Values Are Not Enough: Rollout-Verified Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of a Reasoning Model for Multi-Zone VAV Control
summary: Multi-zone variable-air-volume control must balance thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and electricity use across several continuous actuators. Model predictive control and reinforcement learning are widely studied, but deployment typically requires building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. We first test whether a frontier reasoning model (an LLM trained to use additional inference-time computation) can achieve competitive VAV control from text without building-specific training. With that capability established, we then test whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer control knowledge into a locally deployable open-weight model. Five controllers are evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator. Relative to a Guideline 36-based baseline, TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% while improving temperature and CO$_2$ compliance. Without building-specific training, GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but reduced the ventilation margin. For RFT, deterministic rollouts restore a saved state, apply one candidate, and follow TD3 to score each action. Auditing a learned critic against these rollouts exposed a failure hidden by its near-perfect across-time correlation ($r=0.9998$): within-state ranking was unreliable; the critic selected the rollout-best candidate in only 5 of 10 states. Even with the rollout verifier, 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement in sampled-action return; the open-weight controller used more electricity than the baseline before and after training, and its five-minute predictions remained worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better. Exact rollout scores rank sampled actions but reveal neither next-state effects nor an improvement direction. The unchanged transition errors motivate transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether frontier reasoning LLMs can achieve competitive multi-zone VAV control from text without building-specific training, and whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer such control knowledge into a local open-weight model. GPT-5 reduced HVAC electricity by 6.2% over a Guideline 36 baseline but reduced ventilation margin; TD3 achieved 4.5% reduction with improved compliance. However, RFT failed to produce sustained improvement: a learned critic with near-perfect time-correlation (r=0.9998) had unreliable within-state ranking, selecting rollout-best candidates in only 5 of 10 states, and 200 RFT steps yielded no improvement. The paper recommends transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.
AI.motivation: Model predictive control and reinforcement learning for multi-zone VAV control typically require building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. The authors seek to test whether frontier reasoning models can achieve competitive control from text alone, and whether this capability can be transferred into a locally deployable lightweight model via reinforcement fine-tuning, avoiding the need for per-building training.
AI.method: Five controllers are evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator. The study first tests GPT-5 (a frontier reasoning LLM) for VAV control from text without building-specific training. It then applies TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) to transfer control knowledge into an open-weight model. RFT rollouts restore a saved state, apply one candidate action, and use TD3 to score each action. A learned critic is audited against deterministic rollouts, and sampled-action returns are evaluated before and after 200 RFT steps.
AI.result: TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% relative to a Guideline 36 baseline while improving temperature and CO2 compliance. GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but at the cost of reduced ventilation margin. Critic auditing revealed that despite a near-perfect across-time correlation (r=0.9998), within-state action ranking was unreliable—the critic picked the rollout-best candidate in only 5 of 10 states. RFT with a rollout verifier produced no sustained improvement over 200 steps; the open-weight controller used more electricity than baseline before and after training, and its five-minute transition predictions remained worse than persistence, whereas GPT-5 predicted transitions substantially better.
AI.conclusion: Frontier reasoning models can achieve competitive VAV control from text alone, and TD3 can provide demonstrable energy savings. However, value-based RFT transfer fails because critics can exhibit deceptive across-time accuracy while having poor within-state ranking, and rollout scores rank actions without revealing next-state effects or an improvement direction. The unchanged transition errors motivate transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before attempting value-based RFT.

title: FaithEyes: Towards Faithful Tool Use via Multi-Agent Process-Image Verification
summary: Agentic vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave textual reasoning with explicit tool calls such as cropping and code-based image manipulation, have emerged as a compelling paradigm for reliable and interpretable multimodal reasoning. However, recent studies have revealed that such models often use tools unfaithfully. Many process images are irrelevant to the question (e.g., the tool crops the wrong region or misses the queried target), yet the call still receives full credit and the model still answers correctly. Such decorative or misaligned tool calls waste computation and reveal that the model leans on prior knowledge or the original image rather than the evidence it retrieves. This may stem from two limitations of prevailing methods: the tool reward fails to distinguish useful from useless calls, and tool feedback carries no signal of usefulness. To this end, we introduce FaithEyes, a multi-agent self-judging framework. Concretely, we use a VLM to judge whether each process image helps answer the question. The judgement is injected into the reasoning context as part of the tool observation to help subsequent reasoning, and meanwhile is used to scale the tool reward by the helpful-tool ratio to suppress reward hacking. To keep judgement available at evaluation and thus ensure train-test consistency, we further design a multi-agent framework where the model itself serves as a subagent to judge the tool calls from main agent, eliminating any dependence on an external model at inference. Training via a two-stage SFT + RL pipeline on adapted open-source data, FaithEyes attains competitive or superior accuracy across visual perception and reasoning benchmarks, while markedly improving tool faithfulness. The homepage is at https://github.com/Mosi-AI/FaithEyes.

AI.tldr: FaithEyes is a multi-agent self-judging framework that trains agentic vision-language models to use tools faithfully by having a VLM judge whether each cropped/manipulated process image actually helps answer the question. These judgments are injected into the reasoning context and used to scale tool rewards to prevent reward hacking, enabling competitive accuracy with markedly improved tool faithfulness.
AI.motivation: Agentic VLMs often call tools unfaithfully, producing decorative or misaligned tool calls (e.g., cropping the wrong region) that still receive full credit and yield correct answers. This wastes computation and reveals the model relies on prior knowledge or the original image rather than retrieved evidence. Prevailing methods fail because (1) the tool reward cannot distinguish useful from useless calls and (2) tool feedback carries no signal of usefulness.
AI.method: FaithEyes is a multi-agent self-judging framework. A VLM judges whether each process image helps answer the question; this judgment is injected into the reasoning context as part of the tool observation and used to scale the tool reward by the helpful-tool ratio to suppress reward hacking. To maintain train-test consistency without external models, the model itself serves as a subagent to judge the main agent's tool calls. Training uses a two-stage SFT + RL pipeline on adapted open-source data.
AI.result: FaithEyes attains competitive or superior accuracy across visual perception and reasoning benchmarks while markedly improving tool faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: By injecting usefulness judgments into reasoning context and scaling tool rewards accordingly, a self-judging multi-agent framework can substantially improve tool faithfulness in agentic VLMs without sacrificing accuracy and without reliance on external models at inference.

title: DataClawEval: A Benchmark for Data Engineering Agents in Real Industrial Harness
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly being deployed to automate complex workflows, promising to revolutionize data management and processing. However, existing benchmarks predominantly focus on simplified Text-to-SQL translation or data analysis, leaving the critical and complex domain of end-to-end data engineering largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce DataClawEval, the first comprehensive benchmark designed specifically to evaluate the end-to-end task completion capabilities of autonomous agents in real-world data engineering scenarios. Built upon production-grade code authored by professional enterprise data engineers, it comprises 100 rigorous, end-to-end tasks spanning five execution engines: PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, and FlinkSQL. Rather than non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge scoring, each task is executed within a case-specific, isolated sandbox and graded by deterministic, rule-based scripts. Evaluating 16 frontier agents exposes critical limitations: The strongest model attains only 74.9 overall, and no single model dominates, as each excels on a different engine, revealing strict domain specialization rather than omnipotent proficiency. Thus, autonomous data engineering remains a formidable, unresolved challenge. We release our dataset, containerized environments, and deterministic evaluation scripts at https://github.com/Dicemy/DataClawEval/tree/master

AI.tldr: DataClawEval is the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating autonomous LLM agents on end-to-end data engineering tasks, featuring 100 real-world tasks across five execution engines (PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, FlinkSQL) with deterministic, sandbox-based evaluation. Testing 16 frontier agents shows the best model only achieves 74.9 overall, with no single model dominating across all engines, highlighting that autonomous data engineering remains unsolved.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks primarily focus on simplified Text-to-SQL or data analysis, leaving the complex domain of end-to-end data engineering unexplored. There is a need for a benchmark that evaluates the complete task completion capabilities of autonomous agents in real-world data engineering scenarios.
AI.method: The benchmark is built upon production-grade code from professional enterprise data engineers, comprising 100 end-to-end tasks across five execution engines: PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, and FlinkSQL. Instead of using non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge scoring, each task is executed in a case-specific, isolated sandbox and graded by deterministic, rule-based scripts.
AI.result: Evaluation of 16 frontier agents reveals that the strongest model achieves only 74.9 overall score, and no single model dominates across all engines—each model excels on a different engine, demonstrating strict domain specialization rather than general proficiency across data engineering tasks.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous data engineering remains a formidable and unresolved challenge. The benchmark, dataset, containerized environments, and deterministic evaluation scripts are publicly released for further research.

title: ODEWorld: A Continuous Predictive Architecture via Physical-Time Flow
summary: In the physical world we inhabit, space and time are fundamentally continuous. However, existing machine learning paradigms for world modeling are largely confined to discrete-time prediction, thereby exhibiting significant inefficiency in capturing the dynamics of physical world. We introduce Physical-Time Flow (\textbf{PT-Flow}), a novel approach that learns a continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time. Crucially, the underlying dynamics of sequential data are parameterized by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) embedded in a well-structured representation space. Under this paradigm, the prediction of future can be recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space. Building upon PT-Flow, we construct \textbf{ODEWorld}, a continuous-time latent world model that is both efficient and versatile. By extracting time-variant features and enforcing ODE properties on both the dynamical representation space and the latent velocity field, ODEWorld effectively addresses the long-standing representation collapse issue in latent world model literature. This also enables high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction. Moreover, its continuous nature allows for arbitrary temporal resolution and even backward prediction, which is impossible for most discrete-time models. Lastly, ODEWorld can provide rich planning-oriented information to facilitate downstream policy learning. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control. \href{https://dstate.github.io/odeworld_website/}{Project Website}.

AI.tldr: PT-Flow and ODEWorld introduce a continuous-time latent world model that parameterizes sequential data dynamics via an ordinary differential equation in a structured latent space, enabling efficient arbitrary-resolution prediction, backward rollouts, and improved downstream policy learning.
AI.motivation: Existing machine learning world models operate in discrete time, which is inefficient and mismatched with the fundamentally continuous nature of physical space-time, limiting their ability to capture real-world dynamics.
AI.method: PT-Flow learns a continuous latent velocity field parameterized by an ODE in a well-structured representation space, recasting future prediction as temporal integration via an ODE solver. Building on this, ODEWorld extracts time-variant features and enforces ODE properties on both the dynamical representation space and latent velocity field to avoid representation collapse.
AI.result: ODEWorld achieves high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction, supports arbitrary temporal resolution and backward prediction, and provides rich planning-oriented information; experiments show it excels in both video generation and robotic control.
AI.conclusion: Continuous-time latent world modeling via ODEs can reconcile planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, outperforming discrete-time counterparts in both generative and control tasks.

title: EgoGenesis: Egocentric World-Action Modeling with Online Anchored Projective Memory and Action-3D RoPE
summary: Egocentric video offers rich manipulation experience for embodied AI, yet collecting diverse egocentric data across scenes, objects, motions, and embodiments remains costly. We present \method, an egocentric world-action simulator that synthesizes controllable, high-quality manipulation videos to expand scarce real-world training data. \method{} builds on a pretrained video generation prior and introduces two geometry-aware conditioning mechanisms. Online Anchored Projective Memory (OAPM) preserves a first-frame 3D scene anchor while periodically refreshing a recent state during autoregressive generation. Action-3D Rotary Position Embedding (A3D-RoPE) encodes end-effector motion with camera-aware 3D rotary coordinates, injecting action geometry into skeleton-to-video cross-attention for precise control. Together, these components improve visual fidelity, geometric stability, and action alignment in long egocentric rollouts. Moreover, augmenting 400 real trajectories with 400 \method-generated trajectories improves out-of-distribution real-robot success from 77\% to 84\% on single-arm tasks and from 53\% to 70\% on dual-arm tasks, demonstrating that the synthesized data substantially improve downstream WAM generalization.

AI.tldr: The paper presents EgoSim, an egocentric world-action simulator that generates controllable, high-quality manipulation videos using a pretrained video generation prior with two geometry-aware conditioning mechanisms (OAPM and A3D-RoPE), demonstrating that synthetic data improves real-robot downstream generalization by up to 17% on dual-arm tasks.
AI.motivation: Collecting diverse egocentric manipulation data across scenes, objects, motions, and embodiments is prohibitively costly, limiting the ability to train embodied AI systems that generalize well from egocentric video.
AI.method: EgoSim builds on a pretrained video generation prior and introduces two geometry-aware conditioning mechanisms: (1) Online Anchored Projective Memory (OAPM), which preserves a first-frame 3D scene anchor and periodically refreshes recent state during autoregressive generation; and (2) Action-3D Rotary Position Embedding (A3D-RoPE), which encodes end-effector motion with camera-aware 3D rotary coordinates injected into skeleton-to-video cross-attention for precise action control.
AI.result: Augmenting 400 real trajectories with 400 EgoSim-generated trajectories improves out-of-distribution real-robot success rates from 77% to 84% on single-arm tasks and from 53% to 70% on dual-arm tasks.
AI.conclusion: Synthesized egocentric manipulation video substantially improves downstream whole-arm manipulation (WAM) generalization, validating the effectiveness of the proposed geometry-aware conditioning approach for scalable training-data expansion.

title: SKILL-KD: Contrastive Skill Distillation for LLM Agents
summary: Skill-based prompting has become a practical mechanism for improving large language model (LLM) agents, yet existing skill acquisition methods often treat skills as experience summaries, memory entries, or direct summaries of successful demonstrations. This creates a mismatch for weaker student agents: when a student fails because it lacks task knowledge or operational strategy, its failed trajectory may not contain enough evidence to infer the missing behavior, while the teacher trajectory may be too implicit to be internalized as reusable guidance. We propose SKILL-KD, a contrastive skill distillation framework that treats skills as an explicit distillation medium between agents of different capabilities. Given a student failure and the teacher trajectory on the same task, SKILL-KD distills their actionable discrepancy into a textual skill patch, evaluates the patch by re-running the student, and iteratively refines the patch when the student still fails. To prevent repeated local updates from causing skill drift, SKILL-KD further maintains trace-linked edit histories and performs Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation, deciding whether each patch should add a new rule, delete or modify an existing rule, or be skipped. Across five agent benchmarks and two student settings, SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines.

AI.tldr: SKILL-KD is a contrastive skill distillation framework that extracts actionable textual skill patches by comparing student failures against teacher trajectories, iteratively refines those patches via re-running the student, and uses Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation with trace-linked edit histories to prevent skill drift. It consistently improves frozen student agents across five agent benchmarks and two student settings.
AI.motivation: Existing skill acquisition methods treat skills as experience summaries, memory entries, or direct summaries of successful demonstrations, which mismatches weaker student agents. When a student fails due to missing task knowledge or operational strategy, its failed trajectory lacks evidence to infer the missing behavior, while teacher trajectories are too implicit for the student to internalize as reusable guidance.
AI.method: SKILL-KD treats skills as an explicit distillation medium between agents of different capabilities. It (1) distills the actionable discrepancy between a student failure and the teacher trajectory on the same task into a textual skill patch, (2) evaluates the patch by re-running the student, and (3) iteratively refines the patch when the student still fails. To prevent skill drift from repeated local updates, it maintains trace-linked edit histories and performs Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation, deciding whether each patch should add a new rule, delete or modify an existing rule, or be skipped.
AI.result: Across five agent benchmarks and two student settings, SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines.
AI.conclusion: SKILL-KD demonstrates that treating skills as an explicit contrastive distillation medium enables effective knowledge transfer from stronger teachers to weaker frozen student agents, with drift-aware consolidation ensuring stable and reusable skill acquisition.

title: Harnessing the Potential of Optimizing Data Mixtures via Bayesian Domain Reweighting
summary: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) is fundamentally influenced by the distributional composition of multi-domain pre-training data. While manual heuristics were prevalent in early models, they increasingly fail to capture the intricate synergies between domains as data complexity grows. To overcome the issue, a dominant approach seeks to fit a proxy function mapping between domain weights and their corresponding validation losses, and then find the optimal domain weights to minimize validation losses. These methods rely on strong structural assumptions, such as rank invariance or scaling laws, which are often violated, resulting in non-negligible estimation bias. A promising approach is to directly optimize the weighting scheme from data. However, it suffers from unstable optimization trajectory and prohibitive computational overhead, limiting its potential to search better domain weights configurations. This paper presents a Bayesian domain weighting method to infer the weights from a Dirichlet distribution via introducing Gamma prior information learned from observations. Experimental results demonstrate that proposed method could achieve stable and efficient domain weights learning, and identifies optimal mixtures while consuming substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods, revitalizing optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale applications.
