AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Bayesian domain weighting method for LLM pre-training data that infers optimal domain weights from a Dirichlet distribution augmented with Gamma prior information learned from observations, achieving stable and efficient domain weight learning while using substantially less data than existing search-based function-fitting approaches.
AI.motivation: The performance of LLMs is fundamentally influenced by the distributional composition of multi-domain pre-training data. Existing approaches either rely on heuristic/manual methods that fail to capture complex domain synergies, fit proxy functions with strong structural assumptions (rank invariance, scaling laws) that are often violated and introduce estimation bias, or use direct optimization which suffers from unstable training trajectories and prohibitive computational overhead. A more stable and efficient domain weighting method is needed.
AI.method: The proposed method is a Bayesian domain weighting approach that infers domain weights from a Dirichlet distribution, incorporating Gamma prior information learned from observational data. This allows direct learning of optimal domain weights while avoiding the structural assumptions required by proxy function-fitting methods and the instability/overhead of naive direct optimization approaches.
AI.result: Experimental results show the proposed Bayesian method achieves stable and efficient domain weight learning, identifies optimal domain mixtures, and consumes substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods.
AI.conclusion: The Bayesian domain weighting method revitalizes optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale LLM pre-training applications by providing a stable, data-efficient alternative that overcomes the limitations of both proxy function-fitting and naive direct optimization approaches.

title: Space2Ground 2.0: A Multi-Source Dataset and Framework for Agricultural Monitoring through Fusion of Street-Level and Satellite Imagery
comment: This paper has been accepted for presentation at the 45th EARSeL Symposium, Athens, Greece
summary: Accurate and scalable parcel-level agricultural monitoring remains challenging because satellite Earth Observation alone provides only an overhead perspective of agricultural parcels, while optical observations are further affected by cloud-induced temporal gaps. This paper presents Space2Ground 2.0, a multi-source framework integrating Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 multispectral time series with geo-tagged street-level imagery acquired using vehicle-mounted cameras and shared through the Mapillary platform. A largely automated processing pipeline performs semantic filtering, image quality assessment, viewpoint-based parcel association, and dataset refinement, transforming large volumes of crowdsourced imagery into parcel-linked, analysis-ready data. Applied over Cyprus during the 2022 growing season, the pipeline produced a curated dataset of 46,050 annotated street-level images, selected from an initial collection exceeding 900,000 images and linked with satellite information for 8,581 agricultural parcels. The practical value of the dataset was assessed through parcel-level crop classification experiments using both single- and multi-source observations. The results demonstrate that street-level imagery provides complementary fine-scale visual information that enhances classification when integrated with satellite time series. Overall, Space2Ground 2.0 provides an openly available benchmark dataset and a reproducible methodology for multimodal agricultural monitoring, with potential applications in visual verification, reduced reliance on costly field inspections, and data-driven agricultural policy implementation.

AI.tldr: Space2Ground 2.0 is a multi-source agricultural monitoring framework that integrates Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 multispectral time series, and crowdsourced street-level imagery from Mapillary to enable parcel-level crop classification. Applied in Cyprus (2022 growing season), it produced a curated dataset of 46,050 annotated street-level images linked to 8,581 agricultural parcels, demonstrating improved crop classification accuracy when multimodal data are fused.
AI.motivation: Satellite Earth Observation alone provides only an overhead, top-down perspective of agricultural parcels, and optical observations suffer from cloud-induced temporal gaps, limiting their accuracy and completeness for parcel-level agricultural monitoring. There is a need for complementary ground-level visual information at scale.
AI.method: The framework integrates Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 multispectral time series with geo-tagged crowdsourced street-level imagery from Mapillary. A largely automated processing pipeline performs semantic filtering, image quality assessment, viewpoint-based parcel association, and dataset refinement to transform raw crowdsourced imagery into parcel-linked, analysis-ready data. Crop classification experiments were conducted using single- and multi-source observations.
AI.result: Applied over Cyprus in the 2022 growing season, the pipeline selected 46,050 annotated street-level images from over 900,000 raw images, linked to 8,581 agricultural parcels. Results show that street-level imagery provides complementary fine-scale visual information that enhances crop classification when fused with satellite time series.
AI.conclusion: Space2Ground 2.0 provides an openly available benchmark dataset and reproducible methodology for multimodal agricultural monitoring, with applications in visual verification, reduced field inspection costs, and data-driven agricultural policy. The integration of ground-level and satellite observations yields improved classification performance over single-source approaches.

title: IndustryForge-27B: A Domain-Enhanced Multimodal Foundation Model for Industrial CAD
summary: Automating industrial CAD design and manufacturing places distinctive demands on multimodal foundation models: the model must see engineering drawings and 3D geometry screenshots, write correct parametric-modelling scripts and Windows COM API code, and cover the full range from single parts to assemblies. General-purpose multimodal models fall short on these tasks, while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow to support the diverse calls that upper-layer agents issue. We build IndustryForge-27B on top of Qwen3.5-VL-27B by curating and integrating six industrial-CAD sub-corpora totalling $\sim$52k multimodal samples---CAD Visual QA (CAD-VQA), parametric CAD code (text2cadquery), assembly-level CAD code (text2cadquery-assembly), and three COM sub-corpora for Inventor / SolidWorks (com_2d / com_3d / com_assembly)---and training with a unified multi-task SFT recipe. Across four CAD-domain benchmarks IndustryForge-27B lifts the base model by $+33.65$~pp on average and outperforms the strong closed-source model GPT-5.4 on all four; across eleven general-capability benchmarks it retains, and slightly improves upon, the base model ($+1.56$~pp mean, no catastrophic forgetting). IndustryForge-27B will serve as the common substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects, providing a unified starting point for a full-stack industrial agent that spans from CAD design to industrial-software operation, from parts to assemblies, and from single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement.

AI.tldr: IndustryForge-27B is a multimodal foundation model built on Qwen3.5-VL-27B, fine-tuned on ~52k industrial-CAD samples across six sub-corpora (CAD-VQA, parametric CAD code, assembly CAD code, and three COM sub-corpora for Inventor/SolidWorks) using a unified multi-task SFT recipe. It boosts the base model by +33.65pp on average across four CAD-domain benchmarks, surpasses GPT-5.4 on all four, and retains/improves general capabilities (+1.56pp mean across eleven benchmarks, no catastrophic forgetting). It serves as a shared substrate for downstream full-stack industrial-agent applications.
AI.motivation: Industrial CAD design and manufacturing require multimodal models that can understand engineering drawings and 3D geometry, write parametric-modelling scripts and Windows COM API code, and handle everything from single parts to assemblies. General-purpose multimodal models underperform on these specialized tasks, while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow for the diverse calls issued by upper-layer agents.
AI.method: IndustryForge-27B is built on Qwen3.5-VL-27B by curating and integrating six industrial-CAD sub-corpora totaling ~52k multimodal samples: CAD Visual QA (CAD-VQA), parametric CAD code (text2cadquery), assembly-level CAD code (text2cadquery-assembly), and three COM sub-corpora for Inventor/SolidWorks (com_2d, com_3d, com_assembly). Training uses a unified multi-task supervised fine-tuning (SFT) recipe.
AI.result: Across four CAD-domain benchmarks, IndustryForge-27B improves the base model by +33.65pp on average and outperforms GPT-5.4 on all four. Across eleven general-capability benchmarks it retains and slightly improves upon the base model (+1.56pp mean), with no catastrophic forgetting observed.
AI.conclusion: IndustryForge-27B provides a unified, strong multimodal foundation for downstream industrial-agent projects, enabling a full-stack industrial agent spanning CAD design to industrial-software operation, from parts to assemblies, and from single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement.

title: TriShield: Zero-Utility-Loss Defense Against Privacy Backdoors in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning via Orthogonal Gradient Projection and Optimizer State Entanglement
summary: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) enables collaborative training without exposing raw data. However, a recent attack, NeuroImprint [1] (arXiv:2606.20553), demonstrates that a malicious parameter server can corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor: by assigning a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and ensuring each neuron updates at most once, the server can analytically reconstruct 59\%--79\% of client training data with high semantic fidelity. Existing defenses---including local differential privacy (LDP) [8] and gradient clipping---either fail against this attack or impose unacceptable utility degradation. We present \textbf{TriShield}, a three-layer deterministic defense that completely prevents NeuroImprint-style reconstruction with \textbf{zero model utility loss} and \textbf{no additional communication rounds}. TriShield consists of: (1) a \textbf{Parameter Artifact Detector} that identifies memory-neuron signatures in distributed model parameters before local training begins; (2) a \textbf{Stateful Virtual Iteration} mechanism that forces Adam/AdamW's momentum state to irreversibly entangle gradients across virtual steps, invalidating NeuroImprint's closed-form inversion; and (3) a \textbf{Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection} operator that projects all local gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace computed via SVD, physically eliminating any gradient components that carry private memorization. We prove theoretically that after Layers 2 and 3, the mutual information between the uploaded gradient and any individual training sample is zero. Experiments on GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B verify that TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to \textbf{0\%} across all tested attack variants, while maintaining or improving training accuracy, with less than 5\% additional GPU computation overhead.

AI.tldr: TriShield is a three-layer deterministic defense against the NeuroImprint privacy backdoor attack in federated LLM fine-tuning, achieving 0% reconstruction rate with zero model utility loss and no additional communication rounds.
AI.motivation: Federated fine-tuning of LLMs is vulnerable to a recently demonstrated attack (NeuroImprint) where a malicious parameter server can inject privacy backdoors into PEFT adapters and reconstruct 59%-79% of client training data. Existing defenses like local differential privacy and gradient clipping either fail against this attack or cause unacceptable utility degradation, motivating the need for a defense that is both effective and utility-preserving.
AI.method: TriShield comprises three layers: (1) a Parameter Artifact Detector that identifies memory-neuron signatures in distributed model parameters before local training; (2) a Stateful Virtual Iteration mechanism that entangles Adam/AdamW momentum state across virtual steps to invalidate NeuroImprint's closed-form inversion; and (3) a Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection operator that projects local gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace via SVD, eliminating gradient components carrying private memorization. Theoretical proof shows mutual information between uploaded gradients and individual samples becomes zero after Layers 2 and 3.
AI.result: On GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B, TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to 0% across all tested attack variants while maintaining or improving training accuracy, with less than 5% additional GPU computation overhead.
AI.conclusion: TriShield provides a theoretically-grounded, deterministic defense against NeuroImprint-style reconstruction attacks in federated LLM fine-tuning, achieving complete privacy protection with zero utility loss and negligible computational overhead, making it a practical defense solution.

title: TARS: Timestep-Aware Data Scaling for 3D-Free Video Re-Shooting
summary: Video re-shooting aims to regenerate videos with controllable camera motion and viewpoint. Existing methods rely on explicit 3D priors, which are limited by reconstruction quality and often perform poorly when synthesizing previously unseen regions, or on paired videos with different camera trajectories, whose scarcity hinders generalization. We revisit video re-shooting through text-driven semantic viewpoint specification, enabling control over shot scale, viewing angle, and first-/third-person perspective. To this end, we propose TARS, a 3D-free video re-shooting paradigm. Timestep-wise sensitivity analysis reveals that camera motion is primarily established during high-noise stages, where coarse spatiotemporal structures are formed. Based on this insight, we introduce self-supervised training to learn camera dynamics and fundamental visual representations without paired re-shooting data or 3D reconstruction. Through data scaling and joint textual-camera conditioning, TARS supports robust camera and viewpoint control, plausibly synthesizing regions beyond the source view under large camera motions while enabling reverse-angle re-shooting and perspective switching. Extensive experiments show that TARS provides more accurate and temporally consistent camera control than prior methods. Project Page: https://ymlinfeng.github.io/TARS.github.io/

AI.tldr: TARS is a 3D-free video re-shooting method that uses text-driven semantic viewpoint specification to control camera motion, viewing angle, shot scale, and perspective without explicit 3D priors or paired re-shooting data. It leverages timestep-wise sensitivity analysis showing camera motion is established at high-noise denoising stages, and uses self-supervised training with joint textual-camera conditioning to achieve accurate, temporally consistent camera control.
AI.motivation: Existing video re-shooting methods either rely on explicit 3D priors that are constrained by reconstruction quality and poorly synthesize unseen regions, or depend on paired videos with different camera trajectories whose scarcity hinders generalization. The authors aim to revisit video re-shooting as a text-driven semantic viewpoint specification problem to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: TARS proposes a 3D-free video re-shooting paradigm based on a key insight from timestep-wise sensitivity analysis: camera motion is primarily established during high-noise stages where coarse spatiotemporal structures form. It introduces self-supervised training to learn camera dynamics and visual representations without paired re-shooting data or 3D reconstruction, combined with data scaling and joint textual-camera conditioning for robust control.
AI.result: TARS supports accurate and temporally consistent camera control, plausibly synthesizes regions beyond the source view under large camera motions, and enables reverse-angle re-shooting and perspective switching. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TARS outperforms prior methods in camera control accuracy and temporal consistency.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that text-driven semantic viewpoint specification combined with self-supervised training is a viable and superior alternative to explicit 3D priors or paired data for video re-shooting, offering broader generalization and robust control over camera motion and viewpoint.

title: SemPIC: Learning Semantic Position-Independent KV Caches
summary: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads repeatedly reuse the same documents under changing instructions, histories, and document orders. Prefix caching cannot exploit this reuse, while position-independent caching (PIC) remains unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack the future context in which they will be consumed. Our diagnostics show that a learned boundary-conditioned baseline sharply reduces attention deviation near reusable-block boundaries but leaves interior and task-level residuals, motivating adaptation of the document representation itself. We present \emph{SemPIC}, which trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation while retaining the pretrained decoder as an unchanged Reader. Adaptation is confined to offline cache construction, preserving the standard KV interface and cache-hit decoding path. We further introduce KV Gradient Checkpointing, which reduces peak training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs. Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62.

AI.tldr: SemPIC trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation while retaining the pretrained decoder as an unchanged Reader, enabling reliable position-independent caching for long-context retrieval and agentic workloads. It introduces KV Gradient Checkpointing to reduce peak training memory, raising mean micro-F1 from 0.53 (KV Packet) to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62.
AI.motivation: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads repeatedly reuse documents under changing instructions and orders. Prefix caching cannot exploit this reuse, and position-independent caching (PIC) remains unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack the future context in which they will be consumed. Diagnostics show learned boundary-conditioned baselines reduce attention deviation at block boundaries but leave interior and task-level residuals, motivating adapting the document representation itself.
AI.method: SemPIC trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation, while the pretrained decoder remains an unchanged Reader. Adaptation is confined to offline cache construction, preserving the standard KV interface and cache-hit decoding path. A novel KV Gradient Checkpointing technique reduces peak training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs.
AI.result: Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62. KV Gradient Checkpointing effectively reduces peak training memory while maintaining gradient flow.
AI.conclusion: By shifting adaptation from the consumer side to an offline cache-construction Writer, SemPIC makes position-independent caching reliable enough to approach full-recompute quality, while preserving the standard KV interface for cache hits. This establishes a promising direction for exploiting document reuse in long-context and agentic workloads.

title: AutoPref: Automatic Discovery of Task-Specific Preference Objectives for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
summary: Combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) underpin many real-world decisions, but their exponentially large search spaces make high-quality solutions costly to obtain. Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) learns fast construction policies, typically with reinforcement learning (RL), while preference-based NCO improves sample efficiency by learning from relative solution quality. However, existing preference objectives combine two distinct design choices in manually specified, one-size-fits-all formulations: what learning signal to extract from each solution pair and how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set. We present AutoPref, the first LLM-guided framework for automated preference-objective discovery in NCO. AutoPref factorizes the objective into a pairwise loss program, which defines the learning signal, and a set-aware weighting program, which determines each pair's relative contribution. Their composition forms a unified programmatic objective space containing existing preference objectives as special cases. To make its search tractable, we introduce a staged conditional search strategy with behavioral gates that filter inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation. Across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across problem scales, demonstrating the benefits and scalability of automated objective discovery for NCO.

AI.tldr: AutoPref is the first LLM-guided framework for automated preference-objective discovery in neural combinatorial optimization, factorizing the objective into a pairwise loss program and a set-aware weighting program, and using staged conditional search with behavioral gates to find superior objectives that outperform hand-designed baselines across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP.
AI.motivation: Existing preference objectives in NCO combine two distinct design choices—what learning signal to extract from each solution pair and how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set—in manually specified, one-size-fits-all formulations, limiting performance across diverse problems.
AI.method: AutoPref factorizes the preference objective into a pairwise loss program (defining the learning signal) and a set-aware weighting program (determining each pair's relative contribution), composing them into a unified programmatic objective space. A staged conditional search strategy with behavioral gates filters inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation.
AI.result: AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across problem scales on TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, demonstrating the benefits and scalability of automated objective discovery for NCO.
AI.conclusion: Automated, LLM-guided objective discovery can replace manual preference-objective design in NCO, yielding better and more scalable performance across diverse combinatorial optimization problems.

title: Echoverse: Deep, Evolving Environments for Training Computer-Use Agents at Scale
summary: Computer-use agents learn from what their actions change, so training one needs applications it can act on, break and reset. The applications that matter most are login-gated and stateful, so synthetic environments stand in for them. Recent pipelines generate such environments in bulk, which moves the bottleneck from how many exist to what is inside each one. The returns, we find, come from three properties: how much behavioural depth an environment carries, whether it targets the interaction an agent actually fails, and whether it improves alongside the model. We present Echoverse, which compiles specifications into stateful applications whose tasks are graded against the application's own database, and a co-evolution loop that reads every graded rollout twice: as repairs to the environment, its tasks and its verifier, and as training signal for the model. Trained on twelve such environments, a 9B model improves from $36.5\%$ to $67.1\%$ across fourteen evaluation splits, within fourteen points of the much larger frontier model that taught it. We examine each property in turn. On the same domains, shallow environments push live-site accuracy below the base model ($80.0 \to 75.0$) while deep ones raise it ($80.0 \to 85.0$ and $48.0 \to 65.0$); drilling one interface control across many renderings transfers to held-out widget families and to the open web; and repairing a single environment lifts the model trained on it from $16.2\%$ to $38.5\%$. The same worlds serve as reinforcement-learning environments, where a reward combining the grounded verifier with a dense per-step judge raises held-out score from $58.8\%$ to $68.0\%$. We release four environments as a benchmark, with their applications, seed data and grounded graders. Code: https://aka.ms/echoverse

AI.tldr: Echoverse is a pipeline that compiles specifications into stateful synthetic applications for training computer-use agents, using a co-evolution loop that turns graded rollouts into both environment repairs and model training signal. A 9B model trained on twelve such environments improves from 36.5% to 67.1% across fourteen evaluation splits, within 14 points of a much larger frontier teacher model.
AI.motivation: Training computer-use agents requires applications they can act on, break, and reset. Real applications that matter most are login-gated and stateful, so synthetic environments are used as stand-ins. While recent pipelines can generate environments in bulk, the bottleneck shifts to what is inside each environment; the authors identify three properties that drive returns: behavioral depth, targeted interaction coverage, and co-evolution with the model.
AI.method: Echoverse compiles specifications into stateful applications whose tasks are graded against the application's own database. A co-evolution loop reads every graded rollout twice: once to repair the environment (its tasks and verifier) and once as training signal for the model. The authors examine each of the three properties: depth of environments, drilling one interface control across many renderings, and repairing single environments.
AI.result: A 9B model trained on twelve environments improves from 36.5% to 67.1% accuracy across fourteen evaluation splits, within 14 points of a frontier teacher model. Shallow environments degrade live-site accuracy (80.0→75.0) while deep ones improve it (80.0→85.0 and 48.0→65.0). Drilling one interface control transfers to held-out widget families and open web. Repairing a single environment lifts model accuracy from 16.2% to 38.5%. The worlds serve as RL environments where a reward combining a grounded verifier with dense per-step judge raises held-out score from 58.8% to 68.0%.
AI.conclusion: The quality of synthetic environments matters more than their quantity. Three properties—behavioral depth, targeted interaction coverage, and co-evolution—are decisive for agent training. Echoverse demonstrates strong gains for small models and releases four environments as a benchmark with applications, seed data, and grounded graders.

title: What Makes Graph Unified? Principles and Generative Sliding-Window Transformer for Graph Foundation Models
summary: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose graph learning, aiming to learn reusable knowledge that generalizes across diverse graph domains and downstream tasks, reducing the need for specific model development. Achieving this goal requires reconciling the substantial heterogeneity in node features, graph structures, and semantic information across domains. Among them, heterogeneous node features constitute a fundamental input-level barrier, as their dimensionality and semantics vary substantially across datasets. Existing studies typically project or map heterogeneous node features into a fixed-dimensional space, often implicitly equating dimensional uniformity with effective feature unification. Yet dimensional consistency alone does not ensure that the unified features preserve informative semantics and capture transferable patterns that can support cross-domain knowledge transfer. To bridge this conceptual gap, we distill four desiderata for cross-domain graph feature unification: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility. Guided by these principles, we propose SliGFM, a graph foundation model built upon topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction. SliGFM orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness and scans the reordered features with a shared sliding-window feature encoder, transforming heterogeneous features into a common space of ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens. This formulation enables a smoothness-aware transformer to capture transferable relational patterns among feature tokens within each node, while the generative reconstruction objective encourages preservation of the original feature information.

AI.tldr: SliGFM is a graph foundation model that unifies heterogeneous node features across graph domains via topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction, distilling four desiderata for cross-domain feature unification.
AI.motivation: Existing GFM approaches assume dimensional uniformity implies effective feature unification, but dimensional consistency alone does not guarantee informative semantics or transferable cross-domain patterns. This conceptual gap motivates principled feature unification criteria for graph foundation models.
AI.method: SliGFM introduces four desiderata (formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, backbone compatibility). It orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness, then applies a shared sliding-window feature encoder to transform heterogeneous features into ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens. A smoothness-aware transformer captures transferable relational patterns among tokens, and a generative reconstruction objective preserves original feature information.
AI.result: The paper proposes the SliGFM framework as a solution to the cross-domain graph feature unification problem, though specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: SliGFM bridges the gap between dimensional uniformity and true semantic unification by processing features through topology-aware sliding-window encoding and generative reconstruction, enabling more effective cross-domain knowledge transfer in graph foundation models.

title: MSCM-net: A hyperspectral image classiffcation method based on multi-scale convolution and Mamba
summary: Hyperspectral imaging is widely used in remote sensing and engineering. Therefore, research on its classification methods is crucial. While CNN and Transformer-based methods have advanced, they still face locality constraints and high computational complexity. To address these issues, we propose an innovative hyperspectral image classification model, MSCM-net. Specifically, first of all, a model architecture combining multi-scale CNN and Mamba is proposed. It consists of a multi-scale feature extraction module (MCSE) and multiple stacked Mamba blocks, which integrates the local feature extraction capability of multi-scale CNN and the long sequence modeling advantage of Mamba. Secondly, the proposed MCSE module consists of multi-scale convolution and SENet. Convolution kernels of different scales extract local information with different receptive fields, enhancing the fusion of spatial and spectral information. Meanwhile, the SENet enables the model to automatically learn the importance of each channel in the multi-scale features. Furthermore, we also propose a dual-branch feature aggregation module, which further effectively extracts and integrates the spectral information contained in the central pixel and the spatial information in the surrounding pixels. Our model has undergone numerous experiments on three widely used benchmark datasets. The experimental results show that MSCM-net can achieve advanced classification performance while reducing computational complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MSCM-net, a hyperspectral image classification model combining multi-scale CNN and Mamba (state space model) to overcome locality constraints and high computational complexity of existing CNN/Transformer methods. It integrates a multi-scale feature extraction module (MCSE) with SENet channel attention and a dual-branch feature aggregation module for spectral/spatial fusion.
AI.motivation: Existing hyperspectral image classification methods based on CNN and Transformer suffer from locality constraints and high computational complexity, limiting their effectiveness for remote sensing and engineering applications.
AI.method: MSCM-net combines multi-scale CNN and Mamba. It includes: (1) an MCSE module with multi-scale convolution kernels and SENet for multi-receptive-field local feature extraction and channel importance learning; (2) stacked Mamba blocks for long sequence modeling; and (3) a dual-branch feature aggregation module to extract and integrate spectral information from the central pixel and spatial information from surrounding pixels.
AI.result: Experiments on three widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate that MSCM-net achieves advanced classification performance while reducing computational complexity compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MSCM-net effectively bridges local feature extraction via multi-scale CNN and global sequence modeling via Mamba, achieving superior hyperspectral image classification with lower computational cost.

title: Group-Reflective Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is effective for training large language model agents. However, terminal rewards provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, leaving successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices entangled in the same outcome signal. Existing agentic self-distillation methods enrich sparse supervision with natural-language skills, but skills retrieved externally or extracted from a single trajectory by stronger models may mismatch current experience, exceed the policy's capability, or remain path-specific. We propose Group-Reflective Self-Distillation (GRSD), which derives capability-aligned and outcome-discriminative guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts. For each prompt, the policy reflects on each verified trajectory in an on-policy group, and a stop-gradient snapshot contrasts the resulting reflections from successful and failed rollouts to construct group-level privileged guidance. Conditioned on this guidance, a self-teacher refines turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction. Experiments across multiple agentic environments and model scales demonstrate that GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.

AI.tldr: GRSD is a method that derives capability-aligned, outcome-discriminative guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts to improve RLVR for LLM agents. It uses group-level reflections contrasting successful and failed trajectories to construct privileged guidance, then a self-teacher refines turn-level credit assignment while preserving verifier-determined learning direction. Experiments show consistent gains over baselines and better generalization.
AI.motivation: Terminal rewards in RLVR provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, entangling successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices in the same outcome signal. Existing agentic self-distillation methods using external or single-trajectory skills mismatch current experience, exceed policy capability, or remain path-specific.
AI.method: GRSD operates in three steps: (1) for each prompt, the policy reflects on each verified trajectory in an on-policy group; (2) a stop-gradient snapshot contrasts reflections from successful vs. failed rollouts to construct group-level privileged guidance; (3) a self-teacher refines turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction.
AI.result: Across multiple agentic environments and model scales, GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging the policy's own verified rollouts with group-level contrastive reflection enables capability-aligned and outcome-discriminative guidance, leading to superior performance and generalization in agentic RL training.

title: Beyond Binary Rewards: A Comparative Study of Reward Design for Reinforcement Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning seeks to selectively remove specific knowledge from trained language models without full retraining, a growing necessity under privacy regulations such as GDPR and the EU AI Act. Recent work has reformulated unlearning as a Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) problem, where models are optimized against verifiable rewards computed directly from their outputs. However, existing methods rely on sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal, indicating only whether forbidden content was avoided, and limiting convergence speed. In this paper, we study how reward design affects unlearning efficiency within the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework. We introduce a principled reward decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity, and propose two new reward functions: an exponential reward that provides graded penalties based on the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and a PageRank inspired reward that weights penalties by semantic importance. We conduct experiments on the Real World Knowledge Unlearning (RWKU) benchmark, demonstrating that both rewards consistently outperform the binary setting, while reaching similar forgetting performance up to $3\times$ faster and preserving general model utility. Our results show that reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how reward design impacts unlearning efficiency in the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework. The authors propose a reward decomposition framework decoupling verifiability from sparsity, and introduce two novel reward functions—an exponential reward based on forbidden-concept occurrence counts and a PageRank-inspired reward weighting penalties by semantic importance. Both rewards outperform binary baseline rewards on the RWKU benchmark, achieving up to 3× faster convergence while preserving model utility.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning is increasingly necessary under privacy regulations (GDPR, EU AI Act), but existing RLVR-based unlearning methods rely on sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal, indicating only whether forbidden content was avoided. This limits convergence speed and overall unlearning efficiency.
AI.method: The paper proposes a principled reward decomposition framework that separates verifiability from reward sparsity. Two new reward functions are introduced: (1) an exponential reward providing graded penalties based on the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and (2) a PageRank-inspired reward that weights penalties by semantic importance. Experiments are conducted on the RWKU benchmark.
AI.result: Both proposed rewards consistently outperform the binary reward setting, achieve up to 3× faster convergence to similar forgetting performance, and preserve general model utility on the Real World Knowledge Unlearning (RWKU) benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency, offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning.

title: Beyond Visual Ambiguity: Guiding Robust Monocular Depth Estimation in Challenging Scenarios via Detailed Long Captions
summary: Monocular depth estimation (MDE) faces challenges with non-Lambertian surfaces and adverse weather conditions due to the visual ambiguities inherent in single-image limited information. Existing works address them in isolation via image inpainting or augmentation, yielding limited robustness gains. Language, as a powerful complementary modality to vision, is demonstrated to enhance the visual perception capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) via detailed long captions. However, prior language-integrated MDE methods fail to fully harness this potential due to short text input with limited information, coarse global text feature learning, and limited language guidance during depth decoding. To address these limitations, we propose CapDepth, a novel framework for robust MDE that leverages guidance from detailed long captions to alleviate visual ambiguities in both challenging scenarios. First, we design a detailed long caption input template that explicitly conveys rich spatial relationships among multiple atom sentences. Second, a dynamic caption encoder is introduced to extract fine-grained depth-relevant text features via progressive masked attention. Finally, we propose a text-adaptive decoder that guides enhanced depth decoding with text features via stable adaptive layer normalization. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of CapDepth, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving depth error reductions of 25.0% on non-Lambertian surfaces and 22.0% under adverse weather conditions.

AI.tldr: CapDepth is a novel framework for monocular depth estimation that leverages detailed long captions from language models to overcome visual ambiguities on non-Lambertian surfaces and in adverse weather conditions, achieving 25.0% and 22.0% depth error reductions respectively.
AI.motivation: Existing monocular depth estimation methods struggle with non-Lambertian surfaces and adverse weather due to inherent visual ambiguities in single images. Prior approaches address these issues in isolation via inpainting or augmentation with limited robustness. Language-integrated MDE methods fail to fully exploit language's potential due to short text inputs, coarse global text feature learning, and limited language guidance during depth decoding.
AI.method: CapDepth introduces three key components: (1) a detailed long caption input template that expresses rich spatial relationships across multiple atomic sentences; (2) a dynamic caption encoder that extracts fine-grained depth-relevant text features via progressive masked attention; and (3) a text-adaptive decoder that guides depth decoding using text features via stable adaptive layer normalization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show CapDepth outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving depth error reductions of 25.0% on non-Lambertian surfaces and 22.0% under adverse weather conditions.
AI.conclusion: Detailed long captions as a complementary language modality can effectively mitigate visual ambiguities in monocular depth estimation for challenging scenarios, and the proposed architectural components (long caption template, dynamic caption encoder, and text-adaptive decoder) successfully harness this potential.

title: Distilling Answer Set Programming Theories from Large Language Models
summary: Writing Answer Set Programming (ASP) theories from scratch is a difficult and time-consuming task. We take a neurosymbolic approach to study whether a model can distill complete and correct theories, given a fixed agent harness with the solver in the loop. The protocol is dataset-agnostic: with a single prompt and an empty file as the starting point the model is given a 1-hour time limit to derive a complete theory. We chose VQA as the application domain, three benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER), as these are publicly available and non-trivial. In order to study the model scale required for solving this task we nine different models: four frontier (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5, DeepSeek V4 Pro), two mid-tier (DeepSeek V4 Flash, gpt-oss-120b), and three open-weights (qwen3.6-27b, gpt-oss-20b, qwen3.5-9b). Three of four frontier models reach 100% on CLEVR and 92.8%-98.8% on GQA; on CLEVRER, Sonnet, Opus, DeepSeek V4 Pro score 92.7%-95.3%. GPT-5 reaches 98.7% on CLEVR but drops to 41.8% on GQA and to 86.7% on CLEVRER. Adding handwritten reference theories from other datasets moves the other three frontier models by at most +/-3.4 pp but reduces GPT-5's accuracy by 3-19 pp. We release the code, prompts, and theories distilled.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether language models can distill complete and correct Answer Set Programming (ASP) theories from scratch using a neurosymbolic, dataset-agnostic protocol with a solver in the loop and a 1-hour time limit. Evaluating nine models across three VQA benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER), three of four frontier models achieve strong performance (100% on CLEVR, 92.8%-98.8% on GQA, 92.7%-95.3% on CLEVRER), while GPT-5 shows inconsistent results. Adding handwritten reference theories from other datasets has minimal impact on most frontier models but significantly hurts GPT-5.
AI.motivation: Writing ASP theories manually is difficult and time-consuming. The authors aim to determine whether large language models can autonomously generate complete and correct ASP theories, and what model scale is required for this task.
AI.method: A dataset-agnostic protocol where a model starts with a single prompt and an empty file, with a 1-hour time limit to derive a complete ASP theory, using a fixed agent harness with a solver in the loop. Nine models across four tiers (frontier, mid-tier, open-weights) are evaluated on three VQA benchmarks. A second experiment tests the effect of adding handwritten reference theories from other datasets.
AI.result: Three of four frontier models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, DeepSeek V4 Pro) reach 100% on CLEVR, 92.8%-98.8% on GQA, and 92.7%-95.3% on CLEVRER. GPT-5 reaches 98.7% on CLEVR but drops to 41.8% on GQA and 86.7% on CLEVRER. Reference theories move other frontier models by at most ±3.4 pp but reduce GPT-5's accuracy by 3-19 pp. Mid-tier and open-weights models perform worse overall.
AI.conclusion: Frontier models can successfully distill complete and correct ASP theories from scratch for VQA tasks, but performance varies significantly across models, with GPT-5 showing notable instability. The code, prompts, and distilled theories are released for reproducibility.

title: TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents
summary: Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial paradigm for the post-training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents. However, existing methods predominantly rely on sparse task rewards for policy optimization, failing to fully exploit another class of inherently dense supervisory signals naturally present during online interaction: environmental feedback following action execution. Recent theoretical studies suggest that generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks hinges on predictive knowledge of environmental consequences. Inspired by this, we propose TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents, a unified training framework that alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision. Beyond standard RL updates, TAPO repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model. This approach enhances the model's sensitivity to environmental transition dynamics and action consequences while concurrently optimizing the policy. It serves as a computationally lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement module for existing agent RL algorithms, requiring no additional expert data, extra sampling costs, or inference-time overhead. We conduct systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld, integrating foundation models of various scales with different policy optimization algorithms. Empirical results demonstrate that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.

AI.tldr: TAPO is a framework for LLM agents that augments RL-based policy optimization with action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on shared backbone models, improving performance on WebShop and ALFWorld without extra data or sampling costs.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for LLM agent post-training rely only on sparse task rewards, failing to exploit dense environmental feedback signals available during online interaction. Theoretical insights suggest predictive knowledge of environmental consequences is key to generalization in multi-step goal-oriented tasks.
AI.method: TAPO alternates between standard policy optimization and transition supervision. It repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model, enhancing sensitivity to transition dynamics while concurrently optimizing the policy. It is a plug-and-play module requiring no extra expert data, sampling, or inference overhead.
AI.result: Systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld with foundation models of various scales and different policy optimization algorithms show TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.
AI.conclusion: TAPO demonstrates that incorporating dense transition supervision alongside sparse reward-based policy optimization is a lightweight and effective enhancement for RL-trained LLM agents.

title: Filling the Pareto-Optimal Front for Affordance Segmentation on Embedded Devices Using RGB-D Cameras
summary: While depth sensors have the potential to complement RGB data for affordance segmentation in wearable robots, their usage seems to remain underexplored. The paper proposes two approaches: a reformulated version of hardware-aware neural architecture search, endowed with a newly designed search space to integrate depth (D) information into small-sized deep networks, and a dedicated fine-tuning approach, including a preprocessing layer to merge depth information with RGB data and make it compatible with conventional architectures. In both cases, those methods aim to generate solutions that benefit from modern (portable) hardware accelerators and overcome existing tiny-like approaches, which often fail to tackle critical scenarios due to the severe constraints set by the supporting hardware. Extensive experiments on a pair of real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method as compared with existing solutions. The approach presented in the paper generates, in most cases, solutions that identify the Pareto optimal front to balance generalization performance and hardware requirements. The paper also describes the supporting prototype, including a Jetson Nano board and a RealSense RGB-D camera. When considering the energy profile of the device, the overall system can attain real-time performances within an energy budget that is compatible with standard batteries, such as those used in smartphones.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using depth sensors to complement RGB data for affordance segmentation in wearable robots. It proposes two approaches: a reformulated hardware-aware neural architecture search with a new search space integrating depth information into small networks, and a fine-tuning approach with a preprocessing layer merging RGB and depth data. Both aim to leverage modern portable hardware accelerators while overcoming limitations of existing tiny-model approaches. Experiments on real-world datasets show the methods achieve Pareto optimal solutions balancing performance and hardware efficiency, with a prototype (Jetson Nano + RealSense RGB-D camera) achieving real-time performance within smartphone-compatible battery energy budgets.
AI.motivation: Depth sensors can complement RGB data for affordance segmentation in wearable robots, but their potential remains underexplored. Existing tiny-model approaches fail in critical scenarios due to severe hardware constraints, motivating the need for solutions that integrate depth information into small deep networks while exploiting modern portable hardware accelerators.
AI.method: The paper proposes two approaches: (1) a reformulated hardware-aware neural architecture search with a newly designed search space to integrate depth information into small-sized deep networks, and (2) a dedicated fine-tuning approach that includes a preprocessing layer to merge depth data with RGB information, making it compatible with conventional architectures. Both methods are designed to benefit from modern portable hardware accelerators.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods versus existing solutions. The approach generates, in most cases, solutions identifying the Pareto optimal front balancing generalization performance and hardware requirements. The implemented prototype, using a Jetson Nano board and a RealSense RGB-D camera, achieves real-time performance within energy budgets compatible with standard smartphone batteries.
AI.conclusion: The proposed methods successfully integrate depth information into small deep networks for affordance segmentation in wearable robots, achieving competitive performance and hardware efficiency. The system demonstrates real-time capability with portable hardware and feasible energy consumption, validating the practical viability of the approach for wearable assistive robotics.

title: Diversifying Personalized Research Ideation against AI-Induced Homogenization
summary: AI-assisted research ideation has emerged as a promising paradigm for accelerating scientific discovery, with systems now capable of generating research directions conditioned on papers, topics, or lightweight researcher contexts. Yet current systems largely optimize individual suggestions in isolation. This leaves two blind spots. First, coarse researcher representations may elicit mainstream directions that appear broadly feasible, but lack sufficient researcher-specific grounding. Second, independent recommendations can concentrate a community's portfolio around recurring high-probability themes. To address these blind spots, we propose DivAlign, a four-stage pipeline for alignment-preserving de-homogenization. DivAlign extracts fine-grained researcher profiles, generates profile-conditioned candidate directions, scores them along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential), and surfaces researcher-local directions while reducing redundancy across the community portfolio. On a benchmark we construct from 95 AI researchers across five subfields, DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit. Compared with coarse single-shot ideation, it lowers average pairwise similarity from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608. Compared with the independent top-choice variant, DivAlign reduces nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of the researcher-direction fit score. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ruixxxx/DivAlign.

AI.tldr: DivAlign is a four-stage pipeline for alignment-preserving de-homogenization of AI-assisted research ideation, which extracts fine-grained researcher profiles, generates profile-conditioned candidate directions, scores them on Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential, and reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit.
AI.motivation: Current AI-assisted research ideation systems optimize individual suggestions in isolation, leaving two blind spots: coarse researcher representations elicit broadly feasible but poorly grounded mainstream directions, and independent recommendations homogenize the community portfolio by concentrating around recurring high-probability themes.
AI.method: DivAlign is a four-stage pipeline: (1) extract fine-grained researcher profiles, (2) generate profile-conditioned candidate directions, (3) score candidates along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, Growth Potential), and (4) surface researcher-local directions while reducing redundancy across the community portfolio. Evaluation uses a benchmark of 95 AI researchers across five subfields.
AI.result: DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit. Compared with coarse single-shot ideation, it lowers average pairwise similarity from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608. Compared with the independent top-choice variant, it reduces nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of the researcher-direction fit score.
AI.conclusion: DivAlign demonstrates that it is possible to de-homogenize community-level research direction portfolios without sacrificing alignment to individual researchers, suggesting that community-aware diversity can be achieved alongside researcher-specific grounding.

title: Generalization Bounds on Optimal Control for Transformer Training and Wasserstein Distributional Robustness
summary: We derive finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions. Building on the doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, we view data sets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures, allowing us to interpret the training problem as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. We then analyze a quantized model, derived by quantizing the state, action, and measure-state spaces, and derive explicit finite-sample generalization bounds using concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces together with a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function. These bounds are transferred to the base model at the cost of an explicit approximation error. Finally, we show that the same machinery yields a distributionally robust control formulation of the training problem, connecting Transformer generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper derives finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions using a doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation, treating training as finite-horizon Markovian control, and connecting generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.
AI.motivation: To provide rigorous finite-sample generalization guarantees for Transformers, particularly those trained with dynamic programming-style recursions, by leveraging a control-theoretic and measure-theoretic perspective.
AI.method: The authors use a doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, interpreting datasets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures. They formulate training as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem, then quantize the state, action, and measure-state spaces. They derive explicit finite-sample generalization bounds via concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces combined with a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function. Approximation errors from quantization are explicitly accounted for when transferring bounds to the base model.
AI.result: Explicit finite-sample generalization bounds for quantized Transformer models, transferred to the base model with explicit approximation-error penalties. The framework also yields a distributionally robust control formulation, linking Transformer generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.
AI.conclusion: Transformer generalization can be rigorously bounded via control-theoretic and measure-theoretic tools, and the same machinery reveals a natural connection between training and Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

title: MonoVoc: Decoupling Geometry and Semantics for Lightweight Monocular Open-Vocabulary 3D Gaussians
summary: Open vocabulary 3D scene understanding is essential for next-generation interactive systems, empowering users to intuitively query and navigate reconstructed environments using natural language. However, current 3D Gaussian frameworks are often bottlenecked by restrictive multiview capture requirements, costly scene-specific optimization, and the massive memory overhead of storing dense language features. We present a novel, training-free pipeline that fundamentally reimagines this paradigm by explicitly decoupling 3D geometric reconstruction from semantic integration. Given a standard monocular video sequence as input, our method efficiently outputs a compact, highly interpretable, and fully searchable object-level semantic Gaussian map. Rather than entangling heavy language embeddings within the mapping loop, we extract geometry independently and ground semantics through a lightweight, modular post-processing framework. Extensive evaluations on the Replica dataset demonstrate that this decoupled architecture preserves strong rendering fidelity and competitive segmentation accuracy. Crucially, by replacing dense per-Gaussian storage with modular, object-level semantic embeddings, our approach delivers an order-of-magnitude reduction in memory usage compared to SOTA baselines. This provides a highly efficient, scalable, and practical solution for open-vocabulary 3D retrieval and question answering directly from everyday monocular video.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a training-free, decoupled pipeline for open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding from monocular video. It separates geometric reconstruction from semantic integration, producing a compact object-level semantic Gaussian map. The approach achieves competitive segmentation accuracy and an order-of-magnitude reduction in memory usage compared to state-of-the-art baselines on the Replica dataset.
AI.motivation: Current 3D Gaussian frameworks for open-vocabulary scene understanding suffer from restrictive multiview capture requirements, costly scene-specific optimization, and massive memory overhead from storing dense language features. The authors aim to overcome these bottlenecks with a more efficient and scalable paradigm.
AI.method: The pipeline explicitly decouples 3D geometric reconstruction from semantic integration. Given a monocular video sequence, geometry is extracted independently while semantics are grounded through a lightweight, modular post-processing framework. Instead of dense per-Gaussian language feature storage, the approach uses modular object-level semantic embeddings to create a compact, interpretable, and searchable semantic Gaussian map.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on the Replica dataset show the decoupled architecture preserves strong rendering fidelity and competitive segmentation accuracy. The object-level semantic embedding approach delivers an order-of-magnitude reduction in memory usage compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a highly efficient, scalable, and practical solution for open-vocabulary 3D retrieval and question answering directly from everyday monocular video, addressing key limitations of existing 3D Gaussian approaches.

title: PerturbMap: Cross-Context Transfer of Single-Cell Perturbation Responses
summary: Single-cell perturbation atlases rarely measure every intervention in every cellular context: a query perturbation is often observed in one or more source contexts but missing in the recipient context where its effect is needed. Ignoring those measured responses discards query-specific experimental evidence, whereas copying or weakly calibrating them across contexts risks transferring the wrong signal. We propose PerturbMap, which predicts a missing recipient-context effect by combining a recipient-local low-rank base with accepted proposals that transport the same perturbation's measured source responses through source-to-recipient ridge experts fit on paired training perturbations, with proposal weights determined by route reliability estimated on validation anchors. On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improves full-effect MSE by 4.1\% over a recipient-local low-rank base and achieves lower MSE than FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It remains within $2.82\times10^{-6}$ MSE of our centralized token-matched pooled reference, which uses a stronger training interface. A condition-mean specificity diagnostic shows the same direction: same-recipient top-10 counterpart retrieval by cosine increases from 74.5\% for the low-rank base to 80.5\% for PerturbMap.

AI.tldr: PerturbMap predicts missing cellular perturbation effects by combining a recipient-local low-rank base with transported source responses, using reliability-weighted proposals via source-to-recipient ridge experts, improving full-effect MSE by 4.1% and condition-mean specificity over baseline controls.
AI.motivation: Single-cell perturbation atlases rarely cover every intervention in every context. Queries are often measured in source contexts but missing in the recipient context where they are needed. Ignoring measured responses wastes query-specific evidence, while copying or weakly calibrating them across contexts risks transferring the wrong signal.
AI.method: PerturbMap predicts missing recipient-context effects by combining a recipient-local low-rank base with accepted proposals that transport the same perturbation's measured source responses through source-to-recipient ridge experts fit on paired training perturbations. Proposal weights are determined by route reliability estimated on validation anchors.
AI.result: On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improves full-effect MSE by 4.1% over a recipient-local low-rank base, outperforming FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It stays within 2.82e-6 MSE of a centralized token-matched pooled reference. Same-recipient top-10 counterpart retrieval by cosine increases from 74.5% to 80.5%.
AI.conclusion: PerturbMap effectively leverages cross-context perturbation evidence in a reliability-weighted manner, improving prediction accuracy and context-specificity without requiring a centralized stronger training interface.

title: It's All Just Vectorization: einx, a Universal Notation for Tensor Operations
summary:
Tensor operations represent a cornerstone of modern scientific computing. However, the Numpy-like notation adopted by predominant tensor frameworks is often difficult to read and write and prone to so-called shape errors, i.a., due to following inconsistent rules across a large, complex collection of operations. Alternatives like einsum and einops have gained popularity, but are inherently restricted to few operations and lack the generality required for a universal model of tensor programming.
  To derive a better paradigm, we revisit vectorization as a function for transforming tensor operations, and use it to both lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations, and conceptually decompose higher-order operations to lower-order operations and their vectorization.
  Building on the universal nature of vectorization, we introduce einx, a universal notation for tensor operations. It uses declarative, pointful expressions that are defined by analogy with loop notation and represent the vectorization of tensor operations. The notation reduces the large APIs of existing frameworks to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and enables a clean, readable and writable representation in code. We provide an implementation of einx that is embedded in Python and integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks: https://github.com/fferflo/einx

AI.tldr: This paper introduces einx, a universal notation for tensor operations built on the concept of vectorization. It uses declarative, pointful expressions analogous to loop notation to reduce large tensor APIs to a small set of elementary operations with consistent rules, providing a Python-embedded implementation that integrates with existing tensor frameworks.
AI.motivation: Existing Numpy-like tensor notation is difficult to read/write and prone to shape errors due to inconsistent rules across a large API surface. Alternatives like einsum and einops lack generality as they are restricted to few operations, motivating the need for a universal, consistent model of tensor programming.
AI.method: The paper revisits vectorization as a function for transforming tensor operations, using it to both lift lower-order operations to higher-order ones and conceptually decompose higher-order operations into lower-order operations plus vectorization. This leads to einx, a notation using declarative pointful expressions defined by analogy with loop notation, representing the vectorization of tensor operations.
AI.result: The notation reduces large APIS of existing frameworks to a small set of elementary operations with consistent rules across all operations, enabling clean, readable, and writable code. A Python-embedded implementation of einx is provided that integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Vectorization provides a universal foundation for tensor programming, and einx demonstrates that a small, consistent set of operations based on this principle can replace the large, inconsistent APIs of existing tensor frameworks while improving readability and writability.

title: ObjectStream: Latent Objects as Memory Anchors for Streaming Video Understanding
summary: Streaming video understanding requires models to continuously retain useful visual evidence before future questions are known. Existing approaches primarily manage the growing visual context according to token importance, temporal redundancy, or segment-level relevance, but rarely organize evidence around objects that persist and evolve over time. Thus, in this paper, we introduce ObjectStream, a training-free framework that treats latent objects as memory anchors for streaming video understanding. ObjectStream induces spatially coherent latent objects directly from frozen Video-LLM representations, links them across frames into persistent anchors, and maintains their histories under a bounded memory budget, without requiring external object detectors or segmentation models. Built on these anchors, ObjectStream preserves three complementary forms of evidence: persistent object histories, transient object changes, and recent visual context. This design enables existing Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) to reason over object identities, interactions, and state changes while leaving the underlying model unchanged. Extensive experiments on online streaming and offline long-video benchmarks demonstrate both effectiveness and efficiency. In online streaming evaluation, ObjectStream improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B by 10.0 points on OVO-Bench Real-Time Visual Perception, while reducing peak GPU mem-ory and TTFT by approximately 50%. On offline long-video benchmarks, it surpasses the full-token baseline while discarding 82.5% of visual tokens. These results highlight latent objects as a practical and effective organizing principle for compact streaming video memory.

AI.tldr: ObjectStream is a training-free framework that uses latent objects as memory anchors for streaming video understanding, extracting spatially coherent objects from frozen Video-LLM representations, linking them across frames, and maintaining bounded-memory histories. It improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B by 10.0 points on streaming benchmarks while reducing GPU memory and TTFT by ~50%, and surpasses full-token baselines on offline long-video benchmarks while discarding 82.5% of visual tokens.
AI.motivation: Existing streaming video understanding approaches manage growing visual context via token importance, temporal redundancy, or segment-level relevance, but fail to organize evidence around persistent, evolving objects. Since questions are unknown beforehand, models need a structured memory that preserves object identities, interactions, and state changes efficiently.
AI.method: ObjectStream is a training-free framework that (1) induces spatially coherent latent objects directly from frozen Video-LLM representations without external detectors or segmentation models, (2) links these objects across frames into persistent anchors, (3) maintains their histories under a bounded memory budget, and (4) preserves three complementary evidence forms: persistent object histories, transient object changes, and recent visual context. The underlying Video-LLM remains unchanged.
AI.result: On online streaming evaluation, ObjectStream improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B by 10.0 points on OVO-Bench Real-Time Visual Perception while reducing peak GPU memory and TTFT by ~50%. On offline long-video benchmarks, it surpasses the full-token baseline while discarding 82.5% of visual tokens.
AI.conclusion: Latent objects serve as a practical and effective organizing principle for compact streaming video memory, demonstrating both effectiveness and efficiency across online streaming and offline long-video benchmarks without requiring model modifications.

title: An Instrument to Evaluate Governance Proposals: AI Policy Analysis at Scale
summary:
This paper introduces a policy analysis framework for systematic, transparent assessment of AI governance proposals in an evolving and contested regulatory landscape. AI policy debates often collapse into binary positions that obscure underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions. The framework structures policy analysis around multiple policy attributes, allowing users to surface priorities and tensions without prescribing outcomes. We use a mixed-methods approach that integrates qualitative insights from subject matter experts with computational text analysis to inform the design of policy attribute rubrics. This quantifies the relative emphasis of different policy objectives and presents them through comparative visualizations that support interpretability and cross-policy comparison. The paper also examines the use of commercial LLMs for rubric-based policy analysis, benchmarking their outputs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model with explicitly defined analytical assumptions. Rather than assessing policy effectiveness or desirability, the framework focuses on relevance and alignment across attributes. By making analytical assumptions explicit, including attribute selection, rubric construction, and weighting schemes, the framework enables users to evaluate whether its embedded priorities align with the users' own normative commitments. The approach is jurisdiction-agnostic and intended to support policymakers, analysts, and researchers navigating complex AI governance environments.
  Contributions: (1) multidimensional policy assessment through empirically grounded rubrics that surface tradeoffs rather than resolving them; (2) a transparent hybrid methodology combining feedback from subject-matter experts with computational validation; and (3) use of domain-trained rubric-calibrated models as a benchmark for comparing different general-purpose large language models.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a policy analysis framework for assessing AI governance proposals using multidimensional, rubric-based evaluation. It combines expert qualitative insights with computational text analysis, benchmarks commercial LLMs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model, and focuses on relevance/alignment across policy attributes rather than effectiveness. The framework is jurisdiction-agnostic and makes analytical assumptions explicit to support transparent comparison.
AI.motivation: AI policy debates tend to devolve into binary positions that obscure underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions. Existing approaches lack systematic, transparent methods for evaluating governance proposals in an evolving and contested regulatory landscape.
AI.method: A mixed-methods approach integrating qualitative feedback from subject-matter experts with computational text analysis to design policy attribute rubrics. The framework quantifies relative emphasis of policy objectives via comparative visualizations. Commercial LLMs are benchmarked against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model with explicitly defined analytical assumptions (attribute selection, rubric construction, weighting schemes).
AI.result: The framework enables multidimensional policy assessment through empirically grounded rubrics, surfaces tradeoffs rather than resolving them, and demonstrates a transparent hybrid methodology. Benchmarking of commercial LLMs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model reveals comparative performance for rubric-based policy analysis.
AI.conclusion: The framework shifts focus from policy effectiveness/desirability to relevance and alignment across attributes, enabling users to evaluate whether embedded analytical priorities align with their own normative commitments. It is jurisdiction-agnostic and intended to support policymakers, analysts, and researchers in complex AI governance environments.

title: Building a User Foundation Model for the Open Web
summary: User foundation models have demonstrated strong results in e-commerce and social recommendation, but most industrial deployments assume environments where user identity is stable and persistent. Open-web real-time bidding (RTB) operates on a structurally different data distribution: user identity is fragmented and non-persistent across browsing sessions, and the availability of browsing history depends on user privacy choices. Consequently, a significant portion of traffic carries no historical data, and available records often consist of relatively short, disjointed sessions. As a result, historical signals in this domain are typically represented as aggregated counters and recency buckets, leaving the sequential structure unexploited. To address this limitation, we present a user foundation model that applies self-supervised learning on user browsing histories and show that the learned representation improves multiple downstream production tasks, demonstrating the viability of this approach on the open web. We pre-train a Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective, then fine-tune it on the click prediction task. We optimize the encoder's pre-training pipeline with an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of reviewable, code-level edits (lifters), instantiating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in an industrial setting. The same encoder representation yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker; a 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR, -1.13% eCPC (80% CI excluding zero on both metrics).

AI.tldr: The paper presents a user foundation model for open-web real-time bidding (RTB), where user identity is fragmented and non-persistent. It pre-trains a Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and contrastive learning on user browsing histories, then fine-tunes it for click prediction. The pre-training pipeline is optimized via an LLM-in-the-loop search over reviewable code edits.
