The model yields +1.197% RIG on production bid win-rate and +1.354% RIG on CTR ranker, confirmed by a 7-day live A/B test showing +2.13% CTR improvement.
AI.motivation: Industrial user foundation models typically assume stable, persistent user identity, but open-web RTB operates under fragmented, non-persistent user identity with privacy-dependent browsing history availability. Historical signals are aggregated counters and recency buckets, leaving sequential structure unexploited. The authors aim to leverage self-supervised learning on browsing sequences to improve production tasks in this structurally different environment.
AI.method: The authors pre-train a Transformer encoder using masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective on user browsing histories, then fine-tune it on click prediction. The pre-training pipeline is optimized using an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of reviewable, code-level edits (lifters), instantiating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in an industrial setting.
AI.result: The encoder representation yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker. A 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR and -1.13% eCPC, with 80% confidence intervals excluding zero on both metrics.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised learning on user browsing histories is viable and effective for open-web RTB despite fragmented user identity, improving multiple downstream production tasks. The LLM-as-optimizer approach for pre-training pipeline search also proves practical in an industrial setting.

title: AdaAnchor4D: Anchor-Conditioned Spatiotemporal Feature Aggregation for Monocular UAV 4D Reconstruction
summary: Monocular UAV videos provide valuable observations for dynamic reconstruction of complex urban scenes. However, such scenes exhibit pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity: different regions follow distinct temporal activity patterns, while the motion states of some dynamic regions may further evolve over time. Although dynamic Gaussian methods based on decomposed shared spatiotemporal feature fields have achieved efficient and accurate reconstruction in object-centric or relatively compact scenes, their commonly adopted fixed plane-wise feature combination mechanisms are less suited to the heterogeneous local dynamics of UAV scenes, often leading to ghosting artifacts and blurred dynamic details. To address this challenge, we propose AdaAnchor4D, an adaptive anchor deformation framework for monocular UAV dynamic scene reconstruction. At its core, Anchor-Conditioned Feature Aggregation (ACFA) adaptively aggregates shared spatiotemporal features using anchor-specific aggregation embeddings and temporal information, allowing different local units to obtain dynamic representations tailored to their local and temporal states. Decoupled Local Geometry Deformation (DLGD) separates anchor-state deformation from local Gaussian geometry deformation, while Density-Adaptive Coordinate Warping (DACW) reparameterizes feature-query coordinates according to the axis-wise anchor distributions, alleviating the mismatch between non-uniform geometric sampling and uniform grid parameterization. Experiments on UAV-Arc4D, VisDrone, and UAVDT show that AdaAnchor4D achieves higher rendering quality than representative dynamic Gaussian methods while maintaining real-time rendering performance. The code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: AdaAnchor4D is an adaptive anchor deformation framework for monocular UAV dynamic scene reconstruction that uses Anchor-Conditioned Feature Aggregation, Decoupled Local Geometry Deformation, and Density-Adaptive Coordinate Warping to handle spatiotemporal heterogeneity, achieving higher rendering quality than representative dynamic Gaussian methods while maintaining real-time performance.
AI.motivation: Monocular UAV dynamic scenes exhibit pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity where different regions follow distinct temporal activity patterns that may evolve over time. Existing dynamic Gaussian methods relying on fixed plane-wise feature combination mechanisms from decomposed shared spatiotemporal feature fields are ill-suited to these heterogeneous local dynamics, causing ghosting artifacts and blurred dynamic details.
AI.method: AdaAnchor4D introduces three core components: (1) Anchor-Conditioned Feature Aggregation (ACFA) which adaptively aggregates shared spatiotemporal features using anchor-specific aggregation embeddings and temporal information to tailor dynamic representations per local unit; (2) Decoupled Local Geometry Deformation (DLGD) which separates anchor-state deformation from local Gaussian geometry deformation; (3) Density-Adaptive Coordinate Warping (DACW) which reparameterizes feature-query coordinates based on axis-wise anchor distributions to resolve mismatches between non-uniform geometric sampling and uniform grid parameterization.
AI.result: Experiments on UAV-Arc4D, VisDrone, and UAVDT datasets show AdaAnchor4D achieves higher rendering quality than representative dynamic Gaussian methods while maintaining real-time rendering performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed adaptive anchor deformation framework effectively addresses the limitations of fixed feature combination mechanisms in dynamic Gaussian methods for heterogeneous UAV scenes, delivering superior rendering quality with real-time efficiency. Code will be made publicly available.

title: SciDataSailor: Deep Scientific Data Exploring
summary: Scientific datasets are commonly organized as hierarchical repositories containing heterogeneous and interdependent files, making their inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive and reliant on domain expertise. Although large language model (LLM) agents have advanced substantially in planning, reasoning, and tool use, existing research has largely overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments. We introduce Deep Scientific Data Exploration, an agentic task paradigm in which agents navigate repositories, interpret heterogeneous files and schemas, execute analyses, integrate cross-file evidence, and produce conclusions grounded in executed observations. To operationalize this paradigm, we present SciDataSailor, a framework for synthesizing tool-interactive trajectories by balancing broad exploration with targeted exploitation. SciDataSailor instantiates trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four task-specific mechanisms: difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, dual-feedback first-play urgency, hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and entropy-guided branching. Using this framework, we construct SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation, with the latter comprising 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets spanning the life, earth, and physical sciences.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Deep Scientific Data Exploration, a new agentic task paradigm where LLM agents navigate hierarchical scientific repositories, interpret heterogeneous files, execute analyses, and produce conclusions grounded in executed observations. The authors present SciDataSailor, an MCTS-based framework for synthesizing tool-interactive training trajectories, along with SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation.
AI.motivation: Scientific datasets are organized as hierarchical repositories with heterogeneous and interdependent files, making inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive and dependent on domain expertise. While LLM agents have advanced in planning, reasoning, and tool use, existing research has largely overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments.
AI.method: SciDataSailor synthesizes tool-interactive trajectories by balancing broad exploration with targeted exploitation, instantiating trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four task-specific mechanisms: difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, dual-feedback first-play urgency, hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and entropy-guided branching.
AI.result: The framework produces SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation, comprising 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets spanning life, earth, and physical sciences.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a new paradigm for agentic scientific data exploration and provides both training and benchmark resources to enable LLM agents to operate on real scientific data in executable environments.

title: Flux-OPD: On-Policy Distillation with Evolving Contexts
summary: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize as effective supervision. Contexts can convey such preferences, yet provide little additional supervision once distilled into the student, motivating contexts that evolve with student performance. However, directly using evolving contexts as in-training supervision results in an unstable distillation target and conflicting distributions, requiring mechanisms to stabilize target and downweight conflicts. In this paper, we analyze the effect of contexts through a decomposition of the reverse KL objective, revealing two findings: the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and the objective contains a conflict term that measures conflicts among these teachers. Based on this decomposition, we propose Flux-OPD, an OPD paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to capture task preferences in open-ended domains. Flux-OPD treats the differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, and weights their correction strength using the conflict term as an indicator. Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, highlighting the potential to combine teacher supervision with evolving contexts.

AI.tldr: Flux-OPD is a new Online Preference Distillation (OPD) paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to capture task preferences in open-ended domains where verifiable rewards are unavailable. The method is motivated by a decomposition of the reverse KL objective showing the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers while a conflict term measures disagreements among them. Flux-OPD injects differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as corrections into a context-free teacher anchor, weighted by the conflict term, outperforming existing OPD paradigms on open-ended tasks.
AI.motivation: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize as effective supervision. Contexts can convey preferences but offer little additional supervision once distilled into the student, motivating contexts that evolve with student performance.
AI.method: The paper analyzes the reverse KL objective through decomposition, revealing two findings: (1) the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and (2) the objective contains a conflict term measuring disagreements among teachers. Based on this, Flux-OPD treats differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into a context-free teacher anchor, and weights correction strength using the conflict term as an indicator. It also requires mechanisms to stabilize the distillation target and downweight conflicting distributions when using evolving contexts as in-training supervision.
AI.result: Experiments on open-ended tasks demonstrate that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, highlighting the potential of combining teacher supervision with evolving contexts.
AI.conclusion: Flux-OPD provides a principled framework for using evolving contexts as in-training supervision in open-ended domains by leveraging a theoretical decomposition of the reverse KL objective, and demonstrates that conflict-aware weighting of contextual corrections effectively stabilizes distillation and improves performance over existing OPD approaches.

title: Same Branches, Different Trees: A Bifurcation Connectedness Metric for Coronary Artery Segmentation and FFR-CT Decision Agreement
comment: Accepted at STACOM 2026 (MICCAI workshop). 11 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
summary: Fractional flow reserve derived from CT angiography (FFR-CT) simulates flow through a patient-specific vessel model, so its accuracy depends on the connectedness of the segmented tree, not only on volumetric overlap: a segmentation can reach high Dice yet sever a bifurcation, dropping the downstream subtree and reversing the treatment decision. Topology-aware losses such as clDice and Skeleton Recall act on the global centreline and can miss localised breaks. We study the Bifurcation Connectedness Score (BCS), which scores connectedness at each ground-truth bifurcation, and soft-BCS, its differentiable training surrogate. BCS captures a property of segmentation quality the standard metrics miss: it responds strongly to breaks in connectedness while staying largely unchanged under connectedness-preserving narrowing. Higher BCS accompanies closer agreement between the FFR-CT decisions a solver makes on predicted versus ground-truth geometry, most clearly in severe disease (OR 2.16, CI [1.23, 4.18]). Both decisions come from the same solver, so this reflects geometric, not clinical, fidelity. In training, soft-BCS and Skeleton Recall recover the same branches but build different trees. Recovering branches and keeping them connected are separable properties, so we recommend reporting a measure of each.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Bifurcation Connectedness Score (BCS) and its differentiable training surrogate soft-BCS to evaluate and improve topological connectedness of vessel segmentations in CT angiography, showing that BCS captures segmentation quality that standard volumetric metrics miss and correlates with FFR-CT decision agreement.
AI.motivation: Standard segmentation metrics like Dice fail to capture topological connectedness, which is critical for FFR-CT accuracy. A high Dice score can still result in severed bifurcations that drop downstream subtrees and reverse treatment decisions. Existing topology-aware losses like clDice and Skeleton Recall operate on global centrelines and can miss localized breaks.
AI.method: The authors study the Bifurcation Connectedness Score (BCS), which evaluates connectedness at each ground-truth bifurcation, and develop soft-BCS as its differentiable surrogate for training. They analyze how BCS responds to different segmentation errors and use a FFR-CT solver to compare decisions on predicted versus ground-truth geometry.
AI.result: BCS responds strongly to breaks in connectedness while staying largely unchanged under connectedness-preserving narrowing. Higher BCS correlates with closer agreement between FFR-CT decisions on predicted versus ground-truth geometry, most clearly in severe disease (OR 2.16, CI [1.23, 4.18]). Soft-BCS and Skeleton Recall recover the same branches but produce different tree structures.
AI.conclusion: Branch recovery and keeping branches connected are separable properties of segmentation quality. The authors recommend reporting both a branch-recovery metric and a connectedness metric. BCS captures geometric (not clinical) fidelity of segmentation for FFR-CT purposes.

title: MIND: Lightweight and Effective Memory Injection Defense for LLM Agents via Intent-Aware Information Bottleneck
summary: Memory-augmented LLM-based agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks: Agents may retrieve poisoned memory from attackers, which diverts their behavior from initial user intent and finally causes task failure. However, existing defense mechanisms either incur high computational cost or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts. To address these challenges, we propose Memory Intent-Aware Neural Denoising(MIND), a lightweight defense framework for memory injection attack. Our preliminary analysis reveals that benign and poisoned trajectories exhibit distinguishable relationships between the initial user intent and subsequent behavior. Building on this observation, MIND employs an intent-aware Information Bottleneck(IB) to extract compact intent--behavior representations from the initial intent and turn-level behavior. The IB preserves intent-relevant cross-turn attack signals while filtering task-irrelevant and repetitive information, and a lightweight detector identifies malicious memories from the resulting representations. As such, MIND mitigates information redundancy in multi-turn contexts while avoiding the overhead of repeated LLM auditing. Extensive experiments show that MIND reduces attack success rates while preserving task accuracy and inference efficiency. Notably, on ReAct-StrategyQA, MIND reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3%, respectively, while matching the undefended agent in average accuracy and latency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MIND (Memory Intent-Aware Neural Denoising), a lightweight defense framework against memory injection attacks on LLM-based agents, using intent-aware Information Bottleneck to extract compact representations for malicious memory detection while reducing computational cost and information redundancy.
AI.motivation: Memory-augmented LLM agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks where poisoned memory diverts agent behavior from user intent. Existing defenses are either computationally expensive or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts.
AI.method: MIND employs an intent-aware Information Bottleneck (IB) to extract compact intent-behavior representations from the initial user intent and turn-level behavior. The IB preserves intent-relevant cross-turn attack signals while filtering task-irrelevant and repetitive information, and a lightweight detector identifies malicious memories from the resulting representations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show MIND reduces attack success rates while preserving task accuracy and inference efficiency. On ReAct-StrategyQA, MIND reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3% respectively, while matching the undefended agent in average accuracy and latency.
AI.conclusion: MIND effectively defends against memory injection attacks with reduced attack success rates, preserved task accuracy, and maintained inference efficiency, avoiding the overhead of repeated LLM auditing by leveraging the distinguishable relationship between initial user intent and agent behavior.

title: Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization via Privileged Self-Distillation
summary: Recent advances in post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) or On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD). While OPSD provides dense, logit-level supervision, it inherently suffers from exposure bias due to the privileged information of the self-teacher. In multi-turn agentic settings, this leads to reasoning route convergence and the loss of clear optimization directions. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization (CRPO), which reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective. By leveraging predictive entropy to distinguish between positive positions (reflective exploration) and negative positions (exposure bias), CRPO conducts group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals. Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, significantly enhancing training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

AI.tldr: CRPO reformulates agentic On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) from a contrastive learning perspective, using predictive entropy to distinguish reflective exploration (positive) from exposure bias (negative) positions, yielding group-wise contrast that preserves reliable fine-grained optimization signals. It outperforms existing RL and self-distillation baselines across 13 reasoning and deep-search benchmarks.
AI.motivation: OPSD provides dense logit-level supervision but suffers from exposure bias due to privileged self-teacher information, leading to reasoning route convergence and loss of clear optimization directions in multi-turn agentic settings.
AI.method: CRPO reformulates agentic OPSD as a contrastive learning problem. It leverages predictive entropy to classify positions into positive (reflective exploration) and negative (exposure bias) categories, then conducts group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks show CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, improving training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.
AI.conclusion: CRPO effectively addresses exposure bias in agentic OPSD by contrastively separating reflective exploration from biased supervision, achieving superior training stability and generalization in long-horizon agentic tasks.

title: Capturing Token Tendencies for Training-Free Token Pruning in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: While visual token pruning is essential for efficient Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), existing training-free methods suffer from a critical limitation: they rely on static, instantaneous heuristics to perform irreversible filtering. This approach ignores the hierarchical nature of MLLMs, where token importance often evolves dynamically rather than remaining fixed across layers. Consequently, tokens essential for deep-layer reasoning are often prematurely discarded by shallow-layer estimates. To address this, we propose Trend-aware Pruning, a novel framework that elevates pruning from a local snapshot decision to a temporal trajectory modeling problem. Instead of relying on isolated scores, our method captures the momentum of attention flow. This enables a dynamic rectification mechanism that selectively reactivates "late-blooming" tokens, those initially undervalued but exhibiting rising semantic importance, thereby preventing the loss of critical visual cues. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves a superior efficiency-performance trade-off across diverse multimodal tasks. Notably, it reduces visual tokens by over 77.8%, retaining only approximately 23 tokens in the final layer while maintaining competitive performance, offering a robust and reversible solution for high-efficiency multimodal inference.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Trend-aware Pruning, a training-free visual token pruning framework for MLLMs that models token importance as a temporal trajectory rather than a static snapshot, using attention flow momentum to dynamically reactivate "late-blooming" tokens that were initially undervalued, achieving over 77.8% token reduction while maintaining competitive performance.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free visual token pruning methods rely on static, instantaneous heuristics for irreversible filtering, ignoring the hierarchical nature of MLLMs where token importance evolves dynamically across layers. This causes essential tokens for deep-layer reasoning to be prematurely discarded by shallow-layer estimates, leading to accuracy degradation.
AI.method: Trend-aware Pruning formulates pruning as temporal trajectory modeling instead of local snapshot decisions. It captures the momentum of attention flow across layers and introduces a dynamic rectification mechanism that selectively reactivates "late-blooming" tokens—those initially undervalued but exhibiting rising semantic importance—thereby providing a reversible pruning process.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show the approach achieves a superior efficiency-performance trade-off across diverse multimodal tasks. It reduces visual tokens by over 77.8%, retaining only approximately 23 tokens in the final layer while maintaining competitive performance.
AI.conclusion: Trend-aware Pruning offers a robust and reversible solution for high-efficiency multimodal inference by treating token importance as dynamically evolving across layers, addressing the fundamental limitation of irreversible static pruning in existing methods.

title: Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training
summary: Synthetic textbook data has improved language model pre-training, but prior work largely treats the benefit as a property of generated content or local rewriting style. We study a different factor: whether related content is organized into coherent book-level documents. We contribute both a scalable synthesis pipeline and controlled evidence that this organization matters. The pipeline retrieves source material from a pre-training corpus, clusters it into topical units, plans hierarchical tables of contents, and assembles source-grounded sections into complete books (our Full setting), yielding 686K textbooks (32B tokens) across 15,000+ disciplines. Replacing natural books in a mid-training mix with this corpus improves downstream performance by +1.09 on average. Controlled comparisons then disentangle the relevant design factors. A content-matched Split condition holds generated text and tokens fixed but treats each section as an independent document; Full's +1.02 mean gain isolates document packaging. A length-matched RandomConcat control that joins sections from different books remains below Full, ruling out document length alone. A retrieval-pool-matched Rephrase condition independently rewrites individual retrieved documents under the same audience-by-style scheme, without clustering, TOC planning, or book assembly; Full's +1.17 gain demonstrates the value of structured synthesis. On Llama3-8B, Full likewise outperforms both RandomConcat and Natural Books, supporting book-level organization as a useful axis for synthetic pre-training data design.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether organizing synthetic textbook content into coherent book-level documents (rather than merely generating high-quality content or locally rewriting text) improves language model pre-training. The authors build a scalable pipeline that retrieves, clusters, plans, and assembles source-grounded textbooks, producing 686K textbooks (32B tokens) across 15,000+ disciplines. This corpus outperforms natural books in mid-training by +1.09 on average. Controlled ablations (Split, RandomConcat, Rephrase) isolate document packaging, document length, and structured synthesis as distinct contributing factors, with book-level organization yielding consistent gains of +1.02 to +1.17 over content-matched controls.
AI.motivation: Prior work on synthetic data for pre-training largely attributes benefits to generated content quality or local rewriting style. This paper explores a largely overlooked factor: whether related content is organized into coherent, book-level document structures—and whether such organization matters for downstream performance.
AI.method: The authors build a scalable synthesis pipeline with four stages: (1) retrieving source material from a pre-training corpus, (2) clustering it into topical units, (3) planning hierarchical tables of contents, and (4) assembling source-grounded sections into complete books. This yields 686K textbooks (32B tokens) across 15,000+ disciplines. They then design controlled comparisons—including a content-matched Split condition (sections as independent documents), a length-matched RandomConcat control (joining sections from different books), and a retrieval-pool-matched Rephrase condition (independent rewriting without clustering/TOC/assembly)—to disentangle which design factor drives the gains.
AI.result: Replacing natural books in a mid-training mix with the full book corpus improves downstream performance by +1.09 on average. Full outperforms content-matched Split by +1.02 (isolating document packaging), beats length-matched RandomConcat (ruling out document length alone), and gains +1.17 over retrieval-pool-matched Rephrase (demonstrating structured synthesis value). On Llama3-8B, Full also outperforms both RandomConcat and Natural Books.
AI.conclusion: Book-level organization is a meaningful and useful axis for synthetic pre-training data design, distinct from content quality or local rewriting style. Structured synthesis—clustering, TOC planning, and assembly—matters beyond raw content, token count, or document length.

title: Enhancing Irregular Time Series Forecasting with Continuous-Time Modeling Framework
summary: Irregular multivariate time series are widely encountered in applications such as healthcare monitoring, human activity recognition, and environmental sensing. Their core challenges stem from asynchronous observations, non-uniform sampling intervals, and the fact that temporal patterns themselves carry critical dynamic information. Existing approaches either rely on discretization-based preprocessing (e.g., interpolation, imputation, or aggregation), which disrupts the underlying continuous-time semantics, or adopt continuous-time modeling via ODE-based frameworks, which typically require specialized architectures and incur substantial computational overhead due to numerical solvers. To address these limitations, we propose WrapFlow, a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular time series forecasting. On the input side, WrapFlow introduces Continuous-Time Tokenization, which directly encodes raw observation events and explicitly models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens. The resulting continuous-time tokens are then processed by a standard Transformer backbone to capture long-range temporal dependencies. On the output side, we develop a simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching, which learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions while avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training. This design enables high-quality continuous forecasting using only a small number of fixed rollout steps at inference. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: WrapFlow is a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular multivariate time series forecasting that combines Continuous-Time Tokenization with a standard Transformer backbone and a simulation-free Residual Flow Matching paradigm, achieving state-of-the-art performance without numerical-solver overhead.
AI.motivation: Irregular multivariate time series pose challenges from asynchronous observations and non-uniform sampling intervals. Existing approaches either use discretization-based preprocessing (interpolation, imputation, aggregation) that disrupts continuous-time semantics, or ODE-based continuous-time models that require specialized architectures and incur substantial computational overhead from numerical solvers.
AI.method: WrapFlow has two key components: (1) Continuous-Time Tokenization on the input side, which directly encodes raw observation events into gap-aware tokens that model long unobserved intervals; these tokens are processed by a standard Transformer backbone for long-range dependency capture. (2) A simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching on the output side, which learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions while avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training, enabling continuous forecasting with few fixed rollout steps at inference.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance for irregular time series forecasting.
AI.conclusion: WrapFlow effectively addresses the limitations of both discretization-based and ODE-based approaches by combining continuous-time tokenization with a standard Transformer and a simulation-free flow matching objective, providing high-quality continuous forecasting with low computational overhead.

title: ShadowDancer: Teaching Video World Models Any Action by Learning Unified Dynamics Representations from a Video and Its Shadow
summary: We present ShadowDancer, a novel approach to any-action, frame-level control of interactive video world models. The obstacle is representational: existing interfaces either encode an action loosely, leaving how it unfolds for the model to improvise, or encode it exactly through structured signals that serve one family and are hard to acquire, so precise control across diverse dynamics remains impractical. Demonstration videos are the natural remedy, specifying any dynamics frame by frame; yet a video shows its dynamics only through one particular appearance, a single shadow of the underlying dynamics, so actions learned from demonstrations transfer poorly to new scenes. ShadowDancer addresses this with two key innovations: (1) shadow pairs, video pairs that replay the same dynamics under independently resampled appearance, constructed at scale by our Shadow Library, so that a dynamics family becomes controllable exactly when such pairs can be constructed for it; and (2) cross-shadow prediction, which learns actions by predicting one shadow from the other, so that whatever the pairing resamples is discarded by construction and whatever it preserves becomes the action, yielding a unified dynamics representation that drives a block-causal world model. Any demonstrated clip thus becomes a reusable action asset, replayed in new environments without action labels, motion estimators, or fine-tuning. Experiments demonstrate improved action transfer and long action rollout over strong latent-action and interactive world model baselines across diverse dynamics families, with an average blinded win rate of 86% in rollout comparisons. We show video results at https://ShadowDancer-1.github.io

AI.tldr: ShadowDancer is a novel approach to any-action, frame-level control of interactive video world models. It introduces "shadow pairs" (video pairs replaying the same dynamics under independently resampled appearance) and "cross-shadow prediction" to learn actions by predicting one shadow from another, enabling any demonstrated video clip to become a reusable action asset without action labels, motion estimators, or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing interfaces for action control in video world models are inadequate: they either encode actions loosely (leaving dynamics to model improvisation) or encode them exactly through structured signals that are limited to one family and hard to acquire. Demonstration videos naturally specify dynamics frame-by-frame but transfer poorly to new scenes because a video shows dynamics only through one particular appearance—a single shadow of the underlying dynamics.
AI.method: ShadowDancer uses two key innovations: (1) shadow pairs—video pairs that replay the same dynamics under independently resampled appearance, constructed at scale via the Shadow Library, making a dynamics family controllable whenever such pairs can be constructed; and (2) cross-shadow prediction—learning actions by predicting one shadow from the other, so that whatever the pairing resamples is discarded and whatever it preserves becomes the action, yielding a unified dynamics representation driving a block-causal world model.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate improved action transfer and long action rollout over strong latent-action and interactive world model baselines across diverse dynamics families, with an average blinded win rate of 86% in rollout comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Any demonstrated clip can become a reusable action asset, replayed in new environments without action labels, motion estimators, or fine-tuning, enabling precise frame-level control across diverse dynamics families.

title: BlueprintRepair: Typed Local Edits for Failed Lean Proof Blueprints
summary: LLM-based Lean proving systems increasingly organize a proof as a blueprint: a dependency graph of formal statements. We introduce BlueprintRepair, a repair interface that lets a model change this graph through ten schema-checked local operations. An operation names the node it edits, so the target theorem cannot be changed. Lean checks every applied change, and an accepted repair must declare every blueprint lemma its proof uses. We also construct BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 controlled failures with complete accepted and rejected repair trajectories. We compare typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites under matched source, feedback, model, and budget, one episode per state and interface. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the three interfaces solve almost the same number of the benchmark's localized failures. Typed repair is the cheapest per solved state (patching is 1.30x as expensive, rewriting 2.06x), and within 10,000 completion tokens per task it reaches almost all of its final coverage, while both free-form interfaces are well behind. A second model, Qwen3.6-Flash, solves fewer states but keeps typed repair cheapest, puts it ahead on the proof-authoring states, and repeats the localized pattern.

AI.tldr: BlueprintRepair is a schema-checked repair interface for LLM-based Lean proving that lets models edit the blueprint dependency graph via ten local operations. Alongside BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 controlled failures with full repair trajectories, the paper shows typed repair matches free-form patch/rewrite interfaces in localized failure coverage while being the cheapest per solved state across two models.
AI.motivation: LLM-based Lean provers increasingly use blueprints (dependency graphs of formal statements) to organize proofs, but current interfaces lack a constrained, schema-checked way to repair these graphs. A repair interface that fixes the target theorem and lets Lean verify every change would make repairs safer and more efficient.
AI.method: Introduce BlueprintRepair, an interface with ten schema-checked local operations for editing the blueprint graph. Each operation names the node it edits (so the goal theorem is fixed) and Lean validates every change; accepted repairs must declare all blueprint lemmas used. Build BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 controlled failures with accepted and rejected repair trajectories. Compare typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites under matched source, feedback, model, and budget, running one episode per state and interface, with two models (DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.6-Flash).
AI.result: With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, all three interfaces solve nearly the same number of localized failures. Typed repair is the cheapest per solved state (patching costs 1.30x, rewriting 2.06x) and reaches almost all final coverage within 10,000 completion tokens, while free-form interfaces lag. With Qwen3.6-Flash, fewer states overall are solved, but typed repair remains cheapest, leads on proof-authoring states, and repeats the localized pattern.
AI.conclusion: Schema-checked typed repair is an efficient and effective interface for repairing blueprint-based Lean proofs: it matches free-form rewriting in coverage on localized failures while being significantly cheaper, and these advantages hold across multiple models.

title: Learning features from Newton's algorithm: a way to accelerate nonlinear parametrized PDE solvers
summary: It is well known that Newton's method converges faster when the initial guess is closer to a root of a system of nonlinear equations. In this paper, a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed by learning features from a parameter-space sampling and a database of precomputed solutions. The method uses discrete Newton trajectories to construct two complementary reduced spaces: a solution feature space, built from converged states, and a corrective search direction feature space, built from intermediate Newton increments. For an unseen parameter, a regression model is used to predict a surrogate solution approximation. Then, in a second step, a residual-minimizing correction is computed using a dedicated GMRES-based approach. The resulting state is then used as an initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method, which completes convergence. The corrective step is computationally inexpensive since it only requires residual evaluations and the solution of a small least-squares problem. The methodology is weakly intrusive once the high-fidelity residual fields and a script-based programming interface are available. This strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and decreases the overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization. Significant speedups are observed. This generic approach can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

AI.tldr: A two-stage Newton initial guess strategy that learns features from parameter-space sampling and precomputed solutions, combining a regression-predicted surrogate solution with a residual-minimizing GMRES-based correction to provide high-quality initial guesses for Newton's method, reducing iterations and CPU time.
AI.motivation: Newton's method convergence speed depends heavily on the quality of the initial guess. Poor initial guesses lead to many iterations or divergence, particularly for large-scale nonlinear systems. The authors aim to systematically construct better initial guesses from precomputed solution data rather than relying on ad-hoc heuristics.
AI.method: The approach builds two complementary reduced spaces from discrete Newton trajectories: (1) a solution feature space from converged states and (2) a corrective search direction feature space from intermediate Newton increments. For an unseen parameter, regression predicts a surrogate solution, then a residual-minimizing correction is computed via a GMRES-based method requiring only residual evaluations and a small least-squares solve. The corrected state serves as the initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared to standalone surrogate initialization, with significant reductions in Newton iterations and overall CPU time.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is weakly intrusive (requiring only residual fields and a script-based interface) and provides a generic, computationally inexpensive approach applicable to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

title: Explaining Image Similarity with Automatically Extracted Concept Activation Vectors
summary: Image similarity underlies many computer vision applications, yet it is often unclear why two images receive a high or low similarity score. Existing explainability methods often rely on gradient-based attribution maps to provide local justifications for similarity. These approaches struggle to provide global insights into what specifically drives similarity in regions of an embedding space, such as texture, shape, or color. We introduce a model- and metric-agnostic framework that explains image similarity using Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) extracted automatically via Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). Given a pair of images, we perturb their embeddings along discovered concept directions and measure the resulting change in a chosen similarity function, yielding concept importances. For image pairs, we provide localization with concept attribution maps. We extend this procedure to group-level settings, explaining what drives similarity across a cluster of images rather than a single pair, and further, we introduce Exemplar Retrieval, aiming to recover samples with similar reasons contributing to similarity. Our experiments show that our latent perturbations are more faithful to the underlying data distribution than pixel-space baselines, and that concept importances linearly recover the true similarity score. Qualitative results further confirm the usefulness of our methods in understanding a model's individual and group similarity judgments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a model- and metric-agnostic framework for explaining image similarity using Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) automatically extracted via Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). It perturbs embeddings along discovered concept directions and measures similarity change to yield concept importances, with extensions to localization maps, group-level analysis, and exemplar retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing explainability methods for image similarity rely on gradient-based attribution maps that only provide local justifications and struggle to give global insights into what drives similarity (e.g., texture, shape, color) in regions of an embedding space.
AI.method: A framework that extracts CAVs automatically via SAEs, perturbs image embeddings along discovered concept directions, and measures the resulting change in a chosen similarity function to compute concept importances. It provides concept attribution maps for localization, extends to group-level settings for cluster similarity explanations, and introduces Exemplar Retrieval to recover samples with similar reasons contributing to similarity.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that latent perturbations are more faithful to the underlying data distribution than pixel-space baselines, concept importances linearly recover the true similarity score, and qualitative results confirm usefulness for understanding individual and group similarity judgments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a faithful and interpretable way to explain image similarity both at the individual pair level and group level, with latent-space perturbation proving more aligned with the true data distribution than pixel-space alternatives.

title: ConMem: Contribution-Aware Memory for Long-Horizon Manufacturing Inspection Logs
summary: Long-horizon steel-equipment inspection requires reasoning over heterogeneous records accumulated across repeated inspection cycles. Existing retrieval-augmented generation systems treat historical logs as a static corpus and retain records without estimating their diagnostic value, failing to report early risk. To this end, we propose ConMem, a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted equipment inspection, supporting a human-in-the-loop early-risk screening system. Specifically, our ConMem first segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, then estimates each memory unit's contribution to downstream diagnosis through a Shapley-style estimation, and finally retains high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget. In experiments, we evaluate ConMem on real-world dataset and ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy, exceeding the strongest directly comparable baseline. Relative to the naive 8K-context LLM baselines, it reduces the average number of input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6%. Ablation studies also show that the functional-role-aware segmentation and contribution-based valuation are helping prioritize weak degradation signals for targeted field inspection. Practical deployments further confirm that ConMem retains the weak early signal across three inspection cycles, providing an early-stage seal-wear alert targeted for on-site inspectors.

AI.tldr: ConMem is a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted steel-equipment inspection that segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, estimates each unit's diagnostic contribution via Shapley-style valuation, and retains high-value evidence under a memory budget. It achieves 76.0% QA accuracy, reduces input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6% versus naive 8K-context LLM baselines, and successfully retains weak early degradation signals for targeted field inspection.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented generation systems treat historical inspection logs as a static corpus and retain records without estimating their diagnostic value, failing to report early risk in long-horizon steel-equipment inspection where heterogeneous records are accumulated across repeated inspection cycles.
AI.method: ConMem consists of three stages: (1) segmenting inspection logs into functional evidence units, (2) estimating each memory unit's contribution to downstream diagnosis via Shapley-style estimation, and (3) retaining high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget. It is integrated into a human-in-the-loop early-risk screening system.
AI.result: ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy on a real-world dataset, outperforming the strongest directly comparable baseline. It reduces average input token count by 88.2% and response time by 86.6% relative to naive 8K-context LLM baselines. Ablation studies show functional-role-aware segmentation and contribution-based valuation help prioritize weak degradation signals. Practical deployments confirm early-stage seal-wear alert retention across three inspection cycles.
AI.conclusion: ConMem demonstrates that contribution-aware memory management, rather than static retention, enables early-risk detection in long-horizon equipment inspection while dramatically reducing computational overhead and improving QA accuracy.

title: ClawTrack: Towards Trace-Level Evaluation and Improvement of Real-World Autonomous Agents
summary:
As LLM-based agents are deployed in complex, multi-step workflows, a critical evaluation gap has emerged: most existing benchmarks judge only final outcomes, unable to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies, hindering attribution in long-horizon tasks.
  In this work, we present ClawTrack, a dual-assessment benchmark that simultaneously measures what an agent achieves (Task Score) and how it achieves it (Process Score). ClawTrack comprises 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader scores each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification), anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. Evaluating 21 models over 16,000+ trials, we find that: (1) process scores effectively attribute success and failure to specific reasoning dimensions, filtering lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation; (2) the four dimensions are complementary, with result verification as the systematic bottleneck; (3) the framework is robust to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs; and (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.

AI.tldr: ClawTrack is a dual-assessment benchmark that evaluates LLM-based agents on both task outcomes (Task Score) and reasoning quality (Process Score) across 320 tasks in 8 domains, using a Process Grader that scores reasoning turns on four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, result verification) anchored by 12,541 rubric items, tested on 21 models over 16,000+ trials.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks only evaluate final outcomes, which cannot distinguish genuine reasoning from lucky success, nor attribute failures to specific process deficiencies in long-horizon, multi-step workflows. This creates a critical evaluation gap for LLM-based agents.
AI.method: ClawTrack comprises 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader evaluates each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, result verification) anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. The benchmark uses dual assessment: Task Score for what an agent achieves and Process Score for how it achieves it.
AI.result: Evaluation of 21 models over 16,000+ trials shows: (1) process scores attribute success/failure to specific reasoning dimensions and filter lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation; (2) the four dimensions are complementary with result verification as the systematic bottleneck; (3) the framework is robust to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs; (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.
AI.conclusion: ClawTrack addresses the evaluation gap in long-horizon agent workflows by providing process-level attribution of reasoning quality, demonstrating that process-based evaluation can filter lucky successes, identify systematic weaknesses (especially result verification), and support post-training improvements.

title: Hand-Object Interaction in the Age of Large Foundation Models:Reconstruction, Generation, and Embodied Transfer
summary: Hand-object interaction (HOI) modeling remains challenging because it requires joint reasoning about hand articulation, object geometry, contact, semantics, and dynamics under severe visual uncertainty. Foundation models introduce transferable prior knowledge learned from large-scale cross-domain data, offering new ways to address these challenges beyond task-specific data and models. However, the rapidly growing literature remains fragmented, and existing studies typically describe these methods simply as ``using large models'' without systematically characterizing what knowledge is introduced, where it enters the HOI pipeline, or which HOI uncertainty it helps reduce. This survey presents the first systematic review of foundation-model priors for HOI. We organize the literature into six HOI tasks spanning reconstruction and generation. More importantly, we establish a taxonomy of eight foundation-model sub-priors grouped into geometric, semantic, and visual families. Geometric priors encompass shape retrieval, shape reconstruction, and spatial reconstruction; semantic priors include semantic grounding and language reasoning; and visual priors cover visual representation, image generation, and video generation. Based on this taxonomy, we systematically analyze how different priors are represented, injected, and adapted across HOI pipelines and tasks. Beyond how foundation models empower HOI, we further examine how HOI-derived knowledge is used in robot learning, including human-data pretraining, human-to-robot skill transfer, and HOI-to-robot data generation. Finally, we summarize datasets and evaluation protocols, and discuss limitations and future directions toward more generalizable HOI systems. To support long-term progress, we curate a live repository that continuously aggregates emerging methods and benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic survey of foundation-model priors for hand-object interaction (HOI) modeling, organizing literature across six HOI tasks (reconstruction and generation) and introducing a taxonomy of eight foundation-model sub-priors grouped into geometric (shape retrieval, shape reconstruction, spatial reconstruction), semantic (semantic grounding, language reasoning), and visual (visual representation, image generation, video generation) families. It systematically analyzes how priors are represented, injected, and adapted across HOI pipelines, examines HOI-to-robot learning transfer, summarizes datasets and evaluation protocols, and maintains a live repository.
AI.motivation: HOI modeling is challenging due to joint reasoning about hand articulation, object geometry, contact, semantics, and dynamics under severe visual uncertainty. Although foundation models offer transferable prior knowledge to address these challenges, the rapidly growing literature remains fragmented and existing studies lack systematic characterization of what knowledge is introduced, where it enters the HOI pipeline, or which HOI uncertainty it reduces. This motivates a structured, comprehensive survey.
AI.method: The survey organizes the literature into six HOI tasks spanning reconstruction and generation, and establishes a taxonomy of eight foundation-model sub-priors across three families: geometric (shape retrieval, shape reconstruction, spatial reconstruction), semantic (semantic grounding, language reasoning), and visual (visual representation, image generation, video generation). It systematically analyzes prior representation, injection, and adaptation across HOI pipelines, and extends to robot learning applications including human-data pretraining, human-to-robot skill transfer, and HOI-to-robot data generation.
AI.result: The survey provides the first systematic taxonomy of foundation-model priors for HOI, categorizes existing methods across tasks and prior families, analyzes how priors are integrated into HOI pipelines, reviews their application in robot learning, and summarizes datasets and evaluation protocols for the field.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes by discussing limitations and future directions toward more generalizable HOI systems, and curates a live repository to continuously aggregate emerging methods and benchmarks for long-term progress in the field.

title: AgenticASR: Refining Speech Recognition in Real-World Scenarios via an Agentic Approach
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has achieved substantial gains in transcription accuracy, yet verbatim transcription does not necessarily produce readily usable text. It retains fillers, repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections that increase reading effort, obscure the speaker's final intent, and propagate unresolved or abandoned content to downstream tasks. Existing spoken-to-written methods process completed audio or transcripts but cannot revise emitted text when later speech changes how preceding content should be interpreted. We therefore formulate Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticSR), an audio-to-clean-text task that removes disfluencies, resolves self-corrections, and normalizes written form while preserving the speaker's final intent. AgenticASR implements this task through an ASR--Refiner architecture that repeatedly transforms a bounded active context and replaces its corresponding output span as audio arrives. This enables continual emission and revision over streams of arbitrary duration. We also introduce AASR-Bench, a bilingual benchmark with fine-grained atomic rubrics. Across multiple ASR front ends, AgenticASR attains the highest AASR-Bench scores among evaluated systems. A human--AI agreement study shows that rubric-based judgments align with independent expert assessments. Ablations characterize Refiner capacity, context length, and the quality--latency trade-off between online and offline inference. Together, these results establish AgenticASR as a practical framework for intent-preserving clean transcription during ongoing speech. Code, AASR-Bench, and a demo will be released at https://github.com/AnXMuy/AgenticASR.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticSR), a task to convert speech to clean text by removing disfluencies and resolving self-corrections while preserving the speaker's final intent. The proposed AgenticASR system uses an ASR–Refiner architecture that continuously revises emitted text as audio streams in, and is evaluated on AASR-Bench, a new bilingual benchmark with atomic rubrics.
AI.motivation: Verbatim ASR transcription retains fillers, repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections that increase reading effort, obscure speaker intent, and propagate unresolved content to downstream tasks. Existing spoken-to-written methods process completed audio/transcripts and cannot revise already-emitted text when later speech changes how earlier content should be interpreted.
AI.method: AgenticASR employs an ASR–Refiner architecture that repeatedly transforms a bounded active context and replaces the corresponding output span as new audio arrives, enabling continual emission and revision over streams of arbitrary duration. A new benchmark, AASR-Bench, is introduced with fine-grained atomic rubrics for evaluation.
AI.result: Across multiple ASR front ends, AgenticASR achieves the highest AASR-Bench scores among evaluated systems. A human–AI agreement study shows rubric-based judgments align with independent expert assessments. Ablations characterize Refiner capacity, context length, and the quality–latency trade-off between online and offline inference.
AI.conclusion: The results establish AgenticASR as a practical framework for intent-preserving clean transcription during ongoing speech.

title: GVR-Coder: A Visual-Feedback Framework for Structured SVG Generation in Complex Document and Meeting Scenarios
summary: In demanding professional environments and meeting review scenarios, lengthy text often imposes a high cognitive load. To facilitate efficient information communication, transforming verbose text into logically clear diagrams is essential. Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) provide an effective representation for this purpose due to their editability and resolution independence. However, current research on Text-to-SVG generation remains hindered by three major challenges: (1) the scarcity of datasets for complex, logic-rich diagrams; (2) the absence of explicit layout priors, which leads to chaotic spatial arrangements; and (3) the lack of fine-grained visual feedback to validate rendered outputs and correct aesthetic defects. To address these challenges, at the data level, we introduce DocMeetSVG-100K, a large-scale SVG dataset tailored for document authoring and meeting review scenarios. At the model level, we propose GVR-Coder, a novel framework designed to generate high-quality logical diagrams from lengthy professional texts. Specifically, we adopt a curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning to progressively enhance the model's capability in modeling complex structures, while explicitly incorporating layout constraint knowledge during training. In addition, we introduce reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, a mechanism that provides implicit feedback through reward signals to jointly optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics. Furthermore, we design a generate-verify-repair agent loop, which improves generation quality through explicit, fine-grained feedback and targeted refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines and reliably produces logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams. Code and data are available at https://github.com/CurryaNa/GVR-Coder.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DocMeetSVG-100K, a large-scale SVG dataset for document authoring and meeting review scenarios, and proposes GVR-Coder, a framework that generates high-quality logical diagrams from lengthy professional texts. GVR-Coder uses curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning, explicit layout constraint knowledge, reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, and a generate-verify-repair agent loop to overcome challenges in Text-to-SVG generation.
AI.motivation: Transforming verbose professional text into clear diagrams reduces cognitive load, and SVG is ideal for this due to editability and resolution independence. However, existing Text-to-SVG research suffers from scarce complex diagram datasets, absence of explicit layout priors causing chaotic spatial arrangements, and lack of fine-grained visual feedback for validating rendered outputs and correcting aesthetic defects.
AI.method: The proposed GVR-Coder framework includes: (1) DocMeetSVG-100K, a large-scale SVG dataset for document and meeting scenarios; (2) curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning to progressively enhance modeling of complex structures; (3) explicit incorporation of layout constraint knowledge during training; (4) reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback using reward signals to jointly optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics; and (5) a generate-verify-repair agent loop providing explicit fine-grained feedback and targeted refinement.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines and reliably produces logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams.
AI.conclusion: The combination of dataset construction, curriculum-based training, layout priors, dual rendering feedback reinforcement learning, and an iterative agent loop effectively addresses the three key challenges in Text-to-SVG generation, enabling high-quality logical diagram generation from lengthy professional texts.

title: Large scale cross-regional remote sensing flood monitoring framework for operative mapping and impact analysis
comment: 37 pages, 11 figures, 9 tables. Preprint submitted to Earth Systems and Environment. This version has not been peer reviewed
summary:
Effective flood monitoring is critical for minimizing the impacts of flood disasters on populations and infrastructure. Yet reliable remote sensing across extensive and environmentally diverse regions remains challenging, as most segmentation algorithms lack the generalisation capacity required for large-scale application, while annotated flood data are scarce and unevenly distributed.
  This study presents an end-to-end multimodal framework for Russian Federation territories sustainable flood monitoring and damage assessment based on synthetic aperture radar data, multispectral imagery, and digital elevation models with their derivatives, forming a 21-channel input. Using a self-collected multimodal dataset covering seven Russian regions, two strategies for water surface detection under limited data conditions were compared: a supervised U-Net++ model and the self-supervised AnySat architecture pre-trained and fine-tuned for the segmentation task. Under the data conditions of this study, supervised learning proved more effective, while the AnySat-based approach offered greater stability and retains advantages for settings where larger unlabelled data or missing modalities at inference are expected.
  The best flood area predictions were used to estimate flood impact in urban areas in terms of the area affected, material damage, casualties, and ecological and agricultural impact. The estimations were conducted following the official methodology of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations. Applied to the 2019 Tulun flood, the obtained results closely matched official assessments, except for material damage, due to the open-source databases usage. The results demonstrate the potential of deep learning and multimodal satellite data integration for scalable, reliable flood monitoring across diverse environmental and data-limited conditions.

AI.tldr: This study proposes an end-to-end multimodal framework for flood monitoring and damage assessment across Russian territories, integrating SAR, multispectral imagery, and DEM derivatives (21-channel input). Comparing supervised U-Net++ against self-supervised AnySat under data-limited conditions, supervised learning proved more effective, though AnySat offered greater stability. The framework's flood impact estimates (area affected, damage, casualties, ecological/agricultural impact) were validated against official 2019 Tulun flood assessments.
AI.motivation: Flood monitoring via remote sensing faces two major challenges: most segmentation algorithms lack generalization capacity for large-scale application across diverse environments, and annotated flood data are scarce and unevenly distributed—motivating a need for robust approaches that perform well under limited labeled data.
AI.method: An end-to-end multimodal framework is developed using a 21-channel input composed of SAR data, multispectral imagery, and DEMs with derivatives. A self-collected multimodal dataset covering seven Russian regions was used to compare two water surface detection strategies: a supervised U-Net++ and the self-supervised AnySat architecture (pre-trained and fine-tuned). Best flood predictions were then used to estimate urban flood impact following the official methodology of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations.
AI.result: Supervised U-Net++ outperformed the AnySat-based approach under the study's data conditions, while AnySat provided greater stability and advantages when larger unlabelled data or missing modalities at inference are expected. Applied to the 2019 Tulun flood, results closely matched official assessments except for material damage, attributed to open-source database usage.
AI.conclusion: The integration of deep learning with multimodal satellite data offers scalable, reliable flood monitoring across diverse environmental and data-limited conditions, demonstrating strong potential for real-world flood impact estimation aligned with official methodologies.

title: Chem World: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Physics-Informed Framework for Trustworthy Chemical Property Prediction
summary: Chemical property prediction plays a critical role in accelerating scientific discovery in chemistry, materials science, and drug development. However, existing benchmarks often suffer from limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, making it challenging to systematically assess the reliability and generalization of AI models. In this work, we introduce Chem World, a comprehensive benchmark for chemical property prediction that integrates 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples, covering various properties including density, electrical conductivity, solubility, and other molecular characteristics. Chem World provides a unified platform for evaluating AI models across multiple property prediction tasks. Furthermore, we propose Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network based prediction framework that incorporates chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning, improving the accuracy, robustness, and reliability of chemical property prediction. Extensive experiments on Chem World demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared with existing methods. By combining large-scale standardized evaluation with physics-informed learning, Chem World establishes a foundation for developing trustworthy AI systems for computational chemistry and advancing AI-driven scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Chem World, a comprehensive benchmark for chemical property prediction integrating 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples, and proposes Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network framework that incorporates chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach over existing methods, establishing a foundation for trustworthy AI systems in computational chemistry.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for chemical property prediction suffer from limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, making it difficult to systematically assess the reliability and generalization of AI models in chemistry.
AI.method: The paper introduces Chem World, a unified benchmark integrating 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples covering properties such as density, electrical conductivity, and solubility. Additionally, it proposes Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network framework that embeds chemical prior knowledge into data-driven prediction to enhance accuracy, robustness, and reliability.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the Chem World benchmark demonstrate that Mixture-PINN outperforms existing methods in chemical property prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: By combining large-scale standardized evaluation with physics-informed learning, Chem World establishes a foundation for developing trustworthy AI systems for computational chemistry and advancing AI-driven scientific discovery.

title: Negative controls reveal volume-driven confounding in radiomics and imaging foundation model features
comment: 22 pages (including supplementary), 6 figures, 2 supplementary tables, 5 supplementary figures
summary: Radiomics and imaging foundation models promise non-invasive biomarkers of tumour biology, yet predictive signatures may reflect tumour volume or acquisition artifacts rather than meaningful image structure. We introduce READII-2-ROQC, an open-source framework that uses volume-preserving negative controls to assess whether radiomic and deep imaging features capture independent spatial signals. READII-2-ROQC generates voxel-perturbed images across tumour, background and whole-image regions using configurable randomization strategies, then compares feature behaviour and model performance between original and control images. Applied to three public cancer imaging cohorts, the framework processed 3,552 tumour volumes and extracted PyRadiomics and foundation-model features from original images and nine matched controls. Reproducing published survival and HPV-status signatures, we show that multiple models retain performance after spatial structure is destroyed, revealing volume-driven or contextual confounding, whereas others show perturbation-sensitive signal. READII-2-ROQC provides a scalable quality-control strategy for developing interpretable, biologically grounded imaging biomarkers and reproducible radiomics workflows.

AI.tldr: READII-2-ROQC is an open-source framework that uses volume-preserving negative controls (voxel-perturbed images) to assess whether radiomic and deep imaging features capture independent spatial signals versus reflecting tumor volume or acquisition artifacts. Applied to three public cancer cohorts with 3,552 tumor volumes, it showed that many published survival and HPV-status signatures retain performance after spatial structure is destroyed, revealing volume-driven or contextual confounding.
AI.motivation: Predictive signatures in radiomics and imaging foundation models may reflect tumor volume or acquisition artifacts rather than meaningful biological image structure, undermining their validity as non-invasive biomarkers of tumor biology. A scalable quality-control framework is needed to distinguish signals genuinely derived from spatial image content from those driven by confounding factors.
AI.method: The framework generates volume-preserving voxel-perturbed negative control images across tumor, background, and whole-image regions using configurable randomization strategies. It then compares feature behavior and model performance between original and control images, extracting both PyRadiomics and foundation-model features from 3,552 tumor volumes across three public cancer cohorts, with nine matched controls per original image.
AI.result: Reproducing published survival and HPV-status signatures, the framework showed that multiple models retain performance after spatial structure is destroyed, revealing volume-driven or contextual confounding, while other models exhibited perturbation-sensitive signal that reflects genuine spatial image structure.
AI.conclusion: READII-2-ROQC provides a scalable quality-control strategy for developing interpretable, biologically grounded imaging biomarkers and reproducible radiomics workflows, helping the community identify and avoid confounded predictive models.

title: Qwen-UI-Agent Technical Report: Toward Next-Generation Real-World Centric Foundation GUI Agents
summary:
GUI agents have the potential to become a general purpose executor over existing digital devices. To advance them toward real-world use, we envision agents that operate reliably on real devices, execute workflows across platforms, combine GUI interaction with CLI execution, complete long-horizon tasks, proactively initiate useful services, and autonomously improve their capabilities with minimal human effort. Guided by this vision, we present Qwen-UI-Agent, a real-world centric foundation GUI agent spanning mobile, computer-use, web, and DeepSearch environments. Qwen-UI-Agent combines diverse sandbox environments with a large-scale real-device mobile runtime. Its unified action space interleaves GUI operations with CLI execution and generates batched actions in a single model turn. An AutoResearch-style data flywheel uses agents to construct tasks and environments, diagnose failures, and plan subsequent iterations. Online RL supports training on trajectories exceeding 100 turns, with over 10,000 concurrent environments accelerating rollout. A lightweight harness layer supports proactive service initiation and stateful workflows across mobile and computer.
  Across a broad suite of evaluations, Qwen-UI-Agent sets state-of-the-art performance on mobile-use benchmarks while delivering competitive performance on computer- and browser-use tasks against frontier models, including Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol. On mobile use, it achieves 82.1% on MobileWorld, 92.2% on MobileWorld-Real, and 97.5% on AndroidDaily. On computer use, it achieves 79.5% on OSWorld-Verified and a 40.0% partial-progress score on OSWorld-v2. On browser use and GUI grounding, it achieves 73.6% on WebArena and 81.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, respectively.

AI.tldr: Qwen-UI-Agent is a general-purpose GUI agent spanning mobile, computer-use, web, and DeepSearch environments. It combines diverse sandbox environments with real-device mobile runtime, unified action space interleaving GUI and CLI operations, batched actions, an AutoResearch-style data flywheel, and online RL with over 10,000 concurrent environments. It sets state-of-the-art results on mobile-use benchmarks (82.1% MobileWorld, 92.2% MobileWorld-Real, 97.5% AndroidDaily) while achieving competitive performance on computer-use (79.5% OSWorld-Verified), browser-use (73.6% WebArena), and GUI grounding (81.5% ScreenSpot-Pro) against frontier models.
AI.motivation: To advance GUI agents toward real-world use, the authors envision agents that operate reliably on real devices, execute workflows across platforms, combine GUI interaction with CLI execution, handle long-horizon tasks, proactively initiate services, and autonomously improve with minimal human effort. Existing agents fall short on these dimensions.
AI.method: Qwen-UI-Agent integrates: (1) diverse sandbox environments plus a large-scale real-device mobile runtime; (2) a unified action space that interleaves GUI operations with CLI execution and produces batched actions in a single model turn; (3) an AutoResearch-style data flywheel using agents for task/environment construction, failure diagnosis, and iterative planning; (4) online RL supporting training on trajectories exceeding 100 turns with over 10,000 concurrent environments; and (5) a lightweight harness layer supporting proactive service initiation and stateful workflows across mobile and computer.
AI.result: Qwen-UI-Agent achieves state-of-the-art performance on mobile-use benchmarks: 82.1% on MobileWorld, 92.2% on MobileWorld-Real, and 97.5% on AndroidDaily. It delivers 79.5% on OSWorld-Verified and 40.0% partial-progress on OSWorld-v2 for computer use, 73.6% on WebArena for browser use, and 81.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro for GUI grounding—competitive against frontier models including Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol.
