title: WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning
summary: Pruning is a promising approach for improving the efficiency of LLMs. Existing static structured pruning methods are hardware-friendly and can deliver practical throughput gains, but their input-agnostic computation allocation often causes substantial accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity. Recent dynamic sparsity methods improve quality retention by adapting computation to individual inputs, yet they remain largely limited to coarse-grained structural decisions and their practical acceleration under real-world inference scenarios remains challenging. To address these challenges, we present WIDE, the first end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework designed for both prefill and decode scenarios. WIDE enables fine-grained computation allocation by allowing each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, extending dynamic pruning beyond layer-level decisions to neuron-block-level granularity. Through a two-stage training pipeline, WIDE learns effective token-wise sparse execution patterns and achieves substantially better quality retention than existing approaches. To make such fine-grained dynamic pruning practical, we further propose a pruning--kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, enabling efficient execution across different granularities. At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides 55.1% performance boost when compared to the state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. Under prefill and decoding inference workloads, WIDE achieves close-to-theoretical kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, as well as 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LLM-Pruning/tree/main/WIDE.

AI.tldr: WIDE is the first end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework for LLMs, enabling fine-grained computation allocation where each token dynamically selects attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups. It uses a two-stage training pipeline and a pruning-kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, achieving substantial quality retention and practical speedups (up to 1.98x prefill, 4.95x decoding kernel-level; 1.68x/1.55x end-to-end at 50% sparsity).
AI.motivation: Existing static structured pruning methods are hardware-friendly but degrade accuracy under aggressive sparsity due to input-agnostic computation allocation. Dynamic sparsity methods improve accuracy retention but are limited to coarse-grained structural decisions (e.g., layer-level) and struggle to deliver practical acceleration in real-world inference scenarios.
AI.method: WIDE introduces an end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework for both prefill and decode scenarios. It allows each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, extending dynamic pruning to neuron-block-level granularity. A two-stage training pipeline learns effective token-wise sparse execution patterns. A pruning-kernel co-design framework decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into three components: mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, enabling efficient execution across different granularities.
AI.result: At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides a 55.1% performance boost over the state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. Under prefill and decoding inference workloads, WIDE achieves close-to-theoretical kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, as well as 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration respectively.
AI.conclusion: WIDE demonstrates that fine-grained, token-level dynamic width pruning can achieve both superior accuracy retention and practical, close-to-theoretical speedups across prefill and decode inference scenarios, making it a viable approach for efficient LLM deployment.

title: Chimera: Designing and Chinchilla-Scaling Hybrid Visual Diffusion Transformers
summary: Visual generation increasingly requires high-resolution images, long videos, and multimodal context, making the quadratic cost of full attention prohibitive. We introduce Chimera, a hybrid visual diffusion backbone with a principled scaling recipe. Chimera processes text, image, and video tokens in one raster-ordered stream without positional embeddings. It combines Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) for long-context state tracking with O(N) complexity, interleaved Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) for direct global interaction, and modality-aware short convolutions for local spatiotemporal context. Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers expand capacity while controlling activated compute. To scale this heterogeneous architecture, we introduce HeteroP, a module-wise scheme that transfers hyperparameters across width and depth according to each tensor's functional fan-in and model depth. HeteroP yields a consistently tuned family used to fit Chinchilla-style compute-optimal laws for activated model size, training-token count, and image-video data ratio. Guided by these laws, we train an 11B-parameter Chimera with 2B activated parameters. Experiments show three results. First, measured by pretraining diffusion loss, the dense backbone is 1.7x as compute-efficient as a matched full-attention Wan-2.1 2B baseline, while the complete system reaches 7.3x. Second, without length-specific fine-tuning, Chimera extrapolates zero-shot from 5-second training clips to 30-second videos, with only 6.5% FID degradation in the last five seconds. Third, the fitted laws show that compute-optimal image pretraining divides compute nearly evenly between activated model size and training-token count, whereas video pretraining modestly favors model size at higher budgets. These results establish a foundation for designing and scaling efficient long-context diffusion architectures.

AI.tldr: Chimera is a hybrid visual diffusion backbone combining Kimi Delta Attention for O(N) long-context tracking, interleaved Multi-head Latent Attention for global interaction, and modality-aware short convolutions, scaled via a module-wise hyperparameter transfer scheme (HeteroP) and Chinchilla-style compute-optimal laws, achieving an 11B-parameter model with 2B activated parameters that is 7.3x more compute-efficient than a matched Wan-2.1 2B baseline and zero-shot extrapolates from 5-second to 30-second videos.
AI.motivation: The quadratic cost of full attention becomes prohibitive as visual generation scales to high-resolution images, long videos, and multimodal context, motivating a need for a more efficient yet scalable attention architecture for visual diffusion models.
AI.method: Chimera combines (1) Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) for long-context state tracking with O(N) complexity, (2) interleaved Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) for global interaction, (3) modality-aware short convolutions for local spatiotemporal context, and (4) sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers for capacity expansion. It uses a single raster-ordered token stream without positional embeddings. Scaling is addressed via HeteroP, a module-wise hyperparameter transfer scheme, and Chinchilla-style compute-optimal laws fitted for activated model size, training-token count, and image-video data ratio.
AI.result: The dense Chimera backbone is 1.7x more compute-efficient than a matched full-attention Wan-2.1 2B baseline, and 7.3x for the complete system. It extrapolates zero-shot from 5-second to 30-second videos with only 6.5% FID degradation in the last five seconds. The fitted laws show compute-optimal image pretraining divides compute nearly evenly between model size and tokens, while video pretraining modestly favors model size at higher budgets.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a foundation for designing and scaling efficient long-context diffusion architectures, demonstrating that hybrid attention with principled scaling can achieve substantial compute savings while maintaining quality and enabling zero-shot long-video generation.

title: When Derived Measurements Mislead: Quantifying and Mitigating LLM Over-Trust with Privileged-Modality Reliability Evidence
comment: 25 pages, including references and supplementary material; 3 figures and 19 tables. Code: https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead
summary: Derived measurements increasingly enter large language model (LLM) pipelines as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity. We define derived-feature over-trust (DFOT) as the failure in which a downstream LLM assigns such a measurement the epistemic status of a direct fact or uses it outside its valid scope. Using physiological sensing as a case study, D1 tests acceptance of a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG, whereas D2 tests rejection of an offline-confirmed reliable PPG rhythm under misleading severe history. ECG supplies training supervision and offline reference construction but is never shown to the LLM. Five estimands quantify this chain: conflict over-trust rate (COTR) and context-induced error rate (CIR) characterize D1/D2; correct repair rate (CRR) measures frozen-error repair; evidence-specific repair margin (ESRM) contrasts matched and patient-disjoint shuffled evidence; and utility harm rate (UHR) measures unnecessary verification among HIGH-reliability cases used without verification at baseline. The framework does not depend on a particular reliability generator. We demonstrate it on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as an illustrative baseline and PPG-only inference. On a protocol-locked 187-patient test, the baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points, with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero; UHR increases by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7). DFOT provides a common evaluation target for stronger mitigation methods. The code is available at https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces derived-feature over-trust (DFOT), a framework for evaluating when LLMs inappropriately trust derived measurements (e.g., PPG-derived physiological signals) as if they were direct facts. Using physiological sensing as a case study, the authors define five estimands to quantify this failure mode and demonstrate their framework on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records, showing that a PPG-ECG privileged distillation baseline improves repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Derived measurements (e.g., sensor-derived physiological signals) are increasingly fed into LLM pipelines as if they were direct facts, despite the fact that their validity is instance-dependent and often requires external verification. This over-trust can lead to downstream errors. The authors aim to formalize and quantify this failure mode, which they call derived-feature over-trust (DFOT), to provide a common evaluation target for mitigation methods.
AI.method: The authors define DFOT and construct a physiological sensing testbed comprising two diagnostic tasks: D1 (testing acceptance of a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG) and D2 (testing rejection of an offline-confirmed reliable PPG rhythm under misleading severe history). ECG supplies training supervision and offline reference but is never shown to the LLM. Five estimands quantify the chain: COTR and CIR for D1/D2, CRR for frozen-error repair, ESRM for evidence contrast, and UHR for unnecessary verification. The framework is demonstrated on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as an illustrative baseline compared against PPG-only inference.
AI.result: On a protocol-locked 187-patient test, the ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points, with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero. UHR increases by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7), indicating a mild trade-off in unnecessary verification behavior.
AI.conclusion: DFOT provides a general, reliability-generator-agnostic evaluation framework for quantifying when LLMs over-trust derived measurements. The framework offers a common benchmark for developing and comparing stronger mitigation methods against derived-feature over-trust in LLM pipelines.

title: QAdapt: A Noise-Adaptive Neural Pre-Decoding Framework for Quantum Error Correction
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) relies on quantum error correction to suppress physical errors and preserve logical information at scale. In practice, however, performance is constrained not only by physical noise but also by the latency of classical decoders processing rapidly generated syndrome data. This challenge is exacerbated by hardware noise that is strong, heterogeneous, and nonstationary, as well as by the simulation-to-hardware distribution shift that can substantially degrade fixed neural decoders. We present QAdapt, a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction. QAdapt captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder. Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations for rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt consistently reduces the logical error rate relative to the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data, without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves reductions of up to 5.79 percent in logical error rate and 9.32 percent in backend decoding latency on the residual syndrome. These results demonstrate that QAdapt provides a practical and decoder-compatible approach to improving the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise.

AI.tldr: QAdapt is a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction that captures spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, adapts to evolving noise while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and reduces logical error rate and decoding latency across synthetic and real hardware noise scenarios.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing performance is limited not only by physical noise but also by the latency of classical decoders processing syndrome data, and this is exacerbated by strong, heterogeneous, nonstationary hardware noise and simulation-to-hardware distribution shift that degrades fixed neural decoders.
AI.method: QAdapt employs a neural pre-decoding framework that captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder.
AI.result: Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations for rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt consistently reduces logical error rate versus the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves up to 5.79% reduction in logical error rate and 9.32% reduction in backend decoding latency on residual syndrome.
AI.conclusion: QAdapt provides a practical and decoder-compatible approach to improving robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise.

title: PhiZero: A World Model Built Around Physical Language
summary: We introduce PhiZero, a physical world model built around physical language, a compact discrete representation of world-state transitions. Existing physical world models typically predict future videos directly in pixel space, leaving the underlying world dynamics implicit within high-dimensional visual predictors. Motivated by humans' ability to abstract predictive structure from visual experience and organize it in natural language for explicit reasoning, we learn physical language from in-the-wild videos through self-supervision and use it to explicitly reason about how the physical world evolves. Accordingly, PhiZero adopts a reason-then-render paradigm: it first infers future world evolution as a physical-language sequence and then renders the inferred transitions into videos. Extensive experiments across generation and understanding benchmarks validate the ability of PhiZero to model physically coherent world evolution. We further show its potential for realistic and interactive world modeling, fine-grained action-conditioned simulation, and zero-shot motion transfer.

AI.tldr: PhiZero is a physical world model that uses "physical language"—a compact discrete representation of world-state transitions—to explicitly reason about world evolution before rendering it into videos, following a reason-then-render paradigm.
AI.motivation: Existing physical world models predict future videos directly in pixel space, leaving world dynamics implicit inside high-dimensional visual predictors. The authors are motivated by humans' ability to abstract predictive structure from visual experience and organize it in natural language for explicit reasoning, prompting them to introduce an interpretable intermediate representation.
AI.method: PhiZero learns a compact discrete representation called "physical language" from in-the-wild videos via self-supervision. It then adopts a reason-then-render paradigm: first inferring future world evolution as a sequence in physical language, then rendering the inferred transitions into videos.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across generation and understanding benchmarks validate PhiZero's ability to model physically coherent world evolution. It also demonstrates capabilities in realistic and interactive world modeling, fine-grained action-conditioned simulation, and zero-shot motion transfer.
AI.conclusion: Representing world dynamics in a discrete, language-like intermediate space enables explicit reasoning about physical evolution and supports multiple downstream capabilities including interactive simulation and motion transfer, offering an alternative to purely pixel-space world models.

title: A foundation model of numerical intelligence with cross-disciplinary generalization
summary: Intelligence is commonly understood as the ability to acquire and apply knowledge, adapt to unfamiliar situations and solve new problems. Large language models exhibit this capacity by inferring task-relevant knowledge from textual context and applying it to new tasks. Yet intelligence need not be confined to language. For scientific and social systems, we need models that acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context-an ability we call numerical intelligence. Here we introduce UNified In-Context Operator Networks (UNICON), a foundation model that exhibits numerical intelligence across disciplines. Using graph-based examples from a system as context, UNICON infers the predictive relation shared across them and applies it to queries from the same system. Across scientific and social systems, including those from disciplines absent from training, the same model approaches specialist performance without retraining. Combining UNICON with language-model agents yields further gains, enabling it to surpass state-of-the-art specialists in a discipline unseen in training. We further show that training-corpus diversity improves generalization to unseen disciplines. Together, these results establish UNICON as a foundation model of numerical intelligence and position it as a building block for a broader ecosystem of artificial intelligence.

AI.tldr: Introduces UNICON, a foundation model for numerical intelligence that infers predictive relations from graph-based examples in numerical context and applies them to new queries across scientific and social systems, achieving specialist-level performance without retraining, including on disciplines unseen during training.
AI.motivation: Intelligence extends beyond language; scientific and social systems require models that can acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context. Current large language models excel at language-based reasoning but lack numerical intelligence—the ability to infer task-relevant knowledge from numerical context and apply it to new problems.
AI.method: UNICON uses graph-based examples from a system as in-context context to infer the predictive relation shared across them, then applies this relation to queries from the same system. It is a unified in-context operator network trained across disciplines, and can be combined with language-model agents for additional performance gains.
AI.result: UNICON approaches specialist-level performance without retraining across scientific and social systems, including disciplines absent from training. When combined with language-model agents, it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists in a discipline unseen during training. Training-corpus diversity improves generalization to unseen disciplines.
AI.conclusion: UNICON establishes itself as a foundation model of numerical intelligence, demonstrating that in-context learning can generalize across numerical domains, and positions itself as a building block for a broader ecosystem of artificial intelligence.

title: Kohn-Sham Spectral Embedding on Sparse Graphs at the Nishimori Temperature for Image Classification
comment: 42 pages, 10 figures, 5 tables, was presented at the 10th International Conference 'Deep Learning on Computational Physics (DLCP2026)', under review for the Moscow University Physics Bulletin, Physics series
summary: We introduce Kohn--Sham Spectral Embedding (KSSE), a physics-inspired energy-based model replacing dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding evaluated at the Nishimori temperature of an associated Random-Bond Ising Model. By mapping pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check graphs and constructing a regularized Laplacian acting as a Kohn--Sham Hamiltonian, we solve $D$ independent channel spectral problems in $\mathcal{O}(N\log N + k^2_{\text{mode}} N)$ time via FFT on circulant blocks (leveraging Pontryagin self-duality of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$) and low-order Rayleigh refinement. Graph topology is optimized using \emph{star-domain surgery}: rather than destroying information-carrying codewords by removing frustrated cycles, we construct edge shifts creating local convexity around codewords while bounding residual frustration to $ρ(B_γ)\leq 1+δ$. Multi-scale fractal analysis ($D_2$ spectrum) and fractal learning-rate landscape certifies a landscape transition from rough regimes ($D_2>3$) to star-domain basins ($D_2<1$), enabling Rayleigh refinement with $k_{\text{mode}}=5$ modes. We prove six theoretical results: a generalized Ihara--Bass identity linking belief propagation to the Laplacian; trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence; additive channel separability with an explicit exchange-correlation bound; a surgery theorem bounding frustration with attractor width $Ω(1/\sqrt{d_{\min}})$; a quasi-stationarity perturbation bound; and a fixed-point convergence theorem. In a transductive protocol on ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features ($D=1792$), KSSE achieves \textbf{88.93\%} Top-1 accuracy using $\approx 21.24$M parameters, outperforming Swin-L (197M, 86.4--87.3\%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0--89.5\%) under standard inductive setups, while reducing model footprint by $10\times$ and $30\times$, respectively.

AI.tldr: KSSE replaces dense CNN classifiers with a physics-inspired sparse-graph spectral embedding based on Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians and Random-Bond Ising Models, achieving 88.93% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1000 with ~21M parameters, outperforming Swin-L and matching ViT-H with 10-30x smaller model footprint.
AI.motivation: Dense CNN classifiers are parameter-heavy and computationally inefficient. The authors aim to replace them with a physics-inspired energy-based model that leverages spectral graph theory and statistical physics to achieve high accuracy with dramatically fewer parameters.
AI.method: KSSE maps pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic LDPC graphs, constructs a regularized Laplacian as a Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian, solves D independent channel spectral problems in O(N log N + k²_mode N) via FFT on circulant blocks (using Pontryagin self-duality of Z/pZ), uses star-domain surgery for graph topology optimization, employs multi-scale fractal analysis for landscape certification, and provides six theoretical results including a generalized Ihara-Bass identity, trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence, additive channel separability, a surgery theorem, a quasi-stationarity perturbation bound, and a fixed-point convergence theorem.
AI.result: On ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features (D=1792), KSSE achieves 88.93% Top-1 accuracy with ~21.24M parameters, outperforming Swin-L (197M, 86.4-87.3%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0-89.5%), while reducing model footprint by 10x and 30x respectively.
AI.conclusion: KSSE demonstrates that physics-inspired spectral embedding on sparse graphs can replace dense classifiers, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with orders of magnitude fewer parameters, supported by rigorous theoretical guarantees.

title: ACE-Data-0: Human-Centric Ambient Capture as Embodied Data Engine
summary: Embodied intelligence faces a fundamental data bottleneck. Models must capture how first-person perception, whole-body motion, dexterous manipulation, object state, sound, and touch evolve together as humans pursue goals over time. Existing datasets fragment this experience across viewpoints, modalities, or spatial scales, leaving the full perception-action loop only partially observed. We introduce the Ambient Capture Engine (ACE), a human-centric data engine that transforms real home environments into spatially calibrated, temporally synchronized recording studios. ACE operates at two complementary scales: a table-scale configuration resolves hand-object manipulation, while a room-scale configuration captures whole-body motion, locomotion, and interactions across a furnished home. ACE records egocentric and multi-view exocentric video, full-body and articulated hand motion, object geometry and 6-DoF trajectories, audio, and tactile signals as a unified multisensory stream. Using ACE, we build ACE-Data-0, comprising 150 hours and 17M video frames across 200 task categories, performed by 50 participants in 2 environments, for a total of 75,000 interaction episodes. The dataset spans atomic manipulation, long-horizon chains of household activities, and human-scene interaction, while preserving natural behavioral variation through goal-level rather than step-by-step instructions. We further introduce a hierarchical benchmark that progresses from signals to scene components and then to interactions. Evaluations of state-of-the-art methods expose substantial gaps under contact, occlusion, egomotion, and long temporal horizons. ACE-Data-0 provides synchronized human demonstrations with aligned perceptual, kinematic, and contact supervision, offering a scalable foundation for imitation learning, world models, vision-language-action systems, and embodied AI.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ACE (Ambient Capture Engine), a human-centric data engine that transforms real home environments into spatially calibrated, temporally synchronized recording studios for capturing embodied intelligence data. It produces ACE-Data-0, a large-scale multimodal dataset (150 hours, 17M frames, 75,000 episodes across 200 task categories) with aligned egocentric/exocentric video, full-body and hand motion, object geometry and trajectories, audio, and tactile signals. The work also presents a hierarchical benchmark and evaluations showing SOTA methods struggle under contact, occlusion, egomotion, and long temporal horizons.
AI.motivation: Embodied intelligence faces a fundamental data bottleneck: existing datasets fragment the full perception-action loop across viewpoints, modalities, or spatial scales. Models need to capture how first-person perception, whole-body motion, dexterous manipulation, object state, sound, and touch evolve together as humans pursue goals over time, but no existing dataset provides this unified multisensory stream.
AI.method: ACE operates at two complementary scales: a table-scale configuration for hand-object manipulation and a room-scale configuration for whole-body motion and interactions. It records egocentric and multi-view exocentric video, full-body and articulated hand motion, object geometry and 6-DoF trajectories, audio, and tactile signals as a unified stream. Using goal-level rather than step-by-step instructions to preserve natural behavioral variation, ACE builds ACE-Data-0 with 50 participants across 2 environments covering atomic manipulation, long-horizon household chains, and human-scene interaction.
AI.result: ACE-Data-0 comprises 150 hours, 17M video frames, 200 task categories, 50 participants, 2 environments, and 75,000 interaction episodes. A hierarchical benchmark progressing from signals to scene components to interactions reveals that state-of-the-art methods exhibit substantial performance gaps under contact, occlusion, egomotion, and long temporal horizons.
AI.conclusion: ACE-Data-0 provides synchronized human demonstrations with aligned perceptual, kinematic, and contact supervision, offering a scalable foundation for imitation learning, world models, vision-language-action systems, and embodied AI. The dataset addresses the data bottleneck by providing comprehensive multisensory coverage of the full perception-action loop in natural home environments.

title: Metaphor Tracer: A Theory-Informed Analysis of Hidden States
summary:
What do a language model's hidden states say about the organization of a single text? From one forward pass, without training, we score every token position on two properties. The *aggregator* measures whether the position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration. The *differentiator*, whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace as the model reads: metaphor in its root sense, transport. Constants were frozen on one discovery text; every other is confirmatory.
  The aggregator is not, in the classic sense, an information measure, nor a measure of salience. Across three unrelated models, as a signifier repeats, its surprisal and its attention drain while its aggregator score holds: the channel marks a token's place in the text. That this tracks a reading rests on independent ground truth: an engineered register the aggregator follows across its boundaries (6/6 cells), and a psychoanalyst's marking of clinical transcripts, fixed before the instrument existed, in 34/36 cells, with a graded increment above lexical controls and dissociations no type-level measure reproduces. A transfer test gives the result its shape: the model whose token structure travels with lexical type reads the singular discourse worst, and in a matched base/instruct pair tuning raises fidelity without moving type-transfer. Structural value is a property of a token's place in *this* text, not of its vector alone: a relational rather than essentialist reading of hidden states, operationalizing theory that predated the instrument.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two unsupervised scoring measures computed from a language model's hidden states in a single forward pass: the "aggregator" (whether a token position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration) and the "differentiator" (whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace during reading). Without any training, these scores operationalize a relational rather than essentialist reading of hidden states, marking a token's structural place in a specific text rather than its semantic type.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks to answer what a language model's hidden states reveal about the organization of a single text, and to establish a measure of structural value for token positions that is distinct from classic information measures (surprisal) or salience (attention), grounded in independent ground truth.
AI.method: Using one frozen forward pass and no training, every token position is scored on two properties: the aggregator (text consolidation) and the differentiator (transient carriage of other tokens into its subspace). Validation uses three unrelated models, an engineered register with known boundaries (6/6 cells), and a pre-existing psychoanalyst's marking of clinical transcripts (34/36 cells), plus a base/instruct transfer test comparing pairs.
AI.result: As a signifier repeats, surprisal and attention drain while the aggregator score holds constant across three models, indicating it tracks a token's place in the text rather than its frequency or salience. The aggregator follows an engineered register across boundaries (6/6 cells) and matches psychoanalytic marking of clinical transcripts (34/36 cells) with graded increments above lexical controls that no type-level measure reproduces. In a base/instruct pair, instruct tuning raises fidelity while leaving type-transfer unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Structural value is a property of a token's position in a particular text, not of its vector alone. The aggregator and differentiator operationalize a relational reading of hidden states, translating pre-existing theory into a computable instrument that tracks discourse structure independently of lexical statistics.

title: Oracle-Budgeted Molecular Optimization with Short-Term Graph Memory
summary: Molecular optimization is commonly performed under a limited oracle budget, which makes deciding what to evaluate as important as deciding what to generate. We introduce short-term graph memory, a plug-in module that preserves the generator architecture and native update rule while learning from previously evaluated molecules to prioritize subsequent oracle queries. The module maintains an online graph neural surrogate that pre-screens each round's candidate pool, so the fixed oracle budget is spent on molecules with higher predicted utility. Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard molecular optimization benchmark, it improves the mean top-10 score at no extra oracle cost and never falls behind the base on any oracle; the gain extends to all four generators we tested at a tight budget of one thousand calls. We then analyze how surrogate-guided selection interacts with the exploration and exploitation behavior of different generators. Its benefit at larger budgets is consistent with two properties of the backbone: how broadly it searches, and how effectively its native search already exploits oracle feedback. We provide a simple way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively, and evidence on which generators benefit from it.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces short-term graph memory (STGM), a plug-in module that learns from previously evaluated molecules to pre-screen candidates and prioritize oracle queries under limited budgets. It improves the mean top-10 score across multiple fragment-based generators at no extra oracle cost, with benefits depending on the backbone's exploration breadth and native exploitation efficiency.
AI.motivation: Molecular optimization is often constrained by a limited oracle budget, making the choice of what to evaluate as important as what to generate. Existing generators focus on proposal quality but do not optimally allocate the scarce oracle evaluation budget among candidates.
AI.method: The paper proposes short-term graph memory (STGM), a plug-in module that preserves the generator's architecture and native update rule while maintaining an online graph neural surrogate. The surrogate pre-screens each round's candidate pool so that the fixed oracle budget is spent on molecules with higher predicted utility.
AI.result: Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard benchmark, STGM improves mean top-10 scores at no extra oracle cost and never underperforms the base across oracles. Gains extend to all four tested generators at a tight budget of one thousand calls. Benefits at larger budgets correlate with two backbone properties: search breadth and the effectiveness of native oracle-feedback exploitation.
AI.conclusion: STGM provides a simple, architecture-agnostic way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively, and the analysis offers evidence on which generators benefit most from surrogate-guided selection.

title: ReToken: One Token to Improve Vision-Language Models for Visual Retrieval
summary: Long visual context poses a challenge for vision-language models: performance degrades as the number of distractors grows, and processing all tokens at once is computationally infeasible under GPU memory constraints. We present ReToken, a single learnable embedding trained as an explicit retrieval target that selects a sparse set of query-relevant visual tokens from a pre-filled visual KV cache. Trained on only a small image-QA dataset, ReToken yields consistent gains across image and video benchmarks: on Visual Haystacks it improves Qwen3VL-8B by 13.4 points and InternVL3.5 by 12.4 points (>20% relative), and on LVBench it transfers zero-shot to long video for an 8.0-point gain with Qwen3VL-8B. Thanks to its lightweight design, both training and long-video inference fit on a single H100. Code is available at: https://github.com/avaxiao/ReToken

AI.tldr: ReToken is a single learnable embedding that acts as an explicit retrieval target to select a sparse set of query-relevant visual tokens from a pre-filled visual KV cache, improving vision-language model performance on long visual context tasks while reducing computational cost.
AI.motivation: Long visual context degrades vision-language model performance as the number of distractors grows, and processing all tokens simultaneously is computationally infeasible under GPU memory constraints.
AI.method: ReToken is a single learnable embedding trained as an explicit retrieval target that selects a sparse set of query-relevant visual tokens from a pre-filled visual KV cache. It is trained on a small image-QA dataset.
AI.result: On Visual Haystacks, ReToken improves Qwen3VL-8B by 13.4 points and InternVL3.5 by 12.4 points (>20% relative), and on LVBench it transfers zero-shot to long video for an 8.0-point gain with Qwen3VL-8B. Both training and long-video inference fit on a single H100.
AI.conclusion: ReToken provides consistent gains across image and video benchmarks with a lightweight design that enables feasible training and long-video inference on a single GPU, demonstrating effective sparse visual token selection for long-context vision-language models.

title: SVR: Self-Verifying Refinement via Joint Verdict-Confidence Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Test-Time Compute
summary: Scaling test-time computation can improve language-model reasoning, but uniform budgets waste computation on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback. We introduce Self-Verifying Refinement (SVR), an oracle-free multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that learns to use self-verification as a compute-control policy. At each turn, the model produces a solution together with a discrete correctness verdict and a confidence score; it retains the current answer only when the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold, and otherwise continues refinement using its own self-verification. Ground-truth correctness is used only to construct training rewards and is never exposed to the policy through refinement prompts or required at inference. SVR is trained with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories using rewards that promote solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states; adaptive stopping is activated only at inference. On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 with only 2.99 inference turns on average. In the evaluated complete-system comparison, it exceeds standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference while requiring substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference. These results demonstrate that learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation.

AI.tldr: SVR is an oracle-free multi-turn RL framework where a model learns to use self-verification (discrete correctness verdicts + confidence scores) as an adaptive compute-control policy for test-time reasoning. It achieves 0.563 macro-average accuracy on seven math benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B using only ~3 inference turns on average, outperforming standard GRPO and strong baselines while using far fewer turns than fixed-budget inference.
AI.motivation: Scaling test-time computation improves reasoning but uniform budgets are wasteful on easy inputs, and verifier-guided refinement depends on external feedback which is not always available. The paper aims to replace external verifiers with learned internal self-verification signals for adaptive compute allocation.
AI.method: SVR trains a model with GRPO on fixed-horizon multi-turn trajectories. At each turn, the model outputs a solution, a discrete correctness verdict, and a confidence score. The answer is retained only if the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold; otherwise, refinement continues using self-verification. Ground-truth correctness is used solely to build training rewards (for solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states) and is never exposed to the policy at inference. Adaptive stopping is activated only at test time.
AI.result: On seven math benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves 0.563 macro-average accuracy with only 2.99 mean inference turns. In complete-system comparison, it surpasses standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference while needing substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference.
AI.conclusion: Learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation, eliminating the need for external verifiers or fixed budgets.

title: Cybersecurity Detection Classification with Reasoning-enabled Language Models
summary: A major issue in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) is alert fatigue, as the number of detections reported is more than staff can triage in a given day. Prior work prompts or fine-tunes large language models (LLMs) to emit a triage label directly, but does not train them to reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat. We train a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections by combining automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. We find that CoT reasoning also degrades the label-token probabilities that automated triage relies on, so we separately train a calibrator that reads the full reasoning trace and estimates the probability that the verdict is correct. Our system reaches 82.6% test accuracy and, at the high-confidence operating point that governs automated triage, improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. We further show that the trained calibrator is necessary - an untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero - and that a finetuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models, motivating targeted training over scale.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier for Windows endpoint detections in SOCs, trained via automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. A separately trained calibrator estimates verdict correctness from the full reasoning trace, achieving 82.6% test accuracy and improving benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over direct-label LLM classifiers at high-confidence operating points.
AI.motivation: Alert fatigue in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) arises because detection volumes exceed staff triage capacity. Prior LLM-based triage approaches emit labels directly without training models to reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat, limiting reliability.
AI.method: The system trains a CoT reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections using a combination of automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Since CoT reasoning degrades label-token probabilities relied upon by automated triage, a separate calibrator is trained to read the full reasoning trace and estimate the probability that the verdict is correct.
AI.result: The system achieves 82.6% test accuracy. At the high-confidence operating point used for automated triage, it improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. A finetuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models, demonstrating the value of targeted training over brute-force scale.
AI.conclusion: A trained calibrator is necessary for reliable confidence estimation—an untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero. The results support targeted fine-tuning of moderately sized models with specialized training pipelines over relying on larger frontier models for security triage tasks.

title: LeanCSP: A Framework for Certifying Constraint Reformulation and Solving in Lean
summary: Constraint programming is a core technology for solving complex combinatorial problems in scheduling, planning, configuration, and verification. Trusting its results therefore demands guarantees at two levels: that reformulations applied beforehand are semantics-preserving, and that solvers produce correct answers. In this work, we introduce a framework that addresses both verification levels in the Lean theorem prover: it can be used to prove formulation-level properties, such as equivalence, equisatisfiability, and the correctness of symmetry-breaking constraints, parametrically for entire problem families; and to check solver-produced certificates for individual instances via translation backends to external formats such as MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB. Combining both levels yields an end-to-end workflow that establishes the satisfiability or unsatisfiability of a constraint problem without trusting the external solver. Experimental results show that our framework's verified symmetry breaking also pays off in practice: a single parametric proof per problem family, reused across all instance sizes, reduces solver search effort by a factor of up to 2x10^7, while the entire in-Lean certification stays affordable, taking at most a few minutes for our largest instances.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework in the Lean theorem prover that provides end-to-end verification for constraint programming across two levels: (1) proving formulation-level properties (equivalence, equisatisfiability, symmetry-breaking correctness) parametrically for entire problem families, and (2) checking solver-produced certificates for individual instances via translation backends to MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB. This yields a trustless workflow establishing satisfiability/unsatisfiability without relying on external solvers, with verified symmetry breaking reducing search effort by up to 2×10^7.
AI.motivation: Constraint programming is a core technology for complex combinatorial problems, yet trusting its results requires guarantees at two levels: that reformulations are semantics-preserving and that solvers produce correct answers. Existing approaches lack verification at both levels simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors build a framework in the Lean theorem prover that (1) verifies formulation-level properties such as equivalence, equisatisfiability, and correctness of symmetry-breaking constraints, parametrically for entire problem families, and (2) checks solver-produced certificates for individual instances through translation backends to external formats including MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB.
AI.result: Combining both verification levels yields an end-to-end workflow establishing satisfiability or unsatisfiability of a constraint problem without trusting external solvers. Experiments show verified symmetry breaking reduces solver search effort by up to a factor of 2×10^7, and in-Lean certification remains affordable (at most a few minutes for the largest instances).
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates that full end-to-end trust in constraint programming results is achievable in a theorem prover, with parametric proofs reused across instance sizes providing both correctness guarantees and significant practical performance gains through verified symmetry breaking.

title: Stage-Replay Divergence Follows the KV Cache: Fixed-Prefix Precision Controls and Bidirectional Cache Transplantation
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Reproducibility artifacts (frozen manifests, token IDs, per-item scores, analysis harnesses) described in Section 3.9
summary: Stage-replay diagnostics reconstruct intermediate token prefixes and treat fresh-prefill continuation as continuation from the decoder state that originally reached the prefix. We audit that assumption at a whole reasoning-stage boundary in a Qwen2.5-derived system. A matched 200-item experiment compares retained live cache with one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens and places an exact replica on both sides. In BF16, replicas remain exact while the constructions differ on 166 suffixes and 20 correctness labels; the accuracy difference is only one point (paired 95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). A fixed-prefix 2x2 holds all 200 token states constant while crossing construction and precision. The BF16 disagreements recur, whereas FP32 produces no decoded disagreement (95% Wilson upper bound 1.88%). A prospective bridge makes token-by-token incremental and retained live caches bit-exact on 12/12 rows; an all-200 saved-ledger audit reproduces every retained trajectory and comparison fingerprint. Bidirectional transplantation of all 48 key/value layers makes every tested divergent continuation follow its cache donor, both on a selected set at the primary checkpoint (24/24) and an outcome-blind replication at a later checkpoint (43/43). Exact-token replay can therefore be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity. On the tested states, boundary K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of the divergent trajectory, while numerical precision moderates its behavioral expression.

AI.tldr: The paper audits whether "stage-replay diagnostics" (reconstructing intermediate token prefixes and treating fresh-prefill continuation as if continuing from the original decoder state) hold at a reasoning-stage boundary in a Qwen2.5-derived system. Through matched 200-item experiments comparing retained live cache vs. one-shot prefill, the authors show BF16 replicas can disagree on suffixes and labels (though accuracy differs by only one point), FP32 eliminates decoded disagreements, and bidirectional transplantation of all K/V layers makes divergent continuations follow their cache donor. They conclude that exact-token replay can be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity, and that boundary K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of divergent trajectories while numerical precision moderates behavioral expression.
AI.motivation: To audit the core assumption underlying stage-replay diagnostics—that reconstructing intermediate token prefixes and doing fresh-prefill continuation is equivalent to continuing from the original decoder state that reached that prefix. This is important because if the assumption fails, replay-based diagnostics may misattribute behaviors to token sequences rather than decoder state.
AI.method: A matched 200-item experiment compares retained live cache against one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens, placing an exact replica on both sides. Experiments include: (1) BF16 comparisons measuring suffix and correctness-label divergence; (2) a fixed-prefix 2x2 crossing construction and precision holding all 200 token states constant; (3) a prospective bridge making incremental and retained caches bit-exact; (4) an all-200 saved-ledger audit; and (5) bidirectional transplantation of all 48 key/value layers to test causal sufficiency of cache states, conducted at two checkpoints including an outcome-blind replication.
AI.result: In BF16, replicas remain exact in token content while constructions differ on 166 suffixes and 20 correctness labels, with only a one-point accuracy difference (paired 95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). FP32 produces no decoded disagreement (95% Wilson upper bound 1.88%). The bridge makes 12/12 rows bit-exact, and the saved-ledger audit reproduces all retained trajectories and fingerprints. Bidirectional transplantation makes divergent continuations follow their cache donor in 24/24 cases at the primary checkpoint and 43/43 in an outcome-blind replication.
AI.conclusion: Exact-token replay can be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity. On the tested states, boundary K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of divergent trajectories, while numerical precision (BF16 vs FP32) moderates the behavioral expression of those differences. FP32 eliminates decoded disagreement, suggesting the replay-fidelity assumption is precision-dependent.

title: A report-grounded vision-language foundation model for colonoscopy from 280000 routine reports
summary: Vision-language models remain underused in colonoscopy despite the rich expert descriptions recorded in routine reports. These reports document lesion appearance, size and location but summarise entire procedures rather than caption individual frames, leaving clinical findings only weakly linked to the corresponding images. Here we develop EndoCLIP, a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs progressively recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records. Across lesion-level image-text retrieval, structured report generation and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks, EndoCLIP outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings. On benign-versus-malignant classification, its linear probe approaches the performance of expert readers in a blinded study involving 12 endoscopists. These results suggest that recovering finding-to-frame correspondence can transform routine documentation into scalable supervision, enabling clinical targets to be specified in language rather than separately annotated for each task.

AI.tldr: EndoCLIP is a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy reports. It outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders in zero-shot and linear-probe settings across lesion-level retrieval, structured report generation, and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks, with its benign-versus-malignant linear probe approaching expert reader performance in a blinded study of 12 endoscopists.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models are underused in colonoscopy because routine reports summarize entire procedures rather than caption individual frames, leaving clinical findings only weakly linked to corresponding images and forcing task-specific annotation for each clinical target.
AI.method: The authors develop EndoCLIP, a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs progressively recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records. This recovers finding-to-frame correspondence from routine documentation to create scalable supervision.
AI.result: EndoCLIP outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders in zero-shot and linear-probe settings across lesion-level image-text retrieval, structured report generation, and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks. Its linear probe on benign-versus-malignant classification approaches expert reader performance in a blinded study involving 12 endoscopists.
AI.conclusion: Recovering finding-to-frame correspondence can transform routine documentation into scalable supervision, enabling clinical targets to be specified in language rather than separately annotated for each task.

title: The Role of Causality in Algorithmic Recourse
summary:
Algorithmic recourse aims to provide individuals with actionable changes to improve their predicted outcomes in high-stakes classification settings, such as loan and mortgage applications. However, most existing approaches focus only on flipping a model's prediction, without accounting for whether the recommended changes lead to genuine improvement in an individual's true qualifications or merely enable strategic gaming of the classifier. Consequently, deployed recourse policies can induce behavioral responses that degrade predictive accuracy and become ineffective after model retraining.
  In this work, we formalize this failure mode through a causal performative framework for recourse. We model how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model, capturing interactions among features as well as their effect on the true label. These causal responses induce a non-convex optimization problem, even under standard convex losses. We characterize conditions under which performatively stable solutions exist and can be efficiently computed via simple iterative dynamics. Our analysis reveals that recourse policies that ignore causal structure can induce large, misaligned behavioral responses, whereas causal recourse leads to stable equilibria that reduce incentives for gaming. Experiments on both semi-synthetic and real credit datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization while reducing the need for repeated model retraining to accommodate distribution shifts caused by strategic agent behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes algorithmic recourse through a causal performative framework, showing that standard recourse policies ignoring causal structure can induce gaming and degrade predictive accuracy, while causal recourse achieves performatively stable equilibria that reduce gaming incentives and outperform empirical risk minimization on credit datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing algorithmic recourse approaches only flip model predictions without accounting for whether changes genuinely improve an individual's qualifications or merely enable strategic gaming. This causes deployed recourse policies to induce behavioral responses that degrade predictive accuracy and become ineffective after model retraining.
AI.method: The authors introduce a causal performative framework that models how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model, capturing feature interactions and their effect on the true label. They characterize conditions for performatively stable solutions and efficient computation via iterative dynamics, comparing causal recourse against standard empirical risk minimization.
AI.result: Recourse policies that ignore causal structure induce large, misaligned behavioral responses, whereas causal recourse leads to stable equilibria that reduce gaming incentives. Experiments on semi-synthetic and real credit datasets show the approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization while reducing the need for repeated model retraining.
AI.conclusion: Causal recourse provides a principled solution to the performative failure mode in algorithmic recourse by aligning agent behavior with genuine improvement, achieving stability and better predictive performance than methods that neglect causal structure.

title: Towards Autonomous Aircraft Surveillance from Nanosatellites through On-Board Inference and Generative Data Augmentation
summary: Airborne surveillance from low Earth orbit is hindered by two interconnected bottlenecks: nanosatellites have a limited downlink budget, yet the conventional approach still transmits terabytes of raw imagery to the ground for processing, and open satellite datasets for aircraft are scarce and severely class-imbalanced. These limitations either delay timely decision-making or prevent standard detectors from learning robust representations of rare aircraft classes. In this paper, a workflow that combines on-board inference with generative data augmentation is proposed to address both limitations jointly. Inference is executed on a 6U CubeSat equipped with a low-power edge tensor accelerator, while a diffusion model fine-tuned through low-rank adaptation generates synthetic minority-class imagery. This synthetic output is automatically annotated, pseudo-labelled, by an intermediate detector and merged with classically augmented samples. The results show that the balanced dataset increases global mean average precision from 77.9% to 82.2%, with the minority class rising from F1=0.683 to F1=0.811, and that the quantised detector fits the on-chip memory and projects 25-30 frames per second on orbit. This approach contrasts with the conventional bent-pipe architecture, in which the satellite acts as a passive data collector. Therefore, the computational tests support the proposed workflow as a decision-support tool for real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a workflow combining on-board inference on a 6U CubeSat with a low-power edge tensor accelerator and generative data augmentation via a diffusion model fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation to address the dual bottlenecks of limited downlink budgets and class-imbalanced satellite aircraft datasets. The balanced dataset improves global mAP from 77.9% to 82.2% and minority-class F1 from 0.683 to 0.811, while the quantised detector fits on-chip memory and achieves 25-30 FPS on orbit.
AI.motivation: Airborne surveillance from LEO is hindered by two interconnected bottlenecks: nanosatellites have limited downlink budgets but conventional approaches still transmit terabytes of raw imagery to ground, and open satellite datasets for aircraft are scarce and severely class-imbalanced. These limitations delay timely decision-making and prevent standard detectors from learning robust representations of rare aircraft classes.
AI.method: The proposed workflow combines on-board inference executed on a 6U CubeSat equipped with a low-power edge tensor accelerator with generative data augmentation. A diffusion model fine-tuned through low-rank adaptation generates synthetic minority-class imagery, which is automatically pseudo-labelled by an intermediate detector and merged with classically augmented samples to create a balanced dataset.
AI.result: The balanced dataset increases global mean average precision from 77.9% to 82.2%, with the minority class rising from F1=0.683 to F1=0.811. The quantised detector fits on-chip memory and projects 25-30 frames per second on orbit.
AI.conclusion: The computational tests support the proposed workflow as a decision-support tool for real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites, contrasting with the conventional bent-pipe architecture where the satellite acts as a passive data collector.

title: Same Graph Cross-Task Transfer in GNNs: Protocols and Predictors
summary: Many real-world graphs support multiple predictive tasks over the same underlying structure, creating an opportunity to reuse supervision across node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP). However, existing evaluations often rely on incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and negative sampling rules, making conclusions about same-graph cross-task transfer unreliable. We formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and propose a leakage-free protocol that fixes node and edge splits, uses a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and employs fixed negatives for LP. Across three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS), we find that transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC $\to$ LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP $\to$ NC is fragile and can even degrade accuracy under naive representation reuse. LP $\to$ NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated, suggesting that LP acts as structural pretraining. Finally, we introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility when a shared encoder must serve both tasks, and show that simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes same-graph node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP) transfer, proposing a leakage-free evaluation protocol with fixed splits, a shared message-passing graph, and fixed LP negatives. Across GCN, GraphSAGE, and GPS backbones, NC→LP transfer is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP→NC is fragile and only reliably positive in a structure-dominant regime. The authors introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility and show that graph statistics like homophily can guide mechanism selection to avoid negative transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of cross-task transfer between NC and LP on the same graph use incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and inconsistent negative sampling, making prior conclusions unreliable. A standardized, leakage-free protocol is needed to rigorously assess when and how supervision can be shared across these tasks.
AI.method: The authors formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and design a leakage-free protocol that (1) fixes node and edge splits, (2) uses a shared message-passing graph excluding evaluated edges, and (3) employs fixed negatives for LP. They evaluate three backbone architectures (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS) and introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to quantify joint NC+LP encoder utility, guided by simple dataset statistics such as homophily.
AI.result: Transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC→LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, whereas LP→NC is fragile and can degrade accuracy under naive representation reuse. LP→NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated. CTS and homophily-based statistics effectively guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.
AI.conclusion: Same-graph NC-LP transfer is directionally asymmetric, with NC as a reliable knowledge source for LP on homophilic graphs, while LP serves as useful structural pretraining for NC only under specific regime conditions. The proposed protocol and CTS provide a principled framework for evaluating and deploying multi-task encoders on shared graph structures.

title: A Fuzzy Rule-based Neuro-Symbolic Approach for Pipe Severity Prediction in Sewer Networks
summary:
Standard automated sewer pipe severity assessment relies on direct image classification, creating a "black box" where the link between visual defects and final severity scores remains implicit. This study introduces a modular, fuzzy rule-based neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by decoupling neural perception from symbolic reasoning. The perception module utilizes a Swin Transformer to predict 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees directly from images. For reasoning, a DT, specifically Weka's J48, algorithm is trained on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, and its paths are converted into 19 fixed IF--THEN rules. Inference operates via fuzzy logic: t-norm activations from CODE conditions are weighted by rule confidence and combined with corresponding s-norms to produce interpretable class evidence. We assessed Product, Łukasiewicz, and Hamacher operator pairs using a dataset of 3,244 images spanning five highly imbalanced severity classes. Ground-truth labels were robustly generated via consensus from five independent large language models analyzing original inspector notes. Our results show an improvement of accuracy, balanced accuracy, Macro F1 and MCC by 17.9%, 12.2%, 23.0%, and 17.3%, respectively, over image-only based classification.
  Overall, the framework combines competitive class-balanced performance with traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees to rule supports and severity evidence.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fuzzy rule-based neuro-symbolic framework for automated sewer pipe severity assessment that decouples neural perception (Swin Transformer predicting 14 multilabel CODE degrees) from symbolic reasoning (19 IF-THEN rules extracted from a J48 decision tree trained on ground-truth CODEs). Inference uses fuzzy logic with t-norm/s-norm operator pairs (Product, Łukasiewicz, Hamacher), evaluated on 3,244 images across five imbalanced severity classes, outperforming image-only classification by 17.9% accuracy, 12.2% balanced accuracy, 23.0% Macro F1, and 17.3% MCC.
AI.motivation: Traditional automated sewer pipe severity assessment is a "black box" that classifies images directly without an explicit, traceable link between visual defects and final severity scores. The authors aim to bridge this interpretability gap by introducing a modular framework that separates neural perception from symbolic reasoning, making the decision process transparent and verifiable.
AI.method: The framework has two decoupled modules: (1) a perception module using a Swin Transformer to predict 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees directly from images; (2) a reasoning module where Weka's J48 decision tree is trained on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, and its paths are converted into 19 fixed IF-THEN rules. Fuzzy logic inference applies t-norm activations from CODE conditions weighted by rule confidence, combined via s-norms to produce interpretable class evidence. Three fuzzy operator pairs (Product, Łukasiewicz, Hamacher) are evaluated. Ground-truth severity labels are generated via consensus from five independent large language models analyzing original inspector notes across 3,244 images spanning five imbalanced severity classes.
AI.result: The framework improves accuracy, balanced accuracy, Macro F1, and MCC by 17.9%, 12.2%, 23.0%, and 17.3%, respectively, compared to image-only based classification. The system delivers competitive class-balanced performance while providing traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees through rule supports to final severity evidence.
AI.conclusion: The proposed modular neuro-symbolic framework achieves both competitive performance on imbalanced severity classification and interpretability, offering a principled path from low-level visual defect predictions to high-level severity decisions via transparent fuzzy IF-THEN rules, thereby overcoming the black-box limitation of direct image classification.

title: APO: Unsupervised Atomic Policy Optimization for 3D Structure Prediction of Atomic Systems
summary: Predicting the 3D structures of atomic systems is fundamental to advancing material science and drug discovery. While flow-matching models (, FlowDPO) have recently shown promise in this domain, their performance relies heavily on alignment with ground-truth coordinates via supervised preference learning. However, obtaining experimental labels for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins is prohibitively expensive, creating a bottleneck for structural modeling in data-scarce regimes. In this work, we propose (Atomic Policy Optimization), a fully unsupervised alignment framework that eliminates the need for ground-truth reference structures. APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments, utilizing a novel dual-reward mechanism: (i) a that reinforces the policy's dominant latent structural modes through eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (ii) a that enforces thermodynamic stability. Our framework enables the model to ``self-correct'' by identifying physically plausible configurations within sampled groups. Extensive benchmarks on crystal and antibody structure prediction demonstrate that APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines, achieving a new state-of-the-art in match rates and structural fidelity. Furthermore, we show that APO effectively straightens probability paths, significantly improving inference efficiency. Our results suggest that intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy, supervised coordinate matching.

AI.tldr: APO is a fully unsupervised alignment framework for 3D atomic structure prediction that uses group-relative policy optimization with a dual-reward mechanism (eigen-decomposition of sample similarities and thermodynamic stability) to eliminate the need for ground-truth reference structures, achieving state-of-the-art results on crystal and antibody prediction benchmarks while also improving inference efficiency.
AI.motivation: Flow-matching models like FlowDPO show promise in 3D structure prediction but rely on supervised preference learning aligned with ground-truth coordinates. Obtaining experimental labels for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins is prohibitively expensive, creating a bottleneck in data-scarce regimes.
AI.method: APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments with a dual-reward mechanism: (i) a reward reinforcing the policy's dominant latent structural modes via eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (ii) a reward enforcing thermodynamic stability. The framework enables self-correction by identifying physically plausible configurations within sampled groups.
AI.result: Extensive benchmarks on crystal and antibody structure prediction show APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines, achieving new state-of-the-art in match rates and structural fidelity. APO also straightens probability paths, significantly improving inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy, supervised coordinate matching, suggesting that unsupervised physical constraints can replace expensive experimental labels in structural modeling.

title: SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination
summary: Can supply-chain AI move beyond isolated decision modules toward unified operational planning? A complete replenishment plan specifies which products each location carries, which upstream facility supplies it, how often it is replenished, and how deliveries are routed. These decisions are operationally coupled: the selected assortment changes the demand and load passed to later stages; source assignment and replenishment frequency reshape the delivery requests; and route feasibility and cost, in turn, determine the system value of the earlier choices. Yet in modern supply chains, these decisions are often handled by separate departments and optimized through separate systems, which can lead to stockouts, inventory exposure, and avoidable transportation. We propose SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination, a composite policy model that represents supply-chain entities as tokens, contextualizes them through a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to the corresponding decision interface. Each decision builds on the partial plan formed by earlier decisions while the completed plan is evaluated using a shared system-level utility. We instantiate this framework in urban fresh-retail replenishment, where service frequency, assortment, capacity pressure, and road-network routing interact strongly, and evaluate it on real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com, two large-scale supply chains operating at different replenishment echelons. Across both settings, SCOPE consistently outperforms methods that optimize each decision stage separately, as well as practice-oriented baselines commonly used in supply-chain operations. These results show that learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings lead to more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions.

AI.tldr: SCOPE is a composite policy model that treats supply-chain entities as tokens within a shared operational representation, enabling coupled, end-to-end coordination of assortment, sourcing, replenishment frequency, and routing decisions. Tested on real data from Dingdong and JD.com, it outperforms both stage-wise optimization and practice-oriented baselines in urban fresh-retail replenishment.
AI.motivation: Supply-chain decisions such as assortment, sourcing, replenishment, and routing are operationally coupled but typically optimized by separate departments and systems, leading to stockouts, excess inventory, and avoidable transportation costs. The paper motivates moving from isolated decision modules to unified operational planning.
AI.method: SCOPE (Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination) is a composite policy model that represents supply-chain entities as tokens, contextualizes them through a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to a corresponding decision interface. Each decision is built on the partial plan from earlier decisions, and the completed plan is evaluated via a shared system-level utility. It is instantiated in urban fresh-retail replenishment integrating service frequency, assortment, capacity, and routing.
AI.result: Evaluated on real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com across two replenishment echelons, SCOPE consistently outperforms methods that optimize each decision stage separately, as well as practice-oriented baselines commonly used in supply-chain operations.
AI.conclusion: Learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings leads to more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions, demonstrating that a unified, coupled-policy approach is superior to isolated, stage-wise optimization.

title: $β$-OPSD: Deriving with Policy Optimization, Training with Self-Distillation
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising approach to improve reasoning language models, but it remains brittle in practice: making it work reliably often requires substantial engineering effort. We identify a structural source of this difficulty: vanilla OPSD is precisely the $β=1$ member of a broader policy-optimization family, where $β$ weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. This equivalence turns $β$ from an implicit value fixed at one into a controllable regularization parameter, yielding a more general formulation that trades off proximity to a reference policy against privileged teacher guidance. We introduce $β$-OPSD and derive its optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher. Directly optimizing this objective with reinforcement learning, however, would be costly and high-variance. Rather than optimize the RL objective directly, we turn its closed-form solution into a distillation target.
