Each value of $β$ selects a target along the reference-to-teacher path, which we implement efficiently by mixing their token-level logits. In this way, inexpensive distillation approximates the solution of expensive policy optimization. Return-to-go credit assignment further aligns token updates with the sequence-level objective while retaining the simplicity of OPSD. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that $β$-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, improving optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance. Our results provide a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back without sacrificing the efficiency that makes OPSD practical.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces β-OPSD, a generalization of on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) that frames vanilla OPSD as the β=1 special case of a broader policy-optimization family. By treating β as a controllable regularization parameter weighting the KL penalty against a reference policy, the authors derive an optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between reference and teacher. Instead of costly RL optimization, they turn the closed-form solution into a distillation target via token-level logit mixing. Results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show β-OPSD outperforms vanilla OPSD in both stability and reasoning performance.
AI.motivation: Vanilla OPSD is brittle in practice and requires substantial engineering effort to work reliably. The authors identify a structural reason: OPSD fixes β=1 implicitly, leaving no controllable trade-off between anchoring to a reference policy and following privileged teacher guidance. They seek a principled generalization that makes this trade-off explicit and controllable.
AI.method: The authors (1) formulate β-OPSD by introducing β as an explicit weight on the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy, (2) derive the closed-form optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher, (3) convert this closed-form solution into a distillation target by mixing token-level logits according to β, and (4) incorporate return-to-go credit assignment to align token updates with the sequence-level objective while preserving OPSD's simplicity.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that β-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, improving both optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back, demonstrating that the β parameter enables efficient distillation to approximate expensive policy optimization without sacrificing the efficiency that makes OPSD practical.

title: InfoOps Bench: A live information operations safety benchmark
summary:
In this paper we present an active, constantly updated AI benchmark which measures the integrity of frontier language models against being co-opted for state-backed information operations. We draw on over 2,100 information operations from a live monitoring pipeline which tracks Russian, Chinese and Iranian state-backed information assets. Alongside this paper, we release a companion website that tracks the most prominent claims spread by state-backed media outlets, updated weekly, available from: pattrn.ai/research/infoopsbench. The dynamic nature of the benchmark makes it resistant to saturation.
  In the benchmark, we test 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings. We find that most models can be co-opted for information operations. Integrity scores, defined as the percentage of refused requests, range from 8.8% to 94.5%, an 85.7-percentage-point spread not explained by model size. Model choice also changes the character of the resulting operation. Some models fabricate details and produce output more harmful than the source material, others defuse claims even while complying, and fact-checking rates vary from 2.9% to 72.9%.
  Integrity against information operations is at least partly related to refusal to produce content even for benign claims, illustrating the challenge of balancing model usability with safety. With one exception (Z.ai's GLM 5.2), the Chinese-developed models sharply cut compliance on factually grounded but China-critical claims, dropping 48-70 percentage points relative to matched benign claims.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces InfoOpsBench, an actively updated AI benchmark measuring frontier language models' integrity against state-backed information operations, using over 2,100 tracked operations from Russian, Chinese, and Iranian state media. Testing 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings reveals a massive integrity spread (8.8% to 94.5%), with most models being co-optable, and notably, Chinese-developed models showing sharp compliance drops on China-critical claims.
AI.motivation: State-backed information operations pose a growing threat, and frontier language models may be co-opted to amplify these narratives at scale. Existing benchmarks are static and saturable, failing to keep pace with evolving disinformation campaigns. There is a need for a dynamic, continuously updated benchmark that measures models' resilience against current state-backed information operations.
AI.method: The authors build a live monitoring pipeline tracking over 2,100 Russian, Chinese, and Iranian state-backed information operations. They create a dynamic benchmark (InfoOpsBench) that tests 17 models from 8 providers using four prompt framings. Integrity scores are defined as the percentage of refused requests, and the benchmark is updated weekly via a companion website to resist saturation.
AI.result: Integrity scores range from 8.8% to 94.5%, an 85.7-percentage-point spread not explained by model size. Most models can be co-opted for information operations. Model choice changes the character of operations: some fabricate details and amplify harm beyond source material, others defuse claims while complying, and fact-checking rates vary from 2.9% to 72.9%. Chinese-developed models (except GLM 5.2) sharply cut compliance on China-critical claims by 48-70 percentage points versus matched benign claims.
AI.conclusion: Integrity against information operations correlates partly with overall refusal behavior even on benign claims, highlighting the usability-safety tradeoff. The benchmark's dynamic design resists saturation, and its findings reveal systematic, provider-dependent vulnerabilities in frontier models that warrant ongoing monitoring and mitigation.

title: KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models
summary: Clinical risk models routinely achieve strong aggregate performance while producing materially different error rates across patient subgroups. Audit pipelines have been proposed to catch this, but their components are rarely stress-tested, so it is unclear which parts of an audit can be trusted and under what conditions. We present KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline covering subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring, evaluated to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Four findings follow. (i) Significance tracks each axis's gap against its own minimum detectable effect: rank correlation between significance count and raw equalized-odds difference (EOD) across the 15 axes is rho = 0.56, rising to rho = 0.78 once EOD is standardized by that floor. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48 of 48 held-out runs (paired delta = -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]), while group-wise Platt scaling -- the better calibrator -- behaves as a coin flip on EOD (19 of 48 runs improved, 95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with mean effect near zero, so what an audit should report is the variance, not the average. (iii) The mechanism diagnostic classifies 144 of 144 controlled cases correctly but recovers none of 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no signal that it failed. (iv) CUSUM failures and false alarms track cohort realization far more than disease: at the reference threshold, all 27 false alarms and 7 of 8 missed shifts come from different seeds (chi-squared p = 0.002), so a threshold tuned on one cohort fails to transfer. All results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity. Code, artifacts, and scripts reproducing every number are released.

AI.tldr: KAISEN is a five-phase audit pipeline for clinical risk models tested to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark. Key findings: significance tracking improves when standardized by minimum detectable effect (rho=0.78); per-group threshold optimization reliably reduces EOD (48/48 runs) while Platt scaling does not; mechanism diagnostics fail silently under proxy misspecification; and CUSUM thresholds do not transfer across cohort realizations.
AI.motivation: Clinical risk models show disparate error rates across patient subgroups despite strong aggregate performance. Existing audit pipelines are rarely stress-tested, leaving unclear which audit components can be trusted and under what conditions.
AI.method: KAISEN is a five-phase audit pipeline comprising subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring. It is evaluated on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections, with known ground truth enabling stress testing to failure.
AI.result: (i) Significance correlates with axis gaps only after standardizing by minimum detectable effect (rho rises 0.56 to 0.78). (ii) Threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48/48 held-out runs (delta=-0.285, CI [-0.313,-0.252]), while group-wise Platt scaling improves only 19/48 (mean effect near zero), indicating variance should be reported rather than average. (iii) Mechanism diagnostics classify 144/144 controlled cases correctly but fail all 48 proxy-misspecification cases with no failure signal. (iv) CUSUM failures and false alarms track cohort realization over disease (chi-squared p=0.002), so thresholds tuned on one cohort fail to transfer.
AI.conclusion: Audit pipelines can silently fail in structured ways: mechanism diagnostics fail without warning under proxy misspecification, mitigation method choice drives dispersion rather than average effect, and drift thresholds do not transfer across cohorts. Results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity; all code and artifacts are released for reproducibility.

title: Selective Credibility-Limited Belief Update
summary: Belief update concerns changes in an agent's beliefs induced by changes in the underlying world. Standard Katsuno-Mendelzon update assumes that an epistemic input can be incorporated from every initially possible world, whereas credibility-limited belief update restricts, for each source world, the successor worlds regarded as credible or reachable. Nevertheless, existing credibility-limited approaches treat the epistemic input as an indivisible whole, and therefore cannot represent cases in which only part of a compound epistemic input can be realized. We introduce selective credibility-limited belief update, in which the epistemic input is transformed, relative to each source world, into a weaker proxy before the credibility-limited transition is performed. We provide semantic and axiomatic characterizations of the resulting class of update operators. We then identify two well-behaved sub-classes; namely, consistency-preserving update operators, which require every transformed epistemic input to be credible from its source world whenever the original epistemic input is consistent, and maximal consistency-preserving update operators, which additionally require the selected proxy to be maximally informative among the credible consequences of the original epistemic input. Finally, we establish the generality of the proposed framework by showing that credibility-limited belief update is recovered as a special case, while Katsuno--Mendelzon belief update emerges when credibility restrictions are removed and the transformation functions are taken to be identities. These results demonstrate that the framework provides a unified and strictly more expressive account of belief update, encompassing established approaches while supporting source-dependent selective acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces selective credibility-limited belief update, a framework where epistemic inputs are transformed into weaker proxies relative to each source world before applying credibility-limited transitions, enabling partial realization of compound inputs. It provides semantic and axiomatic characterizations, identifies two well-behaved sub-classes (consistency-preserving and maximal consistency-preserving operators), and shows that both credibility-limited and Katsuno-Mendelzon update emerge as special cases, demonstrating a unified and more expressive belief update framework.
AI.motivation: Existing credibility-limited belief update treats the epistemic input as an indivisible whole, failing to represent situations where only part of a compound epistemic input can be realized. This limitation motivates the need for a framework that supports source-dependent selective acceptance of inputs.
AI.method: The authors introduce selective credibility-limited belief update, where the epistemic input is transformed, relative to each source world, into a weaker proxy before the credibility-limited transition is performed. They provide semantic and axiomatic characterizations of the resulting operator class, then identify two sub-classes: consistency-preserving operators (requiring every transformed input to be credible whenever the original is consistent) and maximal consistency-preserving operators (additionally requiring the selected proxy to be maximally informative among credible consequences of the original input).
AI.result: The framework recovers credibility-limited belief update as a special case and Katsuno-Mendelzon belief update when credibility restrictions are removed and transformation functions are identities. This demonstrates that the proposed framework is a unified and strictly more expressive account of belief update.
AI.conclusion: Selective credibility-limited belief update provides a unified and more expressive framework for belief update that encompasses established approaches while supporting source-dependent selective acceptance of epistemic inputs.

title: MANTA: Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation for Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model-based multi-agent systems improve complex problem solving through task decomposition, agent specialization, information exchange, and intermediate validation. However, existing systems typically treat communication topology as a fixed design choice or an offline optimization target. We introduce MANTA, a framework for Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation that enables communication structures to self-evolve at inference time. Before execution, MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior structural experience. During deployment, it monitors collaboration traces and applies bounded structural updates when the current organization becomes insufficient. These updates can modify agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways while preserving the task interface and agent budget. We evaluate MANTA against representative single-agent and multi-agent baselines on five benchmarks spanning information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, and mathematical reasoning. MANTA achieves the highest average score of 74.0, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and obtaining the best result on PlanCraft. These results show that inference-time self-improvement can extend to the architecture of collaboration itself.

AI.tldr: MANTA is a framework enabling multi-agent systems to self-evolve their communication topology at inference time, achieving 74.0 average score across five benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent systems treat communication topology as a fixed design choice or offline optimization target, lacking the ability to adapt structural organization during actual task execution when the initial setup becomes insufficient.
AI.method: MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior structural experience before execution, then during deployment monitors collaboration traces and applies bounded structural updates when needed. These updates can modify agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways while preserving the task interface and agent budget.
AI.result: Evaluated against single-agent and multi-agent baselines on five benchmarks (information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, mathematical reasoning), MANTA achieves the highest average score of 74.0, beating the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and obtaining the best result on PlanCraft.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time self-improvement can be extended from individual agent behavior to the architecture of collaboration itself, demonstrating that communication structures in multi-agent systems can beneficially self-evolve during deployment.

title: Rethinking Inference-Time Scaling in Local Computer-Use Agents: Failure Modes and Compute Tradeoffs
summary: Deploying autonomous computer-use agents (CUAs) locally is increasingly important for privacy, cost efficiency, and practical usability, yet improving their performance under strict hardware constraints remains challenging. While recent studies show that inference-time scaling can improve frontier computer-use agents through additional computation during execution, its effectiveness for resource-constrained local models remains poorly understood. We present a systematic empirical study of inference-time scaling in local CUAs across contextual, temporal, structural, and parallel dimensions. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, and OpenCUA-7B on the OSWorld benchmark. Our results show that additional computation often yields diminishing returns while changing failure modes. Contextual scaling provides historical grounding that improves trajectory stability and task accuracy, but its gains saturate as token cost increases and failures shift from repetitive or stalled trajectories toward premature false successes. Temporal scaling similarly reduces max-step stalls, yet does not substantially improve task success, indicating that longer horizons often extend erroneous trajectories rather than correct them. We further find that structural decomposition can introduce planning and formatting overhead in local two-stage agents, while parallel scaling partially mitigates these failures at a substantial computational cost. Overall, our findings suggest that efficient local CUAs require selective compute allocation, failure-aware control mechanisms, and agentic frameworks designed around the capabilities and limitations of local models.

AI.tldr: A systematic empirical study of inference-time scaling for local computer-use agents across four dimensions (contextual, temporal, structural, parallel), showing that additional computation often yields diminishing returns and shifts failure modes rather than fixing them, and that efficient local CUAs require selective compute allocation and failure-aware control mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Deploying autonomous computer-use agents locally is increasingly important for privacy, cost efficiency, and practical usability, but improving their performance under strict hardware constraints remains poorly understood. While inference-time scaling can improve frontier models, its effectiveness for resource-constrained local models has not been systematically studied.
AI.method: The authors present a systematic empirical study evaluating inference-time scaling in local CUAs across four dimensions: contextual, temporal, structural, and parallel. They evaluate three model families (Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, OpenCUA-7B) on the OSWorld benchmark.
AI.result: Additional computation often yields diminishing returns while changing failure modes. Contextual scaling improves trajectory stability and task accuracy but gains saturate as token costs rise, shifting failures toward premature false successes. Temporal scaling reduces max-step stalls but does not substantially improve task success, as longer horizons extend erroneous trajectories. Structural decomposition introduces planning and formatting overhead in local two-stage agents, while parallel scaling partially mitigates failures at substantial computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Efficient local CUAs require selective compute allocation, failure-aware control mechanisms, and agentic frameworks designed around the capabilities and limitations of local models, rather than relying on naive inference-time scaling.

title: DualG-MRAG: Decoupling Macro-Reasoning and Micro-Matching for Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation
comment: Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026). 12 pages
summary: While Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (MM-RAG) has shown promising results, it still struggles with complex multi-hop reasoning tasks. Existing methods primarily focus on independent instance-level matching, which often fails to capture explicit relationships across modalities and documents. Although Graph-enhanced methods introduce structural modeling, they face a fundamental challenge in multimodal scenarios: incorporating fine-grained visual features leads to rapid graph expansion and retrieval noise, whereas coarse-grained representations cause the discarding of critical local evidence. To address this dilemma, we propose DualG-MRAG, a Dual-tier framework that introduces a decoupled architecture comprising Macro-reasoning and Micro-matching Graphs for Multimodal RAG. Specifically, to suppress retrieval noise by isolating global structural reasoning from fine-grained evidence matching, we construct a Macro Graph for global topological routing and a Micro Graph for precise local verification. Subsequently, to enable dynamic relevance propagation across heterogeneous evidence sources, we formulate retrieval as a query-driven message passing process via a GNN Retriever. Furthermore, to provide the generative model with coherent structural guidance, we introduce a dynamic programming decoding mechanism that extracts explicit reasoning paths directly from the GNN's forward pass, replacing the standard input of isolated document chunks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DualG-MRAG outperforms baselines in both evidence recall and complex QA accuracy.

AI.tldr: DualG-MRAG is a dual-tier framework for Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation that decouples global structural reasoning (Macro Graph) from fine-grained local evidence matching (Micro Graph) using a GNN Retriever for query-driven message passing and a dynamic programming decoding mechanism for explicit reasoning path extraction.
AI.motivation: Existing MM-RAG methods struggle with multi-hop reasoning tasks because they rely on independent instance-level matching that fails to capture cross-modal relationships. Graph-enhanced methods face a dilemma: fine-grained visual features cause graph expansion and retrieval noise, while coarse-grained representations lose critical local evidence.
AI.method: DualG-MRAG introduces a decoupled architecture with two tiers: (1) a Macro Graph for global topological routing to suppress retrieval noise, and (2) a Micro Graph for precise local verification of fine-grained evidence. Retrieval is formulated as query-driven message passing via a GNN Retriever for dynamic relevance propagation across heterogeneous evidence sources. A dynamic programming decoding mechanism extracts explicit reasoning paths from the GNN's forward pass to provide coherent structural guidance to the generative model, replacing isolated document chunk inputs.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that DualG-MRAG outperforms baselines in both evidence recall and complex QA accuracy on multimodal multi-hop reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling global structural reasoning from fine-grained evidence matching effectively resolves the granularity dilemma in graph-enhanced multimodal RAG, enabling better multi-hop reasoning performance.

title: OSReward: Instituting Standardized Evaluation for Cross-Platform Computer-Use Reward Models
summary: Computer-using agents (CUAs) are advancing rapidly across the digital world. A CUA trajectory records the agent's actions, states, and reasoning. Verifying whether it fulfilled the task instruction is central to CUA evaluation, data curation, and reinforcement learning. Neither human-written verifiers nor human annotators can provide such verification at scale, so the field increasingly turns to vision-language models (VLMs) as judges of CUA trajectories. But a fundamental question has long gone unexamined: are these VLM judges reliable enough? To study it systematically, we introduce OSReward, a realistic, high-quality benchmark that evaluates VLM judges on CUA trajectories. The trajectories come from diverse agent backbones executing human-verified instructions across platforms, then rigorously labeled with ground-truth verdicts through multi-stage human annotation. Building on it, we derive OSReward-Hard, a challenge set concentrating genuinely hard cases, and OSReward-Multi for fine-grained efficiency and alignment scoring. The most comprehensive evaluation of VLM judges to date finds even state-of-the-art models fall short of an ideal judge, sharing a systematic leniency bias that mislabels failed runs as successes. The few reliable enough to trust are too expensive to run at scale, while affordable open models trail far behind. To close this gap, we construct and release OS-Shepherd-100K, an open corpus of reasoning-annotated trajectory judgments for the CUA community. On it, we train OS-Shepherd (9B and 35B), open reward models that supply low-cost, stable, and reliable reward signals, matching commercial judges at 30-60% lower cost than the frontier. Extensive analyses further inform the design of reliable CUA reward at scale. Our code, benchmark, dataset, and model checkpoints are available at https://os-copilot.github.io/OSReward-Home/.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces OSReward, a benchmark for evaluating VLM judges on computer-using agent (CUA) trajectories, revealing that current state-of-the-art models are unreliable due to a systematic leniency bias. It also releases OS-Shepherd, open reward models trained on a curated corpus that match commercial judges at 30-60% lower cost.
AI.motivation: Computer-using agents are advancing rapidly, but verifying whether their trajectories fulfilled task instructions is central to evaluation, data curation, and RL. Human-written verifiers and human annotators cannot provide such verification at scale, so the field increasingly relies on VLM judges. However, the fundamental reliability of these VLM judges has never been systematically examined.
AI.method: The authors construct OSReward, a realistic benchmark of CUA trajectories from diverse agent backbones executing human-verified instructions across platforms, rigorously labeled with ground-truth verdicts via multi-stage human annotation. They derive OSReward-Hard (hard cases) and OSReward-Multi (fine-grained efficiency/alignment scoring), then conduct a comprehensive evaluation of VLM judges. They also build OS-Shepherd-100K, an open corpus of reasoning-annotated trajectory judgments, to train OS-Shepherd (9B and 35B) open reward models.
AI.result: Even state-of-the-art models fall short of an ideal judge, exhibiting a systematic leniency bias that mislabels failed runs as successes. Models reliable enough to trust are too expensive to run at scale, while affordable open models trail far behind. OS-Shepherd models provide low-cost, stable, reliable reward signals, matching commercial judges at 30-60% lower cost.
AI.conclusion: VLM judges for CUA trajectories are currently unreliable at scale, but the gap can be closed with open reward models like OS-Shepherd, which offer reliable scoring at substantially lower cost. The work provides benchmarks and models to inform the design of reliable CUA reward systems at scale.

title: AISPA: User-Centric System Prompt Auditing for Large Language Model Applications
summary: System prompts are instructions configured by developers to govern the behaviors of foundation models in AI applications. They are used throughout commercial AI products, but are rarely disclosed to the public or regulators, creating a serious trust and accountability gap in the wide deployment of AI systems. In this paper, we introduce Artificial Intelligence System Prompt Assurance (AISPA), a user-centric framework for systematically auditing system prompts in AI systems. AISPA examines specific parts of a system prompt and evaluates them along eight dimensions that matter to users. We then use this framework to review 3,249 instructions from system prompts in 88 commercial AI products, classifying each instruction as either protective (of users) or problematic. Our audit surfaces four core findings. First, system prompt design varies substantially across products and developers, with some organizations averaging over 60 protective instructions per product while others average fewer than 5. Second, protective instructions are widely adopted but shallow in scope: 98.9% of products contain at least one, yet only 24% cover all eight dimensions of the AISPA taxonomy. Third, system prompts have grown steadily longer and more protective of users, suggesting that user protection is becoming a more visible concern in commercial prompt design. Fourth, despite this progress, problematic instructions remain pervasive: roughly 40% of products contain at least one instruction that works against user interests, and protective and problematic instructions frequently coexist within the same prompt. Our findings highlight the need for greater transparency, standardization, and independent oversight for system prompts in commercial AI products.
